en: Preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā* (The Conventional Explanation of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*).

Among the six hundred and fifty-seven Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras translated by Ci’en [Xuanzang], such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and others, their prose is for the most part expansive, fluent, and convenient;
reading them leaves no difficulty that catches or irritates the throat or palate. Yet, among them, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* alone...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: from a hundred fascicles of Sanskrit text, it has been condensed into ten fascicles. The language is concise yet the meaning is rich; its arguments are intricate and its essentials are profound.

A reader who studies it with diligent application over months and years, scrutinizing and savoring every word and phrase, is like one who has suddenly entered a winding ravine and a series of overlapping paths, seeing only the forms of deep, secluded thickets and pools, and for whom the destination is not yet suddenly reached.
Only by following it with a meticulous mind and treading it step by step can one finally—though not yet fully—attain it.

I have suddenly become familiar with this location. Among the elders of former generations, there were many who expounded upon it; besides the commentaries and excerpts, those who possessed such knowledge were truly numerous.
Yet, as the study of doctrine declined, these lost texts and fallen traditions vanished without being brought forth.
I once raised this matter to question my teacher, who felt deep regret over it. Now, how fortunate that Master Gao Yuan Yu has opened this slender path, enabling every person...

To traverse the winding paths of the Yangchang Pass is far better than treading upon the broad highways. The Master originated from Tongchuan; he suspended his monk’s staff in the regions of Wu and Yue.

His pure conduct transcended the mundane, and his spiritual insight was peerless. He had for the most part completed his exegesis of the holy texts of the Tripiṭaka; as for their ultimate realization—
It shatters obstructions, guides stagnation, and elucidates the profound; even if Kāśyapa were to be reborn, he would surely break into a smile at this.
At the request of Master Yutai, I have provided an exegesis of this treatise. Cutting through the surface to reach the core, it flows gracefully and penetrates all sides;

upon opening the scroll, it is resplendent, leaving no doubt or obstruction. Thus, Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, which was praised by the Dharma-protector [Maitreya], has, through Cien, attained its full realization.
The transmission of the Buddhist scriptures (brahman-puṭa) began; with the translations of Ci’en, the true texts became even more manifest upon reaching this high plateau.
Is this not indeed a ferry for crossing the ocean of consciousness and a key for unlocking the treasury of knowledge? Some say that what the Master elucidated opened the windows of the sacred texts.
"I have attained what I never had before. Why then do you speak of 'the mundane'? I replied: "When true persons meet, the Way exists in their mutual gaze;
why trouble oneself with words? When a true person listens to the true text, the sound enters and the mind penetrates it—why then trouble oneself with commentaries?
All the establishment and analysis of written characters are designed solely for the sake of the mundane world. The Three Baskets and the Twelve Divisions of the Canon all expound upon the mundane."
Furthermore, it is not that these [conventional expressions] do not elucidate the Truth; rather, by knowing that there are such elucidations, one realizes the Truth within the conventional itself.

Since the elucidation can turn one away from the conventional and cause one to rely upon the Truth, one does not remain oblivious to the conventional elucidations. You, sir, recently resided at the Fahua Hermitage and, noting that I have long cherished this book, presented it to me for inspection.
I was greatly delighted by it and have therefore recorded my praises here, appended to the end of this manuscript. As for the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*...

The intent [of this] is such that the exegesis of both the *Śāstra* and the *Kārikā* is fully present. If scholars seek it, they will naturally find it as clearly as looking at the moon or selecting milk from water;
what further need is there to appoint mediators for the two schools of *Dharmalakṣaṇa* and *Dharmatā*, who have spent their lives in mutual contention?

Autumn of the Gui-chou year of the Wanli era, at Baolin Monastery in Jiangning, the lay devotee [Surname] Qi composed this "Preface to the Vernacular Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*," written in the style of Yuanhe Nan.
Now, every school possesses its orthodox eye; it does not rely on consciousness to perceive, nor upon treatises to discourse, nor upon explanations to expound.
Thus it is. What is there that is not? What is there that exists? What is discarded? What remains? To subsume appearances back into the nature is like a drop falling into the sea;

to manifest the nature within appearances is like the moon reflecting in a river. It can be expressed as both together, yet it can also be revealed singly. It can be cast away in pairs, yet it can also be pointed out alone.
Therefore, while "only" (wei) serves to negate non-existence and "consciousness" (shi) serves to indicate existence, it may also indicate and negate simultaneously, casting away all externalities.

Yet it abides within. Distinguishing the full and the partial, one dissolves consciousness to enter into the nature [of reality]. Contemplating the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm, there are none who are not worldly persons clinging to a self;
these are likened to an army or a forest. When dispersed, they constitute the absence of any grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), just as the substance of a barren woman’s child has never existed.
Whether internal or external aggregates, who can distinguish the intimacy or distance of conditions and objects? Through inference or direct perception, the Dharma remains unfathomable.

Regarding the provisional and ultimate nature of the Dharma, I have contemplated this doctrine in silence; it is truly a matter for lamentation that while the treatise fails to provide an adequate exposition, its flavor is like chewing wax.

If the exposition does not accord with common understanding, one’s progress is like walking upon a precipice; one merely tastes it superficially and stops, ultimately finding the narrow path difficult to traverse.
Master Yù was able to forget the exposition yet possess the exposition, simply because he used the exposition to clarify consciousness.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) possesses characteristics; from what does it arise? Characteristics possess divisions; how could they not differ from one another?

The "spirit" (*śūnyatā* or *ātman*) is like the axle-pin that draws them together; "transforming wisdom" (*jñāna-parāvṛtti*) is like the hub. Luminous lights intermingle within a single room, yet each light maintains its own distinctness;
shadows appear individually upon two pillars, yet the casting of the shadow is not dual. Once pointed out by a finger, the inner truth leaps forth with clarity—this is universal penetration.
This commentary elucidates both nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) as being perfectly complete, while words and thoughts are utterly severed.

The ninety-five heterodox schools are reduced to non-existence, and the thirteen Buddhist sects are collectively found to lack any true name. It may be said that Master Dharmapāla has already exercised his tongue many times over.
Written by the layman You Shi-ren.
Preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) by Susun:
Sentient beings, in every thought-moment, cling to a self; everywhere, they grasp at phenomena. The Buddhas of antiquity spoke to them, saying:

"There is no need for such clinging; this is merely consciousness (*vijñapti*). This discourse, which negates grasping, has no bearing on the manifestation of consciousness itself. Yet, those who pursue shadows and attend to sounds—even unto this point—[remain deluded].
To give rise to attachment based on the banner of consciousness—how excessive this is! Indeed, consciousness is like an illness or a dream regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Since an illness and a dream are certainly not non-existent, how can one say they truly exist? When I seek their origin, the Great Enlightenment is profoundly clear and still.
"Where does consciousness arise? I sought its end, yet Buddha-wisdom was vividly manifest. Where does consciousness cease? Words and thought are cut off; deliberation reaches its limit.
Sitting, I beheld the eight consciousnesses, and suddenly I fell [into realization]. 'Falling' is precisely what is called 'transformation.

This meaning is not like that of a mechanical rotation. Transformation is itself wisdom; the objective realm does not exist through mutual opposition. Before transformation, though it is pervasive wisdom, its entire substance is consciousness."
Outside of illness there is no body; once the pervasive consciousness is transformed, the entire being is wisdom. When awakening arrives, there are no more dreams;

therefore it is said that if one clings to *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) as truly existent, this is equivalent to clinging to external objects—it is an attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) that obstructs the realization of consciousness-only.
Thus, Vasubandhu had no choice but to compose the *kārikās*, and Dharmapāla had no choice but to compose the *śāstra*. (From the *Gaoyuan*).
Even a superior person cannot help but employ conventional explanations. Conventional expressions do not manifest the ultimate truth; explanations do not manifest reality.
By using discourse that is neither true nor real, one reveals a consciousness that is neither true nor real. Only by proceeding thus in a continuous flow can one avoid error.
This clarifies that the healer of illness must rely upon the very spirit of the illness, and that one who awakens from a dream does not depart from the remnants of the dream.
Although those of dull faculties may be hindered by their own capacities, they cannot be granted the ability to count the sands [of the Ganges];
nor is it permitted for those of coarse dhyāna to sweep away [the truth] with wild wisdom. Written by the layman Fu Du, Wu Yongxian, as the preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra Suqian*.

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) was the final compilation and translation by the Great Master Xuanzang. It encompasses all relevant treatises, containing a profound ocean of meaning;
its integration of subtle and vast doctrines is peerless. Since the time of Master Ji (Kuiji), there have been commentaries (*shu*) and sub-commentaries (*chao*).

Beyond these commentaries and sub-commentaries, there are further works such as the *Zhongshu yao*, the *Weishi jing*, and other writings; it is unknown for what reason they were not included [in this collection].

In the Tibetan canon, after the Southern Song dynasty’s relocation [to the south], the Chan school reached its zenith; those who engaged in empty talk were many, while those who practiced authentically were few.

They marginalized the study of Abhidharma (Yixue) and held the Dharma Characteristics school (Xiangzong) in contempt. Consequently, the aforementioned scriptures gradually fell into dispersal and loss.

However, introductory works for beginners appeared during the Yuan period, at which time it seemed that the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the Ci'en school still existed. It was only then that I first heard of the fundamental tenets of the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only).

The Great Master Zibai bestowed this treatise upon me and commanded that I thoroughly investigate it. At first, I was utterly bewildered and found no way of entry. Seeking ancient commentaries and sub-commentaries, I could find none.
Later, while reading the *Kaimeng* and examining the *Zongjing lu* and the *Huayan shuchao*, whenever I encountered discussions of this treatise, I immediately recorded them at the top of my notes.
Through this, a gradual glimmer of insight began to appear. Subsequently, I heard of the circumstances surrounding Chao Songyuan.

He exhorted his fellow masters to apply their minds to this treatise and, forming a group at Mount Jiaozhuang, to conduct an exhaustive study of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) with the intent of providing a commentary.
He then urgently sent a letter inviting them. The two masters each brought forth their own annotated versions of the text, which they compared and verified against one another.
It was for this reason that I produced the edition titled *Correcting Errors and Marking the Meaning*. Thereupon, scholars from all quarters began to regard this treatise as worthy of study.

Those who have thoroughly investigated the matter and sought out woodblock editions have come forth in a continuous stream; yet, as there remain many points of uncertainty, my mind is still not fully satisfied.
Having heard the words of Wang Taigu, I learned that none among the masters of the *Yogācāra* school equals Master Gao Yuan in refinement.

When observing his commentary on the *Ālambanaparīkṣā-śāstra*, it was impossible to find even a single passage he had not explained as clearly as pointing at one’s own palm; from this, one can know that the same must be true for his other works.
At that time, Dongchan Temple was without a presiding master. I consequently left the seat vacant to invite the Master. The Master, perceiving my sincerity, led his disciples there.

I then entrusted him with the task of composing a brief commentary on this treatise. He readily consented, and before a year had passed, the draft of the *Suyuan* (Exposition for the Worldly) was completed.
This work was composed by me because it contains meanings that have been personally verified.

In the summer of the Bingwu year, I received imperial grace and was appointed to the Office of the South (Nancao). At that time, the Master also arrived and began lecturing on this treatise at Juefeng Temple; there were a thousand students in attendance.
Everyone listened with rapt attention, having never before encountered such a thing. In the summer of the Jiyou year, the Master again began lecturing at Waguan Temple.

At that time, he heard that Dharma Master Cheng of Shiziwō on Mount Tai had once commented upon this treatise and wished to go there to visit him. I firmly tried to dissuade him, but the Master would not listen;
he braved the heat and journeyed north. That winter, I too entered the capital to undergo my official performance review.
In the morning, before long, the Master also arrived.
He stayed at Longhua Temple beneath the Northern Gate and further accepted an invitation from Mili An to lecture on this treatise for practitioners from all quarters.
The Dharma assembly was most flourishing, yet I was returning south. In the summer of the following year, having visited Master Cheng, our views did not accord, so he headed south.
I too requested leave from the Southern Palace to return to my rural retreat. The Master took his leave of me to travel to Wulin. Another year passed before I first fell ill.
While in sickness, I heard that the Master was lecturing on this treatise in the Zongjing Hall of Jingci Temple. I...

I was both startled and delighted. At that time, as I was on the verge of death, I had no opportunity to correspond with the Master; even if the Master had sent a letter, I would have been unable to reply.
In the summer of the following year, the Master arrived at Chengyu with a newly carved edition of his secular commentaries and requested a preface for me.

My illness was so severe that I could not immediately fulfill the Master’s request. It was not until early autumn that I began to recover slightly; thereafter, having washed my hands, I opened the envelope and read it.
"Ah! How difficult it was for our Master to undertake this task! Since the time of Master Ji, the lineage of transmission has had its own origins;

his commentaries and sub-commentaries were based on what he received from others, following the principle of 'transmitting without creating. Yet our Master, through his teacherless wisdom (*asat-śāstṛ-jñāna*), traced the fragmentary texts and unraveled their profound and subtle meanings—this was the first difficulty.
Whenever he entered the lecture hall, who among those present did not wrinkle their brows in mutual astonishment, deeming this a lost art? And yet, our Master..."
It was not based on any prior tradition; rather, it was constructed and interpreted through deliberation, like the work of a master artisan—this is the second difficulty.

Although masters such as Chao Song and others, with the mental faculties of three or four men, spent a period of three years examining this treatise, when I perused their original texts, [I found them wanting].
The first two fascicles have been preserved with their headings and records intact, while the remainder is missing. Yet, the Master accomplished it all through his own efforts in less than a year;

this is the third difficulty. Just as that which relies on hills and mounds easily becomes high, and that which relies on rivers and marshes easily becomes low, the ancient commentaries and sub-commentaries have already perished.
Those who study this treatise hereafter may find other teachers from whom to receive its transmission.

Have you forgotten the labor of your master’s foundational construction? Regarding the custom of dwelling in pine nests, Dharma Master Yuyū has compiled an annotated commentary on this treatise, and its carving is nearly complete.
My own verification of the meanings shall likewise soon be set upon the woodblocks. Might these not serve as left and right aides to the *Sushen* (Exegesis for the Worldly)?
Would you, Master, grant permission for this?
Written on the first day of the seventh month in the autumn of the Renzi year of the Wanli era by the lay practitioner Nianxi Wang Kentang of Jintan, while struggling against his illness.
Preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyāna*:

To begin with, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the radiance of the mind. Just as the light of the sun and moon flows forth from their own inherent clarity, so too does the consciousness of divine wisdom.
Manifesting from the mind, consciousness is divided into nine, while the mind itself is but one. Vasubandhu transmitted it to Asaṅga, thereby subsuming consciousness within the mind;
Asaṅga elucidated it for Maitreya, thereby opening consciousness through the mind. Though the verses proclaim the expansion of the treatise, their establishment is no different.

The appearance manifests as the nature’s imitation; empty space is not a fabrication. Thus, one does not realize that the myriad dharmas are but consciousness, and that dharmas are like the trap for fish.
One does not realize that the three realms are but mind, and that consciousness is like chasing a shadow. When consciousness is confused, it is not through treatises that clarity is revealed;

when treatises are obscure, it is not through exegesis that they are explained. Consequently, the vulgar age and the Dharma sink together, and those of superior wisdom fall along with their consciousness. This is the Dharma Master [who speaks].

This is the reason why Master Yù composed the *Sūtra-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (Sōsho). He realized that the light of the mind is distributed among the various consciousnesses, like the radiance emanating from a precious candle;
that the various consciousnesses are elucidated through the manifold treatises, like candles lit upon a broad thoroughfare;

and that the true treatise is dissected by the popular commentary, just as one holds a candle to penetrate the street. This is how Dharmapāla validated Vasubandhu, and how Ci'en illuminated the profound mysteries.
Jian: Master Yù’s continuation of the Cien tradition can truly be said to have harmonized both schools of the One Vehicle and transcended the Three Realms simultaneously.

Like the resonance of the celestial music of Juntian merging as one, or the waters of the ocean becoming a single flavor, how could there be any difference between them? Thus we know that Yongming’s *Zongjing* encompasses both the Nature and Characteristics schools to achieve dual perfection;
and Maitreya’s exposition of the school relies upon the Single Truth to delineate its characteristics. How excellent were the words of Asaṅga!
His younger brother, Devaśarman, said: "In the past, you used this very tongue to skillfully slander the Mahāyāna; now, you use that same tongue to skillfully praise the Mahāyāna.
Thus we know that praising is equal to slandering, and that skillfulness is likewise a flower in the sky (*gaganapuşpa*).

Even if the mind is empty and consciousness is empty, then the thirty [categories] are merely a patchwork; when consciousness ceases, the treatise ceases—this is the great reliance upon the teaching of nature."
Like dregs cast into the Great Clarity, pointing at the marks only serves to add feet to a snake. When the mind and its activities are perfectly realized, what need is there for verbal explanations?
Master Yu’s esoteric intent is to be divined and clarified through spiritual insight; truly, it depends upon the person who possesses it.
In the spring of the *renzi* year, the layman Yu Yong, Huang Ruheng, composed this "Preface to the Vernacular Explanation of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*" with prostrations.
In the autumn of the *jīyou* year, I met the Master on a boat at Qingyuan; we spent the entire day together, forming a friendship beyond the secular world. Thus it was concluded.
He separately transcribed one fascicle of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Subsequently, after I had returned south, the Master also departed for Mount Wutai to pay homage to the Great Being Mañjuśrī;
his traces became lost in the vast wilderness, and four years passed between the seasons of winter and summer garments.

This spring, carrying my book-box to the shores of Lake Hong, I sought a quiet chamber within the monastic quarters of Nanping. As I reached the meditation hall, my feet had not yet crossed the threshold when—
From afar, he beheld this master. I certainly recognized the master, and the master likewise recognized me. As the two men gazed at one another, their joy exceeded all expectation.

After a short while, the master brought forth the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Demonstration of Consciousness-Only) and showed it to me. On that day, the master ascended the Dharma seat and proclaimed this wondrous treatise;

both the wise and the ignorant praised it, exclaiming that they had never before encountered such a thing. It is truly a ferry and a raft for the Chan school, and a guiding finger for those of us who are but beginners.
How profound! I am not clever; how could I know the deep mysteries? For now, I shall briefly set forth my understanding based on what I have learned from my teacher.
Thus, consciousness (*vijñāna*) resides within the mind, and every person possesses it inherently. Since consciousness is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it functions in accordance with the mind.

It is like the light of a mirror, which shines universally so that both Hu and Han appear therein. Therefore it is said: "The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. The Tripitaka and the Ten...

In both cases, there is nothing that is not for the sake of this consciousness. Even if one were to forcibly cause the consciousness to return to the mind, or cause the mind to attach to the consciousness, the seeing of the past would not be the seeing of the present;
why then would the teacher of the past consciousness not be changed in the present?

And even if the seeing of the present were not the seeing of the past, why would the teacher of the present consciousness still remain the same as before? Since the mind does not increase, the consciousness likewise does not [decrease].
The Master Shi’s [experience] at Qingyuan was no different from his experience today.
That they met again after parting, and parted again after meeting—Master Shi’s experience on another day was likewise no different from his experience today.
The mind is itself consciousness; consciousness is itself the mind. Mind and consciousness are non-dual, a single essence mutually interfusing.
Any verbal expression becomes mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); thus, it may be said that the Master need not interpret nor expound upon this.
Nevertheless, these words are addressed to those of sharp faculties and superior capacity. Ordinary beings harbor their consciousness within and remain perpetually deluded by the net of sensory dust.

In the interim, if one does not encounter a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to lift this veil, then one takes the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as one's own nature, rather than taking the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as one's nature.
One emerges and sinks about without awakening. It is like a lute, a zither, or a harp:
though they possess exquisite sounds, without skilled fingers, they can never produce them. Therefore, one must rely upon language and script to realize the primordial source.
Thus, although the Master has explained and lectured upon it, it is also appropriate for me to listen to it. How could this be frivolous discourse rather than a discourse on reality?
This is the preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-sukhāvabodha* (An Easy Explanation of the Treatise on Consciousness-Only) composed by Jin Yunpeng of Yunnan.

In the past, when I read the sayings of the Chan school, I found them direct, incisive, and exhilarating; they resonated profoundly with my mind, leading me to believe that my own nature could indeed be entered directly in a single leap.
Lately, however, I have observed those who discourse on Chan nowadays frequently proclaim that "the present moment is it."

Yet, when I examine his actual practice, it is even more far from being so; thus, I have privately harbored doubts as to whether my own nature is dull and inferior, making me unfit to undertake this task.
This spring, Master Gao-yuan responded to the request of the Provincial Governor, Mr. Wu Benru.
He expounded the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* at Nanping, and consequently produced the *Weishi suquan*. I read it from beginning to end and attained what I had never experienced before;

only then did I realize that one who does not understand the School of Nature (Xingzong) will surely fail through dullness, while one who does not understand the School of Characteristics (Xiangzong)...
To do otherwise would surely be madness. Although the principle may be realized all at once, matters must necessarily be cultivated gradually. Practice and understanding must both be perfected;
those who bifurcate them into two are all followers of external paths. The Master of Gao-yuan was strict in his discipline and maintained tranquility, never treating the world with levity.
This composition regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*—how could it be merely an explanation of the words? It is a definitive commentary. As Mr.
Gong [Gong Jingsun] donated his salary to have it carved into printing blocks, I have respectfully inscribed this upon its covers.
Written by Ge Yinliang of Qiantang at the conclusion of the *Cheng weishi lun suqian*.
I have heard that the Dharma-gate of the three natures is what the Buddhas have taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

It is the locus from which all consciousnesses arise. According to the scriptural teachings, consciousness arises based on conditions; within the essence of the nature of *tathatā*, every phenomenon is consciousness, and every instance of consciousness is the nature.

Therefore, consciousness can both manifest the nature and obscure it; it can be the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). As the ancient masters said:
Delusion arises from the True and is able to obscure the True; the True is manifested through delusion and is able to subdue delusion.

Therefore, the manifestation of the True necessarily depends upon delusion, and the manifestation of the Nature (dharmatā) necessarily depends upon consciousness (vijñāna). For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through their profound intention (*saṃdhi*), skillful means (*upāya*), and expedient methods (*kauśalya*), established the three divisions [of the *Yogācārabhūmi*] to treat the meaning of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
This treatise primarily discusses the profundity of the profound intention; it is not that the profound intention itself is profound.

The ultimate meaning was difficult to fathom. In the spring of the Renzi year, Master Guyuan Yu from Xichu established a teaching seat at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou and elucidated this treatise, further composing a commentary titled *Suyuan* (Exegesis for the Lay).

Once this exegesis appeared, those passages from the original treatise that had been presented as preliminary propositions or extracted fragments were now arranged with perfect order, like silk drawn from a single cocoon or bright pearls strung together.

May readers not laboriously fix their eyes or pause their reflections, but clearly understand the harmonious integration of meaning and insight, so that every traveler passing through a guest inn may recognize the shortcut to their home.
Looking back upon the foreign land, they will realize that what they previously took for familiar is in truth never truly kin.
May they thus attain peace and security, with joy beyond measure. Such a commentary by the Master shall cause gods and humans alike to leap for joy. Three.
The *Zangbao* (Treasury of Jewels) commentary on the *Xiangying* (Correspondence) states that this is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
In the spring of the Renzi year of the Wanli era, the disciple Qin Shunyou respectfully inscribed this colophon for the *Fayin* (Dharma Causes).
All is but mind; all is but consciousness (*vijñapti*). The greedy person’s consciousness grasps; the frugal person’s consciousness relinquishes;

the one on the Path’s consciousness forgets. To forget is to neighbor the Path; to relinquish is to neighbor forgetting. One does not forget by means of sudden forgetting; please begin with relinquishing yourself.

Dharma Master Gaoyuan commented on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* to open up the various forms of consciousness. This is called the Dharma of relinquishing. The Layman Fudu provided the funds for the carving of the blocks.
Picking up gold to inspire the community toward merit-making is what is called "giving away wealth. Only the mind and consciousness are possessed by all living beings;

only the Dharma and material wealth can be relinquished by those with consciousness. If one can inspire others as a good friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is appropriate to harmonize consciousness so that giving becomes taking.
Thus, it shall not be in vain. Inscribed by the Layman Yu Yong, Huang Ruheng.
The Layman Fu Du, Wu Yongxian;
the Bhikṣu of Yunqi, Zhu Hong;
and the Layman Yu Yong, Huang Ruheng.
Qiantang Ge Yinliang, Shaoxing Shen Tuo,
and the Karmadāna layman Gu Sishan.
Han Jingchu of Hexuan,

and Langshi Wu Zhiqing.
Zhou Changji of Changxing; Zhou Chengji of Taicang;
Yang Zhihan; the disciple Xingyuan of Xin’an;
Fang Ruxi; and the disciple Rulian.
Chai Shiji and Chai Shuyan of Wulin;
Guo Dading of Haichang; the disciples Ren Sizhong, Mingguang of Jingci Temple, and Haihui.
Preface to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun): Originally, the three realms are but mind;
the Master’s mind responds to things according to the times. The myriad dharmas are but consciousness; due to consciousness, one encounters delusion and loses sight of the truth.
This is consciousness, this is mind. When the ocean of consciousness is clarified, the water of the mind is still. This is both the true and the delusive; the source of truth is quiescent.
Yet, when the waves of delusion are stilled and the virtues of the mind are equalized, whether speaking or remaining silent, whether acting or withdrawing, one brings about transformation.

Where consciousness and emotion differ, Chan and Vinaya diverge into their respective schools of nature and characteristics. This distinction according to capacity is the sublime skillful means of the Sages regarding names and phrases;

it is the universal path for entering the Way. In this land alone, the benefit lies uniquely in the teachings of sound. For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, from the beginning of the world, have arisen through conditions; they value speech above all else.

It is not that he remained silent; rather, the Maitreya of the Stage of Succession (Kṣetrapratilambha) based himself on the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* to preach the *Saptadaśabhūmi-sūtra*, which he personally transmitted to Asaṅga.
Asaṅga and his brother then passed it down together, and Vasubandhu condensed it into thirty verses. Although the wording of these verses is brief, [the meaning is vast].

The principle permeates the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; therefore, it first refutes the two attachments to self and phenomena, and subsequently clarifies the three names of the "transforming consciousnesses" in just one and a half verses.

The great meaning is already fully and clearly set forth therein—how much more so in the case of the thirty verses! However, because the meaning is rich while the text is concise, those who encounter it find it easy to memorize but difficult to explain.
Consequently, Dharmapāla and others expanded upon the verses to compose treatises, some of which have been completed with purity.

The two names "Vijñapti" (consciousness-only) and "Mātra" (only) emerge [in the title]. Yet, the translator avoided the term "Jing" (pure/only) and designated it as "Cheng" (established). This is because he established "Vijñaptimātra" through the synthesis of the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).

"Vijñapti" excludes the existence of external objects, while "mātra" distinguishes it from a void mind. When compared, these indicate the ultimate aim; when examined, they clarify the essential convergence.

Therefore, the work is collectively titled the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise Establishing Consciousness-Only). This is truly because the sages established [this teaching] to counteract the false attachments of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle.

As for our school’s tradition: even a few words or a single character can stem the surging flood of those who compete for fame; half a verse or the full function of the mind can awaken right faith in those present.

As for the detailed exposition of its subtle refinements—suppressing error and exalting the truth, citing events to illuminate the meaning, and probing deep roots to investigate shortcomings—it is truly unsurpassed.

The mechanism of prolonging and abbreviating [the process] sufficiently attests to his divine acumen. Furthermore, he clarifies that the various consciousnesses follow conditions, using the metaphor of surging waves and receding billows;

by presenting both the Dharma and its analogy, he makes it easy for people to understand. He further initiates five types of question-and-answer sessions, where his polemical arguments fly like the wind.

Establishing the thesis and the reason, he meticulously investigates characteristics and natures, guiding through manifold methods until they ultimately return to *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Only when the hundred stratagems have gradually vanished does one finally awaken.
The profound path clearly reveals the five stages so that one may know how to advance. First, one practices the six perfections to accumulate the provisions for enlightenment;

next, one employs the four immeasurable minds as the preparatory application (*prayoga*). Through the momentary realization of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the two obstacles are suddenly eliminated. This is followed by the cultivation of causes over successive eons.

The co-emergent ignorance is gradually suppressed, the ten layers of obstructions are severed, and the ten aspects of True Suchness are realized; when the cause is exhausted and the fruit is perfected, this is termed "Ultimate.
However, the composition of these verses and treatises extensively adapts to the capacities of various beings. Since the realization of principle depends upon words, how could one remain silent?

When I, a fool, first sought out this meaning, the phrasing proved jagged and the intent remained ambiguous; after several lines of shifting back and forth, it was as if I were climbing a nine-tiered tower.

Translation: Thereupon, he exhausted his thoughts upon the various scriptures and investigated the numerous treatises to their depths. Resting his chin and staring fixedly, he exerted himself with such vigor that he forgot his fatigue.

Seeking further instruction from the Great Masters, he gradually mastered the subtle paths. In the year of Gui-mao, the layman Jin-sha-nian-xi and the Imperial Historian Wang summoned him to reside at Dong-chan, writing in a letter:
"Regarding the *Cheng weishi lun*, I lament that its ancient commentaries have already been lost and the profound meaning is nearly extinguished. [He then resolved to restore it.]
The Master’s labors over several years have been summarized here; I have endeavored to make it concise and clear so that future generations may understand.

Since the Master takes universal transformation as his heart’s purpose, he should not begrudge my request. Thus, as the lectures were given, they were recorded, gradually accumulating until they were nearly complete, though they had not yet reached final completion.
This spring, while the Master held his staff at Nanping, students happened to gather once more, and I further entrusted this task to several great patrons.

At that time, I exhorted others to propagate [this work]. When it was completed in the autumn, I immediately sought out a woodblock edition for publication. However, I am ashamed that there is nothing transcendent or outstanding in it;

the phrasing is often clumsy and obscure. As for the title *Suxuan* (Vulgar Explanations), this does not mean that it is as common as the "Yang" or "Huanghua" melodies merely to suit the ears of the villagers.
If one seeks it as the "Snow from Ying," then the fundamental treatise is indeed present here.

A Popular Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Verses composed by Bodhisattva Maitreya;
commentary composed by Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty by Imperial Decree;
with the Explanatory Subtleties (*Suyǒuquán*) by the Śramaṇa Mingyù of Western Shu.
△ The structural outline (*Kēwén*) is divided into five parts. First: Explaining the Title of the Treatise.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) is so named because this treatise establishes consciousness-only through its exposition;
thus it is called the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. In the Sanskrit language: *vijñapti* means "consciousness," *mātra* means "only," *siddhi* means "establishment," and *śāstra* means "treatise."
The title should have been translated as *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) rather than *Weishi cheng lun* (Treatise Establishing Consciousness-Only).

This is because the sequence of the Chinese terms follows the order of the conditions (*ālambana*) and the direction of the words, whereas the Sanskrit terms follow the sequence of the subjective (*grāhaka*) and the objective (*grāhya*). Thus, the order in the Tang translation differs from that of the Sanskrit original. Now, following the Sanskrit text, I shall first explain the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Thus, there are distinctions between the names and the meanings of consciousness. There are nine names and five meanings. As for the nine names: first, visual consciousness;

second, auditory consciousness; third, olfactory consciousness; fourth, gustatory consciousness; fifth, tactile consciousness; sixth, mental consciousness; seventh, the *manas* consciousness; eighth, the afflicted *manas* (*kliṣṭa-manas*); and ninth, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Regarding the eight ālayavijñānas and the ninth pure consciousness (amala-vijñāna), there are five meanings for each: first, their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, their transformations (*pariṇāma*);

third, their associated mental factors (*samprayukta*); fourth, their states (*avasthā*); and fifth, their true nature (*dharmatā*). Within these nine names, each possesses these five meanings. If considered according to their common gate as own-characteristics, they cannot be differentiated;
however, if considered according to their distinct gates as common characteristics, the names and their meanings each have their respective distinctions. In summary:

Because it is not separate from consciousness, the name "consciousness" is established. Next, there are three meanings for the explanation of the word "only" (*kevala*): first, the meaning of exclusion and retention;

that is, excluding the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) of self and phenomena, while retaining the two natures of *paratantra* (the dependent nature) and *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected nature). Second, the meaning of determination.
This means that there are certainly no objects apart from the mind, and there definitely exists the internal consciousness of the mind. Third, it reveals the preeminence of ultimate reality:
this indicates that the sovereign mind alone is supreme, thereby subsuming the subordinate mental factors. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is termed "consciousness-only."
Next, regarding the combined explanation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only): "Only" (*mātra*) is a term of exclusion, which negates the existence of external objects;

"consciousness" (*vijñapti*) means discernment, which signifies the existence of internal mind. Because it reveals that while objects are empty, the mind exists, they are combined and termed *vijñapti-mātra*.

Question: What constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) of consciousness-only? Answer: Its essence is twofold: first, the object of observation (*ālambana*), and second, the subject of observation (*ālambaka*). As for the essence of the object of observation, it generally comprises the five [aggregates].

Its substance consists of one hundred dharmas, because it universally contemplates both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, and because it takes the nature and characteristics of consciousness as its substance in accordance with the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*.
As for the substance of the contemplating subject, it generally takes the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as its substance, because mental factors are always associated with consciousness.
However, within the context of the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra*, it takes the wisdom that apprehends objects as its substance.

Because it excels in observing the object of contemplation, another explanation is given: "Negation of non-existence" (*pratiṣedha*) functions as the activity (*vṛtti*), while "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) functions as the essence (*svabhāva*).
By subsuming the activity into the essence, it is simply "consciousness"; this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Furthermore, the distinctions of "Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātra*) are explained through ten meanings. The first is the meaning of "eliminating the false and preserving the real," which means eliminating what is illusory and unreal.

1. The meaning of retaining the real and discarding the unreal: "Discarding the unreal" is called *vyañjana* (only); "retaining the real" is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Thus, it is named "True Consciousness-Only" (*yathārtha-vijñaptimātra*).

This means that by abandoning what is confused and retaining what is pure, one discards the confusion and retains the singular; "discarding the confusion" is called *vyañjana*, and "retaining the purity" is called *vijñāna*.

Thus, it is named "Pure Consciousness-Only. 2. The meaning of subsuming the derivative and returning to the fundamental: This refers to subsuming the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and returning them [to the fundamental consciousness].

The essence of the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is called "fundamental consciousness-only" (*mūlavijñaptimātra*). Fourth is the meaning of concealing the inferior and manifesting the superior:

this means that the essence of the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is superior, while the mental factors (*caitta*) are inferior; although both the king and its attendants coexist, by concealing the inferior and manifesting the superior, it is called "superior consciousness-only" (*viśiṣṭavijñaptimātra*).

Fifth is the meaning of discarding appearances to realize the nature: this means discarding the appearances and functions of phenomena to realize the essence of the rational nature (*dharmatā*); it is called "essential consciousness-only" (*svabhāvavijñaptimātra*). Sixth—

1. The meaning of object (*viṣaya*): Because the mind that observes and the mental object observed are one, it is called "object-only consciousness" (*viṣaya-vijñaptimātra*). 2. The meaning of nature (*svabhāva*): Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is consciousness alone, it is called "nature-only consciousness" (*svabhāva-vijñaptimātra*). 3. The meaning of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*): Because the characteristics of all phenomena are consciousness alone, it is called "characteristic-only consciousness" (*lakṣaṇa-vijñaptimātra*).

4. The meaning of time (*kāla*): Because the three times are consciousness alone, it is called "time-only consciousness" (*kāla-vijñaptimātra*). 5. The meaning of number (*saṃkhyā*): Because numbers are consciousness alone, it is called "number-only consciousness" (*saṃkhyā-vijñaptimātra*). 6. The meaning of realm (*dhātu*): Because the realms are consciousness alone, it is called "realm-only consciousness" (*dhātu-vijñaptimātra*). 7. The meaning of teaching (*deśanā*): Because the essence of the expressive teaching explains the meaning of consciousness-only, it is called "teaching-only consciousness" (*deśanā-vijñaptimātra*).

8. The meaning of principle (*yukti*): Because the principle is consciousness-only, it is called "principle-only consciousness" (*yukti-vijñaptimātra*). 9. The meaning of practice (*pratipatti*): Because the contemplative practice is consciousness-only, it is called "practice-only consciousness" (*pratipatti-vijñaptimātra*).

Vijñapti-mātra. Tenth is the meaning of the result (*phala*). This refers to the result of wisdom being vijñapti-mātra; thus it is called "resultant vijñapti-mātra. As for these ten meanings above, none are apart from consciousness.
The two characters *wei-shi* (vijñapti-mātra) have now been explained. Now, the character *cheng* (establishment) shall be explained.

"Establishment" (*cheng*) has the meaning of "positing" (*an-li*). The *Shuyao* states: "To posit the teaching and establish the principle is termed 'establishment' (*cheng*). Question: What is meant by establishing vijñapti-mātra?

What is the purpose? The answer is: In my Buddha-dharma, the mind is the primary principle. Because ordinary beings and non-Buddhists turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust, they wander through birth and death.
Out of compassion for them, the Bodhisattva composed this treatise to establish the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This causes one to return to the original source and attain liberation from birth and death; thus it is established as having great significance and benefit. Question:
By what skillful means can one return to the original source? Answer: There are five gates of contemplation that cause one to contemplate the mind oneself, thereby attaining the original source.

Regarding the five gates of contemplation: within the aforementioned ten meanings, "dispelling the false to preserve the real" is the first contemplation; "abandoning the mixed to retain the pure" is the second contemplation;
"subsuming the derivative to return to the fundamental" is the third contemplation; "concealing the inferior to manifest the superior" is the fourth contemplation;

and "dispelling appearances to realize the nature" is the fifth contemplation. Next, regarding the word "treatise" (*lun*): it refers to the dialogue between host and guest, which definitively discriminates between nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*).
To stir up the ultimate essence of the school and refine its meanings into a unified conclusion, establishing a model for future generations, such a work is termed a "treatise" (*lun*).

Question: Regarding the four characters of the title, which character represents the agent (*neng*) and which represents the object (*suo*)? Answer: The character "treatise" (*lun*) is exclusively the agent; "consciousness-only" (*weishi*) is exclusively the object;

the character "establishing" (*cheng*) applies to both agent and object. Question: How should this be explained? Answer: If "establishing" refers to the act of establishing, then "establishing" belongs to the character "treatise"; "consciousness-only" [is that which is established].
Regarding the term "proof-treatise" (*siddhi-śāstra*): it may be interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "a treatise that is capable of proving [the doctrine of] Consciousness-Only.

Alternatively, it may be a *karmadhāraya* compound, where the function of proving exists within the essence of the treatise; since the function is subsumed within the essence, "proof" is itself the "treatise," thus "proof-treatise.

If "proof" refers to that which is proven, then proof belongs to Consciousness-Only, and Consciousness-Only is itself the proof; or, that which is proven is itself Consciousness-Only—this is likewise a *karmadhāraya*.

This is an explanation. Question: Since the treatise (*śāstra*) is exclusively the means (*sādhana*) and consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is exclusively the object (*sādhya*), does the treatise consist of a root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*) and a derivative treatise (*uttara-śāstra*)?

Which of these is the means? Answer: Both the root and the derivative are the means. If the root treatise is the means, then the Buddha’s sūtras on consciousness-only are the object to be established.
If the derivative treatise is the means, then the root treatise on consciousness-only is the object to be established. Question: This treatise...
What is its thesis? Answer: It takes consciousness as its thesis; that is to say, consciousness definitely exists and is not empty, while objects are definitively non-existent and not real.
Therefore, it takes consciousness as its thesis. What is its essence? Answer: Its essence consists of the words and meanings that express and are expressed. Question:
There are treatises of thesis (*siddhānta-śāstra*) and treatises of commentary (*vyākhyā-śāstra*). What kind of treatise is this? Answer: This is a treatise of thesis. Because...

It relies directly upon various sūtras and comprehensively encompasses the entire Great Canon (*mahāpiṭaka*) to clarify the principles of Vijñaptimātra; therefore, it is a treatise of tenets (*siddhānta-śāstra*).

Since it does not merely explain a single specific sūtra, it is not an exegetical commentary (*vyākhyāna-śāstra*). Question: The teachings consist of three piṭakas: first, the Sūtra-piṭaka (*sūtrapiṭaka*); second, the Vinaya-piṭaka (*vinayapiṭaka*);
and third, the Abhidharma-piṭaka (*abhidharmapiṭaka*). Under which of these is this work subsumed? Answer: [It is subsumed under the Abhidharma-piṭaka.]

This belongs to the third category of the Abhidharma-piṭaka. Question: The teachings speak of either a Single Vehicle (Ekayāna), or three vehicles—namely, the Bodhisattva, Śrāvaka, and Pratyekabuddha—or five vehicles, adding humans and devas. To which vehicle does this belong? Answer: It is precisely the Single Vehicle;
for among the three, it is the Bodhisattva Vehicle, and among the five, it is the first. Thus concludes the first section: the explanation of the title of the treatise.
The following two [sections] explain the author of the verses.

Regarding the statement that "the verses were composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu," the *Vasubandhu-ācārya-carita* states: he was from Puruṣapura in Northern India; this is translated as "Puruṣa" (Man).
In that land, there was a state preceptor who was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan.

He had three sons, all named Vasubandhu—this being translated into Chinese as Tiānqīn (Heavenly Kin). Originally, he was born in Jambudvīpa as the younger brother of the Heavenly King Viṣṇu, sent by Śakra Devendra to subdue the Asuras;
thus, his lineage is divine, and he is therefore called Tiānqīn. Although they were the same...
He had one name, but another distinct name was established to identify him. The third son entered the order in the Sarvāstivāda school and attained the fruit of arhatship;
his distinct name was Pilindavatsa, which means "Mother’s Son.

The eldest son possessed the spiritual capacity of a bodhisattva and also entered the order in the Sarvāstivāda school; later, while practicing meditative concentration, he immediately attained freedom from desire.
He contemplated the meaning of emptiness but was unable to enter it. Desiring to take his own life, the Arhat Piṇḍola was observing this from Pūrvavideha in the east;
he came from that direction and taught him the contemplation of emptiness according to the Hīnayāna.
By contemplating as instructed, he immediately attained entry. Yet his mind remained unsettled, so by means of this vehicle, he traveled through spiritual power to Tuṣita.
In Tuṣita Heaven, he questioned Maitreya Bodhisattva, who expounded for him the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).
Upon returning to Jambudvīpa, he contemplated according to those instructions and immediately attained realization. While he was contemplating, the earth shook in six ways.

Having attained the Mahāyāna contemplation of emptiness, he was thereafter given the distinct name Asaṅga, translated as "Unattached" (*Wúzhù*). Thereafter, he ascended to Tuṣita Heaven several times.
The Deva consulted Maitreya regarding the meaning of the Mahāyāna sūtras. Having gained understanding according to his capacity, he returned to Jambudvīpa to explain them to others;
however, many who heard him did not develop faith. Master Asanga then made this vow:
"I now desire to cause sentient beings to believe in and understand the Mahāyāna. I pray only that the Great Master will descend to Jambudvīpa to expound and explain the Mahāyāna."
To cause all sentient beings to attain faith and understanding, Maitreya, in accordance with that wish, descended to Jambudvīpa during the night and emitted a great radiance.

The layman Xuànjiàn recorded the bequeathed words of the former sage, surely as an entrustment to the worthy of the present.

[The circumstances] were different. Those who received [the teachings] had no reliance upon them; moreover, as time gradually passed, people became increasingly corrupt, life spans shortened, and wisdom became fragmented.

While one might investigate the scattered fragments and achieve some understanding, it was difficult to realize the truth by grasping their divergent pointers. The treatise consists of ten fascicles and contains thirty-two verses. Based on these verses, the text is divided into sections and organized into three parts.

Verse: I prostrate to the one who is perfectly pure in the nature of consciousness-only; I shall now explain that teaching for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.

"Prostrate" (namas) has the meaning of reverent homage. "Benefit and happiness" (hitasukha) has the meaning of compassionate assistance. This refers to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, who was about to compose this treatise.

At that time, one first expresses the sincerity of reverent benefit, and only thereafter provides the explanation. The first two lines concern the veneration of the Triple Gem through the Dharma of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*);

since the Sangha and the Buddha are fundamentally identical, yet there are distinctions in their realization—whether partial or complete—the Buddha is the "complete purity" and the Sangha is the "partial purity.
The latter two lines concern the compassionate benefit of sentient beings through the principle of the One Mind, [applying it] to both the holy and the ordinary.
Individually, there is delusion or awakening regarding karma; thus, delusion results in the endurance of suffering, while awakening results in benefit and happiness.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-bhāṣya* states: "There are two causes and conditions for which this treatise is taught: first, so that the unsurpassed teaching of the Tathāgata may long abide in the world;
second, so as to equally benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings. 1. Presentation of the Title.
The verses are concluded. Below, the second section explains the meaning of the verses and is divided into two parts. First, the general explanation:
"Now, this treatise is composed for the sake of [attaining] the two emptinesses... because by means of the cognitive obscurations, one attains great enlightenment."

The deluded are ignorant of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*); the errant cling to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). Not knowing that self and phenomena are fundamentally non-existent is to be deluded regarding the two emptinesses;
falsely clinging to self and phenomena as truly existent constitutes the formation of the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa*).

Therefore, this treatise is now composed so that sentient beings may necessarily penetrate this meaning and give rise to correct understanding. The two emptinesses—of self and of phenomena—will be explained in the subsequent text. [End of] the preceding section.

To cause the arising of understanding. The intent lies in severing the obstructions; therefore, it is said that "understanding arises. This is for the purpose of severing the two types of heavy obstructions.

From the phrase "due to the self and dharmas" (*ātma-dharma*) onwards, the meaning of the aforementioned "arising of understanding" and "severing the two obstructions" is explained. Attaining the wisdom of the two emptinesses is called "realizing the two emptinesses. Because wisdom arises and delusions are eliminated, it is so named.

"Following the abandonment" means that the purpose of abandoning the higher fetters (*anuśaya*) is to realize the fruit; thus it is called "abandoning the obstacles. This is for the sake of attaining two superior fruits.
By explaining the abandonment of the lower [fetters], the meaning of abandoning obstacles and realizing the two fruits is clarified:

the fruit of true liberation is the entry into parinirvāṇa, and the fruit of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is perfect awakening. Afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to continue the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); by abandoning them, one attains the truth.
Liberation is termed "entering nirvāṇa. That which obstructs correct understanding regarding what is to be known is severed; upon attaining perfect awakening, it is termed "realizing bodhi.
The above constitutes the first section, a general explanation of the meaning of the verse, elucidating the general outline of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

Attachment arises regarding these principles. Some, holding that external objects are not non-existent in the same way that consciousness is, belong to the [Vaibhāṣika] school;

Others, holding that internal consciousness is non-existent in the same way that objects are, such as Bhāviveka and others, rely on the teachings of emptiness intended with a specific underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) to negate consciousness just as they negate objects. Still others hold that the various consciousnesses have distinct functions but a single substance.
Regarding "the same": there is a class of Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who say that although the functions of the eight consciousnesses are distinct, their substance is one.

Or, there are those who maintain that apart from the mind (*citta*), there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*); this is the position held by masters such as Buddhadeva of the Sautrāntika school.

This is because the sūtras speak of the six elements of the person (*pudgala*) and state that defilement and purity arise from the mind, with no separate mental factors. (The term *pudgala* refers to the agent; since the mind is capable of creating things, it is called the "maker.")

The author [states]: "The six elements—namely earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness (each being distinct is termed an 'element')". △ Second, the citation of the four masters is concluded. Below, third, the preceding intent is summarized.
This treatise is composed in order to refute these various divergent attachments and to enable one to attain a correct understanding.
These various divergent attachments belong to the aforementioned ordinary persons, non-Buddhists, and those of other vehicles;

However, the essence of consciousness does not abide in existence or non-existence, nor is it that it does not abide [in them]. Fundamentally, it is neither non-existent nor non-non-existent;

Yet those who employ verbal expressions cannot fully capture it; their wisdom falls short of its true nature, and they merely cling to their own conceptions.

Now, I compose this treatise to lead others to realize *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and attain understanding according to reality. The first section, "The Section on Reverent Preface to the School," is concluded.

It is said that those characteristics depend upon the transformation of consciousness; they are established as various names by way of convention, and are not something separate from the mind.
