It is called "consciousness" because it clearly and distinctly manifests and discriminates the characteristics of objects. Herein, the term "consciousness" also includes the mental factors (*caitta*), because the mind-king (*citta*) and its mental factors are necessarily associated.
Furthermore, the "consciousness" mentioned here consists of the eight types of consciousness and also includes the fifty [mental factors].
Because it is the object of a single mind, the following verse says: "These transformations are only three. Regarding the word "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) in the verse, the commentary explains:

it means that upon the self-verifying essence (*svasaṃvitti*) of each consciousness, there respectively manifest as appearances of the two parts—the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). Because they appear as if they were external objects, they are called "transformations.

Regarding the phrase "based on this," the commentary explains "provisional establishment" (*prajñapti*). Those two refer to the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*). This word— [refers to] the term "this" (*idam*).
"Manifesting as characteristics" (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*) means that based upon the two divisions of characteristics and seeing, one conventionally establishes the names of the "imagined self and phenomena.

This is precisely the "conventional nature of discrimination" (*vikalpa-prajñapti*); therefore, it is said that apart from these two [divisions], there is nothing upon which they depend. Alternatively, the passage beginning with "or again" explains "arising from conditions":
furthermore, it explains that self and phenomena arise from the substance of consciousness through the power of perfuming; this is called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

"Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to that which is conventionally designated through causes and conditions. The section beginning with "the various consciousnesses" explains the aforementioned power of the perfuming of discrimination.

This means that as the various consciousnesses arise, they engage in successive discrimination; this perfuming acts as a condition, whereby there appear what seem to be external objects—namely, the self and phenomena.

Those who, based on these appearances, grasp them as a real self and real phenomena—the word "this" (*etad*) here points back to the aforementioned conventional designations of the *parikalpita* (imagined) nature, which depend upon the *paratantra* (dependent) nature.

Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). The foolish grasp at them erroneously, asserting they possess real substance. "Affliction" (*ābādha*) means illness. Because one perceives objects in a distorted manner when afflicted by illness, this affliction is compared to a dream.
This illustrates that all sentient beings who have not yet realized the two kinds of emptiness are shrouded by ignorance;

this is called the "long night" of birth and death. Just as one suffering from a dream clings to the dream-objects as being truly existent, so it is with these characteristics. If the affliction is removed...
Upon awakening from the dream, one realizes that it was false.

What the deluded commoner (bāla) reckons to be a real self and real dharmas—even down to the objective bases upon which they rely—is conventionally existent; yet for the deluded commoner, these are ultimately non-existent.

The phrase "the deluded commoner" below concludes the preceding discussion on false attachment, establishing that such things definitely do not exist and exist only as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). The phrase "internal consciousness" (*adhyātma-vijñāna*) below concludes [the section].
The superior consciousness transforms; it exists like an illusion and is therefore also termed "provisional" (*prajñapti*). As for the term "resembling," it refers to appearing as if external.

Since it is described as an "external appearance," it differs from that [non-Buddhist] clinging to the substantial nature of a self and dharmas. The statement that "external objects are established according to mental states" reveals that the objective realm is empty;
thus, it is said that they do not exist in the same way that consciousness does. This means that these external objects lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Just as consciousness exists, internal consciousness necessarily arises dependent upon causes and conditions; this clarifies that because the mind exists, it is not non-existent, just as objects are not.

That is to say, this internal consciousness possesses both substance and function; it is not like those who hold that objects exist as a form of exaggeration (samāropa) and hold that the mind is empty as a form of deprecation (apavāda).
Now, by establishing that objects are empty while the mind exists, both of these two attachments are refuted. As for objects—
The phrase "based on the lower" concludes by manifesting the two kinds of existence. "Conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) refers to the provisional; "phenomenon" (*vastu*) refers to the essence.

Objects appear in dependence upon consciousness, yet their essence is fundamentally empty and exists only as a provisional designation. Consciousness serves as the basis; although it manifests all phenomena, it also exists as ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The word "also" implies that its meaning encompasses both types of existence. That which is provisionally established according to conditions is called conventional existence.
"Quiescent and unmoving" is termed "ultimate existence. △ First, the explanation of the meaning of the verse concludes the brief analysis of the self and phenomena.
Below, the second part—raising questions and answers to provide a detailed analysis of the self and phenomena—is divided into two sections. First, the general question and general answer.
How should one know that there are truly no external objects? ... Because neither a real self nor real dharmas can be apprehended.
Through this dialogue, the non-existence of a distinct substantial entity for either self or dharmas is clarified.

Since they both cling to the reality of self and dharmas, the answer refutes them with the three characters "cannot be apprehended" (*anupalabdhi*). △ This concludes the general question and general answer. Below are two [sections].

The section on "Specific Questions and Specific Answers" has four parts. First, the specific question regarding the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) has five parts. First, it cites three types of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
[Question: How is it that a real self (*bhūtātman*) cannot be found? [Answer: ... because it remains hidden within the body and performs its activities.
To the question, "Why is a real self not apprehended? the answer first generally indicates three types of non-Buddhists (tīrthika), and then specifically sets forth their tenets.
First, they maintain that the essence of the self is eternal and all-pervading; therefore, its magnitude is equal to empty space. Because it is identical to space...
Performing karma in various places and experiencing suffering and pleasure therein is what is postulated by the two schools of Vaiśeṣika and Sāṃkhya.

Second, there is the attachment to a self whose substance is permanent yet undergoes transformation according to the body; when the body is large, the substance of the self expands, and when the body is small, the substance of the self contracts.
Therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate. This is what is postulated by the two schools of the Ahrīka heretics and the Nirgranthas (Jains). Third...

These [proponents] maintain that the substance of the self (*ātman*) is eternal and subtle; therefore, they use the atom (*paramāṇu*) as a metaphor. By "concealing and moving within the body," they manifest the eternity of its substance.
By "performing various activities," they manifest the eternality of its function. This is precisely what is reckoned by the two schools—the followers of Paśupati and the Vaiśeṣikas.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) says: "In general, there are three types of false views: first, non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*); second, those who..."
Regarding "Buddhist and non-Buddhist [teachings]": one may study the three trainings of the Buddha-dharma and yet become a non-Buddhist.

These three types mentioned here are the non-Buddhists who exist outside of the Buddha-dharma. As for those outside the Buddha-dharma, even before the Buddha appeared, there were already three or four groups, totaling seven types.
Once the Buddha had appeared, there were six great masters of treatises, which together with the former made thirteen types. The three types referred to now are as follows: [text continues].
These are the six great masters.
First, as for why [the following] is unreasonable: because all phenomena that are cultivated and realized are conjoined with a self.
This refutes the first type of attachment, which clings to a self that is permanent, omnipresent, and equal in magnitude to space; this is the restatement of that attachment.
"Intention (manas) should not experience suffering or pleasure along with the body. This is the opponent's objection, which the Master refutes as follows:

Since [the self] is identical in essence to space—vast and boundless—it would have no basis for the addition of changing suffering and pleasure; how then could it experience various sufferings and pleasures in accordance with a small body?

Furthermore, because it is eternal and omnipresent, it should have no assisting factors to cause its transformation; that is to say, being both eternal and all-pervasive, filling and permeating everything, it cannot be transformed.

[If it is] "active," since it lacks the nature of activity, how could it move from place to place and be able to create various karmas? Furthermore, regarding the [passage] "what is produced below," two further alternatives are established for refutation;
whichever position one adheres to, neither conforms to correct reasoning. If the essence of a single self were identical to all selves...

Since their substance is not different, their functional activity must likewise be the same. Therefore, when one self performs an action, up to and including liberation, all selves should be liberated simultaneously;
this would result in the fallacy that what is done by one is experienced by another. If one self were distinct from all other selves, then being distinct they would not be the same.
Consequently, each should be individually pervasive, and their pervasively omnipresent substances should become intermingled. [If they were to intermingle...]
In this way, they would be identical. Therefore, as before, it should be called "all that is performed and all that is experienced.

If one were to argue—granting even such a counter-argument—that "that which acts is that which experiences," and "this which acts is this which experiences," such that the performance of an action and the experiencing of its fruit do not become confused among various selves, and thus there is no fault of another having acted while a different self experiences the result—the refutation continues: This reasoning is also incorrect.
It is unreasonable for the karmic results and the body to be conjoined with various selves such that they belong to this self and not to others.

That is to say, it is unreasonable for the karmic results to be experienced and the body to be the agent and experiencer, such that among a plurality of intermingled selves, these would be conjoined only with this particular self and not with other selves. Why? It is like a thousand lamps in a single room; their light...
If the light-marks were intermingled, such that the objects illuminated belonged only to this light and not to that light, would this not be logically impossible?
If at the time one is liberated, all should be liberated—this is what is meant by the "intermingling" of the self (*ātman*), where it is difficult to distinguish between "this" and "that.

Since karma, its fruit, and the body must necessarily be conjoined with the self, they would have to be conjoined with all selves. Once conjoined with all selves, when one self is liberated, [all would be liberated].
At that time, all other selves should also attain liberation. Why? Because the dharmas cultivated and realized would be conjoined with those various selves mentioned above.
Furthermore, it is unreasonable [to claim] that this is so; for what reason? Therefore, what they say is like the play of children.
This refutes the second type of attachment regarding the meaning: [the claim] that "the essence of the self is permanent.
The phrase "it should not expand or contract according to the body" is the Master’s refutation. "Tuo ye" refers to a bellows; it is a bag made of leather used as a tool for blowing fire.
Since its essence is permanent, how could there be expansion and contraction? If there is indeed expansion and contraction, it is like a bellows.
The wind in a flute: when it is coiled, it enters within; when it is expanded, it exits without. Since there is both exiting and entering, how can it be called "permanently abiding"?
This uses the concepts of coiling and expanding to refute permanence. Furthermore, regarding the passage "Moreover, the self... and so on:

this means that if the self were identical with the body, then since the body is divisible and not a single unit, one could never find a self-essence that is singular. This uses the concept of being "concomitant with the body" to refute oneness. He then concludes that [view].
He said: "This is merely child's play;
it does not accord with correct principle, nor is it reasonable in the end. Why is this so? (Up to: Because all that comes and goes is neither permanent nor unitary."

This refutes the third type of attachment to the meaning [of a self]: that the measure of the self is as small as a single atom (*paramāṇu*). This restates the intent of that attachment and refutes it, saying:

"Since you admit that its smallness reaches the limit of an atom, by what principle could a large body be moved throughout its entirety? The passage beginning with "If one says... restates a further counter-argument:
that a whirling firebrand (*alātacakram*) serves as a metaphor for the rapid circulation through the body, such that it appears to move everywhere, though it is actually minute.
Regarding this self, it seems that the body moves everywhere; thus one might think that although the self is small, it rapidly circulates through the body.
The Master of the Treatise refutes this: since you maintain that the self is permanent, it should be incapable of movement or transition. How could it be like a fire-wheel?
If you maintain that the self is one, it should remain as a single entity; why then does it move rapidly throughout the body?

To claim that this rapid movement through the body is like a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra) contradicts your own tenet that [the self] is permanent and one. That which undergoes coming and going is not permanent or one.
This explains the meaning of being neither permanent nor one: if a phenomenon goes, it does not remain as a single entity; if a phenomenon comes, it is not [a single entity].

Because it is eternally present, calculating its coming and going contradicts its own nature as constant and unitary. This concludes the first section, which presents the three types of views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Below, the second section presents the three types of views of the other vehicles (yānas).
Furthermore, the self as it is clung to is of three types; therefore, the real self as it is clung to by them is not established.

To distinguish these, the three meanings clung to by other vehicles are cited: first, that which is identical to the aggregates (*skandha*). "Aggregate" has the meaning of a collection, for a collection constitutes the body;

it also has the meaning of covering, for it covers suchness (*tathatā*). These are the five dharmas—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are combined and collected together.
Regarding "the body": the object they grasp is that the body itself is the self, because apart from the body there is no meaning of a self.

Second, regarding "separate from the aggregates": they hold that the essence of the self exists separately from the aggregates; it is precisely because it exists separately that they know it to be real.

Regarding the third [position], that the self is neither identical to nor distinct from the five aggregates: they maintain that the essence of the self is neither identical to the aggregates nor distinct from them, and neither separate from the aggregates nor non-separate from them.
Thus, while they know the aggregates are subject to arising and ceasing, they hold the essence of the self to be eternally one.

First, as for the claim that the self is initially identical to the aggregates, this is logically untenable; it would follow that the self, like the aggregates, is neither eternal nor one. "Eternal" and "one" [are the qualities in question].

This is the internal tenet of other vehicles. If one maintains that [the self] is identical to the aggregates (*skandha*), then since the aggregates consist of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), this contradicts their own established doctrine that the aggregates have the meaning of a "collection" (*caya*).

Furthermore, if matter and mind were combined, they would not constitute a single entity. Moreover, in the section below on the "internal," the fundamental substantial matter (*dravya-rūpa*) is used as an analogy to refute the conceptualized aggregate of matter (*nimitta-bhāga-rūpa-skandha*).
Just as it is with the aggregate of matter, so it is with the aggregate of mind: it is neither continuous nor permanent, but arises through conditions.
This is not real. Form (*rūpa*) is a reflection of the mind. When the mind is active, it is termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*). Apart from form and mind, everything else is termed "the rest.

These remaining formations consist of twenty-four factors such as acquisition (*prāpti*), which are called "dissociated formations" (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). As for the remaining forms, these include shadows, light, and so forth.

Because formations lack substantial resistance (*sapratighatva*), they are like empty space. Because form lacks the capacity for cognition (*ālambana*), it is not of the nature of awareness. Thus, it is distinct from the middle [of the mind].

"The reasoning that the self is the aggregates is likewise untenable. This statement summarizes and refutes the second position as a whole. It follows that [the self] would be like space, lacking both an agent and an experiencer.
"Agent" refers to the performance of action; "experiencer" refers to the receiving of results. Since the self is asserted to be distinct from the aggregates, it is neither form nor mind.
Being non-form, it lacks substantiality; being non-mind, it lacks cognition. Just like the great void, it is inert and devoid of consciousness; yet you insist on holding such a thing to be the self.
"What would it even be for? and "Later, both [the aggregates and the self] would not be mine; this reasoning is also incorrect"—these lines state the third thesis and refute it as a whole.

"Admitting that the self is established in dependence upon the aggregates, yet neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates" means: it is not identical to the aggregates, nor is it separate from the aggregates. This refers to the meaning of what they assert:

the self is established in dependence upon the aggregates, and therefore it is said to be "not separate"; since the self is not the aggregates themselves, it is said to be "not identical. This is the correct [position].
It is like the making of a jar: from a lump of clay the jar is formed; the jar is neither separate from the lump of clay, nor is it the lump of clay itself.

Therefore, one knows that while the clay may be said to be real, the jar is certainly conventional. Thus, your aggregates (skandhas) may be said to be real, whereas the self (ātman) is certainly non-existent.

Furthermore, since it cannot be described as either conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)—the conditioned being identical to the aggregates and the unconditioned being... [the self would likewise be inexpressible].

"It is not the case that [the self] is neither identical with nor separate from the aggregates, yet cannot be described. This means: since it is neither identical with nor separate from the aggregates, why further insist on whether the self exists or does not exist?
Therefore, the following section concludes that this is irrational. △ Second, the three types [of views] regarding other vehicles are concluded.
Below, the master of the treatise provides a general analysis in three chapters and two syllogisms (*prayoga*).
Furthermore, regarding the "body of a self" (ātman) that is asserted to be real:

[the passage from] "hence the principle of the asserted self is in both cases unestablished" means that one must interrogate whether this asserted self possesses volition (cetanā) or not. If it possesses volition, it must be impermanent (*anitya*).
This means that the presence or absence of volition occurs only upon arising and ceasing; since there is already arising and ceasing, how could it not be impermanent? Therefore.
Another explanation states: It is not at all times [that the self exists], because it possesses volition (*cetanā*). If it were devoid of volition, it would be like empty space.
This means that the activity of the faculties is rooted in volition, and their arising and ceasing are based on the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
If there were no volition, it would be unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and thus identical to empty space—without arising or ceasing, unable to perform actions, and likewise unable to receive results.
Therefore, the self as it is grasped is not established by reason in either case. This concludes the section [showing] that both the "possessing volition" and the "lacking volition" are irrational.
Furthermore, regarding the substantial self-body as it is grasped by all [proponents], [it is shown that] the self as it is grasped is not established in either of the two ways.
Furthermore, [the text] below interrogates whether the substance and function of the self (ātman) exist or not.

If it possesses function—just like hands and feet—it means that the self as you conceive it, if it possesses function such as the hand being able to grasp or the foot being able to run, would have a nature that is produced;
thus, the self would certainly be impermanent. How then can you maintain that the substance of the self has the quality of being truly eternal? If it lacks function, it is like a rabbit’s horn.

Regarding the "horn": it arises based on a substance (*dravya*), and a substance must necessarily have a form. A rabbit's horn exists as a mere name; it serves as an analogy for that which lacks functional activity (*kāritra*).
Since functional activity is absent, a real self (*ātman*) is not established. Thus, the self as it is grasped by [the opponent] is unestablished in both respects.
This concludes the section showing that [the self] is untenable whether it possesses or lacks functional activity. Chapter Two ends.
Furthermore, regarding the substantial self-body (ātman) as it is clung to by various [schools], [it leads] up to right view, yet instead causes one to sink and wallow in birth and death.
"Not" (*na*) signifies the sense of uncertainty. One interrogates these views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) concerning whether they take the self-body as their object or not.

If [the opponent claims] "no," this is a refutation by restating their position and challenging it: only when the apprehension of an object is clear and distinct can one know it to exist substantially; since the view of self does not directly apprehend [the self-body], [it cannot be established].
Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*): how is reality known? If it is inferior, this is stated as a restatement of the [wrong] view to establish its nature.

Because of the self, views arise; views arise from delusion (*mṛṣā*). Based on views, one clings to a self; the self exists through conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). Therefore, the Buddha taught the Dharma that "all things are without self.
Within that which is selfless, to falsely give rise to the view of a self is called perversion (*viparyāsa*)—it is not knowing according to reality (*yathābhūtam*). Now...

Since you maintain that the substance of the self (*ātman*) is real and that it serves as the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), then the nature of this view of self should not be inverted;
it would constitute a knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*). Below, the text restates this point regarding its non-inverted nature and proceeds to refute it. That is to say:
since you of the Hīnayāna admit that the view of self can take a real self as its object, then the nature of the view of self is not inverted and constitutes [correct] knowledge.

[This is] truly known. How is it that the authoritative teachings you yourselves believe all condemn the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) while praising non-self (*anātman*), yet do not contradict one another?
The passage beginning with "The statement 'there is no view of self'" explains below how the holy teaching praises non-self and condemns the view of self.
How could there be... [this would be] contrary to the norm. If one were to allow that the nature of the view of self is not inverted, it should...
[They] realize nirvana. If those with false views can realize nirvana, then it would follow that those with right views should sink into saṃsāra; how could there be anyone who reverses this?
This refutation based on the principle of contrariety to the natural order concludes the third chapter. Below, two formal arguments (prayoga) are established to provide a comprehensive refutation.
Furthermore, various views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) do not take a real self as their object; rather, they are various conceptual constructions following one's own deluded sentiments.
First, by refuting that the apprehending view of self is false and illusory, it follows that a real self cannot serve as its objective referent.

Therefore, taking the "view of self" as the subject (*dharmin*) under discussion, we establish as our thesis (*pakṣa*) that it does not take a real self as its object. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it possesses an objective referent."
Just as taking other minds as an analogy, this demonstrates that the grasping subject—the view of self—is false, because its object—the self—is likewise false. Why is this?
Because the false view of self has an object; since the grasping subject and the grasped object exist in mutual dependence and are merely conventional designations, how could they be said to be real?
"As with taking other minds" refers to [minds] other than a real self—namely, the three [types of mind].

Since all dharmas of the realms—the mind and its mental factors—have false conceptualization as their intrinsic nature, if the [subject] is already false, then the real self that is the object of perception must also be false.
In the section on "the view of self," the author next refutes the unreality of the self as the object;
because the false view of self acts as the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), the object of perception is presented as the *dharmin* (the subject of the proposition).
It is established as our thesis that the self (*ātman*) is not real. "Because it is an object of cognition" is the reason. "Like other phenomena" is the example.
This intends to show that the self, as an object of cognition, is unreal, because the self that performs the cognition is itself a false construction. Why is this so?
Because an unreal self is an object of cognition, and since the object of cognition and the cognizing subject are mutually dependent and merely conventional, how could it be a real self?
Regarding "other phenomena" (*anye dharmāḥ*): this refers to all other phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), excluding a real self (*ātman*).
Since these others arise from conceptual conditions, and since they are dependent on conditions, the self that is their object is likewise not real.
Therefore, below [the text] concludes that the view of self does not take a real self as its object; rather, that which is its object is merely—
Based upon the *paratantra-svabhāva*, one falsely gives rise to conceptual constructions. How could that which is the object of such false construction be taken as the real essence of a self?
△ The Master of Treatises has finished his general analysis. Below, there are four sections summarizing the common attachments, divided into two parts. First, the enumeration of the categories.
However, there are briefly two types of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*): first, the innate (*sahaja*), and second, the conceptual (*vikalpita*).
Although the varieties of all self-grasping held by the world’s śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others are numerous, when summarized, they do not exceed these two types:
the innate and the conceptual. △ The enumeration is concluded above; below follows the actual [explanation].
The explanation has three parts. First, innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).
Innate self-grasping has existed since beginningless time [and can only be eliminated] when one attains the superior contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*).

This explains the meaning of "innate" (*sahaja*) indicated above. Because it has existed since beginningless time, it does not depend on false teachings; because it arises through internal causal power, it does not depend on false conceptualization;
and because it is always concomitant with the body, it functions spontaneously. Since it possesses these aforementioned characteristics, it is called "innate. Furthermore, regarding its two types:
although there is one innate [affliction] in total, it is divided into two aspects according to the cognizing consciousness that takes it as its object.

There are two types: continuous and intermittent. The meaning of "continuous" refers to uninterrupted continuity. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses have been revolving constantly since beginningless time;

therefore, they are called "continuous. Regarding "arising as the marks of one's own mind": this means that when the seventh consciousness takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object, it relies upon that seeing-part as the objective essence (*bhāva*).
From its own self-verifying substance (*svasaṃvitti*), the seventh consciousness transforms and gives rise to reflected images (*pratibimba*), which it then grasps as real.
This "I" is called a truly substantial object (*saviṣaya-vastu*). It is intermittent because it takes only the mind as its object; it is not constant in meaning.

Since the sixth consciousness arises dependent upon various conditions, it is interrupted when those conditions are lacking. Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness enters a state of neutrality (*avyākṛta*), it does not give rise to the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*);
thus, it is also termed intermittent. Although the seventh [consciousness] is neutral, it is obscured (*nivṛta*) and clings to [the self] at every moment.

Therefore, that continuity [is maintained]. This is called "interruption. Regarding that which is transformed by consciousness: this refers to the manifestation of the aggregates of form and mind within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
The sixth mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) either takes the five aggregates as a whole to be the self, or takes one specific aggregate individually to be the self.

Among these, the characteristics of the mind and the explanation of their meaning are the same as before. It is also called an "object consisting of mere images" (*kevala-chāyā-viṣaya*), because it is perceived concurrently with...

Because it is a form (*rūpa*). The passage "these two below" concludes by clarifying that it is difficult to sever. Because it is established through the power of internal causes, it is called "subtle.
Because it has existed from beginningless time, it is said to be difficult to sever. After ascending the stages (*bhūmi*), one repeatedly cultivates this contemplation within the first seven stages.

When one ascends the eighth stage, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is permanently suppressed and no longer manifests; therefore, it is called "emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). As for the term "superior birth":

Regarding [the two types of self-grasping], that which arises from discrimination is secondary; innate [self-grasping] is primary. Since the emptiness of self and the emptiness of persons are identical to the emptiness of sentient beings, [the former are subsumed therein].
△ The first section, on innate grasping at a self, is concluded. Below are the two sections on grasping at a self arising from discrimination.
The grasping at a self through conceptual discrimination is also eliminated by the true suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*) in the present.

This explains the meaning of "conceptual discrimination" in the aforementioned heading. Because [beings] grasp at the existence of internal and external [phenomena], which arise from conditions, it is said: "also by."
The present external conditions consist of the conceptualizations of false teachings; it arises only after these [conditions], and therefore is not co-existent with the body.
The phrase "existing only in the sixth consciousness" excludes the non-conceptual nature of the preceding seventh consciousness. "This also has two kinds" refers to...

In summary, this single category of discrimination is divided into two types according to its objective referent. First is the characteristic of the aggregates of false teachings, which are mistakenly held to exist as real entities apart from the mind;
they differ from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) in that they are merely manifestations of the mind, arising from causes and conditions.

Taking up the previous point, the refutation by way of the difficulty that [the result] should not be three is as follows: If it were not three, then when the three combine to form one, they would lose their original individuality.
Since the capacity to establish the distinction between cause and effect has been lost, the single characteristic of that which is established must also be lost in accordance with its substance.
When both characteristic and substance are lost, how can one speak of "one" or "three"?

One cannot say that each of the three possesses two characteristics (up to the point where) the substance would likewise have to be threefold for each, because the substance is identical to the characteristic.

Regarding the statement that "the three [poisons] cannot be said to each have two characteristics," this is said for fear that the opponent might further argue that within each of the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—there are two characteristics, such as "greatness" and so forth, or "greed" and so forth.
Therefore, it first suppresses their argument by stating, "cannot be said," and so on. Below, the text takes up and refutes this further argument:
if there were two characteristics within a single entity, they would necessarily be mutually identical; if the general were identical to the particular, then the general...
"There ought to be three; how then can one be seen? If the particular is identical to the universal, then the particular should also be one; how then can three be seen?

If it is argued [as follows], this restates their counter-argument that each of the specific characteristics possesses all three natures, in order to refute the difficulty regarding the inconsistency between 'one' and 'three':
namely, that within greed there are hatred and delusion; within hatred there are greed and delusion; and within delusion there are greed and hatred."
The three dharmas are mixed together; therefore, each is seen as one. Furthermore, the refutation states: "If there is a single substance with three characteristics, why is only one seen?

If each of the three [substances] has its own three characteristics, how then could they be different? The passage beginning "If that" below restates the objection that it is irrational for each of the three substances to possess its own three characteristics.
Each one refers to greed and so forth; that is to say, since a single dharma such as greed already possesses the three characteristics, it should be one...

This concludes the point that if the essence were identical to the characteristic, each individual [element] would necessarily undergo transformation.
Furthermore, since the dharmas such as "greatness" (mahat) are all composed of the three [qualities], they ought to be without distinction; this would constitute a grave error.
Moreover, because there is no differentiation among these dharmas, the composition of those three factors is refuted.

That is to say, since the transforming capacities of the dharmas such as "greatness" are identical, the manifested characteristics resulting from that transformation must necessarily be without difference. This explains the characteristic of non-differentiation mentioned above. It says:

The "subtle elements" (*tanmātra*) refer to the five subtle elements; the "greats" (*mahābhūta*) refer to the five great elements; and the "faculties" (*indriya*) refer to the eleven faculties. These all pertain to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

It is logically necessary that matter and mind are each distinct. For those who maintain that all phenomena are composed of the synthesis of these three [aspects], it would follow logically that there is no distinction between them.

If this were so, then according to the principle above—that essence and aspect are not distinct—since the essence is already without distinction, the function (*vṛtti*) must likewise be without distinction.
However, it would follow that a single sense organ could perceive all objects, because all objects are equally the conjunction of the three [organ, object, and consciousness].

This completes the first part above: the Sāṃkhya’s conception of the *puruṣa* (spirit-self) as a unity. Below follows the second part: the Vaiśeṣika’s conception of the six categories (*padārtha*) as distinct entities, divided into five sections.
First, the tenets of the Vaiśeṣika school.
Regarding the categories such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth, which the Vaiśeṣikas maintain to be substantially real and perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
the Great Master Qingliang stated that the Sanskrit term *Vaiśeṣika-sāstra* translates here as "Superior Discourse" (*Shenglun*). This [school] was founded by...

The *Śītalāvatī* is also considered the second. As for the term "Vaiśeṣika" (Excellence Treatise), it is so called because its six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) are preeminent, or because it was composed by an eminent person.
This author of the treatise lived at the end of the *vivartakalpa* (the aeon of formation), when the lifespan of humans was immeasurable.
A non-Buddhist (tīrthika) appeared in the world named Ulūka, which in this language means "owl. By day he avoided sounds and forms, concealing his traces in mountains and marshes;
by night, when his sight and hearing were suspended, he would go out to beg for food. Because people of the time took him for an owl bird, he was called the Owl Ascetic (Ulūka-ṛṣi);
he is the same as Vārṣagaṇya of the *Śataśāstra*. Some call him Kaṇāda; *kaṇa* means "grain."
*Taṇḍulakiñjalka*. "Kiñjalka" is translated as "grain-heart" (the core of the grain). Formerly, he would roam at night and alarm young women; thus, he no longer begged for food at night.

Instead, he took the *taṇḍulakiñjalka*—the heart of the rice grains found amidst the bran and chaff from threshing floors—and ate it. Consequently, he was known at the time as the Rice-Heart (*Taṇḍulakiñjalka*) Sage.

Having practiced the Way for many years, he claimed to have realized *bodhi* and joyfully entered parinirvāṇa. He merely lamented that, regarding what he had awakened to, there was no one to whom he could transmit it, and he felt pity [for this].
Sentient beings in this world are deluded and lack the eye of wisdom; therefore, [the Buddha] contemplates these seven virtues and bestows the Dharma so that it may be transmitted:
first, being born in a central land; second, having complete parents; third, belonging to the Brahmin caste; fourth, possessing the marks of a noble body;
fifth, being intelligent and quick-witted; sixth, practicing faith with gentleness and flexibility; and seventh, possessing a heart of great compassion. After an immeasurable period of time...
One who lacks the seven virtues will, after many kalpas have passed, appear in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as a brahmin named Maṇavaka, which means "The Youthful Scholar.
This youth has a son named Pañcaśikha, which means "Five-Crested";
his hair on the crown forms five curls, and he has five points upon his head. This person is fully endowed with the seven virtues, yet his faculties ripen somewhat slowly.
Having become so deeply attached to his wife and servants, he was extremely difficult to convert. After immeasurable years had passed, [the Rishi] waited for their faculties to ripen.

Then, after another three thousand years, while entering a garden for recreation, he encountered a quarrel between the husband and his wife over flowers. Taking advantage of this, the Owl-owl (Pūtanā) utilized the power of spiritual penetration to transform him;
however, as he would not comply with the five peaks, the Seer returned. Again, after three thousand years, having failed to convert him, he once more—
For three thousand years, the two schools vied with one another most intensely. As their mutual resentment became acute, they looked up in thought to the Empty Immortal (Kongxian).

The Immortal responded at that moment, using his supernatural powers to guide them; he transported them through the air to the mountain where he dwelt and expounded for them the Dharma of the six categories of realized meaning:

first, reality (*tattva*); second, qualities (*guṇa*); third, activity (*karma*); fourth, great existence (*mahāsattā*); fifth, identity and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*); and sixth, conjunction (*samavāya*). Regarding "reality": all...

The substance (*dravya*) is real; it is called "real" because it is that upon which qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karma*) depend. This is because qualities and activities do not depend on [categories such as] "existence" (*sattā*) and so forth.
"Qualities" refers to moral virtues, and "activities" refers to functional operations. There are nine kinds of substances: first, earth; second, water; third, fire; fourth, wind;
fifth, space; sixth, time; seventh, direction; eighth, the self (*ātman*); ninth, the mind (*manas*). There are twenty-four qualities: first, color; second, ... [and so forth].
1. Odor; 2. Taste; 3. Taste-constituents; 4. Tangible objects; 5. Number; 6. Dimension; 7. Distinctness; 8. Conjunction;
9. Disjunction; 10. Thatness; 11. Thisness; 12. Cognition; 13. Pleasure; 14. Pain; 15. Desire; 16. Hatred.
Seventeen: diligence. Eighteen: heaviness. Nineteen: fluidity. Twenty: moisture. Twenty-one: formations. Twenty-two: phenomena.
Twenty-three: non-phenomena. Twenty-four: sound. Karma has five types: first, grasping.

Second, abandonment; third, contraction; fourth, extension; fifth, motion. Great Existence (*mahāsattā*) is one. Substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and activity-ness (*karmatva*) are three, because they share the same existence.
Apart from substantiality, quality, and activity, there exists a separate dharma as their essence. Because of this Great Existence, substantiality and the others exist.

Likewise, commonality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) are also one: for example, earth has the sense of commonality in relation to earth, and the sense of particularity in relation to water and so forth.

The identity and difference of the earth element: this is earth and not water; the same applies to water and the other elements. Furthermore, there exists a distinct substantial entity apart from [the categories of] substance and so forth.
Regarding the "phrase of conjunction" (*saṃyoga-pada*): it refers to a collection of dharmas.

By means of the phrase of conjunction, just as a bird flying through the sky suddenly reaches a tree branch and stays there without departing, it is by virtue of the phrase of conjunction that stability is produced. These six are what belong to the self (*ātmiya*).
Having received full ordination, until one attains liberation, one experiences the former six [categories]. If one attains liberation, one becomes separated from these six, which is termed *nirvāṇa*.

Now, this treatise cites those six categories of meaning; they maintain that these six categories all possess substantial entities (*dravya*) and are apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, regarding that which you cling to as earth, water, fire, and wind (up to) "because they are admitted to be perceived by the sense organs of form," it is like earth, water, fire, and wind.

That is to say, since they have already conceded that all categories (*padārtha*) are unobstructed, then within the category of substantiality, earth, water, fire, and wind—
It should not be non-obstructive; yet, because it was originally obstructive, to insist that it is non-existent is called "should-be-non-existent.

[The same applies to] solidity and so forth. Solidity and the others should also be like earth and the other [elements]. Originally, solidity and the others are without obstruction; if they were like earth and the others, they would consequently become obstructed.

Therefore, it is said that they "should not be unobstructed. Since they have become obstructed, they are subsumed under the category of *guṇa* (quality) as objects of contact for the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), just like earth, water, fire, and wind.
Furthermore, one may formulate the following formal argument (*prayoga*): Solidity and the others are the subject (*dharmin*); they should not be unobstructed.

Resistance (*pratighāta*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because it is subsumed under the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) and is that which is touched by the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

The concordant example (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Like earth, water, fire, and wind. Its fallacy lies further in the fact that that which is non-resistant cannot be established as resistant. Regarding the passage "earth, water, fire...
and below, it refutes the claim that hardness and so forth possess the same nature as earth and so forth. The *Daśapadārthī-śāstra* states: "Thus, there are nine real entities (*dravya*)."

How many are with form (*rūpin*) and how many are without form (*arūpin*)? Three are with form, namely earth, water, and fire. Six are without form, namely wind, space, time, direction, self, and mind.

Since you maintain that it possesses resistance, and since resistance is like coarse earth, when analyzed it is no longer coarse; how, then, can there be the property of permanence?

Therefore, one establishes the formal argument (*prayoga*) as follows: "Because all [entities] possess resistance" is the reason (*hetu*); "like coarse earth and so forth" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); and "it must be impermanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Following the various statements below, we next refute the existence of obstructive matter. Regarding that which is apprehended by the material sense organs: among the various entities such as light and shadow, all visible forms are seen by the eye precisely because they are non-obstructive.
If one were to grant that the eye apprehends them while maintaining that they are obstructive, they would have to be like earth and other such elements.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that what they grasp as "existence" must be the "Great Existence-nature" (mahāsattā), and that it should have no distinct self-nature apart from substance and so forth.

As for the phrase "because it is admitted not to be non-existent," this means that the opponent themselves admits that the existence-nature is not non-existent, just like substance, quality, and so on.

This is an example of a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). The intention is as follows: if it is granted that "existence" (*sattā*) is not non-existent, then it should follow that the category of substance (*dravya-pada*) possesses characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the category of quality (*guṇa-pada*) possesses existence (*sattā*), and the category of activity (*karma-pada*) possesses function (*kāritra*).
Only then could one maintain that the category of existence (*sattā-pada*) is substantially real. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: Thesis (*pakṣa*):

Existence (*sattā*), as the subject (*dharmin*), must have no distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) apart from substance and the other categories. Reason (*hetu*): Because it is granted that it is not non-existent.

Therefore, the concordant example is like substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth. If they insist that existence-nature (*sattā*) must certainly exist apart from substance, quality, and action, [the author] refutes this further, saying:

"If it were separate from substance and the rest, it would not be existence-nature. If you insist that it is distinct from substance and the rest, then it would be like an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the other four types of non-existence:

namely, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), and total non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). This refers to prior non-existence... [text continues].

Non-existence through cessation; non-existence through mutual exclusion; non-existence through non-encounter. The formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: "Existence (*sattā*) is the subject (*dharmin*). It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that if it were separate from substance (*dravya*) and so forth, it would not be existence.
The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it is admitted to be distinct from substance and so forth. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and the like.

As for the phrase "as with the lower [categories]," this uses the nature of existence itself as an analogy to refute the position that existence exists as something external and separate from substance and the other categories.
If that which exists is not non-existent, then one must admit the existence of "existence-nature" (sattā). However, apart from existing things themselves, there is no separate existence-nature;
it is simply the nature of existence inherent in those things. How then could there be a separate existence-nature apart from real entities and so forth? If it were separated from them...
Furthermore, one uses the non-existence of phenomena (*dharma*) as an analogy to refute the intrinsic nature of existence (*bhāva-svabhāva*). This means:

if you admit that there is a distinct intrinsic nature of existence apart from phenomena, then there should likewise be a distinct intrinsic nature of non-existence apart from phenomena. Since phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, the internal and external are utterly severed;

how then could there be a non-existence apart from phenomena? Moreover, since that [non-existence] is not so, how could this [existence] be so? This establishes the aforementioned non-existence of phenomena.
Since this is not the case, what "existence-nature" (sattva) could there be apart from these existent phenomena?
Therefore, the following section concludes that the category of "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) is a false conceptualization and lacks reality.

Furthermore, regarding their adherence to the nature of substance, quality, and action (up to the point of "because..."), the nature of generality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is merely a conventional designation.

They maintain that the nature of generality and particularity exists as a distinct real entity apart from substance, quality, and action, capable of making the collection of various phenomena such as substances identical and making each individual phenomenon distinct.
Moreover, that which they adhere to as the nature of substance, quality, and action is [identical to] the nature of generality and particularity.
Furthermore, as for the claim that it is logically impossible for "sameness" and "difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) to exist apart from substance, quality, and action:

this is because it would follow that these [categories of] sameness and difference are likewise not of the nature of substance, quality, or action, simply because they are distinct from substance and so forth—just like qualities and actions themselves.
That is to say, one cannot assert that this nature of sameness and difference is anything other than what was previously maintained regarding substance and the rest.
The nature of *mahābhūta* (great elements) is admitted to be distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth, just as qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karman*) are distinct from substance.

Furthermore, it would follow that substances and so forth are not subsumed under the category of "substance" and so on; this clarifies that such a distinction is logically improper. One should state that the three—substance, quality, and activity—manifest the nature of generality and particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Thus, the generality and particularity of what is not substance and so forth should be subsumed within substance and so forth, and substance and so forth should likewise be subsumed within generality and particularity.

They are distinct, because they possess the nature of being distinct from substance (*dravya*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as in the case of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and substances (*dravya*)," this means that if the three—substance, quality, and action—are distinct from the nature of substance and so forth, then, just as qualities and actions each possess their own separate essence before one can speak of their identity or difference, they are distinct from substance and the like.
The examples below, such as earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth, clarify this: their natures are solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.

The substance consists of earth, water, fire, and air. If one knows that outside of solidity and so forth there is no earth and so forth, and outside of earth and so forth there is no solidity and so forth, then by this analogy it should be understood that outside of substance and so forth there is no generality-and-particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), and outside of generality-and-particularity there is no substance and so forth.

As stated below regarding "substance" (*dravya*): one then combines the meaning of "substance" and so forth with "generality-and-particularity," and the meaning of "earth" and so forth with "solidity" and so forth; this applies equally to "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and the rest.
This refers to the nature of substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*). The "nature of substance and so forth" refers to the nature of identity and difference (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Furthermore, the term "substance and so forth" also refers to substance, quality, and action. The first phrase restates and refutes the claim that there is no nature of identity and difference apart from substance, quality, and action—just as there is no nature of solidity and so forth apart from earth and the other elements.
The second phrase restates that there is no [nature of identity and difference] apart from substance, quality, and action.

Regarding substance, quality, and action: just as there is no separate essence of earth and so forth external to qualities such as solidity, if one were to depart from this [principle], then by means of the analogy of "sameness" (sāmānya) and "difference" (viśeṣa), one would refute the existence of sameness and difference external to substance and the rest.
What is called "non-substance" and so forth is precisely the nature of sameness and difference.

If there were a nature of sameness-and-difference (sāmānya-viśeṣa) apart from substance and so forth, then there would have to be another nature of sameness-and-difference existing outside of that [first] sameness-and-difference.

Since that is not the case, how could this be so? To establish the above point: since there is no sameness-and-difference apart from sameness-and-difference itself, how could there be a sameness-and-difference apart from substance, quality, and action?
Therefore, the following section on sameness-and-difference concludes that it is a false conceptual construction (parikalpita).
Furthermore, the category of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) as maintained by them—up to the point reached by the preceding reasoning—is also not substantially existent.
Next, the category of conjunction is restated and refuted. They maintain that it is through conjunction that all phenomena (*dharma*) are able to aggregate;
yet the nature of conjunction exists as a distinct entity, not subsumed under the phenomena themselves. Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] establishes an inference.

This is refuted by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Taking the "referent of a composite expression" as the subject (*dharmin*) of the thesis, it is established that it is certainly not substantially real.

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is not subsumed under [the categories of] 'substantially real' and so forth. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like that which is absolutely non-existent (*atyantābhāva*).

That is to say, if something is not subsumed under [the categories of] "substantially real" and so forth, it is like that which is absolutely non-existent; for apart from all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is no such thing as a "composite referent. Why? Because [it would be devoid of any basis].

They maintain that the "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) exists as a distinct substantial entity. They illustrate this with the following examples: the category of substance (*dravya-pada*) possesses an essence;

the category of quality (*guṇa-pada*) possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and the category of action (*karma-pada*) possesses a function (*vṛtti*). Thus, they claim these three categories can be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

However, when analyzed through reasoning, the category of substance is subject to disintegration, the category of quality is non-obstructive, and the category of action is impermanent; none of them exist substantially. Since the meaning of the category of conjunction...
It is separate from all dharmas; it is not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and its unreality can be known.
How much more so for that which they themselves admit—the referent of the term "combination" (*saṃyoga*)—which is not apprehended by direct perception and yet is claimed to be truly existent?

Even if one were to maintain that this combination, like the aforementioned "reality" (*satya*) and so forth, is subsumed under direct perception, since we have previously demonstrated through reasoning that direct perception is not ultimately real, this [combination] must likewise be so. △ Fourth, the specific refutation of the three propositions.
[The previous section] concludes. The following five points refute the [distinction between] subject and object.

However, those "realities" (*tattva*) and so forth are not objects that exist independently of consciousness; they too are merely conceptual constructs (*prajñapti*) established according to conventional sentiment.

Now, regarding the phrase "those realities" and so forth: this collectively refers to the six categories of meaning as the objective conditions (*ālambana*). It does not mean that there are realities existing apart from consciousness that serve as objects.

Regarding those things obtained through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of self-nature: this refers to the six categories, such as "substance" (*dravya*), which are the objects of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*). [The opponent argues:

"These are not obtained through direct perception, because they are admitted to be objects of cognition, like a tortoise’s hair. This means that those six categories are admitted solely as objects known through false conceptualization;
therefore, the tortoise’s hair is used as an analogy. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: "The six categories, substance and so forth..."
It is asserted that there are phenomena which are not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) existing apart from consciousness.

The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they are admitted to be objects of knowledge. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like a tortoise’s hair and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "cognition of a real entity":

this refers to the cognition of the category-meaning (*padārtha*) of a real entity. It is not subsumed under the cognition of a direct perception of the intrinsic nature of a real category-meaning existing apart from consciousness; that is to say, the object...
If the real referent (*vastu-pada*) is not an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the cognizing mind is likewise not subsumed under direct perceptual cognition.

Because it arises from a conceptual synthesis, like the knowledge of solidity and so forth—meaning that the cognizing wisdom and the meaning of the real referent arise through a conceptual synthesis, just as the knowledge of solidity and other qualities arise together from mental construction—and are not attained through direct perception. Thus it is established.

The *Pramāṇa* states: "The cognition that takes as its object [an entity] is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it is not subsumed under a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that realizes a real entity existing apart from consciousness.
The reason (*hetu*) is: 'because it arises through conceptual synthesis. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is, for instance, the cognition of virtues and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "explained at length up to... this abbreviates the cognitions of the four phrases within the section on virtues; the inferential reasoning (*anumāna*) is the same as before, and thus the wording is not repeated here at length. As for "taking as an object" (*ālambana*)...
"Conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), the following [term] refers to the cognition of conjunction. This too is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it arises from a conceptual synthesis.
Likewise, the cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is also not direct perception, because it takes the cognition of reality as its object, just like the cognition of virtue (*guṇajñāna*).

Therefore, regarding the Vaiśeṣika [system], the following summarizes how all these propositions are false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*). △ Five: The refutation of the subject and object is complete. This concludes the two Vaiśeṣika sixfold propositions.
The section on "Differences" concludes. The three lower heavens are able to produce the notion that things are permanent; in total there are eight such types.
There are those who maintain that there is a single Mahādeva (the Great Sovereign God) [who produces all phenomena]; this is refuted in the same manner as the following.
The ash-smearing heretics (Ājīvikas) hold such views; both the *Kaisheng* and the *Qingliang* treatises list them as the third school. They maintain that the deity possesses four attributes:
first, its essence is real; second, it is all-pervasive; third, it is eternal; and fourth, it is capable of producing all phenomena. Furthermore, they maintain that the deity has three bodies.
First is the Dharma-body, which is able to give rise to the myriad things. Second is the Enjoyment-body, which resides in the heavens of form.

Third is the Transformation-body, which teaches and transforms sentient beings by assuming various forms according to the six paths. The opponent clings to these [three bodies]. The Master of the Treatise refutes them collectively, demonstrating through inquiry and explanation that they are irrational.
If a dharma that is capable of giving rise [to something] must necessarily be impermanent, then the dharma capable of giving rise possesses functional activity; [a permanent dharma] cannot.

Regarding what is produced: by what adherence can it be brought forth? If one grants that it can be produced, it certainly would not accord with the principle of permanence. [The passage] "Those which are not inferior," etc., successively restates and refutes [the opponent's position].

Since phenomena (*dharma*) are impermanent, there is no logical possibility for them to be omnipresent; thus, the meaning of reality is entirely absent. [The passage] "Since its essence is... restates the opponent’s thesis and presents a refutation.
Because they adhere to the notion that the essence of the deity (*deva*) is permanent, it is difficult to maintain that [the effect] is produced at all times. Due to this...
Regarding their claim that the divine essence (*devatātman*) is omnipresent and thus difficult to produce in all places, and that it can only arise by depending on desire or conditions:
"desire" refers to longing, which is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*); "conditions" refers to various causal factors, which also include material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*).

If one asserts that the mind arises depending on matter, this contradicts the theory of a single cause, for they hold that the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) alone is the cause. Alternatively, [it may refer to] desire...

[The opponent] replies: "Furthermore, even if one grants that the conditions for transformation do not require waiting, if you claim that causes and conditions arise instantaneously without anything upon which they depend, then the cause would be eternal and the fruit should be constantly produced.
If these were to fill the world, what space would there be to contain them? [The author] refutes this further below.
This section summarizes the seven types of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*). Each of them postulates a permanent, substantially existent power that gives rise to all phenomena;
all such views are refuted by means of the same reasoning used against the *ābhyanga* (ash-smearing) sect. 1. **Brahmā**:

This refers to the Vedic scholars (*vedavādin*), here called the "Scholars of the *Vidyā*" (or *Ming-lun-shi*). According to the *Kaisheng* and *Qingliang* commentaries, this is the fourth [type]. Bodhisattva Āryadeva refutes the minor non-Buddhist...
The *Nirvāṇa-samaya-śāstra* states: They reckon that from the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa a great lotus flower arises.
Upon this flower is the progenitor Brahmā; they claim that Brahmā is the ancestor of all things.
That Brahmā creates all sentient and insentient beings. From the mouth of Brahmā are born the Brāhmaṇas (the Pure Practitioners); from his two arms are born the Kṣatriyas.

The *kṣatriya* (royal caste) is produced from the waist; the *vaiśya* (merchant caste) is produced from the two thighs; the *śūdra* (agriculturalist caste) is produced from the two feet. Regarding the "two times":

this refers to the immediate dispersal of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The opening of the ignorant is the fifth [time], and the cooling [of afflictions] is the sixth. They maintain that all phenomena arise from time;
that is to say, they observe that things such as grasses and trees produce flowers at certain times and bear fruit at certain times. Thus, [they claim] time exists.
When it expands, it rolls up; sometimes it flourishes, sometimes it withers. Although time is subtle and invisible, by observing flowers, fruits, and so forth, one knows that time exists.
Therefore, one calculates that time is eternal and unitary, the cause of all things, and the cause of nirvana.
Regarding the "Three Directions": this refers to the Fang (Direction) school of masters. They posit Fang as the sixth, and Qingliang as the seventh.
According to their reckoning, when a person is born, they are born from the Directions; when they die, they return to the Directions. Therefore, the Directions are eternal and singular.
This is the cause of all phenomena; this is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the four "Original Limits" (*pūrvakoṭi*):
Āṭanāyika is the seventh [teacher] for beginners, while Qingliang is the fifth. "Original Limit" refers to the very beginning of the past;
it is the calculation that at the very outset of the world there was only a great expanse of water, and then a Great Āṭanāyika was born, shaped like a chicken's egg.

It is golden in color. It is subsequently divided into two parts: the upper becomes heaven, and the lower becomes earth. Within this, a Great Brahmā is born, who is capable of creating all things animate and inanimate.
Therefore, heaven is the cause of all phenomena. Fifth, regarding "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*): this refers to the proponents of the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*).
Jizang classifies them as the eighth [school], while Chengguan classifies them as the eleventh. They reckon that all phenomena...
"Things arise spontaneously and cease spontaneously, without cause and without condition. Therefore, this spontaneity is the cause of all phenomena and the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

This view maintains that there is no cause for either purity or defilement in anything; it is like the natural sharpness of a thorn, or the black color of a crow which is not a result of dyeing, or the white color of a crane which is naturally so.
6. Regarding "Empty Space": This refers to the teacher Kaulūta (or Kaulika), who opened the way for the *Kṣapaṇaka* (the Mundane Purifiers).
The "Cool" (Śīta) school constitutes the ninth. They maintain that space (*ākāśa*) is the cause of all things;
it is a distinct entity, real, eternal, and unitary, serving as the cause of all things. From space arises wind; from wind arises fire; and from fire arises heat.
Heat produces water; water produces ice; ice becomes solid earth; from earth grow the five grains; the five grains produce life; when life perishes, it returns to emptiness.
Therefore, empty space can act as the cause of the myriad things; it is the cause of *nirvāṇa*. 7.

As for "I," this refers to the proponents of the theory of past actions (*pūrvakṛtavādin*). They calculate that all sentient beings receiving the retribution of suffering and pleasure all derive from their past days.

This is due to the causal conditions of one's original karma (*pūrvakarma*). Therefore, if there are those who maintain the precepts and exert diligence, undergoing physical and mental suffering, they are able to destroy their original karma.
Once the original karma is exhausted, all sufferings are extinguished. When all sufferings are extinguished, one immediately attains *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, past actions serve as the cause for everything. [The section on] "Opening the Ignorant" was the tenth; Qingliang did not record it, but I have now cited it according to our own school.
This collectively subsumes other schools, all of which maintain the doctrine that [the creator] is capable of producing all phenomena; therefore, they are established as a single section.
The aforementioned seven types of non-Buddhist tenets are all refuted in the same manner as the critique of Maheśvara.
The section on the four views that sound can express and signify permanence concludes above. Below, there are two types of views asserting that sound is permanent.

There are others who hold a biased attachment to the claim that the sounds of the *Veda* (the *Śruti*) are eternal. [This extends to] the claim that the essence of sound is like that of jars, garments, and so forth, because it depends upon various conditions.
The "sounds of the *Veda*" (*vidyā-śabda*) are precisely the sounds of speech; based on sound, one utters words to express and define all phenomena.

Because these do not change across ages and can serve as a valid authority (*pramāṇa*), they are reckoned as eternal. This was listed as the eleventh [view] by Kaīmōng. Qingliang [Huayan Jingying] did not [accept this].

[Record: All sounds refer to the sounds of bells, drums, and the like. "Waiting for conditions" means, for example, that a bell or drum awaits being struck, or that birds and beasts await being called.

"Expressing meaning" means, for example, that ringing a bell gathers the assembly, striking a drum signals entry into the hall, the chirping of birds determines good or bad fortune, and the sound of the wind indicates fair or rainy weather.
Although they depend on conditions, sound is of a single essence; therefore, it is reckoned as permanent. [Opening:]
It was listed as the twelfth [position] by Mōng (Mingquan), but Qingliang did not record it. The two schools mentioned above share the same name, "Sāṃkhya" (Sound-Theory);

therefore, they are established collectively as one section. Below that, the Master [Xuanzang] refutes both theories of the permanence of sound in general, examining and explaining their irrationality.

Furthermore, in the section "Clarifying the Sound of Treatises," he specifically refutes the former theory: if sound is permanent, there can be no "action performed," nor can there be an "agent. If there is no agent...

That which is neither [of the two extremes] is precisely the meaning of permanence; therefore, a formal inference (*prayoga*) is established to refute it. Taking "the sound of the treatise" as the subject (*dharmin*), the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it must not be eternal.
The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is admitted to be expressive. The similar example (*sapakṣa*) is like all other sounds;

that is to say, whatever possesses the nature of being both the agent and the object of expression must necessarily be non-eternal. Furthermore, since other sounds depend upon conditions, they likewise possess the characteristic of non-eternality. Below the section on "other sounds," this is refuted.
The second position: They maintain that the substance of sound is eternal and is manifested in dependence upon conditions. To refute this, he establishes the following inference (*anumāna*):
"Sound as a subject (*dharmin*) must also be non-eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*). "Because it depends on various conditions" is the reason (*hetu*).

"Like jars, garments, and so forth" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). [This concludes] the fourth section: the refutation of the position that sound, as a signifier, is eternal. Below follows the fifth [section]: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
They are able to give rise to the notion of permanence.
There are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who cling to earth, water, fire, and wind [claiming they are permanent]; how can it be said that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal?
These are the Lokāyata masters; here they are called the "Worldly Non-Buddhists" (*Lokāyatika*). In the *Kaifeng* [catalogue], they are listed as the tenth.
Third: Śīta (Coolness) is the eighth. They reckon that all phenomena, such as form and mind, have the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the four great elements as their cause.
Among these four great elements, that which is most refined and intelligent, capable of cognitive reflection (*ālambana*), is the mental phenomenon (*citta-dharma*).
It is like the element of fire: although all are fire, the lamp emits light while others do not.

Therefore, among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is that which can take objects as its cognitive focus; this is certainly without error. "The measure of the cause" refers to the atom (*paramāṇu*).
"Impermanence" refers to the coarse effect. That is to say, arising from the atom, it returns to the measure of the cause; hence it is so stated.
"It truly exists. This is also irrational; below, the Master of the Treatise refutes it in general. He investigates and demonstrates its irrationality. The refutation consists of two parts:

first, the refutation of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) that produce [gross matter]; second, the refutation of the gross matter (*sthūlarūpa*) produced [by them]. Under the heading "The grasped [object]," he first refutes the atoms.

this means that the effect is equal in magnitude to its cause and is naturally not coarse. It would necessarily be impossible for the material sense organs, such as the eye, to perceive it.
