If it is argued that [the object] becomes coarse because many parts conjoin—[a claim that extends] from "it is merely a false conceptualization following worldly sentiment" up to this point—where you previously granted that many causes had accumulated but were not yet conjoined, and now maintain that they become coarse through the conjunction of those many causes; we refute this by saying:

Since the many causes themselves are not subtle, they are already sufficient to constitute the coarse, resistant matter of the sense-faculties and their objects. What need is there for your insistence on a "productive cause" (*janaka-hetu*)?
It would mostly result in unreality; this is necessarily so by principle. Since the preceding cause is reckoned as permanent while the subsequent effect is unreal, they are mutually contradictory.

Furthermore, in the section on "the effect," the author restates and refutes the doctrine of distinct causes and effects: if the cause possesses material obstruction, the effect must likewise possess material obstruction.

As with two atoms, how could they be combined? If it is argued that [the cause and effect] mutually receive one another—whereby the effect receives the cause as sand receives water, and the cause enters the effect as medicine enters copper—this addresses the previous objection that cause and effect are distinct entities.
Therefore, it is refuted by asking: "Who allows that the substance of sand or copper receives water or medicine? That is to say, the substance of the sand...

It is complete and sealed with molten copper; how could water or medicinal substances enter it? As for the claim that it must undergo transformation through separation, this means the preceding cause cannot accommodate the effect.
Furthermore, to calculate that the effect transforms by separating from the cause contradicts the attachment to [the atom] being unitary and permanent.

If it does not exceed the measure of its cause, it is one; to separate would contradict this. If the essence of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) were real and permanent, then to undergo transformation would contradict this.

Furthermore, [the argument] is coarse and inferior, as it refutes the adherence to a single substantial entity. Regarding "coarse material effects," this refers to all effects. "Obtaining one part" means perceiving a single object.
That is to say, if the substance were one, then when perceiving one object, other objects should also be perceived.

Why? Because both [the perceived and the unperceived] would be identical to that same one. To allow that one perceives everything is not permitted; otherwise, it would contradict the principle that the substance of the effect is one. [If you] admit...

By depending on one, one attains all. Furthermore, this contradicts the fact that "this" and "that" are distinct entities. Therefore, in the following section, the refutation of false conceptualizations is concluded.
"Advancing and retreating" refers to the aforementioned granting and non-granting [of the premise]. This concludes the fourth refutation regarding the synthesis of the majority.

△ Fifth, the refutation of the notion that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) can produce permanence is concluded. Below, the sixth section generally enumerates the pervasive attachments to the conceptualization of identity, difference, and so forth.

However, although the categories of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are numerous—up to ninety-five types, which were previously condensed into eleven schools or thirteen schools—they are now further condensed into four types.
If these are condensed once more, they consist of two causal lineages: those who assert existence and those who assert non-existence. As the *Śata-śāstra* states: "First..."

All worldly categories and meanings are expressed by names and conventions and are known by the mind and wisdom; yet, due to differing emotional attachments, there are briefly four types. These are: existence, non-existence, both, and neither.
One should understand that these correspond, respectively, to the four false attachments: namely, oneness, non-oneness, accepting both, and accepting neither.

Regarding the calculation of "oneness," this refers to the view that the effect exists within the cause. As for the category of "existence": [The text continues with further definitions of the remaining categories.]

That is to say, one first posits a single dharma. As for those who maintain that all dharmas other than this single dharma are identical in essence—that is, that the substance of this single dharma and all dharmas is definitively one—it refers to the claim that this single dharma and all dharmas are necessarily of one and the same substance.

This is like the Sāṃkhya school, which holds that the *pradhāna* (the primal nature), endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*), transforms into the twenty-three principles; thus, from the beginning, it is simply the one *pradhāna*.
Regarding the "entity" (*tattva*), this too is a calculation of oneness. The Master of the Treatise refutes that position in its entirety; he challenges and explains why it is irrational. He states:
"Let it not be that all phenomena are identical to the nature of existence. That is to say: do not claim that all phenomena are precisely the one existent entity you maintain.

If you assert that all phenomena constitute a single essence, (1) it contradicts your own tenet, and (2) it contradicts common worldly understanding. Furthermore, as for the section below, he restates [the opponent's position].
The counter-argument is difficult to refute. "Color, etc. refers to the remaining [objects] such as sound, smell, taste, and touch. "Blue, yellow, etc.
refers to the remaining [qualities] such as clarity and turbidity, pleasant and unpleasant, sweet and bitter, cold and warm.

That is to say, if one further argues that color is one with blue, and so on up to touch being one with cold, then since the five sense objects are distinct, this refutes the objection regarding their difference from worldly convention. To refute [this], it says: "Then..."
"In your view, the dharma of form has no blue, yellow, red, or white; the object of sound has no clarity or turbidity, nor high or low pitch;

and even the object of touch has no cold, warmth, roughness, or smoothness. If this were so, it would contradict worldly convention, for in the world, various forms such as blue and so forth are each distinct.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the *Śataśāstra*) states: "The Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists maintain that there exists a universal nature (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)."
If [a thing] were identical with all phenomena, it would then be a category of existence (*astitva-pada*). This attachment is not true. Why is this?
If colors such as blue were one with the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*), they should be identical in essence, just like the nature of form.

If sounds such as the five kinds of music were one with the nature of sound, they should be identical in essence, just like the nature of sound. Fragrance, taste, touch, and so forth should be understood accordingly. The eye...
If the various faculties (*indriya*) were one with the nature of the faculties (*indriyatva*), they should be like that nature; their essence would all be identical.

Consequently, each individual faculty should perceive all objects, and each individual object should correspond to all faculties. Furthermore, if all phenomena (*dharma*) were one with the nature of existence (*astitva*), they should be like that nature;
their essence would all be identical. Moreover, pleasure, pain, delusion, volition (*cetanā*), and the self (*ātman*) would likewise [be one with] existence...
Their nature is one; they should possess a nature as such, and their essence is entirely identical. Consequently, the distinctions established by your own school are all unestablished.
Therefore, that which you cling to is certainly not true.

Second, the adherence to the existence of a substratum (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*), such as "existence" (*sattā*), [leads to the conclusion that] it should not be an object of the eye and other senses, just like sound and so forth.

Second, the calculation of difference refers to the view that the effect does not exist within the cause (*asatkāryavāda*). Regarding the substratum and its properties such as existence, they are as previously described;

however, their essence is definitely distinct, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas. For they maintain that the category of substance (*dravya-pada*) constitutes the essence, serving as the locus for qualities (*guṇa*) and activities (*karma*), whereas qualities and...
It must be distinct from substance (*dravya*) and the others, which constitute its essence and serve as the basis for the category of "great existence" (*mahāsattā*).

Yet, great existence must be distinct from substance and the others; the same applies to generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, that which is distinct from existence must belong to the category of non-existence (*asat*).

Therefore, the subsequent refutations employ the category of non-existence as the primary challenge. The opponent’s adherence to these [categories] will be refuted in general below; their attempts at interrogation and explanation are irrational and must not be accepted.

Regarding the statement that "all phenomena lack the nature of existence": this means one should not say that all phenomena exist; for there is no essence to the "existent phenomenon" (bhāva) as you conceive it.

If a phenomenon and the essence of an existent phenomenon were definitively distinct, then, like a non-existent cessation (nirodha), it would contradict the principle that its own essence is not non-existent according to the six categories, and it would also contradict what is perceived by the world as existing things.
Furthermore, if you further argue that [the essence] exists upon the substance of form (*rūpa*), such as blue...
Yellow, red, and white are established as having distinct physical natures; therefore, it is said that they are "not form," etc. The word "etc. includes the other four sense-objects (*viṣaya*).

This also demonstrates that the five sense-objects exist substantially, thereby refuting the objection that [the claim] contradicts worldly consensus regarding the existence of things. Thus, he further refutes [that position], saying:

Since it is not the nature of form (*rūpa-dharmatā*), it should—like sound and other such phenomena—not be an object of the eye and other sense faculties. The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Commentary on the *Śataśāstra*) states:
"The Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists claim that the category of 'existence' (*sattā*) is distinct from its dharmas; this should fall under the category of 'non-existence.
Yet even this is not true. Why? If blue and other forms were different from the nature of form, they would—like sound and so forth—not be within the range of the eye."

The sounds of the five kinds of music and so forth would differ from the nature of sound itself; consequently, like form and other [sensory objects], they would not be the objects of the ear and other faculties.
Furthermore, if all phenomena lacked an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their essence would be fundamentally non-existent, like a rabbit’s horn.

This would mean that you are identical to those who propound emptiness and selflessness, or to the heterodox teachers of other paths. Is it not the case that an intrinsic nature is not simply the phenomena themselves? [Phenomena...]
If it is not existent, yet there is existence, then since the substratum (āśraya) does not exist, how could the dependent (āśrita) exist?

Furthermore, upon an intrinsic nature (svabhāva), there is no distinct intrinsic nature; thus, it should not be called "existent. As for all other cognitions and phenomena, although they possess an intrinsic nature, because that intrinsic nature is not [ultimately] existent, their essence should be non-existent.
In this way, all established categories and meanings fail to be established, and thus they become identical [to non-existence].
Because they negate [reality], these non-Buddhist outsiders hold false views; therefore, what they grasp is certainly not true.

Third, their attachment to the existence of dharmas and their possession of a nature such as "existence" (sattva), up to [their claim that] these constitute a real principle, is definitively unestablished.
Regarding the third thesis—that cause and effect are both identical and different—this means that the effect exists within the cause and yet does not exist within it.

The following section of the treatise refutes this position as a whole; the Master demonstrates that such a claim is irrational. If one holds to identity or difference, one incurs the same faults as the two previous positions.

The two phenomena of identity and difference are mutually contradictory in their characteristics; therefore, their substance must be distinct. If one insists that they share the same substance, then both [characteristics] would fail to be established.
Why is this? Identity and difference are not one, and identity is not difference. Therefore, it cannot be said that all phenomena are [identical].

All are of one and the same substance. Or rather, it should be understood that we admit they are conventional and not real; thus, speaking of them as "one" or "different" is merely a matter of provisional designation (*prajñapti*).
If, regarding a single phenomenon, one provisionally designates it as "one" and also provisionally designates it as "different," there is fundamentally no fault or difficulty.

However, to grasp these as being real is logically untenable. The *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra* states: "The Nirgrantha heretics maintain that there is a 'universal nature' (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*)..."
Those dharmas are both identical and different; this must fall under the category of "both existent and non-existent. Yet even this is not true. Why?
If the nature of existence were identical with form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it would share the same fault as the Sāṃkhya school.

If it were different from form and so forth, it would incur the same error as the Vaiśeṣika school. Since identity and difference are two mutually exclusive characteristics, to claim that their essence is the same is logically untenable.
It is established that "one" should not be identical to "many," for it would then be like "different"; and "different" should not be different from "one," for it would then be like "one.

Since neither "one" nor "different" can be established, how can "existence" or "non-existence" be established? To claim that the characteristics of "one" and "different" are distinct while asserting their substance is the same is a contradiction.
Then all phenomena (*dharma*) would necessarily be without distinction. Since distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) do not exist, how could a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) exist?

The two characteristics of unity and difference are established through mutual dependence (*apekṣā*). If you claim that a single phenomenon is called "one" or "different" based on differing points of reference, then both "one" and "different" would not be real.
Alternatively, they would obstruct one another as mere designations; for a single phenomenon to possess two characteristics is mutually contradictory. Both...
To claim that this is true would necessarily be unreasonable; therefore, what they grasp must certainly not be true.
Regarding the four attachments to the existence of phenomena and their nature as "existent" and so forth, let no wise person mistakenly grant them assent.
Regarding the fourth point—that cause and effect are neither identical nor different—this means that within the cause, the effect is neither existent nor non-existent.

The Master refutes their position as a whole below, demonstrating through inquiry and explanation that it is irrational: if they are not identical, they must be different; if they are not different, they must be identical.

Thus, being both identical and different, the statement that they are "neither identical nor different" serves either to negate or to affirm. [The text] asks for the definitive meaning of what is negated and what is affirmed. If only...

"Affirmation" (*vidhi*) means the sense of manifestation. That is to say, it does not manifest the many as one, nor does it manifest the one as many. Since it is a negation of both, how can it be called "affirmation"?
If it were merely a negation (*pratiṣedha*), then negation has the sense of cessation; it would simply be a cessation. Why then would you insist that it is real?
If you maintain that it is both affirmation and negation, then affirmation cannot admit negation, and negation likewise is not affirmation; therefore, they are mutually exclusive.
It is contradictory. Negation is not negation, and affirmation is not affirmation; is this not mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)?

Furthermore, [the passage] "nor inferior" generally rebukes the faults of contradicting worldly convention and one's own school. Therefore, [the passage] "hence" concludes by warning later worthies not to give rise to superficial faith.
The *Vyākhyāyukti* on the *Śataśāstra* states: "The heterodox Ājīvikas maintain that there is a 'nature' (*svabhāva*) which is neither identical to nor different from those phenomena. When...
Regarding the position that it is neither existent nor non-existent, this too is not true. Why is this so?

If the nature of existence and so forth were not identical with the phenomenon (*dharma*), it would share the same fault as the Vaiśeṣika school; if it were not different from the phenomenon, it would be the same as the Mahat of the Sāṃkhya school.

Furthermore, the characteristics of identity and difference are commonly known to exist in the world, yet you alone deny them, thereby incurring the fault of contradicting worldly consensus. Moreover, what you have stated is not consistent.

This is a different statement. Is it merely a term of negation (*paryudāsa*), or does it partially possess affirmation (*vidhi*)? If it partially possesses affirmation, it should not be a "double negation" (*ubhayapratiṣedha*).
If it is merely a negation, there would be nothing to which one clings. To have both negation and affirmation is logically contradictory;

to have neither negation nor affirmation renders the statement mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). You maintain that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are not empty, yet you say that the double negation is intended merely for...
To avoid this error, this "neither-nor" statement should likewise not be discussed, for it contradicts the nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) of your own tenets.

If the nature of all phenomena is such that each is individually "neither," then even this statement of "neither-nor" should not be uttered; for the very act of raising speech necessarily possesses the nature of being "neither-nor.
Thus, you and your followers should remain perpetually tongue-tied, as the mere utterance of words would destroy your own doctrine.
Even silence does not establish the thesis, for it is likewise non-existent; thus, both speech and silence fail. How bitter this is!
What wise person would not feel compassion? Therefore, that which they cling to is certainly not true.

Thus, these four kinds of worldly outsiders, with their heterodox arguments and evil views, disturb and destroy their minds, vainly and falsely seeking the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.

All of these are inconsistent with reason; they are contentious and confused, giving rise to four kinds of denial regarding all phenomena: namely, [denying] existence, denying non-existence, affirming both, and affirming neither.
These involve superimposition, repudiation, contradiction, and frivolous proliferation. Therefore, what is grasped by worldly people is not real.
This concludes the sixth section, the general summary of the four types of universal attachments. This also concludes the preceding section on the individual inquiry into non-Buddhists.
Second, the specific inquiry into the clinging to the reality of other vehicles’ dharmas is divided into two parts. First, the question and answer that introduce the topic:
Because the objects clung to by other vehicles as being substantially existent apart from consciousness (up to) and the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) do not exist according to reason.
The author of the treatise poses a hypothetical question to provoke the tenets held by other vehicles. In the response, he refutes their irrationality as a whole.
For the sake of beginners, it is said that these other vehicles accept only seventy-five dharmas out of the one hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna:
namely, eleven material (rūpa) dharmas, fourteen non-associated (viprayukta) dharmas, three unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas, and forty-six mental concomitants (caitta).

Mental factors (citta-dharma) total seventy-five in all. Therefore, in the following refutation, only the enumerated number of those [factors] categorized as dissociated (viprayukta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is cited to refute them;
the others are not cited. As for the forty-six mental concomitants (caitta):

That is to say, there are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*): namely, five of each from the universal and object-specific categories. There are ten great wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*):
namely, the eleven beginning with faith, excluding non-delusion (*amoha*). There are six great afflictive mental factors (*kleśa-mahābhūmika-dharma*):

namely, delusion (*moha*) from among the root afflictions, along with negligence (*pramāda*), laziness (*kausīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) from among the great secondary afflictions. [There are also] the great unwholesome mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika-dharma*).
There are two [categories]: namely, the two medium-universals (*madhya-anuśaya*). There are ten minor-affliction grounds (*parītta-kleśa-bhūmi*), namely the ten minor-followers (*parītta-anuśaya*).

There are eight in the indeterminate grounds (*aniyata-bhūmi*), namely: among the root afflictions, greed (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*); and among the indeterminate factors, regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), vitarka, and vicāra.

In total there are forty-six [categories]. Herein, the *rūpadharma* (material phenomena) are first refuted; the remainder will be analyzed and refuted in various ways in the subsequent text. △ First, the question-and-answer section that introduces the subject is concluded.
Second, the actual explanation of the grasped objects (*grāhya*) is divided into three parts according to their number. First, the *rūpadharma* are divided into two.
First, the actual presentation of *sapratigha-rūpa* (resistant matter) and *apratigha-rūpa* (non-resistant matter) is divided into two. First, the enumeration of their numbers.
Furthermore, the grasped [objects], namely form (*rūpa*), are generally of two kinds—[up to] the second, which is non-obstructive and not composed of atoms.
This is a general heading that divides the category of form-dharmas into two types. That which is called "obstructive" refers to the ten kinds of form:

the five sense organs and the five sense objects. The organs are the respective bases for the five consciousnesses; therefore, they are called the "five organs. The objects are the [bases for] the five consciousnesses...

Because each has its own distinct object, they are called the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are forms (*rūpa*) produced from the seed of form;

because they possess material obstruction, they are called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*). That which is said to be "without resistance" (*apratigha*) refers to the form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*).

Since it is exclusively the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and is termed a "sense object of phenomena" (*dharma-viṣaya*), it is called "form included in the sphere of mental objects. This is of five kinds. First:

The first is *paramāṇurūpa* (extremely subtle matter). This refers to analyzing the matter of the sense faculties and their objects through conceptual meditation until reaching the state of the ultimate atom;

thus, it is designated by the name "extremely subtle. The second is *paramāvacchinnarūpa* (extremely remote matter). This likewise involves analyzing the matter of space, light, shadow, and so forth through conceptual meditation until reaching the state of the ultimate atom;
thus, it is designated by the name "extremely remote. The third is *vijñaptisamādānarūpa* (matter derived from what is undertaken), which refers to...

1. The form of the current activity that possesses the functional capacity for restraint and initiation, which arises from the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) at the place of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) during the reception of the precepts; this is established as "form derived from undertaking" (*samādāna-saṃgṛhīta-rūpa*). 2.

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the form derived from them (*upādāya-rūpa*), which are the objects of the five sense-consciousnesses; these are established as "form perceived by the senses" (*sanidarśana-rūpa*). 3. The form of the current activity that possesses the functional capacity for restraint and initiation, which arises from the seeds of volition at the place of the preceptor during the reception of the precepts;

this is established as "form derived from undertaking. 4. Form as the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-rūpa*); this refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which universally conceptualizes various types of form-phenomena as being truly existent; it is established with the name "pervasively conceptualized. 5. The fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).

"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the various objective spheres that manifest within the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the noble ones (*ārya*); these are designated by the name "fruition of concentration.

The five types mentioned above are all transformations produced by the cognizing consciousness (*vijñāna-jñāna*) which takes them as objects; because they arise from the seeds of the mind, they are called "non-obstructive" (*apratigha*).

△ The enumeration is concluded. Below, the second section, the "Detailed Explanation," is divided into two parts. The first part, "Refuting the Obstructive," is divided into four sections. The first is "The Establisher."
Regarding atoms (*paramāṇu*):
those resistant forms (*sapratigha-rūpa*) certainly do not exist as real entities. [This continues until: How could they combine to receive light and cast shadows?

Intending to refute resistance (*sapratigha*), one first refutes the atom; since the atom is not real, resistance must necessarily be non-existent. This is stated in the passage beginning with "As for all those below..."
That which is obstructive, such as a jar, and that which is non-obstructive and non-material—both of these are absent in ultimate reality. Furthermore, regarding "parts":
that which has parts is divisible, while that which lacks parts is non-material. How can that which is non-material undergo conjunction? How can that which lacks parts receive light?
Only that which has parts may be admitted to receive light; moreover, that which is divisible is not ultimately real.

When the sun’s orb first rises and illuminates pillars and other objects, [it is said that] "thereby the atoms (paramāṇu) must necessarily possess spatial dimensions," explaining the aforementioned reception of light and the casting of shadows.

Since atoms are fundamentally not objects apprehended by the sensory consciousnesses—being admitted only as a collection—there must necessarily be the manifestation of shadows within a beam of light passing through a crack.
When light comes from the east, one part receives the light while a shadow appears from the west.

There are spatial divisions (*digbhāga*) because the substance and its location are distinct; thus, spatial divisions must necessarily exist. Furthermore, [the text] below further clarifies that atoms (*paramāṇu*) must possess spatial divisions:
either when light strikes them, or when one perceives their contact with walls and so forth, or when they constitute composite objects—thus, the fact that atoms possess spatial divisions is evident.
Moreover, [the text] below proceeds through successive reasoning to clarify that their position regarding atoms...

If there is even a slight degree of collective aggregation, such that spatial divisions are not entirely absent and they may interpenetrate one another, this restates their counter-argument: they allow for a collective aggregation in which [atoms] mutually interpenetrate, thereby avoiding the aforementioned difficulty regarding the impossibility of aggregation. As for the interpenetration of other particles: [This is followed by the refutation: If atoms were to interpenetrate, they would occupy the same location; thus, they would become a single atom, and no accumulation would be possible.

Furthermore, if they do not interpenetrate, there must be a gap between them, and thus no true contact occurs. Therefore, the notion of a collective aggregation of atoms is untenable. *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, specifically concerning the critique of the Vaibhāṣika theory of atomic aggregation.*
Coarse matter would not arise; therefore, it is refuted by saying that [coarseness] would fail to be established. Regarding "interpenetration":
suppose one atom is primary and the remaining atoms all enter into that single atom. While there are no other atoms, the fundamental substance of that single atom is not non-existent.
Consequently, this single atom must possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*).
If one maintains that resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) consists of atoms (*paramāṇu*), then the real existence of resistant form is not established.
This is because, if one maintains that gross form—which is admitted to be obstructive—can be constituted by atoms, those atoms must necessarily possess spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*).

If they lacked spatial dimensions, they would not be obstructive and resistant. Therefore, [the author] concludes below that both the subject (the atom) and the object (resistant form) are equally devoid of reality.
The first [section], "The Proof that Atoms Exist," concludes. Below, the second [section] concerns the correct meaning: the transformation of consciousness.

How could the five consciousnesses lack a supporting basis (*āśraya*) and an objective condition (*ālambana*) consisting of form? ... [up to] "...that which is able to induce the arising of something resembling its own consciousness."
Below the section on the five consciousnesses, an opponent asks: "The meaning is that the bases and objects of the five consciousnesses must necessarily be real matter (*rūpa*).
If there were no resistance (*sapratigha*), would the five consciousnesses not then lack an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)? The Master’s intended answer is: "Although matter exists..."

This is not as you maintain—that it is composed of atoms—but rather it is a manifestation of internal consciousness. The phrase "consciousness [arises]" below explains the meaning of the aforementioned "transformation of consciousness.
When consciousness arises, it refers to the time when the eight consciousnesses manifest. "Internal causes and conditions" refers to the mutual perfuming of the agent and the object.
The eyes and so forth are the faculties (*indriya*), termed the "basis" (*āśraya*). Form and so forth are the objects (*viṣaya*), termed the "object-condition" (*ālambana*). Therefore, the...

All that arises based on conditions is a transformation of consciousness. Question: If, at the time consciousness arises, it always takes internal form as its object, why is it also said that the eyes and other sense organs serve as conditions?
Therefore, the answer states: "However, the sense organs such as the eyes are not apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

... This [organ] is merely a functional capacity (*śakti*), not something produced externally. Here, "produced" refers to form (*rūpa*), while "functional capacity" refers to the organ (*indriya*). Thus, the organ and the form—

There are no two [entities]. Originally, they arise from a single consciousness and are likewise of one substance. However, based on the distinction between that which possesses cognition and that which lacks cognition, they are divided into the two categories of faculty (*indriya*) and object (*viṣaya*).
Because it possesses cognition, it can give rise to consciousness; because it lacks cognition, it can serve as an object. "Externally there is...
answers the question regarding the basis (*āśraya*) mentioned above. "These eyes, etc. answers the question regarding the focal object (*ālambana*) mentioned above. [This] induces [the following]:

"Appearing as itself": "itself" refers to the object. The object can attract the mind, and the mind evolves in a manner resembling that object; therefore, it is called a consciousness produced by an object that appears as itself.
△ Second, the correct doctrine regarding the transformation of consciousness is concluded. Below, the three [points] cite the attachments and provide refutations.
"You maintain that those [atoms] are the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this [consciousness]... because when they are not in conjunction, this characteristic does not exist.
This passage raises an objection based on the opponent's position to refute it. The word "those" (*te*) refers to the atoms (*paramāṇu*). It means that they are not merely producers;

that is, they do not function solely as causes of production, but also serve as objects of cognition. Having raised the opponent's position above, the intent of the subsequent refutation is as follows:
Since your insistence that atoms lack substantial reality has been refuted, there can be no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Do not attempt to claim that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) serve as the object-condition for this consciousness. The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states:

"Just as the visual faculty and so forth do not possess the aspect of those [objects] with respect to the visual consciousness and so forth, likewise, atoms do not [possess the aspect of the object] with respect to the visual [consciousness]."
The [consciousnesses] such as visual consciousness have no objective referent (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is known that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not the objects of the five consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "even those which, through combination, appear like them" (*yāvat saṃhatās tannirbhāsāḥ*): the word "appearance" (*nirbhāsa*) refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the transformation of consciousness (*vijñānapariṇāma*).

"Combination" (*saṃhata*) refers to matter (*rūpa*) external to consciousness as asserted by other schools. It should be stated: "[They are not objects] because they take as their object only the objective aspect of matter which appears like that [external object] through combination."
This refers to the meaning that internal form appears as if it were external; it is not a phenomenon produced by combination (*saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "reaching a state where [cognition] definitely does not arise," this refutes the non-Buddhist (Bāhyaka) tenet that combinations are unreal and lack the functional capacity to produce consciousness; thus, they are without an object-condition (*anālambana*). As stated in the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*:

That [combination] lacks substantial reality because it cannot produce [cognition]. Thus, regarding the combination with respect to visual consciousness and the others, there is no sense in which it functions as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Below that discussion of combination, it is concluded that since it is not real, it cannot serve as a condition.

Furthermore, using the analogy of a second moon, it is shown that combination lacks the function of producing the five consciousnesses. Below the section on "not all atoms," the common combination of atoms is refuted.

[This refers to] the stage [of atoms]. There is no objective referent (ālambana). Since the aggregation of atoms is originally nothing but atoms, visual consciousness and the other cognitions lack the status of having an objective referent.

The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states: "Because that image does not exist upon visual consciousness and the others, it is likewise logically impossible for the various aggregated images of atoms such as form to exist there;
for both [the Vaibhāṣika and Sautrāntika] maintain that these are the images of atoms. Furthermore, it is not...
Below the section on "All Atoms" (paramāṇu), it refutes that the substance of an atom possesses conjunction; nor is it an object of cognition (ālambana). Therefore, it says:
"Because this characteristic does not exist when they are not in conjunction."

Because the substance and characteristics [of atoms] are identical whether they are in a state of combination or in a state of non-combination (up to their state of not yet being gathered), it is explained that there is no distinction in the substance of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Regarding the states of combination and non-combination, they lack the status of being an object (*ālambana*) for visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions.
Having raised the objection below, the term "some who maintain" (*kecit*) is cited to explain that within the substance of the ultimate atom, the capacity for combination is fully present.
This is consistent with the meaning. "Form and so forth" refers to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Each one is also distinct among the five sense objects;

that is to say, when the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of each of the five sense objects are not yet aggregated, although they possess the characteristic of aggregation, this characteristic is not manifest and they do not constitute the objective domain of the five consciousnesses.

When the atoms converge and mutually support one another, the coarse characteristic (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) finally becomes manifest, and thus they become the objective domain of these [five] consciousnesses. Coarse...
The appearance of characteristics [occurs] because the substance possesses the characteristic of combination (*saṃyoga*).
One should know that the substance possessing combination is identical in principle to aggregation (*saṃghāta*). Aggregation may be subtle, while combination may be coarse.

As for those who maintain that these characteristics are substantially existent, it is because they are present within the substance of the atom (*paramāṇu*), thereby serving as the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the five consciousnesses. The author of the treatise refutes this position in general as follows:
Whether atoms are aggregated or not yet aggregated, their essence is no different; how, then, could there be a coarse appearance that serves as the object of the five consciousnesses?

The Bodhisattva Dignāga says in verse: "Aggregation is like hardness and so forth; even if it appears to the visual consciousness and others, it is a condition but not an objective support (ālambana), because it is admitted to have the nature of atoms."
Regarding objects such as vases and bowls and their constituent atoms, [the text asks] how much more so for atoms that lack reality apart from consciousness.
Furthermore, the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Object-Condition) raises the counter-argument of the external school’s shifting position to refute it, stating:

"They maintain that visual and other consciousnesses can take as their object the aggregated characteristics of atoms, which arise separately. That treatise further counters this by examining the essence of the atom."
[The opponent] maintains that [the atom] possesses the characteristic of being a composite. The Master of the Treatise refutes this with verses using the analogy of hardness and so forth.

Consequently, [the opponent] shifts their position and calculates that the characteristic of aggregation itself is the atom; they hold that the atom arises as consciousness by taking aggregation as its object, which constitutes the meaning of the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya).
The Master again refutes this with verses using the analogies of jars, bowls, and so forth. What is cited here is the commentary on those verses from that treatise.

Refutation of the argument: Regarding objects such as jars and bowls, since their constituent atoms are equal in number regardless of whether they are large or small, the cognitive appearances arising from them should likewise be without distinction.

If it is argued that there is a distinction in appearance because consciousness arises in relation to jars and bowls, then in the state where atoms are gathered together to form jars and bowls, those objects should exist independently of the atoms.

Because of their characteristics. If one were to exclude the atoms (*paramāṇu*), would the conventional characteristics (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*) of a jar or a bowl give rise to cognition? Therefore, that treatise states:
"It is not the case that jars, bowls, and the like can constitute atoms with distinct dimensions and forms, because they abandon the spherical nature of the minute.

The coarse characteristic is the jar or bowl; the subtle characteristic is the atom. If it is argued that atoms do not abandon [their nature] and thus produce cognition without being separated from the jar, [that is incorrect].

The *ōu* (jar) is similar to the appearance of a jar; thus, there is a distinction [between them]. Refuting this, it is said: "A consciousness characterized by coarse features does not take an object characterized by subtle features as its condition.

This means that the two types of consciousness—the coarse and the subtle—do not serve as mutual conditions for one another. If they were to serve as mutual conditions, the same would apply to other consciousnesses.

Therefore, it is further suppressed [by the argument]: "Do not allow that a consciousness of one object takes another object as its condition. If it were to take another object as its condition, one would again challenge that position, saying: "One consciousness..."

Because it must take all objects as its conditions, one must admit that there are [atoms] below [the threshold of perception]. This establishes the point that outside of consciousness there are no atoms.
From this, it is definitively known that what is transformed by one's own consciousness consists of a multitude of atoms combined to form a single object.
This establishes the meaning of the five consciousnesses having a direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). To arise in dependence upon that [object] is the meaning of "condition";

to arise bearing its image is the meaning of "objective. The *Ālambanaparīkṣā* states: "Although external objects do not exist, there is internal form appearing as if it were an external object, serving as the objective condition.
It is admitted that the visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing its image and [originate] from it."

[The text] arises. However, below the section on consciousness, it concludes by manifesting the characteristics transformed by consciousness, while simultaneously refuting the existence of dharmas external to the mind. Regarding "according to measure":

because the measure of the objective sphere follows the power of one's karma, the forms thus transformed differ in size—some small, some large. "Not separately" below [the text] refutes external attachments.
△ Third, having concluded the citation of attachments and the analysis of their refutation, the following four sections clarify that atoms are merely provisional designations.

For those who cling to the notion that coarse matter possesses substantial reality [up to] the point where it is shown that all is a manifestation of consciousness and not composed of atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is clarified that the doctrine of atoms is provisional and not ultimate; therefore, there are no real atoms existing external to consciousness.

*Yogācāra* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "correspondence" (*xiāngyìng*). This is because the Buddha’s teaching corresponds to all things, and one should practice in accordance with the teachings. Furthermore...
It is called "concordant with names" (nāma-saṃprayukta); it is a wisdom of conceptualization (parikalpita-prajñā), which is precisely the discriminating mind (vikalpa-citta).

By means of this discriminating mind, one universally analyzes gross form, successively breaking it down until the notion of an atom (paramāṇu) is formed; therefore, the various holy teachings provisionally designate [this] as an "atom. Although below this—
These are merely successive layers of conceptualized images within a false imagination. From "thereby" (*yīcǐ*) downward, the conclusion refutes the preceding argument.

△ Fourth, the provisional establishment of atoms is finished. This concludes, together with what precedes it, the first refutation of those with resistance (*sapratigha*). The following two sections refute those without resistance (*apratigha*).
The other non-obstructive forms (*apratigha-rūpa*) belong to this same category; therefore, they can be described as truly existent form-dharmas.

This "category" refers to the aforementioned atoms (*paramāṇu*), which are of the nature of conceptual constructs (*prajñapti*). These other non-obstructive forms are provisionally admitted to exist and are termed "non-obstructive," just like mental factors (*citta-dharma*).
Furthermore, they are not substantial form; rather, they are designated as such in relation to the obstructive forms mentioned above, just as consciousness is so designated.

Manifestations can only be described through conventional designation; apart from consciousness, they definitely do not exist. How much less could that which lacks form and characteristics be truly existent?
II. The refutation of non-resistant matter (*apratigha-rūpa*) is concluded. This concludes the preceding section on the correct presentation of resistant (*sapratigha*) and non-resistant matter.
Below follows the secondary inquiry into manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) matter, divided into two parts. I. Refuting the existence of manifest matter.
Are informative and non-informative form not substantially existent? (Up to: Because they manifest the mind, bodily intimation is designated as "body.

"Intimation" (*vijñapti*) means "to manifest," because its characteristics are visible. Non-intimation is the opposite of this. First, regarding the body, the author of the treatise poses a definitive question.

Thereafter, it is refuted separately. There are two types of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*): first, bodily [informative matter], and second, vocal [informative matter]. Therefore, the question is asked regarding the nature of the real existence of bodily informative matter.
If one says [it is shape], this refutes the tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school which maintains that shape constitutes bodily informative matter;

that is to say, if it were shape, it would necessarily be analyzable, and thus, by principle, it would not be substantially real. Regarding the phrase "length and so forth," this explains the aforementioned meaning of being analyzable; that is, length is analyzed...
[The opponent] asserts that [the object] is short; however, when one analyzes the large into the small, down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it cannot be found.

If [the opponent] says "below," this refutes the Saṃmitīya school’s reckoning of motion as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). That is to say, if motion were taken as the material form of bodily intimation, then motion would not be a permanent principle.

Cessation has the meaning of being immovable, whereas the conditioned has the meaning of movement. Movement takes wind as its cause; that which has a cause does not move further by depending on another cause.
That which lacks a cause need not depend on a cause for its cessation. Birth, cessation, and movement are like a flowing stream;

why should they depend on the presence or absence of wind? Therefore it is said: "If cessation depended upon a cause, it would not be cessation. What is now called a "cause" is stated only to clarify this point.
Bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is an effect. An effect necessarily depends on a cause; when the cause is exhausted, the effect arises, and as the effect arises, the cause ceases.

Therefore, the notion that "motion" constitutes bodily intimation-color (*kāyarūpa*) is incorrect, because motion and cessation do not depend upon a cause. The passage beginning with "If one says... represents the subsequent counter-argument of our own school (*svayūthya*).

This refers to material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) that are neither manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*) nor shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), but which are produced by the mind and are capable of moving the hands and other limbs.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "There are three kinds of resistant matter (*sapratigha-rūpa*): namely, manifest color, shape-color, and informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
Manifest color refers to blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brightness, darkness, clouds, smoke, dust, mist, and the uniform manifest color of space."
"Shape-color" (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) refers to long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, regular, irregular, high, low, and so forth.

"Informative color" (*vijñapti-rūpa*) refers to taking up, putting down, bending, extending, walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and so forth. As for the claim that "neither manifest nor shape" refers to informative color, this is logically untenable;
the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this in general. Regarding the phrase "this, if... and below, it means movement is refuted as previously stated. Wind... [text fragment].

Nor is it informative (*vijñapti*). Regarding the imagined existence of form (*rūpa*), in what respect could it be similar [to informative form]? The preceding section refuted that the sense faculties (*indriya*) do not possess informative form.
Furthermore, below the discussion on tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), it is refuted that the objects (*viṣaya*) do not possess informative form. Tangibility refers to the object of the body-faculty;

it is exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), unlike bodily action (*kāyakarman*), which permeates both wholesome and unwholesome natures. Since their natures are different, tangibility is not bodily informative form. As for why it does not apply to odors or tastes: [the same logic follows].

This refers to the objects of odor and flavor. Furthermore, it is not a manifest bodily action (*vijñapti-kāya-karman*). As for that which is analogous to touch, it is also of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*);

therefore, under the section on the body, this concludes the refutation of the [opponent's] incorrect position. However, under the section on the mind, the correct meaning is established. This is distinct from the Hīnayāna insofar as it concerns the transformations of the mind.
When one speaks of "the continuity of arising and ceasing," this refers to the characteristic of movement, such as the raising and lowering of the hands or the stepping forward of the feet.

Afterward, when the preceding characteristic has arisen, the succeeding characteristic immediately ceases; as soon as the preceding characteristic ceases, the succeeding characteristic arises. This is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*).
While it appears to move, it merely represents the mind; however, what is this so-called "name"? It is certainly not a real entity.
Vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) is likewise not substantially real; [this holds] up to the point that vocal intimation as a mere designation does not contradict reason.
Having generally stated that vocal intimation is not real, he further refutes the claim that sound possesses expressive power (*abhilāpa*). "Moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the minimum unit of time.
The *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "Within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*; within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred instances of arising and ceasing.
Through the accumulation of many *kṣaṇas* of sound, a single syllable is formed; a single syllable forms a name; and many names form a phrase."
Only then can there be expression. If one maintains that sound constitutes vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*), it is refuted as follows:
the nature of sound lasts for only a single moment, and sound alone lacks the capacity for expression; rather, speech is constituted by multiple moments, and furthermore, [sound] is not substantial.

As for the previously refuted external resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*), it is further refuted here as being color-form (*rūpadharma*) and not vocal intimation. Thus, following the discussion on the mind, the correct meaning is concluded and revealed.
These are transformations of consciousness-only. △ First, the conclusion of the informative [action]. Second, the non-informative [action].
Since the informative [action] is actually non-existent, how could the non-informative [action] be real? (Up to: because it is established based on manifest volition, it is a conventional existence.
By using that which exists as an analogy for that which does not exist, one can know it to be unreal. Regarding "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*), other sources state:

it is "form derived from what is undertaken" (*samādāna-śīla-ākṣipta-rūpa*), because it is form produced by undertaking the precepts. When one contemplates the dharma of undertaking the precepts, wishing to protect the good and ward off evil, there appears a form characterized by the limits of good and evil;
yet, because it lacks any manifest expression, it is called "unmanifest. The following passage provides the explanation.
The meaning of *avijñapti* (non-informative action) is established as follows: it consists of the volitions (*cetanā*) of body and speech, which are themselves the three types of karma.

At the moment of receiving the precepts, because this is the most excellent form of the three karmas, even though there is no outward manifestation, the seeds of the color-form (*rūpa*) of the precepts are known to increase within oneself; therefore, this name is established.

As for "one who manifests evil conduct," this refers to one who performs evil deeds with the body and utters evil words with the mouth, whereby the visible forms and sounds are manifest; [the term] may be used to indicate their cessation.
It is merely the volition that initiates bodily and vocal actions; it is non-informative (avijñapti) and can only be brought to rest while in meditative concentration.
It is also called "non-manifest" (avijñapti). Both of these aforementioned types are conventional designations; why then do you cling to them as being real?

In the sūtras, the Blessed One taught that there are three types of karma (up to: ...there is only internal consciousness transforming and appearing as form). An opponent cites a sūtra to raise an objection, stating:
"As for bodily action (*kāyakarman*), it is established in terms of its basis. 'Body' refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*); since action arises based on the body, it is called 'bodily action.
As for vocal action (*vākkarman*), it is established in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); because speech itself is the action."

Regarding "mental action" (*manas-karman*): it is established based on its origination (*samutthāna*). Action is *cetanā* (volition); that which is associated with the mind and originated by the mind is called mental action.

It is not denied as being non-existent; rather, when it is said to be "non-material" (*arūpin*), the Master [Vasubandhu] answers the purport of the previous question, meaning that while the three types of action taught in the Sūtra do exist, they are not the substantial matter (*rūpa*) as you assert.
"Able to move downward" (*adhaḥ-preraṇa-samartha*) explains the aforementioned point.

The meaning of the three types of action (*trikarma*) being non-material (*arūpa*) is as follows: action is volition (*cetanā*); volition is the mind (*citta*). This demonstrates that the three types of action are solely mind.

Therefore, the volitions that move the body and initiate speech are designated as "bodily action" (*kāyakarma*) and "vocal action" (*vākkarma*). The two types of volition—thorough deliberation (*saṃtīraṇa-cetanā*) and determination (*niścaya-cetanā*)—are respectively the volition of investigation and the volition of decision;
these are associated with the mental faculty (*manas*), demonstrating that they are solely mind. The agent (*kartṛ*) initiates and produces speech.
It is said: that which moves refers to the ability to move the hands and body; because these are all [driven by] the mind (*manas*), they are called mental action (*manas-karman*).

The passage "giving rise to body and speech" below explains the establishment of the name "action. The passage "this is deliberative determination" below refers to deliberative volition (*cetanā*), which is precisely the mind.

Because the mind travels through the domains of body and speech, and because this path of action (*karmapatha*) universally induces both suffering and pleasure—possessing these two meanings—it is further established as being called a "path" (*mārga*).

Therefore, regarding the fact that the first seven courses of action (*karmapatha*) also have volition (*cetanā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this provides a general explanation that the courses of action are exclusively mental.
Thus, it is said that volition is their intrinsic nature. The "first seven" refer to the three of the body and the four of speech. Volition is the mind (*manas*).

Since the two types of action—body and speech—take the mind as their essence, they are called "intrinsic nature. Alternatively, [the phrase] "body and speech" below explains the aforementioned manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) as well.

Included within the paths of action (karmapatha) are the manifest forms (vijñapti) of body and speech; since there is no volition that does not initiate them, and because they involve listening, reflecting, and coming and going, they are termed "that which is traversed.

From this point downward, the conclusion is reached: the manifest and unmanifest forms (vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa) do not possess a real substance external to the mind, but are merely transformations manifested by internal consciousness.

[The section on] the second, the unmanifest [forms], is concluded. Together with the above, the first category, material phenomena (rūpadharma), is concluded. Below are the two categories of non-associated formations (viprayukta-saṃskāra).
The Dharma is divided into two parts. First, the restatement of the thesis and its general refutation:
"Conditioned factors dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are also not substantially existent (until: like other conventional phenomena, they lack a substantial essence."

Regarding the statement that "non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are also not substantially existent," this is a general refutation of their asserted existence. Question: What are called non-associated formations? Answer:
[Factors such as] acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth are not capable of being cognitive objects (*ālambana*). They do not associate with the mind (*citta*) or mental factors (*caitta*).

Because they lack material resistance (*sapratigha*), they do not associate with matter (*rūpa*). Because they possess arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*), they do not associate with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, they are called "non-associated."

[The section on] "Conditioned Forces Disassociated from Mind" (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra). Below, [the author] generally refutes that these disassociated forces do not possess a real substantial entity (*dravya*).

"Acquisition" (*prāpti*) means the sense of accomplishment; "non-acquisition" (*aprāpti*) means the sense of non-accomplishment. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the remaining twenty-two factors. These disassociated forces are merely manifested by form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*);
therefore, they lack a substantial characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), just like form and mind themselves. Furthermore, they lack any functional activity (*kāritra*) distinct [from those two].
Form, mind, and so forth, because they lack intrinsic nature and lack functional activity, are known to be unreal; they exist only as provisional designations.

Regarding this "definite inferiority," it refers to the attainment of such states and so on: apart from form, mind, and so forth, there is necessarily no substantial entity. One should understand that this pertains to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

They are subsumed within the [factors] dissociated from mind; they are definitely not manifested apart from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). Therefore, it is said: "Because you admit they are included within the aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, among the four categories—mind, mental factors (*caitta*), matter, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—those not subsumed therein are ultimately non-existent in essence.

As for other real dharmas, such as *tathatā* (suchness) and the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality), since these are not subsumed [within the aggregates], they are conventional designations and not real. △ 1. Restating the Opponent’s Position.

The general refutation is concluded. Below, there are six sections for the specific refutations based on their respective tenets. First, regarding acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*):
how, then, do they know of acquisition and non-acquisition? [It is because] one must necessarily possess seeds of the wholesome in the present, and so forth.
"Furthermore, 'that which is below'"—this is the Master of the Treatise’s question. "'The Sūtra'"—this refers to the citation of a sūtra from another vehicle as an answer.

it refers to the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). The ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) are: right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right view. Right... [text ends]
Right thought, right effort, right liberation, and right knowledge—because these ten are all correct, they are called the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
Ordinary beings dwell in defilement and completely lack these noble dharmas; Arhats have emerged from the entanglements and their afflictions are forever severed.

As for the claim that the Sūtra does not state this and thus it cannot serve as proof, the Master of the Treatise refutes it based on the Sūtra in general, and further cites the Sūtra as an example to raise a challenge.
This demonstrates that there is attainment without being separate from form and mind. As for the seven treasures:

the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the minister-treasurer treasure, and the minister-general treasure; it is also said there is the blue-food-tree treasure.

The precious trees that provide yellow food, red food, and white food; the precious trees that provide drink; and the precious trees that provide clothing and vehicles—these are the fruits of the tree.
This refers to what is stated in that sutra: that a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) accomplishes the seven treasures. How could it be that he accomplishes the non-sentient bodies of others?
The bodies of others are different from [his own] form, and non-sentient things are different from mind. "How could it be that" means that they are not different from form.
If attainment exists within the mind, and since it is not distinct from form or mind, why do you insist that attainment exists as a reality separate from the mind?

If you argue that—according to the calculations of other vehicles—attainment and so forth must necessarily be distinct from form and mind, and that "accomplishment" is a conventional designation for the power of mastery over jewels (which resides in the jewels themselves), yet this attainment does not reside in the king;
then why do you find it difficult to accept the principle that attainment exists without being separate from form and mind?

If you claim that the seven treasures possess sovereign power, then wholesome karma likewise possesses sovereign power;

why not then speak of "accomplishment" as being conventionally designated based upon that karma, rather than persistently clinging to the view that there is an actual existence of acquisition and so forth apart from the mind? If you claim that it is because the seven treasures exist in the present...
One may provisionally say that "attainment" (*prāpti*) exists as a designation for jewels; however, how can it be known that good and evil exist apart from the present?
This is because wholesome and unwholesome karma pervades the three periods of time. Furthermore, one may rely on the wholesome to establish its name provisionally.

Below this, it is explained that wholesome and unwholesome states must necessarily exist in the present; even if they do not arise as active manifestations (*samudācāra*), their seeds (*bīja*) constantly persist.
Furthermore, what superior function does "acquisition" (*prāpti*) have with respect to phenomena? [Up to: Since it is truly non-existent, acquisition also does not exist.

Regarding the question, "What superior function does acquisition have with respect to phenomena," the author of the treatise poses an inquiry as to what the superior function of acquisition toward all phenomena is like.
The phrase "that which has already been lost" refers to the past; "that which has not yet been acquired" refers to the future.
[Objection: "That which is non-sentient (*asattva*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This is said in contrast to sentient beings, because sentient beings are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
