It should never arise. The two periods of past and future are likewise unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and thus never produced.
If one were to claim that both periods arise simultaneously, taking attainment (*prāpti*) as their cause, then to maintain that these two are causeless would render that [attainment] useless.

Regarding the statement "two types of arising": they claim that both "arising from what originally existed" and "arising from what originally did not exist" are instances of arising without a cause (*ahetuka*).
Now, by taking "attainment" as the cause, one calculates that what was previously unobtained or has already been lost arises simultaneously [with its cause];
this is therefore "arising with a cause. Consequently, those two types of causeless arising they cling to become useless. Thus, the *Śataśāstra* says: "If it originally did not exist..."

Regarding "arising": why does that which previously did not exist not arise? If that which already exists inherently arises, then that which exists later should likewise arise. Furthermore, the section beginning with "Moreover, possessing" provides a second refutation of the meaning of simultaneous arising (*sahaja*).

This means that if things in the past and future were to arise simultaneously by taking possession (*prāpti*) as their cause, then if they possess the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of those three natures should all manifest simultaneously. If, however, they arise sequentially depending on other causes, [the claim of simultaneous arising is untenable].

If one maintains that the "accompaniment-acquisition" (*sahaja-prāpti*) is the cause [of the non-disappearance of dharmas], it would be rendered useless. If one were to concede the following, this would be a restatement of the counter-argument of other vehicles:
namely, that "acquisition" (*prāpti*) is the cause for the non-loss of these various dharmas, and that by virtue of this acquisition, those dharmas are accomplished. To refute this:

if you claim that sentient beings accomplish various dharmas, one should know that those dharmas do not exist apart from sentient beings; if they were apart from sentient beings, they would not truly [exist].
It can be obtained. How then can you maintain that there is an "obtaining" (prāpti) and so forth existing apart from form (rūpa) and mind (citta)?

Therefore, since obtaining is useless with respect to dharmas, it is concluded that the dharma of obtaining lacks both superior and common utility. Since obtaining is truly non-existent, non-obtaining (aprāpti) is likewise non-existent.

However, based on the states (*avasthā*) of various phenomena that can be established in relation to sentient beings—up until the point where they have not yet attained the various noble dharmas (*āryadharma*)—it is shown according to the lower [text] that both acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are, in their true meaning, all merely nominal designations (*prajñapti*). The seeds are the cause of karma;
sovereign karmic power is the cause; and present karma is the fruit. The following section explains and establishes the meaning of non-acquisition (*aprāpti*).
The seeds to be abandoned through seeing are precisely the afflictions of conceptual discrimination. If these afflictions are abandoned, one accomplishes the dharmas of an ārya;

yet, because they have not been permanently eradicated, the non-possession of the dharmas of an ārya is termed "the nature of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjanatva*). △ The first section on acquisition and non-acquisition is concluded. Below are the two [sections] on the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Furthermore, how is it known that the distinctions of states among different forms, minds, and so forth are conventionally designated as "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*)?
[The text continues: "Furthermore, how..."—here the Master of the Treatise poses the question. "In the Sūtra..."—here the proponents of other vehicles cite a sūtra as an answer:

namely, that "devas are similar to devas" and "humans are similar to humans"; therefore, one knows that homogeneity exists. "This sūtra..."—here the Master of the Treatise refutes it in general: [it refers merely to] a commonality of cognition.

"Speech" refers to cognition as discrimination and speech as verbal expression. If it were due to a homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) that causes the speech of gods to be identical to that of gods and the speech of humans to be identical to that of humans, then grasses and trees and so forth should also possess a homogeneous character;

why then does the speech of grass not accord with grass, and the speech of wood not accord with wood? If verbal expression arises only by virtue of a homogeneous character, then it must likewise arise from a homogeneous character.

"Distinct [instances of] generic similarity (*sabhāgatā*) arise; distinct [instances of] generic similarity arise. Since it has already been stated that this is not so, what then is meant by saying they arise together?

If one were to say: "Below," this refers to restating their alternative position. "Desire" (*chanda*) means longing or aspiration. That is to say, this desire is the same as that, and that desire is the same as this;
only by taking generic similarity as the cause does one give rise to a common desire. The refutation states: This is also illogical. [The previous argument regarding] past...
Habitual practice serves as the cause. The arising of the desire for common engagement is the seed of past habituation; the desire for common engagement is the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
This means that, for example, having previously seen a person, a seed is perfumed; later, upon seeing that person again, a corresponding manifest activity arises.

Having previously seen wholesome [objects], a seed is perfumed; later, upon seeing the wholesome again, a corresponding manifest activity arises. This is the sameness of person-to-person within this body.
It is similar. Goodness is identical with goodness; this is the similarity of the mind. One should understand that this principle arises from perfuming (*vāsanā*);

do not laboriously insist on a separate cause. However, based on sentient beings [as mentioned] below, it is established as a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) to complete the correct doctrine; it has no separate, substantial existence.
△ The second section on the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) is concluded. Below follows the third [section] on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, how is it known that the life-faculty is established as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) for the determination of the duration of abiding, distinct from matter, mind, and so forth?

"Furthermore, how so? [The Master of the Treatise] asks. "The Sūtra... [The proponents of other vehicles] cite the sūtra in response. "Consciousness" refers to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) of the eighth [consciousness];

"heat" refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective portion) of the eighth; "life-force" (*āyus*) refers to the seeds of the eighth. Now, by citing the "root of life," it is precisely these seeds that are meant.
"In this sūtra... [The Master of the Treatise] refutes them in general. "That which has already been established" refers to the principle previously discussed.

Furthermore, even material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) do not exist apart from consciousness; how then can one insist that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exists as something distinct from consciousness? Moreover, the following analogy does not establish the actual meaning:

while it might be said that mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) are "different" because they are associated with the mind and arise and perish moment by moment, [the case of the life-faculty is not analogous].

The substance [of the mental factors] must not be real. Since the mental factors (caitta) are separate from the mind (citta) and are not substantially existent, they are used as an analogy for the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), which is not real apart from the mind.
To this, the proponents of other vehicles raise an objection: "The Sūtras state that there are three [realms]; how can they lack distinct substances? The Master replies:

The meaning is explained as threefold, as in the case of the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*). That is to say, the eighth [consciousness] has its seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) named "cognition" (*vijñāna*), its image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) named "warmth" (*uṣman*), and its seeds named "life-force" (*āyus*). Although there are three meanings, their substance is not distinct, just like the four right abandonments:
causing unarisen wholesome states to arise quickly, causing arisen wholesome states to increase, and causing unarisen unwholesome states not to arise. Once arisen, [they are maintained].
The arising of evil should be swiftly eliminated. Although there are four meanings [to diligence], they originate from a single essence of vigor; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.

Regarding the objection that "in the state of non-conceptualization (*acittaka*), life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) should be absent," this is a challenge from other vehicles (*anyayāna*). They argue:

"Since you admit that life-force is not separate from consciousness (*vijñāna*), then in the state of non-conceptualization, life-force and warmth should be absent. To this, the treatise asks: "Does the Sūtra not say that consciousness does not depart from the body?"

The Master explains: Since the sūtras state that consciousness does not depart from the body, it is known that these three—vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—possess the quality of non-separation.
Other vehicles further raise the objection: "If it is said that consciousness does not depart from the body, how can there be what is called a 'mindless state' (*acittaka-avasthā*)?

The Master answers: "That state is called mindless because the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) have ceased; it is not that the eighth [consciousness] is absent. This will be explained in detail later.
This meaning is extensively elucidated in the texts on the two lower meditative absorptions and in the third fascicle. Following this [passage], the refutation of the previous position is concluded:
namely, that this very fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) alone is sufficient to serve as the substratum for the experience of results within the three realms and five destinies;

there is no need to laboriously maintain the separate existence of a real life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) apart from consciousness. Following "However, based on... (*kintu*), the conclusion establishes the correct position: that [the life-faculty] is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).

Regarding "established": the determination of the duration of abiding refers to the limited span of one's lifespan. Regarding "distinction in function": this refers to the inequality of karmic forces.
"Proximate seed" refers to the eighth consciousness-seed; based upon this seed, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established.
△ The third section on the life-faculty is concluded. Below follow four [topics]: the two mindless absorptions and the maturation of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-vipāka*).

Furthermore, how is it known that the two mindless attainments (nirodhasamāpatti) [and the state of non-conception]—up to the point where it says "like a jar" and so forth—are also able to obstruct [the arising of mental states], even though they are provisional (*prajñapti*)?
Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, how," the Master of the Treatise asks a question. Regarding the phrase "If there were none," this is the objection from other vehicles (*yāna*). It means:

if the aforementioned three states are not substantial entities (*dravya*), by what dharma are the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) obstructed from arising as manifest activity (*samudācāra*)? Regarding the phrase "If there were none," this refers to the treatise.
The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes that definition of "mindless absorption" (acittaka-samāpatti) by means of the "formless absorptions" (ārūpya-samāpatti).
While the name "mindless absorption" is commonly known in the world, the term "formless" applied to an absorption has not been heard of in principle.

Furthermore, he rebuts the opponent's argument regarding obstruction from below, demonstrating that what acts as an obstructor is merely conventional (prajñapti). For example, even a mere dam can obstruct water; why then must a real entity (dravyadharma) obstruct the mind?

This means that when practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because one proceeds through the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of concentration, these three factors are also not substantially existent (*dravyasat*).
Regarding the explanation of the correct meaning of the names established for the two concentrations: "the coarse and agitated mind" refers to the first six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñāna*).

The reason the seventh [consciousness] is not mentioned is that it is explained in the same way as the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), because the discussion concerns only the meaning of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).

"One who has formed a superior aspiration" refers to the arising of a mind of superior resolve, aspiring to be born in a tranquil realm. "Subtle and minute" means that coarse perception (*saṃjñā*) has already been eliminated.

"At the time of the extremely subtle mind" signifies that the perfuming (*vāsanā*) has already been established; thus it is said: "it establishes the seeds of an extremely predominant mind of revulsion (*udvega*), and so forth."

The following passage clarifies that these are provisionally established based on specific stages and do not possess a real substantial entity (*dravya*). They suppress and eliminate coarse conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), and their seeds are of a wholesome nature;

therefore, both of these meditative attainments are designated as "wholesome" (*kuśala*). Regarding the section on "Non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñika*) below, it specifically explains the correct meaning of the designation for the maturation (*vipāka*) of non-conceptualization.
This means that when one cultivates the meditative concentration, one seeks the fruit of that celestial realm; this perfumes the seeds that summon the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Having received the retributive fruit of the heavens, [the text] below explains that the establishment of "non-conceptual attainment" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) receives the name of "retribution" (vipāka).

Therefore, the section below concludes that these three factors—the two mindless attainments and the retribution of non-conceptualization—are not substantial entities; they are merely provisionally established based on the states of matter and mind.
△ Four: The Two Mindless Attainments and the Retribution of Non-conceptualization concluded.

In the preceding section on the attachment to the factors of other vehicles (*yānāntara-dharma-abhiniveśa*), the formal explanation of that attachment is divided into three parts: first, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); second, non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*);

and third, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Within the second [category], there are three further divisions: first, citing the attachment and refuting it generally; second, refuting it specifically according to the attachments;

and third, concluding the remaining points by citing the attachments. This second [division] is further subdivided into six: first, acquisition and non-acquisition (*prāpti-aprāpti*); second, the homogeneous character of a group (*nikāya-sabhāga*); third...

The life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the four [meditative attainments], the two mindless attainments (acittaka-samāpatti), and the maturation of non-conception (āsaṃjñika-vipāka). The first fascicle’s explanation is concluded.
Within this, the fifth section, "The Threefold Analysis of Conditioned Phenomena," is divided into five parts: first, a general refutation through question and answer.
Furthermore, how is it known that the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) [are identical to] the substance of matter and mind?
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, how" is the Master’s question. The passage beginning with "The Sūtra" is the response provided by other schools citing scripture.

Regarding the phrase "As stated in the Sūtra," the Sarvāstivādins say: "The three characteristics of the conditioned possess distinct, real entities," and so forth. Thus they speak of the "three conditioned [characteristics]."
"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to the three dharmas of arising, abiding, and ceasing; because they are impermanent and possess the sense of transformation, they are called "conditioned.

This sūtra refutes this [view] below in general. Regarding the term "sixth case" (*ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*): according to the *Kaimeng yin*, among the eight grammatical cases (*aṣṭau vibhaktayaḥ*), the sixth is called the "possessive case" (*śeṣa*).
For example, a servant belongs to a master; thus it is called the possessive case. Since the servant and the master are distinct, it expresses a difference in substance (*bheda*).

Now, regarding the statement that it is not the sixth case (ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti): because the substance of form and mind is identical to the substance of arising and so forth, they do not differ in their belonging to the category of "sound" (*śabda*).

This is unlike the case where the master and the servant have distinct substances. According to the enumeration used in *Hetuvidyā* (Logic), the "dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣa*) is called the sixth case;
the "subject" (*dharmin*) is the first case, the "thesis" (*pakṣa*) is the second case, the "reason" (*hetu*) is the third case, and the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the fourth case.
The "homogeneous class" (*sapakṣa*) constitutes the fifth case; the "heterogeneous class" (*vipakṣa*) constitutes the sixth case.

Because that heterogeneous class is distinct from the homogeneous class, it carries the sense of being separate and individual, unlike [the categories of] arising and so forth, which are identical to form and mind. Therefore, it is said that it is not the sixth case.
△ The general refutation through question and answer is concluded. Below follows the specific refutation of the agent and the object.

The nature of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is not definitively different from the characterized (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, the functions of abiding, change, and cessation should not occur simultaneously.
The characteristics are birth and the others; the characterized are form and mind. Solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are the natures of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*):
earth, water, fire, and wind. Solidity and so forth are the natures of earth and the others; thus, nature and characteristic are not distinct. Birth and the others are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
How could it be that form and mind are different? Since conditioned and unconditioned phenomena exist only in mutual dependence, a single unconditioned dharma is neither subject nor object;
how then could there be a "characterized" (lakṣya) that is distinct from the unconditioned? This is intended to clarify that the conditioned is not different from the characterized.

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "arising and so forth" refutes the co-existence of the essence of the characterizer (lakṣaṇa). If those of other vehicles cling to the three types of conditioned phenomena... [the three]... three.

The essence [of these factors] exists simultaneously. It is not necessary that form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) constitute the essence of these three dharmas. The refutation states: they should all function simultaneously at all times.

To say they "exist simultaneously" means that within the essence of arising there are abiding and ceasing; within the essence of abiding there are arising and ceasing; and within the essence of ceasing there are arising and abiding.
Because these three dharmas share the same essence, they are said to exist simultaneously. As for their "functions," these are the dharmas of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Their functions coexist, yet they do not accord with one another; therefore, they are collectively refuted by being raised simultaneously. The *Śataśāstra* states:

"When the essence of a phenomenon arises, its abiding and cessation do not yet exist; when it reaches the stage of abiding and cessation, the characteristic of arising has already ceased. Yet you claim their essence is identical."

This is extremely erroneous. As for the passage beginning "If it were contrary," [the author] refutes the opponent's tenet that the essence [of a phenomenon] exists simultaneously with its attributes by means of the two factors of arising and abiding, which are contrary to cessation. First, he refutes this by means of arising, change, and cessation;

that is to say, if arising and cessation are contrary phenomena and cannot coexist, then the same principle applies to the essence as well. How can you maintain that they constitute a single essence existing simultaneously?

[The argument against] arising and ceasing is next refuted by means of abiding, change, and cessation. That is to say, if abiding and cessation have distinct functions, they likewise ought not to coexist;
how then can one maintain that their substance is identical? Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, regarding abiding and change in relation to cessation, their functions likewise ought not to coexist."
"The essence of both the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) is primordially existent" (up to) "because a cause for their mutual distinction cannot be found.
This refutes the claim that the essences of both the characteristic and the characterized exist simultaneously.

If one asserts that the characteristic must exist as a real entity distinct from matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), and thus clings to the two dharmas—the characteristic and the characterized—as having essences that are both primordially existent, then if the essence is primordially existent, the function (*kāritra*) must also [be so].

It should be so. Why? Because there is the substance of form and mind, and there is the function of the conditioned; there is the substance of the conditioned, and there is the function of arising and ceasing.

Since substance and function do not possess distinct natures, why would they not arise simultaneously? The passage beginning with "If one says" refutes the alternative position that things such as arising are produced by causes and conditions.
If [arising] depends on causes and conditions, then it is produced by causes and conditions; why then do you cling to [the notion of arising] as being separate from the mind?
Because there would be a separate substantial entity, it is further refuted as follows: Furthermore, to maintain that arising and so forth exist substantially apart from the mind is useless.

If you claim that while the characterized phenomena—matter and mind—are eternal, arising and so forth only occasionally conjoin with them, thereby avoiding the objection that they arise all at once, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would likewise be eternal and would also conjoin with arising and so forth. Even if one were to grant that unconditioned phenomena...
Because a distinct cause for the conjunction of birth and so forth between this and that cannot be found, and because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are devoid of arising and ceasing.
△ Second, the specific refutation of the agent and the object is concluded. Below follows the refutation by means of the difficulty of the three time periods.
Furthermore, the past and future worlds are neither manifest nor permanent; therefore, their [proponents'] assertions are irrational from every perspective.
Previously, it was refuted that both time-periods belong to the meaning of cessation: the past has already ceased, and the future has not yet arisen;

thus, both time-periods are equally non-existent, and non-existence is precisely cessation. The Master’s intent in this refutation is as follows: setting aside for a moment arising and abiding, it is just as with the cessation of the past and future.

Phenomena have already ceased and are impermanent; they do not exist in the future nor are they present. Their essence is like a flower in the sky. Why then do you cling to the notion that there is a real intrinsic nature apart from the mind?
The term "arising" refers to existence. Next, by means of the three periods of time, this refutes their attachment to the idea that the essences of arising and ceasing both inherently exist.
If you claim that arising and ceasing share the same essence, since arising is designated as "existence," how could it be identical to that which has already ceased?
Regarding the future: since cessation is defined as non-existence, it should not be the present that has already arisen.

If you concede that cessation is not non-existent in the same way that what has already arisen is not non-existent, then you must concede that arising is not existent in the same way that what has already ceased is not existent.

Therefore, to maintain that they share the same essence contradicts the three time periods. Furthermore, below [the section on] cessation, he again refutes the abiding dharma: advancing, it is the same as cessation; retreating, it is different from arising; both are untenable.
This is the principle. △ The refutation of the three time periods is concluded. Below, the four [sections] correctly clarify the provisional establishment [of time].
However, because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise through the power of causes and conditions... (up to) the last one is non-existent, and thus it exists in the past.
The section "Concluding by revealing the correct meaning: it is merely a provisional designation" (結顯正義唯假立名) explains that [the four names] are fundamentally non-existent.

The section "The first three... further combines these four dharmas into two periods. The intent is to reveal that all dharmas are impermanent, shifting and flowing according to the world, and are provisionally established as moments (*kṣaṇa*).
△ This concludes the fourth section, which correctly clarifies the provisional establishment. Below, the fifth section provides a question-and-answer explanation of the manifestation (*vijñapti*).
"How can [the characteristics] not be associated with conditioned phenomena? (up to) "Therefore, the four characteristics are all conventionally established.

Regarding "How can," etc.: the followers of other vehicles ask. "With what do they share? This means: since cessation (*nirodha*) is a non-existent thing, how can it share the characteristics of present conditioned phenomena?
Regarding "To indicate this," etc.: the Master of the Treatise answers. That is to say, the past phenomenon that has ceased indicates this present arising.
Regarding the dharma of "abiding-and-changing": if that which is subsequently definitely non-existent were to serve as a characteristic of existence, what fault would there be?
[The text] "The arising indicates the lower" explains and establishes the meaning of indication (*vijñapti*). Furthermore, it concludes by clarifying that the meanings of indication differ.

[The text] "This depends on the lower" concludes the previous provisional establishment of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) and introduces the subsequent provisional establishment of a single lifetime (*ekajīvitāntara*). A "single lifetime" refers to the beginning and end of the retribution of one birth.
[This is] so. "First existence" and below explain the four characteristics established as provisional within a single life-span (*ekakalpa*). "First existence" refers to the time of birth.
"Subsequent non-existence" refers to the time of death. "Similar continuity" means that once born, one subsequently grows gradually.
From infancy one becomes youthful; from youth one becomes old. Although the appearance undergoes transformation, the underlying physical characteristics remain similar.

Taken as a whole over this long duration, it is collectively termed "abiding" (*sthiti*). Within this state of abiding, there is a continuous transformation, which is further termed "alteration" (*anyathātva*). Alternatively, it may simply be called "abiding," as this term subsumes "alteration.
Therefore, the following section concludes by establishing these as provisional designations (*prajñapti*), demonstrating that they do not exist substantially. △ Five.

The questions and answers clarifying the [preceding] exposition are concluded. This completes the five sets of three regarding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) mentioned above. Below, the section on the divisions of names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) is divided into two parts.
First, the extensive refutation through questions and answers:

Furthermore, how is it known that [these] are distinct from matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth? [This concludes up to: "This alone is sufficient to express meaning; what use are names and the rest?"
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "How so? below, the Master of the Treatise poses a question. Regarding the phrase "The Sūtra says" below, those of other vehicles cite a sūtra in response.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "What is called a 'name-group' (*nāmakāya*)? It refers to the verbal expressions that arise in accordance with the intrinsic nature and specific characteristics of all phenomena; this is called a name-group."
Just as with the terms "eye" and "ear," which each express a distinct meaning, what is a phrase-group (*padakāya*)?

It refers to the establishment of the virtues and faults of defilement and purity based upon the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those very phenomena; this is called a phrase-group. For example: "The eye can see forms."
The ear is able to hear sounds because of the distinction in their meanings. What is the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*)?

It refers to all bodies of syllables (*akṣarakāya*) that serve as the basis for both names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*). Furthermore, with respect to the objects of knowledge and the things expressed, a brief conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is a phoneme;

it merely apprehends the vocal tones and is unable to discern the distinctions of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). A middle-length conceptualization is a name (*nāman*); it... [apprehends]... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist Abhidharma treatise, likely discussing the three linguistic components—phonemes, names, and phrases—and their functions.)*

One thoroughly understands intrinsic nature and masters phonemes; this is the "extensive contemplation" of these phrases. One completely realizes both the intrinsic nature and the distinctions of phonemes.
That which is attained by the Buddha is free from the characteristics of names and phrases, and free from the characteristics of letters; therefore, it is called "extraordinary.
As for what is conceived by other vehicles—that there exist real entities of name-bodies, phrase-bodies, and letter-bodies external to form and mind—the following scripture is cited [to refute this]:

[The opponent] cites this sutra as proof. Below this, the Master of the Treatise refutes it in general. He says: In this sutra, it is stated only that the Buddha attained rare and marvelous sets of names, phrases, and phonemes;
it does not state that there exists a substantial entity separate from the mind. Therefore, as proof, it is unestablished.
If [the opponent] argues that these names and so forth exist apart from sound, or arise based on sound: if they existed apart from sound, they would have to be like form and other such phenomena.

It is not a real designator (*vācaka*). Since there is no designator of meaning apart from sound, if [the designation] arises in dependence upon sound, then the sound itself—possessing its own phonetic cadence—is sufficient to constitute the designator.
Why, then, must one separately maintain that names (*nāman*) and so forth exist as real entities to serve as designators?
If it is argued that the phonetic modulations upon sound (up to the point of) grasping the distinctness of the expressive [words] belong only to the "Heavenly Affection" (the gods) and not to others;
or if it is argued as follows— that by analogy with the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), one refutes the sense-base of sound (*śabdāyatana*)—

and if it is further argued that while the phonetic modulations produced in dependence on sound are indeed names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*), yet these exist as real entities separate from sound, then this is what you perceive.

The shapes and configurations of matter would have to exist as substantial entities even apart from the locus of matter; however, since there are no configurations apart from the locus of matter, this is not the case.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage refutes that counter-argument and further challenges the claim that sound cannot produce names and so forth.
That is to say, the previous position held that the configurations of phonemes do not exist substantially apart from sound; thus, it is understood that those [phonemes] are themselves sound.
[The opponent’s position is] convoluted, like the sound of stringed instruments or pipes; it is not a real designator (*vācaka*).

Therefore, he further refutes it, saying: "Since these vocal sounds are like stringed instruments or pipes, they do not produce names and so forth.
Why then do you insist that based on sound, names and so forth can be produced? Furthermore, who says that those [sounds] are definitely incapable of designating?"

The proponents of other vehicles maintain that the "syllable" (*akṣara*) is simply sound. Their intention is to accept that names (*nāman*) and so forth, which are produced by sound, function as the expressive agents.

The Master [Vasubandhu] cites and refutes this: "If it is accepted that sound acts as the expressive agent, then the sounds of wind-chimes and the like should also possess the capacity for expression.
This being not the case, why do you insist that these vocal sounds—just like those of wind-chimes and the like—are the basis upon which names and so forth are produced?
If it were only the lower [view], the Master would employ skillful means to reveal the principle while simultaneously censuring their clinging attachment.

That is to say, they are deludedly attached to the idea that names and so forth arise from the sounds of speech, failing to realize that speech itself is capable of signification. "By what principle?"—this is the interrogation by those of other vehicles; that is, by what reasoning?
Regarding the claim that "speech is the expressive agent," this is because they maintain that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are the expressive agents.

Since they do not realize that speech and names are like the two sides of a brocade—differing only in their orientation—how could they know that something other than speech possesses the capacity for expression?

"Speech is not different from that which follows below. This is the Master’s explanation. "That which is understood by both humans and devas" means that humans and devas together hear the speech and comprehend its various meanings.

within the sounds of speech, there are high and low, clear and dull, granting and withholding, suppression and exaltation, single names and multiple names, short phrases and long phrases;

"Phoneme" signifies the manifestation of meaning, because it manifests and expresses both. If one asks: "Since these three are established as conventional designations, their substance is simply sound (*ghoṣa*);

They are neither identical nor distinct. Because the three arise from sound, they are not distinct; because the provisional and the real are each separate, they are not identical.

"The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid) takes provisional names and the like as its object; the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) takes actual sounds and the like as its object. Although...
The two natures are mutually inseparable. Because a *dharma* (phenomenon) corresponds to its signified meaning, it takes names (*nāman*) and so forth as its object.

Because speech (*vyañjana*) mostly corresponds to the capacity of the listener, it takes sound (*śabda*) alone as its object; this is because once the ear has heard the sound, the mind comprehends the meaning.

Thus, while the two are said to differ because their respective objects differ, they do not differ in essence. Their essence is simply sound. Sound, along with names and so forth, is subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

That which consists of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*), and the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*) belongs exclusively to sound, because sound is a phenomenon of form (*rūpadharma*).

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) belong to names, phrases, and syllables, because among the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), there exist [the factors] such as name (*nāman*) and so forth. For now, this is based on the lower [treatise].
This establishes that both [the name-body, phrase-body, and syllable-body] are merely conventional designations. That is to say, for the time being, this is based on this world-system;

it is based on sound that the name-, phrase-, and syllable-bodies are conventionally designated, not implying that they are established based on sound in all world-systems. Suppose one asks: "In other world-systems..."

Upon what basis are they provisionally established? The answer is: In other buddha-fields as well, the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes are provisionally established based on light, sublime fragrances, tastes, and so forth;
for by means of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing that light, fragrance, and taste, one is able to comprehend the meaning.

"Those who hold the lower [view]"—this raises their position. "Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)" refers to defiled mental factors such as greed; "latent" (*anu*) has the meaning of co-arising, and "disposition" (*śaya*) has the meaning of a seed.

The phrase "separate from... and below summarizes the remaining formations. There are other non-associated formations, namely the ten types not yet refuted:

namely, flux (pravṛtti), distinctness (anyathātva), association (samyoga), momentum (java), succession (anukrama), time (kāla), direction (deśa), number (saṃkhyā), and the nature of combination (sāmagrī).

Regarding the statement that the "collection of names" (*nāmakāya*), "collection of phrases" (*padakāya*), and "collection of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*) should all be refuted, this is also according to the same reasoning as above; it refutes the latter ten [categories].
△ Third, the conclusion by citing the [opponent's] adherence to their position. This concludes the two types of dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Below are the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), divided into three parts. First, the general refutation.

This restates the previous section to provide a general thesis and a general refutation. Now, regarding "the definitively existent dharmas, which are briefly of three kinds":

The mind is the subject that cognizes; form is the object of cognition. That which is known in the present is the meaning of "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*).
Examples such as a jar or a garment refer to things currently being used: a jar can contain substances, and a garment can cover the body; this present utility is the meaning of "conditioned.
These two types of phenomena are commonly known by the world to exist, and their existence does not depend on further proof through logical reasons. This concludes the discussion of what is known.
The experience of these two factors is commonly known by worldly people; it does not require the formulation of a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) before it can be understood.
Therefore, it is said that they do not depend on a logical reason for their establishment. Regarding those phenomena that possess functional activity, such as the eyes and ears:

this means that through the five sense organs, such as the eyes, consciousness is produced which takes the five sense objects as its conditions. Through each respective organ, a corresponding consciousness is produced. By means of this activity of producing consciousness, one employs inference (*anumāna*).
One should know that there are five supreme faculties (paramārthendriya) which differ from the former two; they are established without depending on causes.
These are dharmas possessing activity in the present, and they also carry the sense of being conditioned (saṃskṛta).

The phrase "unconditioned [phenomena] are not commonly known by the world to definitely exist" (up to) "there is no real unconditioned nature apart from matter, mind, and so forth" correctly refutes the claim that unconditioned phenomena are not substantially existent. This means:

your adherence to unconditioned phenomena—which are neither of the two aforementioned categories and are not commonly known to exist in the world—constitutes an adherence to their existence that contradicts worldly consensus. Furthermore, your adherence to unconditioned phenomena...

Just like the eye and so forth, because they possess functional activity. If something possesses functional activity, it must be impermanent. Since it is impermanent, it contradicts your own tenet of permanence;

therefore, one cannot maintain that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) exists as a real entity. Now, the passage beginning with "However, all... concludes by demonstrating that the unconditioned is not real.
Regarding "the nature of being an object of knowledge" (*jñeyatva*): this refers to the mental apprehension of the presence or absence of the term "unconditioned" following its hearing from others.
It is their nature. As for the nature that is manifested, it consists of form and mind, which exhaust the meanings of cause and effect within the conditioned;

or, when conditions are lacking, they lack the function of being conditioned, thereby manifesting as unconditioned. This nature of the knowable and this manifested nature are like form, mind, and so forth.
All these are impermanent; therefore, one must not cling to the notion that they exist substantially apart from the mind. △ The general refutation is complete. Below follows the specific refutation.
Furthermore, as for space and so forth, are they one or many? (Up to: Because it would logically follow that if one clings to their essence as being one, such a principle ought to be so.

The nature is fundamentally pure; it is not purified by the power of analytical discernment, for its essence is inherently pure. Why then do you cling to the view that unconditioned phenomena are truly eternal? Furthermore, space (*ākāśa*) would likewise not be all-pervasive or capable of containing all things. This specifically refutes the existence of space.
It has many essences. If the essence of space were manifold, then many spaces and many phenomena would each occupy and contain their own respective places; how then could it be called "empty space"?
It is called "pervasive" because it is able to universally contain and receive, being one that contains the many.

As for what is clung to by other schools—since those of the Hīnayāna admit only the first three [types of space]—the mention here of "other schools" may refer to those who cling to the latter three types, namely: [The text continues with the enumeration of these three.]

Below, three points cite the correct meaning of the scriptures.

This means that upon hearing the names of the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) spoken, the mind immediately transforms into the images (*nimitta*) of those six unconditioned phenomena.
From this transformation based on hearing, repeated perfuming (*vāsanā*) occurs; through the long-term power of such habitual practice, they are clearly remembered without forgetting.

This is a designation. It refers to the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) characteristics that manifest from consciousness.

From the time one first hears them taught, through their manifestation at a later time, and throughout the interval when they repeatedly appear, these characteristics remain similar and undergo no change; thus they are conventionally called "unconditioned.
While they possess the sense of being real and permanent, they do not exist apart from the mind as entities with a substantial self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, because they are provisionally established based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) things are not definitively real existents.

This explains the meaning of their provisional existence based on the nature of phenomena. That is to say, it is the suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the emptiness of persons and the absence of a self.

because its essence and characteristics are distinct, it is not identical; because it is both essence and characteristic, it is not different. This intends to reveal that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the true rational nature of the characteristics of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). From the phrase "detached from all... below, there is a separate explanation of the five [elements], beginning with space.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are all merely provisional designations. That is to say, the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is vast and boundless, accommodating all things without obstruction;

it is thus metaphorically named "space" (*ākāśa*). "Discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to analytical discernment, and "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the cessation through abandonment. This means that the noble ones (*ārya*) realize the nature of *tathatā*.

Obscured by various hindrances and defilements, [the nature of reality] is covered and not made manifest. By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one discriminatively extinguishes all afflictions (*kleśa*).

When the hindrances of affliction are ultimately eliminated, one is able to sever the fundamental ignorance and directly realize *tathatā* (suchness). One then attains an equal union with the essence of *tathatā*, which is conventionally designated as "discriminative cessation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, the essence of *tathatā* is the very nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is inherently pure from the beginning; it is not something severed through the power of discrimination.
It is manifested by cessation. Alternatively, when conditions for various phenomena are lacking and they do not arise, this reveals suchness; this is the meaning of "non-arising.
Therefore, the name "analytical cessation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is provisionally established.

Furthermore, the suchness manifested by the fourth dhyāna—which, being distinct from the three preceding concentrations, transcends the three calamities and eight afflictions, and is free from the movements of joy, pleasure, and so forth that agitate body and mind—is designated as such because it is revealed by these [qualities].
It is given a name; "immovable" is provisionally established. Furthermore, in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), ideation and sensation do not function;

this very state is provisionally established and named the "cessation of ideation and sensation. Thus, these five kinds [of names] are provisionally established based on the ultimate truth (*tathatā*).

As explained below, it is further clarified that the ultimate truth (*tathatā*) is also provisionally designated with various names and meanings. That is to say, the meaning of *tathatā* is free from the provisional and free from the real; it is neither existent nor...
Emptiness is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and transcends all dualistic oppositions. How can it be expressed through names?

These names are established merely as provisional designations to negate attachment; they are provisionally termed "existent" to negate those who deny the nature of phenomena, and they are provisionally termed "empty" to negate those who cling to the existence of a phenomenal nature.
As for the term "illusory," "illusory" refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Illusion is precisely the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). One must not grant that sentient beings are [mere] illusions;

rather, it is said that *tathatā* (suchness) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the true reality of all phenomena, which is truly not inverted or false. It is with respect to this very principle that the provisional name "suchness" is applied.

This differs from the [views of] the lower vehicles, which refute the false attachment to unconditioned phenomena as being separate from the mind. [Therefore,] these [unconditioned phenomena] are certainly not substantially existent. Thus, all...

Unconditioned [phenomena] can only be provisionally established. △ This concludes the third section on unconditioned phenomena. Together with the preceding two sections, this concludes the discussion regarding other vehicles.
Below, three points collectively refute the aforementioned attachments.

these are not of a truly existent nature. [The text asks: "When you take the mind as its object—such as mountains, rivers, and so forth—and grasp them as distinct, real objects existing outside the mind, why [is this not also an attachment to phenomena]?"
When one perceives that object, does one immediately realize that the object is the grasping mind? The intent here is to point out that there are no phenomena external to the mind;
there is only the perceiving mind. As will be explained below, the text subsequently refutes this very perceiving mind.

Herein, the innate clinging to phenomena and the subsequent conceptual clinging to phenomena are identical in wording to the preceding discussion on the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*), differing only in that they involve the clinging to a self versus the clinging to phenomena, and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) versus the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The [section on] grasping is concluded. Below, the two types of conceptual attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) are distinguished.
Conceptual attachment to phenomena is also eliminated by means of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), once it has reached the present.
△ The second section, the detailed analysis of the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), is concluded. Below follows the third section, which summarizes the internal and external [graspings].
Thus, all the aforementioned graspings at phenomena (up to) the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) being like illusory things and so forth.

Since the *Zongjing* was previously cited to explain the identity of self and phenomena, it will not be explained again here. However, as for the passage "yet they appear," which explains that all these phenomena arise from conditions:

they are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and because they exist [as appearances], they are like illusions. The real phenomena that are grasped are the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); they are certainly not substantially existent. Therefore...

"World-Honored One," etc., cites the words of the Sage as proof to make it known that all phenomena are merely manifestations of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), so that one does not cling to the notion that there are real entities existing separately from the mind.

△ This concludes the third section, the summary of the internal and external; and together with the preceding two sections, this concludes the specific inquiry regarding the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
The following three lines provide a summary of my doctrine:

Thus, that which is grasped by non-Buddhists and those of other vehicles (up to the point where it is said) revolves as if resembling those [external objects] because the mind is turbid due to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

This collectively concludes that both the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) do not exist apart from the mind. Furthermore, a formal inference (*anumāna*) is established as an illustration to clarify this: "External forms and so forth... [is as follows].
Those external phenomena grasped by them, which possess a real substantial nature, are precisely the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent origination) arising from conditions.

In contrast to that false attachment, it is said that the dependent is "real"; yet in contrast to the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected reality), it is said to be "like an illusory phenomenon. Regarding the term "that collection":
every sentient being necessarily possesses the eight consciousnesses and the fifty-one mental factors gathered together; therefore, it is called "mind" (*citta*).
The aggregate refers to that person’s mental aggregate. Although it exists as a real entity, it is not the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for this [other] person’s mind;

how much less so could it be an objective condition if it were a distinct substantial entity apart from the mind? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows: The mental aggregate of another person is the subject (*dharmin*).

It is not the direct objective condition for one's own consciousness, this is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is comprised within the aggregate of another. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is as follows: [Whatever is comprised within the aggregate of another is not the direct objective condition for one's own consciousness].

Just as that which is not an object of cognition (*ālambana*) is not the mind’s object, so too the mind is the cognizer; because it is not an object of cognition, it is like [other factors] gathered in the same assembly.

"Gathered in the same assembly" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*) of one's own mind, which are not the direct objects of cognition for the primary mind (*cittarāja*), let alone external phenomena.

To establish this through formal inference (*pramāṇa*): the mental factors gathered in the same assembly are the subject (*dharmin*); the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are also not the direct objects of cognition for their own consciousness; the reason (*hetu*) is "because of their own nature."
Because they are distinct. A common analogy is like other things that are not objects of apprehension (*anupādeya*).

"A person is like fire. This is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*) that does not establish itself based on a substantial reality (*dravya*). This concludes the refutation of the conventional as not being based on the substantial.

This is conventional cognition. When one speaks the word "fire," this constitutes verbal expression; yet the fire does not burn the mouth, nor does it burn the mind.

This is because conventional cognition and its expression both fail to apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Why is this? Because the specific characteristic of fire consists in its capacity to burn objects.

Regarding that which functions solely based on common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*): it relies upon the substantial entity (*dravya*) to manifest a reflected image (*pratibimba*), and this is termed a "common characteristic.

This is a characteristic that arises together with the substantial entity for conceptual cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*). It is only upon this characteristic that names and expressions arise; therefore, conceptual cognition and its designations rely solely upon common characteristics.
Furthermore, this does not mean that apart from these common characteristics, there is no other means for the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) of specific characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*).

It serves as the basis for conventional cognition and linguistic expression. Now, regarding the phrase "where linguistic expression does not reach," this refers to the meaning of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, while conventional cognition and linguistic expression arise by means of sounds, that which is beyond the reach of sound is called the self-characteristic of phenomena (*dharmasvalakṣaṇa*).
If there were no locus for sound, conventional cognition (*prajñapti-jñāna*) and its designations (*abhilāpa*) would have no basis to function.

Since both the designator (*vācaka*) and the designated (*vācya*) lack intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), the designator is speech itself and the designated is conventional cognition; that is, conventional cognition as the designator cannot apprehend an intrinsic characteristic, and thus they are said to "both lack" it.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "Hence we know" concludes by establishing them as mere conventional designations (*prajñapti-vāda*). They rely solely upon "semblance-objects" (*pratibimba-vastu*); "semblance" refers to what follows.

Because it superimposes a characteristic upon that [basis], it is called "resembling" (*sadṛśa*). Sound gives rise to cognition that expresses [meaning] solely by relying on this superimposed resembling characteristic.

Therefore, it cannot be said [that they are identical]. A provisional designation must necessarily rely upon the real. Thus, the following concludes that the refutation of the objection is irrational. △ Four:

Because they do not arise simultaneously, the three ripen in different categories; this category and that category are distinct from one another.

The first of these is exclusively the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), while the latter two pertain to both the death and rebirth of fragmentation (*bheda-jarāmaraṇa*). Regarding "constantly and thoroughly deliberating": "constant" means uninterrupted;

the detailed explanation of the three names. Below follows the third section: the transformation as cause and effect, which is divided into two parts. First, the enumeration of the numbers.

First, *causal transformation* (*hetu-pariṇāma*) refers to the eighth consciousness, wherein impure wholesome and unwholesome [seeds] are perfumed (*vāsita*) and caused to grow.

Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are themselves seeds; therefore, they are called the "causally transformative. When, at the time of perfuming (*bhāvanā*), one receives their subtle influence, it is termed "habitual tendency.

Regarding "outflow" (*niṣyanda*): it refers to that which is of the same kind and possesses the sense of being a direct producer. Regarding "maturation" (*vipāka*): it refers to that which is distinct.

There is the sense of mutual assistance. Regarding "the habit-energies of equal outflow" (*nisyanda-vāsanā*): this refers to the first seven consciousnesses, which, by the power of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), perfume the eighth consciousness to form seeds that subsequently grow.
Later, from these seeds, the active states (*pravṛtti*) of the first seven consciousnesses arise;

because cause and effect are of the same kind, they are called "equal outflow. Regarding "the habit-energies of maturation" (*vipāka-vāsanā*): this refers to the first six consciousnesses, which [perfume it] solely through contaminated wholesome [states].
The two natures of evil permeate the eighth consciousness, forming seeds of good and evil and causing them to grow.

Subsequently, from these two types of karma—good and evil—the eighth consciousness is summoned to experience the fruits of suffering and pleasure. Being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), where cause and effect are distinct, this is termed "ripening" (*vipāka*).
The second [type], the fruit-transforming [consciousness], refers to the aforementioned two kinds [of consciousness] up to what is called the *vipāka-phala* (maturation fruit).

Because the fruit differs from its cause, the fruit undergoes transformation in accordance with the cause; thus, the aforementioned two kinds of latencies act as the causes that project the eight consciousnesses as the fruit.

Regarding "various characteristics," this refers to the manifest characteristics of the eight kinds of consciousness. Below, "equal outflow" (*nisyanda*) provides a detailed explanation of production through causal conditions.
This is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*). Regarding the "direct causal condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*): it refers to the arising of its own manifest activity from its own seed;

that is, each of the eight consciousnesses arises as a manifest activity from its respective direct seed, and is thus called an "outflow. Because cause and effect are of the same category, the fruit is said to resemble the cause.
Below, regarding "ripening" (*vipāka*): this explains the ripening fruit produced by the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). As for the "dominant condition," it means...

Wholesome and unwholesome karma draws the eighth consciousness to repay the projecting karma (ākṣepaka-karma) of others; because it continues for a long duration without interruption, it is designated by the name "vipāka" (maturation).

Because the fruit is perfected.

It is subtle and obscure, because it is difficult to discern both in terms of its appropriation (*upātta*) and its locus (*āyatana*).

It is always associated with contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), because among the six classes of mental factors (*caitasika*), this consciousness is associated only with the universal class.

It is exclusively the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because it lacks suffering and pleasure. It is non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), among the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*).
Because it is singular. "Contact and so forth are also thus" means that the mind-king and its mental factors are of the same nature.

Explaining the three names.

it is established based on the characteristic of being a fruit of reliance, because it produces its own fruit in accordance with the causal karma of others. This [section] below distinguishes [this consciousness] from the rest.

This interrogates what kind of phenomenon the "seed" (*bīja*) is. The answer clarifies that the seed is a specific functional capacity (*śakti-viśeṣa*) within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) that directly produces its own fruit.
Thus, it is called a "seed" by virtue of being this functional capacity that gives rise to manifest phenomena as its fruits.
The "fundamental consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness. "Directly producing its own fruit" means [producing] from its own seeds.
Because it produces the manifest fruit of its own kind. Regarding the distinction of functional capacity (*śakti-viśeṣa*), this indicates that these seeds are not of a single type.
This and what follows mean that these seeds, the eighth consciousness, and the fruits they produce are neither identical nor different.

The essence is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the fruit is the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*). The essence of consciousness is the function (*kāritra*) in relation to the seeds, while the manifest fruit is the cause (*hetu*) in relation to the seeds.
Therefore, these three dharmas, according to principle, should be neither identical nor different. The *Zongjing* states: "The fundamental consciousness is the essence."
The seed is the function; the seed is the cause; that which is produced is the fruit. These three phenomena, according to reason, must be neither identical nor different.
If they were identical, one could not speak of the existence of cause and effect, because they would possess the same substance and nature.
If they were entirely different, then rice, wheat, and so forth would be able to produce beans and the like, since you [the opponent] admit the existence of cause and effect.

Because they would be entirely distinct. This is not so; for if it were otherwise, the dharma would only have its function once it has ceased, since you admit that essence and function are entirely distinct.

Where essence and function resemble one another, their momentum and influence must necessarily be identical; where cause and effect resemble one another, their capacities and characteristics can correspond with each other. They are not entirely distinct.

Although this does not resolve the objection raised below, it addresses the concern expressed above regarding [the principle of] being neither identical nor different. Otherwise, one might fear it would be the same as...
Regarding the Bodhisattva’s reckoning: there is a nature that is both existent and equal to existence; it is neither identical nor different. Therefore, he himself explains:

"It is substantially existent because it arises from the transformations of one's own mind. As for "provisional phenomena," these refer to what is conceptually imputed by others as existing externally to the mind.
Just as that which is ultimately non-existent does not arise from causes and conditions,
if this [ultimate] were neither identical to nor different from all phenomena, then it would follow that there is no such thing as true ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).
The opponent objects: Since this seed and the manifesting consciousness (vijñāna-pravṛtti) are neither identical nor different, they must be like a jar and so forth.
Just as a lump of clay and a jar are neither identical nor different, you must admit that the essence of the jar is a conventional designation (prajñapti).

If so, then your fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna) is likewise conventional, like the jar; and the untainted seeds of true suchness (anāsrava-tathatā-bīja) within that consciousness would also have to be conventional. This would lead to a logical fallacy.

According to our own school’s true ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), however, all seeds exist only conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). [They are] subsumed under the category of being exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) because they are associated with the wholesome nature.

The Master [Vasubandhu] explains: "However, it is said that the seeds of all phenomena within consciousness are neither identical to nor different from it, and that they are substantially existent (*dravyasat*)."

This is because the nature of *tathatā* is free from the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of identity and difference. Although seeds are explained below as being based on the defiled (*sāsrava*), they are not the same as *tathatā*.
This is because the defiled seeds are the objects of perception (*ālambana*) for the eighth consciousness, whereas *tathatā* and the undefiled seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are not.

Regarding the object within the causal state, it is only when the subsequent transformation of the basis occurs that the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) becomes perfectly luminous and is then able to take [the object] as its condition.

Thus, concerning all impure states below, the relationship between the seeds of clarity and consciousness is neither identical nor different. This means that the seeds and consciousness are of the same substance and both possess an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).

This is called "non-different. Regarding the phrase "both cause and effect exist," this means that the cause, which is the seed, is the perfuming consciousness and it encompasses all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The effect, which is the manifesting consciousness, likewise possesses the three natures. Therefore, [it is non-different] from the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
It is described as "not one. This "not one" refers to the seeds of the out-flowing (sāsrava) dharmas, not to suchness (tathatā).

The True Dharma distinguishes itself from the false. This refers to that which arises through the perfuming of similar True Dharmas, caused by hearing the untainted, pure Dharma.

"The Pure Dharma-realm" refers to the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas, because it is eternally free from all adventitious obscurations. Regarding the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), it means [arising] from the Dharma-realm.
The teachings that have arisen are heard without error; such teachings are therefore called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).

Based on this correct hearing, the resulting perfuming (*vāsanā*) is termed "perfuming. This very perfuming is able to produce the supramundane, untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), and is thus called a "seed" (*bīja*).
As it is said: "For all bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon awakening..."

There exists the seed of the permeation of correct hearing; although it is termed "worldly," one should know that it is subsumed within the Dharma-body and is capable of directly producing the seeds of supramundane mind.
△ The first section, establishing the thesis and citing proof, is concluded. Below, the second section refutes the previous attachments by restating them.

Sentient beings possess inherent distinctions in their fundamental natures (gotra) from the very beginning; these arise based on perfuming (vāsanā), rather than existing as pre-existing substantial entities.

The nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). The two vehicles do not abandon the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), but only abandon the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The wick can produce the flame, and the flame burns and consumes the wick; the seed produces the manifest activity, and the manifest activity perfumes the seed.

It is an *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition), not a *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition). To illustrate this by analogy with the aforementioned "perfuming for growth," it is likewise an *adhipati-pratyaya*, not a *hetu-pratyaya*.

Third: First, refuting by means of correct reasoning.

If only that which first arises were the cause of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena, wholesome states, and so forth, then they would have to be the seeds of unwholesome states and so forth.

This refutes Nanda’s position that only that which first arises is the seed. If only that which first arises [were the seed], it must necessarily be produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*), and thus there would be a cause [for its arising].
Regarding the timing [of their arising]: conditioned uncontaminated phenomena arise through perfuming. If there were no causal conditions, conditioned uncontaminated phenomena could never arise.
How, then, could currently existing contaminated and uncontaminated seeds exist? If they were to begin to arise without causal conditions, they would have a beginning in time.

The seeds of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) should produce one another; likewise, the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, would mutually serve as seeds for each other.

If this were admitted, then the outflowing [seeds] of the Buddhas would arise once again, which would constitute a great error; therefore, it is said that the outflowing cannot be the cause of the non-outflowing, and so on.
The above constitutes the refutation. Its intent lies in revealing that the seeds are inherently existent; therefore, it raises the objection based on their mutual production.

If [the mind] were produced through perfuming, it would necessarily contradict one's own school’s tenets. As for the Vibhajyavādins, they are those among the four Nikāyas who engage in analytical discussion.
Regarding the statement that "the nature of the mind is originally pure," this refers to the essence of the true mind, which is inherently pure from the beginning;

this reveals that the untainted seeds are innately present. Just as a guest depends on a host to establish itself, and dust is manifested by space, the metaphors of the "host" and "space" illustrate their innate existence.
Suchness (*tathatā*). The metaphor of adventitious dust refers to afflictions newly perfumed; therefore, at the time of being freed from defilement, it transforms into the untainted (*anāsrava*).

This reveals that the untainted seeds are simply this very Suchness, designated by the term "transformation. For this reason, the Master of the Treatise further clarifies its primordial existence, stating:
Therefore, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not arise without a cause; True Suchness (*tathatā*) is their cause. This is the meaning of "inherently existent" (*prakṛti-stha*).
[Section One: The Correct Doctrine of that School concluded. Below follows two successive refutations.

They maintain that the primordial nature (prakṛti) is eternally unitary, while the twenty-three principles undergo transformation in their characteristics.

The substance of your mind is one and the same, yet there occurs a transformation between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as between the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, it would follow that these [latter] states must be wholesome (*kuśala*). That is to say, the untainted is wholesome; the mind thus possesses all three natures (*tri-vidha-svabhāva*).

They should act as causes for one another; hence it is said: "Do not [assume] that the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth, are mutual causes.
This is because if a contaminated mind has an uncontaminated nature, their seeds and their manifesting natures and characteristics are identical.
Furthermore, they are mutually refuted by means of the distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, if an outflowing mind is by nature non-outflowing, and thus one allows that an outflowing mind serves as the cause for a non-outflowing mind, then a non-outflowing mind should likewise be by nature outflowing, and the two would also serve as causes for one another.
Therefore, it is further challenged: "Because no distinct causal conditions can be found. If...
If you grant that the nature [of the mind] is untainted (*anāsrava*), then the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would also be untainted by nature.
While in the state of an ordinary person, if the untainted were to manifest, they should be called a noble one (*ārya*); why then would they be called an ordinary person?

If you argue that because the characteristics of an ordinary person are defiled, it is not called untainted, then the seeds of the mind would likewise not be untainted. Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of seeds and their manifestations are identical.

Because they are identical. Since one who manifests through the seeds of an Ārya must necessarily be an Ārya, and since those whose characteristics (*nimitta*) are defiled must necessarily be defiled in nature (*svabhāva*), it follows by logical inference that the seeds and their manifestations must be identical.

This objection refers to Nanda, who maintains that the meaning of "possessing" (*samanvāgama*) refers to the fact that the seeds—both the perfumed (*bhāvya*) and the perfumer (*bhāvaka*)—have been established from beginningless time.

External grains such as rice and wheat are transformations of consciousness; therefore, they are fruits produced by common-characteristic seeds.

Excluding external seeds, they possess only a nominal existence. Both internal and external seeds possess two types of causes: the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) and the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*).

With respect to the sprout, the external seed acts as the cause of production; with respect to the stem and so forth, it acts as the cause of projection. As for the ālayavijñāna, [it functions similarly].

This internal seed is the direct cause for the production of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); it is the indirect cause for the subsequent stages from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

It is like shooting an arrow: the force exerted when releasing the string is the cause of production; that which causes the arrow not to fall immediately to the ground after leaving the string is the cause of projection.
