This is because the explanation of the term "cognition" (*vijñapti*) includes it within the seeing division;

since there must necessarily be an object-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its objective condition (*ālambana*), Nanda established these two divisions to refute Sthiramati’s position that there is only one division. Now, regarding "contaminated," this is because [it has not yet...]

The transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) necessarily possesses two aspects. That which resembles the objective support consists of the two aspects of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), appearing as the two aspects of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
The statement that "the associated [factors] are likewise" indicates that mental factors (caitta) also arise based upon the mind (citta).

Below the section on "resembling the object of cognition" (*ālambana*), the names of the two parts are explained and established. Regarding the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*), there are generally four types:

1. The "image" named after its true nature (*lakṣaṇa-nimitta*): Its essence is *tathatā* (suchness), because it is the true characteristic. 2. The "image" named after its objective field (*viṣaya-nimitta*): It serves as the objective field for the mind and the sense faculties.

3. The "image" named after its formal appearance (*ākāra-nimitta*): Only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess this image, because they have formal characteristics and appearances. This applies universally.

Because the image (*pratibimba*) and the substance (*dravya*) are transformations of consciousness, there are four meanings for the term "aspect" (*nimitta*): first, the aspect as the signifier; second, the aspect as the signified meaning;

third, the aspect as the objective part (*nimittabhāga*), which refers to the latter three among the aforementioned four; and fourth, the aspect as the subjective part (*darśanabhāga*). Regarding the subjective part, there are five categories in total:

first, that which is called "seeing" in the sense of realization, namely fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); second, that which is called "seeing" in the sense of illumination, which applies generally to the faculties...
1. That which illuminates simultaneously with consciousness is called "view" (*darśana*), because it is capable of perceiving; this refers to the three internal [aspects of consciousness]. 2.
That which possesses both mindfulness and discernment is called "view," because the mind that possesses mindfulness and discernment understands the signified meaning. 3.

That which involves inferential deliberation is called "view," because the mind of inference (*anumāna*) deliberates upon its object. Among these five types, one excludes the five material sense organs and two of the internal [aspects]. The remainder...
This is called the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*).

If the mind and mental factors lacked the characteristic of an object of cognition (*ālambana-nimitta*), then the various parts—the cognizing subject and the cognized object—would each function spontaneously.
This refutes the position of Sthiramati, who asserts that there is only a single part. If there were no object of cognition, it would be impossible for [the mind] to cognize its own object.
Regarding the object of cognition: if it does not take its own object as its condition, it must take another object as its condition.

Therefore, it is further argued: otherwise, each individual mind would be able to take all objects as its conditions. Why? Because its own object would be like other objects, and other objects would be like its own object.
If there were no capacity for cognition, it would be like space and so forth; for the essence of space lacks the functional capacity for cognition. If the mind and mental factors were like space...

[Objection: Space is empty; therefore, space should be like the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Furthermore, it is argued: "Alternatively, space and so forth are also capable of being cognitive subjects (*ālambaka*).
Why? Because space is like the mind and mental factors. Thus, following the section on the mind and mental factors, [the author] establishes his own position and further cites a sūtra as proof.
The first two lines of the verse refute the existence of external objects; the third line proves the duality of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The division into the perceiving subject and the perceived object constitutes the fourth phrase, which clarifies that [the object] arises through the transformation of consciousness. △ This concludes the first section on Nanda’s two-fold division.
Below follows the second section on Dignāga’s three-fold division, which consists of three parts. First, it explains the meaning of the three-fold division according to external adherents.

Regarding those who maintain that there exists an objective referent (ālambana) distinct from consciousness: [up to] because the characteristics of consciousness, sensation, perception, and so forth, are each distinct.
The external opponent maintains that the external object is the objective referent (*ālambana*), which constitutes the first part.

From the transformation of that object, the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is called the "aspect" (*ākāra*), which constitutes the second part. The perceiving-seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is called the "self-substance" (*svabhāva*), which constitutes the third part. This refers to the mind (*citta*).
"Shared with the mental factors" (cittasādhāraṇa) and below means that the mind and its mental factors share the same sense faculty as their basis and share the same object of perception;

this is called "similarity of aspect" (ākārasādṛśya). "Entity" refers to the mind-king (citta-rāja), while "number" refers to the mental factors (caitta). "Equal" means they are equally termed the "seeing portion" (darśana-bhāga).

This indicates that although the mind and its mental factors are equally the seeing portion, their specific characteristics—such as discernment (*vijñapti*) for the mind and experiencing (*anubhava*) for sensation (*vedanā*)—are each distinct. Thus, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is defined as discernment.

Regarding the modes of activity (*ākāra*): sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, take the acts of experiencing and so on as their respective modes of activity; therefore, they each differ.
This is because one realizes that there is no object of cognition apart from consciousness, and thus the essential natures of consciousness, sensation, and the others possess distinct differences.

Second, the internal establishment of the threefold division (*triprakāra*). This refers to those who have attained penetration that there are no objects apart from consciousness; they have already understood the meaning of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). The *Zongjing* says:

"Taking consciousness-only as the thesis (*siddhānta*), one does not take the primary object (*bimba*) as the objective support (*ālambana*), nor is the reflected image (*pratibimba*) the aspect (*ākāra*).
Therefore, the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is taken as the objective support, and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) is taken as the aspect. Thus, the image-part and the seeing-part...
[The parts] all arise as manifestations from one's own consciousness; therefore, the substance of the consciousness that serves as the support is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
The phrase "if this were non-existent" below means that the meaning of the self-verifying portion must necessarily exist. This intends to refute Nanda’s position of establishing only two portions.

For example, when the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*)—by means of the aspect of blue—induces the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) to perceive the color blue, there must necessarily be the visual consciousness's own...
When the aspect of the object (grāhyabhāga) ceases, the aspect of seeing (grāhakabhāga) immediately perishes, because the aspect of seeing is produced by the aspect of the object;
since it has arising and ceasing, when the aspect of seeing is subsequently induced by a yellow aspect and takes that yellow as its object, it necessarily does not take the blue as its object.
Therefore, the self-cognizing aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) alone remembers the objective aspect of the previously experienced blue, for the essence of the self-cognizing aspect is non-dual.
Because [the mind] arises and ceases while remaining in constant succession, there is no self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), for it would necessarily be impossible to recollect [it].

Regarding the statement that "the mind and its mental factors have distinct modes of activity" (*ākāra*): although the primary consciousness (*rāja*) and its mental factors (*paryāpanna*) share the same sense organ and object, their modes of activity differ.
The mode of activity of consciousness is discernment (*vijñapti*); the modes of activity of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are experiencing (*anubhava*) and so on. This is because...

Because their functions differ—whether taking objects collectively or individually—they are not the same as the previous position which held that the transformed image (*pratibimba*) and its objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) arise as the subjective mode of apprehension (*ākāra*).

Yet, they are said to be "similar. Now, when it is said that the modes of apprehension are distinct, this means that even though the preceding objects may be equal in number and so forth, [the modes of apprehension remain different].
Because their characteristics are each distinct and so forth, it is stated again to show that they differ from the preceding [definitions].
However, when each mind and mental factor arises, the agent of cognition, the object, and the fruit are such that the three entities are without distinction.

Dignāga, the Master of the Three Vedas, established his own system of the threefold nature (*tripuṭī*). The object of cognition (*prameya*) is the image-part (*nimittabhāga*); the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*);

and the fruit of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*). Thus, every mind and mental factor possesses these three parts. As cited in the lower section of the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*, the proof for this threefold nature is as follows:
the first line of the verse proves the object of cognition, the image-part; the second line proves the means of cognition and the fruit of cognition.
This [distinction between] the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) constitutes the third phrase, which establishes the meaning of the second phrase;
the fourth phrase reveals the principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). △ Second, the three parts according to Dignāga are concluded. Below follows the four parts according to Dharmapāla.
Furthermore, if one minutely analyzes the mind and mental factors up to their realization of their own essence (*svasaṃvitti*), they must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"Realization" (*saṃvitti*) refers to the essence; it is the verification of that object. The "self-verifying portion" (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is precisely *tathatā* (Suchness).

Since the eight consciousnesses are not separate from *tathatā*, the essence of *tathatā* is able to realize the eight consciousnesses. The passage beginning with "If this were non-existent" below clarifies this point.

There must necessarily be a fourth aspect (*caturtha-bhāga*), namely the third, the self-cognizing aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*). Since this is of the same nature as the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—both being consciousness—it should likewise be cognized by a fourth aspect.
Furthermore, the self-cognizing aspect would then have no result. Thus, he again refutes [the opponent] by challenging them with the difficulty that the third aspect lacks a result.
Fearing that the opponent might offer the defense that the seeing aspect itself serves as the result of the third, he first suppresses [that argument] by saying:

"One should not [assert] equality," etc., because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) penetrates all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus it is said that the seeing-part is sometimes not subsumed under valid cognition;
it does not realize the third [cognition]. To verify its own essence, it must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The *Zongjing* says: "It must possess four meanings."

This constitutes the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). [The four aspects are: first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); second, internal object-conditioning; third, not manifesting as a mental image (*anākāra*); and fourth, being the essence of mind.

△ The three sections on Dharmapāla’s fourfold division are complete. This concludes the second part: the general presentation of the tenets established by the three masters regarding the internal and external subject and object.

Among these four divisions, the first two are external; herein, "seeing" refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), and thus both the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-division function toward the external sphere and are termed "external nature.
Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are exclusively internal realization and are termed "internal nature.
Therefore, the subsequent verse states: "The mind of sentient beings has two natures; the former is exclusively the object-condition (*ālambana*)."
The image-part (*nimittabhāga*) is not part of the mind itself, because it lacks the function of being a cognitive subject; it is exclusively the object of cognition.

The latter three parts belong to the mind itself, encompassing both the meanings of being a cognitive subject and an object. This refers to the section below the second part, which explains the relationship between subject and object regarding the first two parts.

Because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is common to all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is described as "direct perception," "inference," and so forth. Regarding the third [part], which is the capacity to cognize what is below it:
this explains the meaning of the object and subject of cognition for the latter two parts. As for the third cognizing the second and the fourth:

this refers to the eight kinds of consciousness, each of which possesses a self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that can cognize the seeing-part, as well as a verifying-the-self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*). Otherwise, one would have to establish a fourth [part].

5. The fourth [consciousness] takes the third as its object, and this succession is infinite. The fourth takes the third as its object because both are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). As for why the fourth does not take the second as its object:
because that [second consciousness’s] seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is generally inferential and non-valid cognition (*anumāna-apramāṇa*), it is not a resultant entity and thus lacks utility.
Therefore, below the section on mind and mental factors, the four parts are established to demonstrate the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā*. Previously, one [part] was established.

Because there is no distinction between the means and the result [of cognition], a two-part model cannot be established. Because there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), a three-part model cannot be established.

Because there is no measure-result (*pramāṇaphala*), a four-part model cannot be established. Now, by establishing a four-part model, none of these faults apply. Furthermore, if the third and fourth parts were mutually the measure and the result, the fault of infinite regress would follow.
Therefore, the following section cites scripture to prove the meaning of the four-part model. As for the "two natures," they refer to the two external parts.

The external constitutes the external nature (*bāhya-svabhāva*). The internal is divided into two parts, which constitute the internal nature (*ādhyātma-svabhāva*). As for "all parts," this refers to the four parts; thus, the internal and external are each explained separately.

Each has its own objects of grasping (*grāhya*) and subjects of grasping (*grāhaka*), forming bonds. Only the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is common to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and so forth;
therefore, it is said to be "various. Below this verse, the Master of the Treatise himself provides an explanation. The first three lines of the verse clarify the internal and external respectively.

The meaning of the two divisions. From "Seeing that there are various [objects]" onwards, the meaning of the fourth line of the verse is explained. △ Second, the internal and external agent and object is concluded.
Below, third, the conclusion is returned to *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Thus, these four divisions may be subsumed into three: [the first] up to "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness.

As for their subsumption into three: self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are originally one entity; however, two names are established based on the distinction between the true and the false. Question:
Since there are now three divisions, does this not incur the same fault as that of Dignāga? Answer: He maintained that there were only three [divisions], whereas this [system] merely...
Because they are subsumed [within the same category], there is no such fault. In the following text, the two are subsumed as one; the objection raised there is the same as here.

As for subsuming them as two, there is only a single subject and object, because the latter three parts are identical in being the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and are thus all subsumed within the seeing-division.

As for subsuming them as one, both subject and object are forgotten, manifesting the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Question: Since they are subsumed as one, manifesting the principle of consciousness-only, [how is this so?]
Furthermore, why are four parts established? The answer is: establishing four parts clarifies the phenomenal aspects (*ākāra*) of Vijñapti-mātra;
subsuming them into one establishes the tenet that Vijñapti-mātra exists. For example, in the latter part of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the meaning of Vijñapti-mātra is cited as proof.
The first two lines manifest the existence of the subject and object; the latter two lines manifest the principle of Vijñapti-mātra. Thus, the following explains the establishment of Vijñapti-mātra.

The meaning of *citta* (mind) subsumes all mental factors (*caitta*). Furthermore, the preceding [section] concludes by stating that "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is the meaning of the aspect (*ākāra*) of consciousness.
△ Third, the conclusion returning to *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is complete. This concludes the first part: the extensive explanation of the character *liao* (to discern).
Below, the second part—the extensive explanation of the character *chu* (place/locus)—is divided into two sections. First, the formal explanation of the meaning of *āyatana* (locus).
What is called the "locus" refers to the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness), up to [the point where it is said]: "like the light of many lamps, each pervades while appearing as one.
This locus is the environment and its resources (*bhājana-pratītyasamutpāda*) upon which sentient beings depend; all are produced by the collective karmic power of sentient beings.

Regarding "external primary elements" (*bāhya-mahābhūta*), this is stated in contrast to "matter as an object of the sense faculties" (*indriya-rūpa*). Although the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organs) are also matter, they are not objects of perception (*ālambana*); therefore, they are so named [to distinguish them from external matter].

Internal matter refers to the sense organs, while external matter refers to the objects; thus, they are called "external matter. Both internal and external matter are composed of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); therefore, it is said that the primary elements exist both internally and externally.

Although [the text] states "all the lower [realms]" and so forth, this refers to the transformation from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) into the semblance of the sense organs, the body, and the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), which involves four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
First, there is the collective transformation within the common [world], such as mountains, rivers, and so forth, which are not experienced by a single individual alone.

1. Transformation within the uncommon among the common: because it can function independently; for example, one's own fields and houses, which ghosts do not see as fierce fires, but humans see as water.
2. Transformation within the uncommon among the uncommon: such as the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), which is the support for its own consciousness alone and not the support for others.
3. Transformation within the common among the uncommon: such as one's own physical sense organs (*bhautika-indriya*), which others also [perceive].
Because they are experienced. What is now called "the distinct transformations of each" refers to the non-common transformation within the common [realm], such as one's own fields and houses.
The analogy of "many lamps and their light" illustrates the common transformation within the common [realm], such as mountains, rivers, and so forth. △ This concludes the first section:
the formal explanation of the meaning of the "locus. Below are two questions and answers for further clarification.
"Who is it whose maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) transforms into this appearance? [This question continues through to: "Because all those with identical karma transform it together.

This question asks which realm’s appearance is transformed. In the response, two meanings are presented, yet they are not yet correct. Regarding the second meaning of the response, it refutes the preceding position through reasoning:
if one claims that everything is transformed by all in common, then the noble and the ordinary, the pure and the defiled, would become mutually confused, which contradicts reason.

The *Nyāya* (Correct Principle) states: If it were granted that noble ones transform impure lands while they themselves dwell in pure realms, what further need would there be for them to descend and be born here?
Therefore, [the author] establishes his own position below, stating: "Only those who are firmly established [in their respective realms] are capable of such transformation.
The Sūtra cited below explains the meaning of the scriptural passage quoted by the previous master; it simply uses the term "all" to refer to those with common karma.
One interpretation holds: "If that were so, when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed, what benefit would there be in transforming this [world] into that?

The correct position refutes the former. If it is argued that [the world] must necessarily remain stable, then as soon as this land is transformed, why would it not remain stable when the receptacle world is about to be destroyed?
Furthermore, if the receptacle world is being destroyed, there will certainly be no one remaining to dwell there; by which consciousness, then, is this deficient realm transformed?
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, those below" raises the objection regarding birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If it is claimed that those currently residing [in the form realm] or those who will be born there generate a revulsion for the world of form and are thus born in the formless realm, then what purpose would their formless bodies serve for the previously transformed world of form?
Even if one were to grant that there is a body within the formless realm, its coarse or subtle characteristics would be incompatible with those of the world of form.
What benefit does this transformation of the coarse vessel-world provide for that subtle substance?
However, the transformed earth is originally intended for the physical bodies [of beings], as it is seen differently by ghosts, humans, devas, and so forth.

This establishes the correct principle. However, the transformed land does not transform for its own sake; it exists solely as a basis and object of enjoyment for the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) of all [beings].
Therefore, it can serve as a support and object of enjoyment for those physical bodies, and thus transforms into the appearance of that receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Consequently, because it is not dedicated exclusively to itself, the aforementioned objection does not apply—just as in the case of a person.
The construction of houses is originally for the sake of human habitation; it is not the exclusive domain of a single individual. When the inhabitants leave, the house may still remain.
As vessels decay or are formed, what concern is this to sentient beings? Therefore, it is said: "Although there are no sentient beings, the appearance of the world nevertheless exists.
This statement below concludes by clarifying the meaning of common and uncommon transformations. If one considers them as objects of individual enjoyment, then...
Just as with a single form: humans see it only as water; hungry ghosts see it as a river of pus or as a raging fire; and devas see it as a palace for fish and dragons made of lapis lazuli.
Although it is a single substantial entity, these different perceptions arise because they are not shared [perceptions]. △ The second section, the question-and-answer clarification, is concluded.

The preceding two sections have completed the detailed explanation of the term "locus" (*sthāna*). Below, the three [sections] provide a detailed explanation of "appropriation" (*upādāna*), which is divided into two parts.
First, the appropriation of seeds:
"All seeds" refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*)... [continues] ...just as the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) does not contradict *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).

The seeds of outflows (*sāsrava-bīja*) are of the same nature as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth [consciousness] constantly takes its objects;

being untainted and wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*), it is not the same as the indeterminate. The seeing-part of the eighth [consciousness] is false by its very nature (*svabhāva*) and does not take *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, because the untainted seeds depend upon *tathatā*.
If one were to ask: "Since it is not an object (*ālambana*), it should be the same [as the indeterminate]."
"Is there a dharma existing separately outside of the mind? The answer says: "Although it is not an object of perception (*ālambana*), it is a seed sustained by the eighth consciousness;
because it is not separate from consciousness, it encompasses both the real and the false, thereby establishing the principle of *Vijñaptimātratā*.
[The section on] "1. Grasping Seeds" is concluded. Below follows "2. Grasping the Root-Body."

That which possesses the faculties (sendriya-kāya) refers to the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*). [This continues] until: "Even after that, the remaining corpse is still seen as a continuity.

Here, "faculties" (*indriya*) refers to the ultimate faculties (*paramārthendriya*), while "body" (*kāya*) refers to the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*). This is based on the seeds of specific characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*) and the internal great elements (*ādhyātmika-mahābhūta*).

It is said in reference to the ultimate faculties; for it is only the ultimate faculties that are "specific characteristics" and are termed "internal matter" (*adhyātma-rūpa*). Furthermore, it is called "body" (*kāya*).

The locus (*āyatana*) is also comprised of internal form and is called the "seed of common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*), because the loci of one's own and others' bodies transform into one another.
"Appropriation" (*upabhoga*) has the meaning of being the object-condition (*ālambana*). If they did not transform into one another, they would not mutually serve as objects.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In this context," [the author] misinterprets the meaning of the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, asserting that even the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*) transform into one another; this principle is not correct. Regarding the passage beginning with "There is another interpretation," he refutes the former view.
This means they transform into one another; however, only the *bu-chen* (tangible, physical) aspect transforms, while the *sheng-yi* (ultimate, essential) aspect does not.

There is no principle by which the sense faculties (*indriya*) of another could be experienced by oneself, because they are neither the support (*āśraya*) nor the object (*ālambana*) of one's own consciousness. The phrase "resembling those of self and other" below explains the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*.

This explains the meaning that the consciousnesses of oneself and others each undergo transformation independently. How could the mutual transformation [of objects] be confused with one's own independent transformation?

Therefore, the following section is introduced to establish the previously stated meaning of the transformation of seeds into common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). When [the consciousness] arises in another realm, it takes the bodies of others as its object;
at the time of parinirvāṇa, it takes the corpse as its object. This is the sense of "appropriating" (*upabhoga*) those [objects]. As for the term "continuum" (*saṃtati*), it refers to that corpse.
Because they do not perish immediately. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* verse states: "These external and internal seeds should be known as capable of both producing and projecting;
their withering and death result from the projecting [force], just as things naturally cease later. As An-hui explains:

"In this way, both external and internal seeds serve as causes for production (*janana-hetu*) and as causes for projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*). If it concerns external seeds, in relation to the sprout, they act as..."

The productive cause (*janana-hetu*) is the direct cause with respect to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is the indirect cause with respect to the stalk and so forth. The ālayavijñāna is the internal seed;
it is the direct productive cause with respect to name-and-form, and the indirect projecting cause with respect to the six sense bases up to old age and death.
Such is the productive cause. As for the projecting cause—how is it? To answer this question, it is said that [the body] withers and perishes due to the [projecting] cause.

Introduction. If the two types of seeds were solely causes of production (*janakahetu*) and not causes of projection (*ākṣepakahetu*), then seeds such as barley stored in granaries and the like would not continue in a similar succession for a long time;
nor would a corpse after death undergo successive transformations such as the appearance of livid discoloration (*vinīlaka*).
Furthermore, there should be no such thing as "concomitance through successive states. Why? Because [the entity] would have to perish immediately upon death.

This is illustrated by the analogy of something that perishes spontaneously later on; for example, like an arrow shot from a bow, where the force of being released from the string acts as the productive cause.

The arrow leaves the bowstring but does not immediately fall to the ground; this serves as an analogy for the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) that explains the continuity of the corpse, whether it appears as a bluish discoloration or remains withered and decayed for many years—all of which signify the principle of continuity.
△ Second, the section on the appropriated sense-faculties and the body is concluded.
The three preceding sections on the detailed explanation of appropriation (*upātta*) are concluded. The following four sections conclude by clarifying the two types of transformation.
Thus far, we have discussed the matter of what is transformed by the power of karma (up to the point where) actual matter (*rūpa*) appears within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
This concludes the preceding inquiry and response, which clarifies the meaning and provides an extensive analysis of the three categories beginning with "appropriation" (*upātta*).

Regarding the passage "If [the body] were fixed," etc., it means that for the noble ones (*ārya*), the bodies, elements, and other phenomena manifested through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are for the most part not fixed.
Below the section on the transformed bodies and environments, the meaning of "indeterminacy" is explained and established. Regarding the transformation of bodies and environments:

one's own body and the bodies of others, as well as realms such as heavens and hells, pure and impure worlds, and so forth—all these supporting retributions (*niśraya-vipāka*) and the like—are firmly manifested through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*), spiritual powers (*ṛddhi-bala*), and manifest appearances (*prabhāvana*).
Thus, they transform and appear to benefit sentient beings for one kalpa or many kalpas, existing in a state of mutual dependence. Therefore...
It is constantly continuous. Sound and light preach the Dharma; for the most part, they manifest briefly, appearing and changing in accordance with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.
"Briefly explained below" reiterates the preceding meaning: the ten bases of form consist of the five internal faculties and the five external objects.
These are the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the form included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Among these, there is both the conventional and the real.
What is here termed "real" refers to the forms of the bodies, utensils, and so forth, which are transformations produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Why is it that this consciousness cannot manifest as resembling [the object], and why does that [subsequent] consciousness also take this form as its objective condition (*ālambana*)?

Question: Why does the transforming consciousness not manifest as resembling mental factors (*caitta*) to serve as its objective condition? Answer: It is divided into two types within the middle [category]. Regarding transformation by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*):
this refers to the spontaneous mind (*svarasa-citta*) which arises solely through the power of prior karma and the actual seeds of names and speech (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*).

The first five [consciousnesses] and the eighth [ālayavijñāna] take their respective dominant and maturation causes as conditions; they transform [objects] because they have the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) as their cause.
As for "transformation through discrimination," this refers to the arising of mind through mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.

Because they arise through mental attention that conforms to their own discrimination, those two—the sixth and seventh—give rise to the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) through discriminative transformation. There is no... [end of fragment].
There may be a substantial entity that does not necessarily possess a function; therefore, it serves merely as an object (*ālambana*).
However, in the case of the eighth consciousness, the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) transformed by causes and conditions do possess a truly real objective function.

Conversely, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) transformed by causes and conditions within the eighth consciousness lack a truly real objective function, because the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) cannot itself act as the perceiving subject.

"Those" refers to the characteristics of the mind and so forth that have been transformed. These cannot be apprehended by the eighth consciousness as causes, because they lack the actual utility of an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
"Must require their actual utility" means that they must separately arise from this [eighth consciousness] based on its actual utility. "Must" signifies what is intended.

If one intends for them to possess the actual utility of an object of cognition, then only when form and so forth are separately transformed and produced from these eighth causal conditions do they come to exist.

Regarding the practical utility of objects of cognition: even transformations such as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) lack practical utility. If they were real unconditioned phenomena, they would not have been realized during the stage of the causal path;

if they were merely conventional unconditioned phenomena, they would lack both substance and function. Therefore, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) does not take mind and mental factors as its objects.

This concludes the response to the intended meaning of the question, clarifying that within the eighth cause (*hetu*), the [eighth consciousness] does not take the preceding seven minds and mental factors as its objects, nor does it take uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) as its objects;
therefore, it is said that the mind and so forth, as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), have no actual objective reality (*ālambana-prayojana*).

Suppose one asks: "If the eighth consciousness in the causal state does not take the mind and so forth as its objects, is it admitted that it can take them as objects during the stage of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)? The answer is as follows:
It says: "Reaching the untainted [dharmas], etc. This refers to supreme wisdom, which is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

When the essence of this wisdom is limpid and pure, although it is free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), the images of all the conceptually discriminating minds and mental factors belonging to the [other] seven consciousnesses appear within it.

Because the Buddha’s universal wisdom is able to take as its object all phenomena—whether true or false, existent or non-existent—it is said that [the Mirror Wisdom] exists below the level of the tainted [dharmas]. This concludes the section.

This clarifies that within the eighth cause, [the storehouse consciousness] does not take the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, but takes only three objects. It exists below the realms of desire and form, thereby establishing that the objects of the three realms are distinct.
Specifically, both the realm of desire and the realm of form take all three objects—seeds, the body with its faculties (*indriya-śarīra*), and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*)—as their objects.
Within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), it takes only contaminated seeds as its object; it does not take uncontaminated seeds as its object while in the causal state.

Therefore. △ Fourth, the conclusion that clarifies the two transformations is finished. Together with the preceding, the explanation of "appropriation" (*upādāna*) and "cognition of objects" (*vijñapti*) is finished. Below, the second part explains "the unknowable.
Regarding "the unknowable," this refers to these mental aspects (*ākāra*); it should be understood that the same applies to states such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Transformation of Consciousness) states: "The mode of activity (*ākāra*) and the object (*ālambana*) of this consciousness cannot be distinguished;

they are of one essence and not different. If this is so, how is it known that this consciousness exists? Answer: It is known that this consciousness exists by virtue of its functional effects (*vastu*).

This consciousness is able to sustain all matters of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and karmic retribution (*vipāka*). For example, in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*), its characteristics and objects cannot be distinguished, yet it nonetheless exists.

Regarding matters such as anger and so forth, one knows that ignorance exists; the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is likewise. There is no distinction between its characteristics (*nimitta*) and its objects (*viṣaya*);

it is known to exist solely by virtue of its activities (*kārya*). Or, from "or this" below, there is another explanation of the meaning of "unknowable" with respect to the object of cognition (*ālambana*).
An opponent asks: "If you admit that this consciousness apprehends an object of cognition, why do you further state that its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is difficult to know?"

The analogy answers the intent of the previous question as follows: Just as in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness that does not depart from the body must be believed to exist;

since one believes that in the attainment of cessation there exists consciousness that does not depart from the body, and it is thus comprised within the category of sentient beings, it must have an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Since it has an object of cognition, just as when there is mind, why is it not known? It is because it cannot be known; therefore, we know the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Subtle and hidden, it is difficult to comprehend. The meditative attainment of cessation is thus; one should know that the same applies to states such as the non-conceptual (*asaṃjñika*).
The two explanations regarding the "unknowable" are concluded. This concludes the explanation of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) according to both interpretations above.

Within the first section on the "Initial Transformation," the explanation of the verse’s meaning is divided into eight topical divisions. First, the explanation of the three names;

second, the explanation of the modes of activity (ending at the conclusion of the second fascicle). Herein, the third section—the explanation of the associated mental factors—is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation through question and answer.
"With how many mental factors (*caitta*) is this consciousness associated? [The answer continues] up to: "Because it is subsumed under the universal (*sarvatraga*) mental factors.

This question and answer clarify with which [factors] the King (the *ālayavijñāna*) is associated. That is to say, from beginningless time until the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), this storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is termed "the state prior to the transformation of the basis" (*aśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Within the first seven stages, as well as the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the six destinies (*ṣad-gati*), these are termed "all stages."

Throughout all stages [of consciousness], it is always associated with these five mental factors (*caitasika*), because these five are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*). Therefore, they accompany the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) in all its states.
The first part, the general explanation through question and answer, is concluded. Below follows the second part, the detailed explanation of the five factors, which is divided into six sections.
The first is the explanation of the mental factor of contact (*sparśa*), which is further divided into two: its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its function (*karma*).

Contact (*sparśa*) refers to the differentiation of the transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three. (Up to: At the time when contact arises, it excels the object of that consciousness.

When the sense faculty and the object produce consciousness, it is called the "conjunction of the three. "Transformation" is the functional capacity of this conjunction. "Differentiation" has the meaning of discerning;
that is, contact discerns a portion of the functional capacity within the conjunction of the three. Therefore, it is able to cause the mind...

Its nature is the object contacted by the mind. Since all other mental factors arise based upon contact (*sparśa*), it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*) and the rest.
In the passage beginning with "root and object," the meaning of how the aforementioned threefold conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*) and contact mutually serve as conditions is explained.

In the passage beginning with "contact depends," the point is established: namely, that contact arises depending on the threefold conjunction, and the threefold conjunction achieves its union through contact. Therefore...

This is explained as the meaning of their mutual production; that is, the "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*). Following the section on the threefold conjunction, the text explains the aforementioned "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) and "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
This transformation is the functional capacity of the mental factors (*caitta*) produced by the threefold conjunction.

Since the contact factor (*sparśa*) also resembles the threefold conjunction in its ability to produce sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, it is said that the contact factor discriminates the functional capacity for transformation within the threefold conjunction.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the function of the three [faculties] belongs solely to the predominant faculty, there are four reasons: first, by way of being primary; second, by way of proximity;
third, by way of pervasiveness; and fourth, by way of continuity. Although the object can produce both mind and mental factors, it is neither primary nor proximate.
Although the mind is primary and proximate to the production of mental factors, it cannot produce the mind itself, and furthermore, it is not pervasive.
The object and consciousness both lack the meaning of continuity; therefore, only the sense faculty is preeminent. △ This concludes the section on the nature and function of the single entity.
Below follows the distinction between the Sūtras and Śāstras.

Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises state that "discrimination" (up to) is not identical to the nature of sensation and so forth, just as it is not the same as the triad of conjunction.

Therefore, in the lower volume of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it cites scriptural evidence to show that the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*) are uniquely preeminent, while simultaneously explaining the essential nature and function of contact (*sparśa*).
Regarding the statement from the *Udayin-sūtra*, the *Pañcaskandhaka* states that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of seventy-three factors;

that is, among the fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*), excluding the two aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), the remaining forty-nine factors, together with the dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*), constitute this aggregate.
There are twenty-four formations (*saṃskāra*), totaling seventy-three factors, all of which are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

When it is now said that "all" refers to the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) along with formations, this excludes the factor of contact (*sparśa*); thus, there are seventy-four factors. With contact as a condition...
Regarding consciousness, contact, feeling, and so forth, which arise in groups of two, three, or four: this means that from the two factors of the sense faculty and the object, consciousness arises;

from the three factors of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness, contact arises; and from the four factors of the sense faculty, the object, consciousness, and contact, feeling arises. From feeling onwards, all mental factors [arise].
All [mental factors] arise from four dharmas. In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, only "volition" (*cetanā*) is mentioned, and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is not explicitly named;
this is because volition is the primary factor within the aggregate of formations, and by citing this single dharma, the others are subsumed.

As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* stating that contact (*sparśa*) alone is the basis for feeling (*vedanā*), it is because at the time of contacting an object, there is necessarily an experience; since contact is the immediate and predominant basis for feeling, it is specifically mentioned. This is explained as follows below.

The preceding [section] touches upon the proximity to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). However, regarding "contact" (*sparśa*) below: others claim that the nature of contact is simply the conjunction of the three (*trikasamnipāta*), and thus it lacks a real substantial entity (*dravyasat*).

The Master [Vasubandhu], however, specifically demonstrates that the substance of contact is truly existent. He states that among the six stages (*ṣaḍavasthā*), contact is a mental factor (*caitasika*).
Regarding these "six stages," both the Southern and Northern editions erroneously transcribe them as "six-sixes" (*liuliu*); I have now corrected this according to the meaning. Among the four...
Among the [four] nutriments (*āhāra*), this is subsumed under the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).

Since seventy-four dharmas take contact as their condition, we know that the essence of contact is real, just like feeling (*vedanā*) and the others, each of which has its own distinct essence and is not merely the conjunction of the three. △ The second section, "Distinctions between Sūtra and Śāstra," is concluded.
This concludes the first part, the general explanation of the mental factor of contact. Below follows the second: the mental factor of attention (*manaskāra*).

Mental attention (*manasikāra*) has the nature of being able to arouse the mind. (Omitted) It should not be considered a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), because it does not differ from concentration (*samādhi*).
This explains the essential nature and function of the mental factor of mental attention: that which, when the mind has not yet arisen, arouses the mind so that it arises;
and once the mind has arisen, leads it toward its object. The following section explains the aforementioned nature and function, thereby clarifying mental attention.
Regarding this name: if it were asked, "Since attention (*manasikāra*) can also give rise to mental factors (*caitta*), why is it here called specifically 'that which draws forth the mind'?

The answer is: because the mind is the sovereign, it is said only to draw forth the mind; where the mind is, the mental factors are present there as well. "Turning toward" (*āvarta*) has the meaning of being non-pervasive;

"pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) has the meaning of being universal and all-encompassing. "Holding the mind so that it abides" has the meaning of stability (*niyata*). The Master of the Treatise cites another [view].

Regarding the section on the "clinging to words," the text refutes each point individually. As for the phrase "both [are] below," it means that the two types of clinging contradict the intended meaning; therefore, they are said to be "neither.
If one claims that it "turns toward," meaning turning from this and proceeding toward that, then it should not be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

If it causes the mind to abide, it would be no different from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); how, then, could it be termed "attention" (*manasikāra*)? △ The second section, on the mental factor of attention, concludes. Below, the third section explains the mental factor of sensation (*vedanā*).

Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*): it refers to the experiencing of what is favorable, unfavorable, or neutral. It is called "feeling toward objects" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) because it is not shared with other [mental factors].

This explains the essential nature and function of the mental factor of feeling. Since there are three types of feeling: when one experiences a favorable object, it is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

When experiencing an object that is disagreeable, it is called the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhā-vedanā*). When experiencing an object that is neither [agreeable nor disagreeable], it is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Because feeling is the basis for desire, its function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Regarding the phrase "capable of giving rise to the desires for union, separation, or neither": this explains the aforementioned arising of craving. It follows that there are three types according to the feelings;
"neither" refers to the meaning of the feeling of equanimity, which is neither suffering nor pleasure. The passage beginning with "There is... refers to another location.

It is said that the remaining characteristics are the objective sphere (*ālambana*). Because one experiences the objective sphere through the experience of the objective sphere (*viṣayavedanā*), it is "concomitant" (*sahaja*).

This refers to the triad of the three [faculties, objects, and consciousness] coming together. "Contact" (*sparśa*) is the locus of contact; that is to say, feeling arises from the four factors consisting of the triadic conjunction and contact.

In contrast, experiencing that which produces [feeling] along with the concomitant contact is called "intrinsic feeling" (*svabhāvavedanā*), because it possesses the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of feeling alone, unlike the experience of the objective sphere, which shares [its nature] with others.

Because of their characteristics. That [opponent] says it arises from the "lower" [contact]. The Master of the Treatise refutes this: although the object is what is perceived by feeling within the triadic conjunction, feeling definitely does not perceive contact itself.
Therefore, it is said: "Feeling certainly does not take the simultaneously-arisen contact as its object.

If it is argued that feeling arises resembling contact—meaning that the fruit (feeling) resembles its cause (contact), arising from the triadic conjunction and causing the three to harmonize—then one must maintain that the fruit of feeling proceeds from contact.

That which is produced [from contact] and is able to experience contact would mean that all worldly results, which resemble their causes, should possess the nature of feeling (*vedanā*) and should likewise experience the cause;

for a result produced by a cause mostly resembles its cause. Since it is asserted that contact is the cause of feeling and feeling experiences contact, it should be called "feeling as cause" (*hetu-vedanā*).
Why then is it called "feeling as self-nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*)? If one were to say, "It is like a king..."—the "king" serves as a metaphor.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consumes various kingdoms and cities; this is a metaphor for sensation (*vedanā*).

Although this intention metaphorically represents the sensation of intrinsic nature, it cannot represent the contact (*sparśa*) that produces it, because a king is not produced by the various kingdoms and cities.

Therefore, it is refuted as being contrary to one's own tenets, since they maintain that it is the sensation that apprehends the producer. As for "not self-attesting," it also does not establish the proof that sensation apprehends the producer.

Regarding the meaning: if one were to claim that feeling which does not abandon its own nature of contact is called "feeling by way of its own nature" (*svabhāva-vedanā*), then all phenomena would be of the nature of feeling, because all phenomena do not depart from their own nature. Therefore, what he has said merely deceives the infant;
his refutation is irrational. Now, below the section on "objects," the text reiterates and explains "feeling of objects" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) as having a meaning distinct from other characteristics.
This refers to when one experiences a favorable object (*anukūla-viṣaya*). At that time, the characteristic of that favorable object is definitely attributed to oneself;

this is called "feeling of a favorable object" (*anukūla-viṣaya-vedanā*). When experiencing what is favorable, one does not experience what is unfavorable or neutral. If one were to experience the unfavorable or neutral, the same would apply to the favorable.

Therefore, the feeling of an object is definitely attributed to oneself, as it is not shared with other characteristics. △ This concludes the third section explaining the mental factor of feeling (*vedanā-cetasika*). Below, the fourth section explains perception (*saṃjñā*).

Mental factors (*caitta*). Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): its nature is to apprehend the image of an object (up to: it is only through this that one can subsequently give rise to various names and expressions).
This explains the essential nature and function of the mental factor of perception. Perception has the apprehension of images as its essence; it establishes names and expressions.
*Vṛtti*: This explains the meaning of the preceding [term] by means of the following. *Pratisthāpana* (establishment) refers to the grasping of an image (*nimittodgrahaṇa*).

Having grasped the defining characteristics (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) such as squareness or roundness, one subsequently gives rise to conventional designations (*vyavahāra*) such as "square" or "round. △ The fourth section, the explanation of the mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*), is concluded.
Below, the fifth section explains the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*).
Volition (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to engage in activity (up to: driving one's own mind to perform wholesome deeds and so forth).
This explains the essential nature and function of the mental factor of volition. "Engaging in activity" refers to the act of deliberation and investigation; this is the essential nature of volition.
It governs the mind and mental factors, serving as the functional activity of volition (*cetanā*). Therefore, it is said elsewhere: "Attention (*manasikāra*) is like a horse in motion;

volition is like the rider," meaning that [volition] is able to direct [the mind]. This explains and establishes the aforementioned meaning: namely, taking the apprehension of objects—whether correct or erroneous—as its cause.

Thereafter, the mind is engaged to bring about [the action]. △ Fifth, the explanation of the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*) is complete. Below, the sixth section provides a summary of the five universal factors.

Since these five are subsumed under the category of universal factors (from "since" to "because"), they are termed "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they share the same object of perception (*ālambana*) and other such characteristics.
The universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) should be associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), for the storehouse consciousness also pervades all states.

Their characteristics as universal factors shall be explained in detail in the fifth fascicle. Regarding the difference in their modes of activity (*ākāra*): consciousness has the apprehension of objects as its mode of activity;
attention (*manasikāra*) has the alerting of the mind as its mode of activity; and so on, up to volition (*cetanā*), which has the performance of action as its mode of activity.
Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "simultaneous dependence on the same basis" (*samāśrayatva*), as well as "having the same object" (*samālambanatva*):

this refers to the primary mind (*citta*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) arising simultaneously, sharing the same supporting faculty (*indriya*), the same perceived object (*viṣaya*), and the same substance of the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Therefore, they are called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).

△ This concludes the sixth section, the summary of the five objects. This also concludes the preceding two sections, the detailed explanation of the five objects. Below follows the third section: Questions and Answers for Clarification.
[This is] distinct. The text [on this] appears later in the chapter on the "Abandonment of Feeling" (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Fourth, the explanation of the feeling of equanimity:
the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely indistinct, just as neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) bring about both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The five characteristics of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) are identical to those of this eighth aspect; therefore, they are appropriately associated. The five characteristics are:
first, lack of clarity, because it lacks wisdom and mindfulness; second, non-discrimination, because its object is within the range of perception;
third, subtlety, because its characteristics are not manifest; fourth, uniformity, because there is no shifting or release; fifth, continuous progression, because it flows without interruption.

Because it has been severed. Furthermore, from "this below" onward, the text explains the meaning of its association with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). The phrase "only maturation" (*vipāka*) excludes that which is not born of maturation;
that is, it refers to the indeterminate state of maturation (*vipāka-avyākṛta*).

Being projected by prior karma, it does not depend on present conditions of wholesome or unwholesome karma, but is driven solely by the power of wholesome or unwholesome karma from previous lives. Therefore, it is associated only with neutral feeling, and not with the two feelings of suffering or pleasure.

It does not have the meaning of being associated (*saṃprayukta*). As for that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), namely the first six consciousnesses, the two feelings of pleasure and pain arise in dependence upon present conditions and are associated with them; this eighth [consciousness] cannot be so associated.

Furthermore, because it is below—that is, because the eighth is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*)—it is without transformation. Because it is without transformation, sentient beings constantly grasp it as "self" from moment to moment.
If it were associated with the feeling of change (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*), it would undergo transformation along with that [feeling]; how then could sentient beings grasp at a self moment by moment?

Therefore, this [state] is associated only with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Thus, it is established that its association consists exclusively of the feeling of equanimity. If so, [the following objection arises]: below...
An opponent raises an objection, saying: "The eighth consciousness is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Since equanimity is a tranquil phenomenon, it should be identical to the tranquility of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). How then can this consciousness also bring about evil results?

If you claim that the feeling of equanimity does not bring about evil results, then since you previously admitted that wholesome karma can bring about equanimity, it would likewise follow by logic that this [eighth] evil karma brings it about."

However, [the opponent] says that the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is inferior. The Master of the Treatise replies: Although equanimity is tranquil, it does not differ from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in its ability to sever hindrances and defilements;
therefore, it is not in contradiction with either suffering or pleasure, just as indeterminate phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*) can give rise to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
△ The fourth section, the explanation of the sensation of equanimity, is concluded. Below, the three preceding questions and answers regarding their associated factors are distinguished.
How is it that this consciousness is not [of the category of] specific objects (viṣayaviśeṣa), etc.? Because it is intermittent, it is certainly not maturation (vipāka).
Through this question and answer, the meaning of its non-association with other mental factors (caitta) is clarified. Among the specific objects, desire (chanda) is the aspiration for something;
since this consciousness follows karma as it is, it lacks desire. The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is dull and indistinct, unable to maintain [its object], and thus lacks excellence.

Regarding the understanding of meaning: because the dull and inferior consciousness lacks clear recollection, it is devoid of mindfulness (*smṛti*). Because this spontaneous mind does not abide with one-pointed focus, it is devoid of concentration (*samādhi*).
Subtle and obscure discernment (*pravicaya*) is certainly incompatible [with such a state]; therefore, it co-exists with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Regarding the statement that there is no mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) and that this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*):

this provides a general explanation of the mutual contradiction between the wholesome and afflicted states. Since the nature of maturation is itself indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it lacks the logical possibility of being associated with either wholesome or afflicted factors.
The passage beginning "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) below explains the contradiction among the mental factors in the state of non-determination; it means that although those mental factors are likewise...
[Commentary: It is intermittent and does not coexist with the maturation [consciousness], because the maturation consciousness is uninterrupted.

Therefore, it coexists only with the five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*). △ The third section, the question-and-answer distinction, is concluded. This concludes the three preceding explanations of association (*samprayoga*).
Below follows the fivefold explanation of the non-obscured (*anivṛta*).
There are four kinds of phenomena, namely: wholesome, unwholesome, [up to] non-obscured-neutral, and maturation-natured.
Herein, the four natures are first indicated, followed by a series of questions and answers to clarify that the primary evolving consciousness is associated with only one nature.
Question: Why is it stated elsewhere that it is common to both the wholesome and the defiled? The answer is provided in the following text.
If the maturation (*vipāka*) were of a wholesome or defiled nature, [it would follow that it could not be the basis for all seeds]...

therefore, this [eighth consciousness] is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). By means of the statement from another source, the Master cites the opponent's position—that the eighth consciousness is of a wholesome or unwholesome nature—and refutes it.

Flowing-on (*pravṛtti*) is the gate of defilement; returning-extinction (*nivṛtti*) is the gate of purity. It flows by reason of karma; it evolves by reason of suffering; and it is transformed through cultivation.
Therefore, it returns. It ceases through realization. This is because the essence of the eighth consciousness is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

by receiving the perfuming of the wholesome and the defiled, it becomes capable of the phenomena of saṃsāra and cessation. If it were itself wholesome or defiled, its own nature would be so powerful that it could not receive perfuming from others.

Thus, both of these two positions are unestablished. Furthermore, below this, the argument proceeds by refuting [the opponent] through the difficulty of the relationship between the support (*āśraya*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*).

Regarding their mutual contradiction: the wholesome contradicts the unwholesome, and the unwholesome contradicts the wholesome. That which is neutral by nature (*svabhāva-avyākṛta*) may serve as the support for either the wholesome or the defiled;

however, if it were itself wholesome or defiled, neither would be possible. The "extremely fragrant" is a metaphor for the wholesome, while the "extremely foul-smelling" is a metaphor for the defiled. Its essence is not...

Fragrance and stench: being perfumed by fragrance and stench, whether extremely foul or extremely fragrant—how could there be perfuming? Because there is no perfuming, both cause and effect are absent.
"Obscuration" (*nivṛta*) means that defiled phenomena obstruct the Noble Path; because these are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
"Obscured" (*nivṛta*) means "inferior. This explains the meaning of "unobscured" (*anivṛta*). That is to say, this eighth consciousness maintains the seeds of the untainted (*anāsrava*);
therefore, it does not obstruct the Path. Furthermore, as the basis for True Suchness (*tathatā*), it does not veil the mind; thus, it is called "unobscured.

Regarding "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), to explain the indeterminate, one first clarifies the determinate (*vyākṛta*), and subsequently uses that as an analogy to reveal the indeterminate. That is to say, what is desirable is the fruit of the wholesome, whereas what is undesirable is [the fruit of the unwholesome].
These are the evil fruits. Those two [wholesome and unwholesome dharmas] both possess a potent intrinsic nature that can be designated and distinguished;

this consciousness lacks those, and is therefore called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). △ The fifth section, explaining "unobscured" (*anivṛta*), is concluded. Below, the sixth section explains "of the same class" (*sabhāga*), which is divided into two parts.
First, the correct explanation of the "sameness of nature" (*sabhāgatā*).
Regarding the phrase "contact and so forth are also like this," this statement is made because contact and the other [mental factors] are necessarily of the same nature as the King (the mind).
This refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It is...

They are of the nature of non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). The same applies to contact (*sparśa*) and the others, because the mental factors associated with them must necessarily share the same nature.
Furthermore, below the section on contact, the meaning of the verse is explained again: "Maturation" refers to the neutral nature.

Regarding the statement that "the object and the mode of activity (*ākāra*) are both unknowable," it is because consciousness has "discernment" as its mode of activity, and since this is subtle and hidden, it cannot be known; the same applies to contact and the others.
Because they take the mental factors (*caitasika*) as their mode of activity (*ākāra*), and because they are also subtle and hidden, they cannot be known.

That which cannot be known is precisely the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, it is said that they take three kinds of objects. These five factors are associated with the unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

For this reason, the verse states that contact (*sparśa*) and the others are likewise. △ The first part, the direct explanation of the "commonality" (*sabhāgatā*), is finished. Below, the second part is the detailed [explanation].
Distinguishing Errors:
There is an interpretation that holds that since contact and so forth are like the ālayavijñāna, how could they be the same as consciousness in being able to maintain seeds?
This interpretation is a biased attachment. As for the phrase "those which are likewise," it refers to contact and so forth, which likewise possess all such [kinds of] maturation (*vipāka*).

The six lines of verse establish the meaning [of the preceding]. Therefore, it says: "Because there is no distinction. Regarding the phrase "That which is taught below," it first refutes the inability to receive perfuming and maintain seeds:
namely, that mental factors (*caitta*) are not the mind-king (*cittarāja*), and thus lack autonomy; furthermore, greed (*lobha*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Faith and the other [wholesome factors] are wholesome. Since both the wholesome and the defiled are not susceptible to perfuming, contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] likewise cannot be perfumed.
How then could they, like consciousness, be able to maintain seeds?
Furthermore, if contact and the others were also capable of receiving perfuming, [it would follow that they do so] because they arise simultaneously with the six visual consciousnesses and the rest.

Within this context, even granting that those [six consciousnesses] undergo perfuming, they further refute it through various arguments. First, they refute the notion that six types [of seeds] produce a single fruit:
if the five [sensory consciousnesses] that undergo perfuming are identical to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna), then there would be six kinds of seeds;
since there are six kinds of seeds, it is logically untenable for them to produce only a single fruit. Next, they refute the production from a single seed: since [the fruit] arises from one...

As for arising, the other five [causes] are all useless; how could they be identical in receiving perfuming? If they are not identical in producing results, this also cannot be accepted, as it would undermine the production of results in succession.
That is to say, if the power [of the causes] were equal at the time of perfuming, the arising of the results would necessarily be simultaneous; how then could there be succession?

Furthermore, it cannot be said that they descend [into the womb]. If they were to descend, it would result in six fruits arising simultaneously. If one were to claim that the six fruits arise all at once, then a single sentient being would possess six visual consciousnesses;
the same would apply to the sense organs and their objects. Consequently, the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) would become one hundred and eight elements.
Since this is not the case, how could they possibly arise all at once?
"Who says that contact and so forth can also receive perfuming? (up to) "it is also like fire having no power to burn. "Who says... and below, the opponent argues.
Because the Master has raised the objection that [contact etc. receive perfuming and maintain seeds, he devises a different strategy to falsely preclude the aforementioned fault.
"Not so," and below, the Master counters with a question: namely, since you do not maintain that contact and so forth receive...
"Infusion. How can it be said that contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors] are "all-seeds" (*sarvabījaka*), just like consciousness? This refers to what follows below:

the opponent offers a defense, stating that those which possess a semblance of seeds refer to the eighth consciousness. When the eighth consciousness perceives seeds, the associated contact and other factors take those seeds as their basis and manifest as images;
these are called "having a semblance of seeds. It is precisely this semblance of seeds that is termed "all-seeds. As for the phrase "the objects of perception and so forth," it refers to those...
When the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) takes seeds as its object, the five mental concomitants (*caitta-dharma*) necessarily share that same object.
This proves that the foundational consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) must take seeds as its object. The *Zongjing* states: "In the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there is no form to rely upon;

therefore, there is no remote object-condition (*parokṣālambana*). This clarifies the meaning of the eighth [consciousness] having a direct object-condition (*sākṣādālambana*). It further states: "The eight [consciousnesses] and the five [mental] concomitants rely upon..."

Because the three objects serve as the substantial basis for the mind-king (citta-rāja) when it takes them as its conditions, this demonstrates that mental factors (caitta) possess a remote objective support (viprakṛṣṭālambana).
The phrase "resembling [the eye]" and so forth concludes by clarifying that one should not raise the objection that there is no causal basis. Regarding "resembling the eye-faculty" and so on:

this also refers to when the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) takes the eye-faculty and others as its object; at that time, the associated contact (sparśa) and other factors rely upon the faculty as their substantial basis and transform into something resembling the eye and so forth.

It is not the support for consciousness, because it has the immediate sense faculty (*indriya*) as its support. Like fire that does not burn, it is also analogous to a seed that lacks the capacity to produce [a sprout].
That defense is irrational; regarding the objects of contact and so forth, one should state [the exception] according to what is appropriate, rather than claiming it applies to all.

The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "Regarding the objects of perception such as contact (*sparśa*), which appear as seeds and appear as sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, they possess a relationship of proximity or distance with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) only at the time of subsequent appropriation (*upādāna*) and location.

Why, then, do you speak of 'appearing as images' (*nimittapratibhāsa*) in relation to all seeds? As for 'subsequent appropriation,' it is stated in contrast to the aforementioned 'all seeds. This is because within subsequent appropriation there exists..."
Regarding the "seed as object" (*ālambana-bīja*): the term "all kinds of seeds" (*sarvabījaka*) mentioned previously is definitively designated as that which undergoes perfuming (*vāsanā*).

If it were not so designated as that which undergoes perfuming, yet were still called a "seed as object," then the root verse would incur the fault of tautology (*punarukta-doṣa*), because within the "appropriated" (*upātta*) [consciousness], there is already that which is a "seed as object.
How could one say "the aspect resembling the seed" again after having already explained the aspect of the "object resembling the seed"?

Furthermore, the phrase "and those below" cites the opponent's previous position to refute it. That is to say, if one maintains that all things are mutually analogous, then one must state that dharmas such as contact (*sparśa*) are like consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Therefore, he further refutes this by saying: "Let it not be that the five [factors] beginning with contact are also capable of discerning;

let it not be that the five [factors] beginning with contact are each associated with the five [factors] beginning with contact. From this point downward, he concludes and clarifies the meaning within the verse.
It is also stated thus: "according to what is appropriate," not meaning that all are exactly like the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

△ Second, the detailed analysis of errors is concluded. This concludes the six preceding explanations on the "sameness of nature" (*sabhāgatā*). Below, the seven explanations of the "section on citing analogies" are divided into two parts:
first, the formal explanation through question and answer.
Is the ālayavijñāna subject to annihilation or eternal? (Up to: It is like a torrent; such is the nature of cause and effect.

Through this dialogue, it is clarified that the first transforming consciousness is by nature neither annihilated nor eternal. "Constant" refers to the following: an explanation of the meaning of the character *heng* (constant).
