The nature of mind is not [substantial], like a sound that lasts for only a single moment, or like light which lacks a real entity. How could it be capable of receiving perfuming or maintaining seeds?

Furthermore, the passage beginning with "Moreover, below" reiterates the refutation of the previous argument: form is a transformation of consciousness, and non-associated formations are manifestations of consciousness.
These two, being separate from consciousness, lack a real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since they lack a real nature, they cannot serve as the basis for seeds.

Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*): this distinguishes the mental factors from that which possesses the nature of holding seeds (*bīja-dhāraṇa*).

That is to say, since the various mental factors are intermittent—just like the consciousnesses themselves—and, being termed "mental factors," lack the sense of autonomy (*svātantrya*), and furthermore are not the substance of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*), how could they possess the capacity to be perfumed (*vāsya*) or to hold seeds?
Therefore, it stands to reason that the mind which holds seeds must exist separately; this concludes the demonstration that [the ālayavijñāna] is distinct from the evolving consciousnesses.
Regarding consciousness and so forth: there exists separately an eighth [consciousness] called the "mind that holds seeds. △ This concludes the section on citing scriptures and inference.
Below, the second part—entitled "Citing the Opponent’s Tenets and Refuting Them"—is divided into four sections. First: "The Homogeneous Receiving of Impregnation."
Some say that since the six consciousnesses have existed from beginningless time [up to the present], why is it necessary to insist on the existence of an eighth consciousness-nature?
They claim that other vehicles teach that the first five are the perfumers (*vāsaka*) and the sixth is the perfumed (*vāsya*).
Although the functioning of the first five undergoes transformation, they are not distinct from the sixth consciousness in terms of their own kind; therefore, the sixth consciousness is the perfumed.
[It is] the nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, it can maintain the seeds (*bīja*). This refutes the Mahāyāna tenet that clings to the existence of an eighth [consciousness].
Why is that statement meaningless? Because the nature of distinct categories must be identical to the nature of distinct entities.
The author of the treatise first uses the distinction between the provisional and the real to refute what is unreasonable.

If one maintains that categories (*jāti*) are real, then one is identical to the Sāṃkhya school, for whom things undergo transformation while their essence remains one. If one maintains that they are provisional, by what principle could they sustain a truly real seed?

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "if one maintains [them as such]," the question is asked: among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), to which nature do they belong? If they belong to the wholesome or the unwholesome, then the wholesome and unwholesome would be predominant.

[The storehouse consciousness] is "intense" (*sābhisyanda*) and thus certainly cannot receive perfuming (*vāsana*). Furthermore, the natures of the wholesome and unwholesome are "determinate" (*vyākṛta*) dharmas;

because they possess a fixed continuity of mindfulness (*smṛti*), and since this mindfulness is like analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), how could they receive perfuming? If [the storehouse consciousness] belonged to the neutral (*avyākṛta*), then at the time of wholesome or unwholesome minds, the neutral mind would cease, and its corresponding [perfuming] should likewise cease;
how then could it receive perfuming? This is not the case. [The author] first suppresses [the opponent's position] below, fearing that they might formulate a further counter-argument. If...

If the categories of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena are of the same nature as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they ought to constitute a distinct category [of their own]. If they were a distinct category, they would necessarily be distinct entities;
how then could they serve as the perfumed (*bhāvya*)? This is because the perfuming agent (*bhāvaka*) and the perfumed must necessarily be of the same category.
Furthermore, in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), this category [of consciousness] is definitely absent; therefore, it also lacks the capacity to maintain seeds.

Moreover, because the homogeneous [series] is interrupted, the state of mindlessness is refuted as being incapable of maintaining seeds. Since the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are interrupted, they lack the quality of stable persistence;

thus, the process of being perfumed and maintaining seeds is not established for them. If one were to allow that the six consciousnesses are of the same category [as the storehouse consciousness], [the following would apply].
Regarding the perfuming [of seeds]: since the categories of consciousness are identical for both Arhats and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they should mutually perfume one another.

Consequently, an Arhat would be like an ordinary being and should be perfumed by defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) to become an Arhat; likewise, an ordinary being would be like an Arhat and should be perfumed by untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) to become an ordinary being.
To admit such mutual perfuming leads to logical fallacies. Furthermore, if the six consciousnesses were to be perfumed by their own kind, it would follow that...
The sense faculties, such as the eye, are of the same category as other phenomena and would likewise mutually perfume one another.

Consequently, the eye and so forth, being identical in category to other phenomena, should perfume those other phenomena to produce the eye and so forth; and other phenomena, being identical in category to the eye and so forth, should perfume the eye and so forth to produce those other phenomena.

However, you do not accept this. Therefore, one should not maintain that consciousness is perfumed by its own kind. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains: "That is to say, the sense faculties, such as the eye..."

The nature of pure matter (*viśuddha-rūpa*) is always accompanied by the category of the faculties (*indriya-jāti*). Consequently, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) should also be established as having the nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), because its status as a faculty is equivalent [to the other faculties].
What is here referred to as "the remaining phenomena" (*śeṣa-dharma*) refers precisely to the meaning of the mental faculty as explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.

Furthermore, following the discussion of the six consciousnesses, the doctrine of mutual perfuming (*anyonya-vāsanā*) is again refuted. Since the first six [consciousnesses] arise and perish together, what dharma could serve as the perfumable (*bhāvya*)?
This is because the perfumable consciousness lacks arising and perishing. Regarding the two moments—preceding and succeeding—this refers to the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Since they either perish first or arise later, they are necessarily not simultaneous; being separated by these moments of arising and perishing, how could they mutually perfume one another? Because the [perfuming] agent...
Regarding the object of perfuming (*vāsyam*), it must necessarily be simultaneous. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains:

"If one were to say that a preceding moment perfumes a succeeding moment and thereby constitutes perfuming, this meaning is not tenable, because those two moments do not exist simultaneously. If one insists on their occurring together,"

This establishes [the impossibility of] the seeds being both the perfumed and the perfumer. Previously, this was refuted by reasoning: the six evolving consciousnesses are all intermittent and lack the quality of stable abiding;

they are likewise not susceptible to perfuming. How, then, could they maintain the seeds? △ This concludes the first section on the perfuming of homogeneous [seeds]. Below, the second section concerns the former serving as the seed for the latter.
There are those who maintain that within the uninterrupted succession of their own respective categories, matter and mind are not subject to perfuming, as has already been explained.
That is to say, they hold that previously ceased material phenomena serve as the seeds for the subsequent arising of material phenomena, with no interval between them;
this is intended to refute the objection raised in the preceding chapter regarding the interruption of moments. Just as it is with material phenomena, so it is with mental phenomena. Thus:

The principle that the preceding is the cause and the succeeding is the effect is established; conversely, the proof cited from the Sūtra stating that "the collection and arising of defiled and pure seeds is called mind" is unestablished. Regarding their position, the Master refutes it as follows:

Since they maintain that within their own category there is neither the perfumer nor the object of perfuming, and since perfuming is thus non-existent, from what could seeds arise? Therefore, one cannot maintain that the preceding serves as the seed for the succeeding. Thus...
If one maintains that the preceding moment serves as the seed for the subsequent one, then that which is interrupted should not arise again.
Furthermore, the final matter and mind of those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) of the Two Vehicles are comprised within the outflowing (sāsrava);

since they must be permanently severed, it cannot be said that the outflowing matter and mind at the moment of death serve as the seeds for the subsequent non-outflowing (anāsrava) matter and mind. Nor should it be claimed that such matter and mind [necessarily] descend [to lower realms]. This refers to matter, mind, and so forth.

It is not that which is perfumed; since this has already been refuted above, one should not resort to such a revised hypothesis. △ Second, the conclusion of the preceding section on the prior serving as the seed for the subsequent.
Below follows the third section: cause and effect across the three periods of time.
Some say that if all phenomena of the three periods of time exist [simultaneously], then all causes and effects cannot be established.

This refers to the position that one clings to past phenomena as the cause capable of producing an effect, and present phenomena as the effect toward which it moves; or that present phenomena are the cause capable of producing an effect, and future phenomena as the effect toward which it moves.
In such a view, the causes and effects of the three periods would naturally produce and move toward one another [without functional distinction].

Why labor to separately maintain a separate eighth consciousness as the repository of seeds? However, the passage "But the Sūtra... [indicates that] the commentator explains the meaning of the Sūtra cited by the previous master of the treatise.
The passage "That says... [indicates that] the master of the treatise refutes it: since past dharmas have already ceased, they are not permanent; why then are they maintained as causes?
Since future dharmas have not yet arisen, they are not present; why then are they maintained as effects? Therefore, the analogy of a flower in the sky is used.
It does not exist as a substantial reality. Furthermore, since the past and future do not possess substantial reality, they also lack practical efficacy.

How, then, could they serve as causes and conditions? A cause is a seed, which must necessarily be a substantial reality; a condition is a manifest activity, which must necessarily have practical efficacy. If [these] were non-existent...
This concludes the summary of cause and effect: [the effect] must arise from seeds, and seeds must exist within the consciousness that sustains them.

If the eighth consciousness did not exist, neither the seeds nor the relationship between cause and effect could be established. △ This concludes the third section: Cause and Effect across the Three Times. Below follows the fourth section:
Dispelling Characteristics to Reveal the Principle of Emptiness.
There are those who hold that the principle of emptiness which dispels characteristics in the Mahāyāna—that very mind—is this eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The intent of the Mahāyāna sūtras is to negate and dispel [clinging] according to specific instances. When sentient beings cling to existence, the Buddha says it is empty in order to dispel that clinging to existence.
Fools do not understand this; taking it as the ultimate, they rely on fallacious inference (*tarka*) to deny everything. They, in particular...

[The opponent] objects: "No. The Master refutes this, stating that to deny the existence of this consciousness contradicts and undermines the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras cited previously, which teach that this consciousness exists.

Furthermore, to deny the arising of wisdom, the abandonment of afflictions, the cultivation of causes, and the realization of fruits—such that both the defiled and the pure are non-existent—is a great false view.
The World-Honored One declared such persons to be incurable. [The opponent], being inferior, refers to those with the view of emptiness who completely deny [the teachings].
No. To disparage [these teachings] is merely untrue; the superiority [of the Mahāyāna] is manifest.

As for "all phenomena," this refers to the categories of saṃsāra, nirvāṇa, and the provisions for awakening. If these were all non-existent, the bodhisattva would have no reason to apply himself with diligence to their cultivation.
"Who has... and so forth introduces a simile: a barren woman cannot conceive; her child is necessarily non-existent.

How could a wise person employ an army that is necessarily non-existent to eliminate illusory enemies? Here, "the wise person" is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva, and "illusory enemies" are a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The analogy of the military expedition represents the provisions for enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Since it is said that [the self] "should not exist" and yet it is asked "who possesses [them]," one knows that all dharmas such as cause and effect are not entirely non-existent; they must manifest based on the eighth consciousness, which maintains the seeds.

How could there be no eighth consciousness as the mind that maintains the seeds? Therefore, the following section concludes with an exhortation to believe. △ Four: Dispelling Characteristics and Emptiness.
The principle is concluded. This concludes the first pair of citations regarding the mind that maintains the seeds; the following two citations concern the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*).
Furthermore, a sutra states: "There is a ripening consciousness... (up to)... based on what further phenomenon is a sentient being perpetually established?"
By citing scriptures and inferring their meaning, one establishes the existence of the eighth consciousness-substance.

The passage beginning with "As for the eye and so forth" distinguishes the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna), such as the visual consciousness, from the nature of the maturation-consciousness (vipāka-citta). The analogy of lightning and so forth illustrates that the evolving consciousnesses are impermanent;

by showing that they cease and then resume, it demonstrates that these evolving consciousnesses possess the characteristic of arising and ceasing. The phrase "In those [states] such as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), this matter does not exist" serves as a distinction.

Regarding the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*): because they do not have the function of being produced by wholesome or unwholesome karma, [the text says] "the eye and so forth," meaning the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth.
Although these are produced by completing karma (*pūrṇaka-karman*), they are merely termed "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).

This is because the true maturation-consciousness (*bhūtavi-pāka-citta*) is constantly continuous. The eye and so forth, like sound, are not constantly continuous. [The phrase] "it must certainly... concludes by clarifying that the essence of the true maturation-consciousness is constant.

[Pervasive]: It can transform the bodies and the vessel-world to serve as the support for sentient beings. This is because all sentient beings rely internally upon the body of faculties and externally upon the vessel-world.
Having thus negated [the preceding], it is stated that those dharmas which were previously excluded lack substantial reality and are not eternally present.

If the eighth consciousness did not exist, what would transform the bodies and the vessel-world? If there were no bodies or vessel-worlds, further relying on what dharma could sentient beings be established?
Furthermore, whether in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or not, that mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.

This passage cites bodily and mental sensations (*vedanā*) to verify the existence of a maturation-consciousness (*vipākacitta*). "Exhaustion and impairment" refers to painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*); "tranquility and satisfaction" refers to pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*);

and "the absence of both pain and pleasure," occurring both in a state of concentration and when there is no discursive thought, refers to neutral sensation (*upekṣāvedanā*). When not in a state of concentration [and there is no such neutrality], it is likewise [neutral].

At that time, when there is volition, these are feelings of suffering or pleasure. If a truly resultant (*vipāka*) mind were not constantly present during those aforementioned states, who would possess the bodily sensations?
Since the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are intermittent and sometimes absent, one might fear an objection such as:

"If the Buddha lacks a resultant mind, how could he give rise to wholesome thoughts? To explain: it is not the case that when the Buddha gives rise to other wholesome minds and so forth, [the resultant mind] must necessarily...
The true resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) manifests. Just as when such a manifesting resultant consciousness occurs, it is certainly not the Buddha, because it is a sentient being.
From this point downward, the conclusion clarifies that the true resultant consciousness is ever-present;

therefore, that sutra states that there is a resultant consciousness produced by the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma, which is precisely this eighth consciousness. 2. Citation [of Scriptural Authority]
The exposition of the resultant consciousness is concluded.

Regarding the nature of rebirth within the realms of the three lower worlds, the Sūtra further states that the actual, constant, pervasive, and unmixed flow of sentient beings is the true and ultimate process of rebirth.
Citing scriptures and inferring their meaning, it is proven that there exists an eighth [consciousness] which undergoes the process of transmigration and rebirth (*gati*).
To establish this process of rebirth, four criteria must be met: first, it must be substantially real; second, it must be constant; third, it must be universal; and fourth, it must be unmixed.

The eighth consciousness possesses these four aforementioned characteristics and can therefore be established as the true, substantial subject of rebirth. First, the possibility of confusion is refuted: if it were not a maturation-dharma (*vipāka-dharma*) possessing these four criteria...

This refers to the confusion of rebirth within the various realms of existence (*gati*). Why is this? Because while abiding within one realm, one further gives rise to the dharmas that constitute rebirth in other realms.

This demonstrates the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); for as long as it abides, it is necessarily not separated from the body. Following the discussion of maturation, the text next distinguishes the non-universal nature of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*).
"Maturation-form" refers to the form of the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya-rūpa*). "That which is induced by karma" refers to the form of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya-rūpa*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because this [physical] form does not exist, it is said to be "not pervasive. Regarding those born in lower realms, next we exclude the meaning of "constant" with respect to wholesome karma.
Wholesome karma acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) refers to innate wholesome karma; karma of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-karma*) refers to discriminative wholesome karma.
That which leads to rebirth in all destinies (*sarvagati-gāmin*) is so called because such karma pervades the three realms. "Without confusion" means that wholesome [karma] is necessarily...

Because it is a virtuous retribution, it does not exist constantly; this is because karma is subject to exhaustion. Next, [the text] distinguishes the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), whose essence is not substantially existent and which lack the meaning of "going toward birth.
Only the eighth [consciousness], both the sovereign and its objects, possesses these four meanings;
therefore, it is the true "going toward birth."
If this mind did not exist, it would not arise in the formless realm; therefore, we know that there is this distinct eighth consciousness. Regarding the "states of the wholesome and so forth":

these refer to the states of the wholesome, the indeterminate, and the contaminated (*sāsrava*). Within the formless realm, there exists only the seed, which carries the meaning of "destiny" (*gati*) and "birth" (*upapatti*).

If there were no ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) to sustain those seeds, it would follow that the formless realm could not exist. Thus, it is said that [without it] the formless realm would not be possible.

Regarding the realms of rebirth (*gati*): even granting your position, that is to say, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), setting aside for a moment the impure (*sāsrava*) states, at the time of an untainted (*anāsrava*) mind, there would be no maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Consequently, one should realize awakening (*bodhi*); and once awakening is realized, one should not belong to any realm of rebirth. This applies if [you maintain] the formless realm...

To claim that [the formless realm] is entirely devoid of rebirth in a destination (*gati*) contradicts correct reasoning. According to principle, there must be a realm (*dhātu*), because a realm necessarily entails rebirth in a destination.

The aforementioned fault consists of four types: confusion, lack of pervasiveness, lack of constancy, and lack of reality. This deficiency is precisely the fault of asserting that the formless realm lacks rebirth in a destination.

Only by admitting the existence of the substance of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which possesses these four characteristics, can both of the aforementioned pairs of faults be avoided.
This is a fault. For this reason, [the text] below cites scriptural evidence that at the time of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), there are no dharmas of maturation (*vipāka*);

one must realize enlightenment because it is not a rebirth within the realms of existence (*gati*). One who has transcended the three realms should not be subject to rebirth within the realms. The Truths of Suffering and its Origin are the causes and effects of the mundane world;

the non-forgetting of cause and effect is called the seed of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Only the Buddha has eternally severed this. This is intended to clarify that those remaining within the three realms [are still subject to such seeds].

Because it necessarily leads to rebirth. "Correctly and truly" (zhèngshí) and below concludes by revealing the retributive consciousnesses (*vipākacitta*) and so forth that have been discussed; that is, this eighth [consciousness].

One should know that this eighth consciousness exists as a distinct entity. △ The section on the substance of the realms, destinies, and births is complete. Below follows the four types of bodies possessing material sense organs.
Furthermore, a sutra states that there is a body possessing material sense-faculties (up to the point where it says) "only because of the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-citta*).

By citing this sutra and inferring its meaning, it is proven that the eighth consciousness is that which performs "appropriation" (*upādāna*). Specifically, regarding the five material sense-faculties mentioned below, this explains that the sutra contains the sense of "appropriation.
The "five material sense-faculties" refers to the *paramārtha-indriyas* (ultimate sense-faculties). Their "bases" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are the... [floating organs].
The sense faculties (*indriya*) are like dust. Because those of the past have already ceased and those of the future have not yet arisen, they lack appropriation (*upādāna*).

Only those of the present exist as definitely appropriated. Regarding "they are definitely subordinate," this means that those material faculties are definitely appropriated by the mind of maturation (*vipākacitta*).

This ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*) is projected by prior karma of both wholesome and unwholesome types; therefore, in the realms of existence characterized by form, the body possessing the sense faculties (*indriya*) is exclusively appropriated (*upātta*) by it.

The phrase "the eye and so forth" below serves to distinguish this from the fact that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) lack the quality of being appropriated. This statement follows below.

The Master of the Treatise himself explains the preceding meaning. Herein, he merely provides a general indication; the detailed explanation will follow later in the text. Fearing that one might object:
"If the Buddha has no maturation [of karma], then his physical body (rūpakāya) should not be 'appropriated' (upātta)," he answers: "This does not indicate that it is capable of being appropriated."
Only the ripening consciousness (*vipākacitta*)—the stainless, pure, and white consciousness—is also able to appropriate the form-body (*rūpakāya*) of the Buddhas;
however, regarding the contaminated body, only the ripening consciousness is capable of appropriation. Therefore, it is stated thus in the Sūtra:
The physical body possessing the sense organs is that which is appropriated;
this is because the various evolving consciousnesses arise as present conditions. That mind is precisely this eighth consciousness.

This explanation clarifies the meaning of the following section. It refers to the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which are induced by present conditions and are not drawn forth by prior karma as is the case with maturation (*vipāka*).
This illustrates the meaning of impermanence, like sound, wind, and so forth.

When it says that those [consciousnesses]—whether wholesome or defiled—are not induced by karma, it means that the nature of those evolving consciousnesses is itself wholesome or defiled, rather than being induced by the karma of another, just as [the nature of sound and so forth is not].

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is pure by its own nature; it does not arise from severing other afflictions, because it manifests the purity of the fundamental nature. The evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are likewise:

they are wholesome or defiled by their own nature, rather than being made wholesome or defiled by others, because they induce what is wholesome or defiled. The evolving consciousnesses arise solely based on the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*);

thus, they possess the nature of being either wholesome or unwholesome, unlike the ripening consciousness, which is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, the evolving consciousnesses do not rely upon everything; they are not universal supports. The evolving consciousnesses...
Because it does not pervade the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), and because it is non-continuous—having interruptions like a flash of lightning—it is a metaphor for impermanence.
Based on these various meanings, [the ālayavijñāna] cannot grasp (*upādāna*) the contaminated physical body (*rūpakāya*).

Following the mention of "all mental consciousnesses" (*citta-vijñāna*), this serves to distinguish the mental factors (*caitta*) from being the grasper; the meaning is that since the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) itself lacks grasping, the mental factors likewise do not.

Follow this. Generally speaking, the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) encompasses all phenomena; therefore, it is said that according to the principle of consciousness-only, its meaning includes the mental factors (*caitta*).

The phrase "not the various [physical] bases" (*na tu... adharāḥ*) serves to distinguish them from the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) and the formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), as they lack the quality of being appropriated (*upātta*).

If the material sense organs were capable of self-appropriation, there would be no body of material sense organs that is not appropriated; and if there were nothing appropriated, [the body] would not exist.
The objects of perception, the formations dissociated from mind, and those manifested by form and mind have no substantial reality from the outset, being like space and so forth;
therefore, one should descend [to the next level]. This concludes the summary that clarifies the "appropriating mind" mentioned in that sutra, which is precisely this eighth consciousness.
△ Fourth, the section on the physical body with material sense organs is complete. Below follows the fifth section on the triad of life-force, warmth, and consciousness.

Furthermore, a sūtra states that life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—[up to]—are [the three that sustain existence]; if it were merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), how could this not contradict correct reasoning?

By citing the sūtra to investigate its meaning, it is proven that the eighth consciousness is able to maintain life-force and warmth. Life-force is the seed of consciousness; warmth is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); and consciousness is the active manifestation (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
This means that the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) lack the power to maintain life-force and warmth; only [the eighth consciousness] possesses it.

"Vipāka (maturation) below" indicates that the eighth consciousness is able to sustain life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*). As for life-force and warmth, they share the same indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and are of a single, continuous stream (*ekajātīya-saṃtāna*).
"The Sūtra says below" refutes the externalist attachment that there is no substance of the eighth consciousness, asserting instead that the sixth consciousness alone sustains life-force and warmth.
However, the sixth consciousness is subject to interruption, unlike life-force and warmth, which are of a single, continuous stream.
Therefore, it is said: "The theory of Consciousness-Only is not so; how could it accord with correct principle?
Although it is taught that the three dharmas mutually support one another, [the passage] up to "that consciousness is precisely this eighth consciousness" [is established].

The opponent from another vehicle raises an objection: "Among the three factors [of the aids to penetration], since you admit that the 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*) factor does not pervade the three realms, why do you not likewise admit that the sixth consciousness also has interruptions and transitions? Why do you grant this quality of interruption and transition to the 'Heat' factor alone?

The Master answers this collectively: "Because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there being no material substance, the characteristic of 'heat' is also absent; therefore, it is said not to be pervasive."

Regarding the previous reasoning, it is not intended as a formal objection (*dūṣaṇa*). This is because "reasoning" (*yukti*) refers to what is accepted by intention, rather than being restricted to the verbal expression of an objection.

That is to say, the following section restates the meaning cited from the preceding sūtra: namely, that the three factors—vitality (*āyu*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—are uninterrupted and undergo no transformation, and are thus able to support one another constantly.
If they were subject to transformation, they would lack the function of constant support. Such is the meaning of the sūtra. This is...
This is the correct principle (*nyāya*). The following section explains the meaning of why the response given in the previous passage does not constitute a logical fault (*dūṣaṇa*).

The Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*) offers two intentions when citing this locus: first, the literal expression (*vāc*), and second, the intended implication (*abhiprāya*). Although the literal expression states that the three factors support one another, the intended implication holds that this is spoken only with reference to a single consciousness (*vijñāna*).
That is to say, while the word "consciousness" is used, it does not denote the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). Now, [the text] cites the factor of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*)...

[The opponent replies: "It pervades. [The author asks: "Does this not contradict the previously accepted principle? Since that principle remains unrefuted, it is universally established (*prasiddha*).

Furthermore, from "the three lower realms" onwards, the text refutes the attachment of other vehicles (*yāna*) which hold that the sixth consciousness can maintain vitality (*āyuṣ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Vitality is the functional capacity to continuously maintain matter and mind without interruption;
it is the seed of the eighth consciousness. Warmth is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. Both of these types...

It belongs to the outflowing (sāsrava). If it is granted that the sixth [consciousness] can sustain the outflowing when one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and gives rise to an outflow-free mind (anāsravacitta), then this sixth [consciousness] would also be capable of sustaining.
Since the sustaining mind has already become outflow-free, by what consciousness would the outflowing life-force (āyus) be sustained?
This is because, among the eight causes, it always belongs to the outflowing. Therefore, it is the [seventh consciousness] that sustains life and warmth. From this point downward...

The conclusion clarifies the eighth [topic]: the ability to sustain vitality (*āyuṣ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). △ This concludes the fifth section on the triad of vitality, warmth, and consciousness.
Below, the sixth section concerning the mind at the time of birth and death is divided into two parts. First, a general explanation of birth and death.
Furthermore, the sūtras state that for all classes of sentient beings, [the mind]—up to what is called the "mind of birth-and-death"—does not contradict correct reasoning.

By citing the sūtras and inferring their meaning, it is proven that the eighth consciousness is named the "mind of scattered existence. This means that at the time of taking birth and at the time of death, when all other minds have separated, only this mind remains;
thus it is called the "mind of scattered existence. It is not the case that this refers to the mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), because...
Regarding the concentration of non-mind (*acittaka-samādhi*): upon entering this concentration, there is no mind; upon emerging from it, there is mind.

Now, at the time of birth and death, the mind must certainly not be absent within the body of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), and it must certainly not exist within the state of death-existence (*maraṇa-bhava*) where the body has ceased. Therefore, it is not the concentration of non-mind. Furthermore, the *Zongjing* states:
"The affairs of birth and death necessarily abide in a distracted and agitated mind. The Sūtras speak of two paths: that of distraction and that of tranquility.

All [mental states] exist in dependence upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). This refers to the passage "birth and death below," which distinguishes the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) from the mind at the time of birth and death.
One who is "extremely fainting" refers to the moment of birth and death; it is like being asleep without dreaming, serving as a metaphor for the time of birth and death.

At this time, the evolving consciousnesses necessarily do not manifest. Furthermore, the passage "in this state below" explains why the evolving consciousnesses do not arise during the state of birth and death mentioned above.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are extremely coarse and violent; therefore, they must necessarily be cognizable.

Below the section on the true maturation (*vipāka*), [the text] correctly reveals that both the mode of activity and the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the eighth consciousness cannot be discerned. Although this mind exists during the period of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is as if there were no mind.

Regarding the term "one lifetime" (*eka-janman*): it refers to the duration from the beginning to the end of a single retribution. This consciousness remains without transformation from its beginning to its end.
Therefore. △ First, the general explanation of birth and death is concluded. Below, the second section distinguishes birth and death.
Some say that the five consciousnesses are definitely absent at this stage (up to the point where it is established); however, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not like this.
Other vehicles raise this objection: "If the sixth consciousness does not exist during the state of birth, it is because the first five consciousnesses are absent;
for other teachings state that the first five evolving consciousnesses are the causes of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since the state of birth lacks the first five as causes, even if the mental consciousness exists, its modes of activity (*ākāra*) do not arise, and thus it cannot be known. This argument implicitly demonstrates that the eighth consciousness must necessarily exist.
Regarding the "essence of consciousness": if that were so, the Master of the Treatise refutes it as follows.

If one maintains that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) necessarily arises only with the five sensory consciousnesses as its cause, then for those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), subsequent mental consciousness would never arise at all. Why?

Because other teachings state that in that formless realm, the five sensory consciousnesses are necessarily absent; since there is no basis for the arising of either concentrated or distracted minds, [if mental consciousness depended on them], it would not occur. If that...

A concentrated mind must necessarily be induced by the mental faculty (*manas*). One should know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) does not have the five [sensory] consciousnesses as its cause.

If it is argued—granting even such a counter-argument—that the concentrated and distracted minds manifest abruptly at the time of emerging from meditative absorption due to long-standing habituation, the Master of the Treatise objects:
"When one is first born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), why would they not manifest? This refers to the formless realm.
At the time of initial birth, although the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) exists, it is not clear because the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is absent.

If, through habitual practice, the mental consciousness arises when emerging from meditative absorption in that realm, then the mental consciousness habitually practiced at the time of initial birth in the desire and form realms should likewise arise.
Since the mental consciousness arises at the time of initial birth, its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its object (*ālambana*) must both be present.

There is something known. What is called "distracted mind"? Both are unintelligible. If one follows the lower [position] and further indulges in speculative reasoning, [it is argued that] although there is mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) at the moment of birth, because it is obscured and dull, it does not yet manifest initially. [The author] refutes this, saying: This characteristic of obscuration...
This refers back to the eighth original cause mentioned previously; why then take the trouble to state separately that there exists a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?

Among certain other Hīnayāna schools, it is maintained that during states such as birth and death, there exists a subtle mental consciousness. The Master of the Treatise explains: "One should know that [it is] subtle."

This refers precisely to this eighth consciousness. If it were argued that both its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its object (*ālambana*) are unintelligible, we reply that the well-established mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not like that.
Furthermore, because one reaches [a new state] at the time of death due to wholesome or unwholesome karma, we know for certain that this eighth consciousness exists.
Citing sutras and śāstras as proof: the occurrence of the sensation of cold at the time of death can only be established if the eighth consciousness exists.

A verse from the *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* says: "In the case of the sages, it leaves from the crown; for those born in the heavens, from the eyes; for humans, from the heart; for hungry ghosts, from the abdomen;

for animals, from the knees; and for those in hell, it exits from the soles of the feet. This verifies the distinctions among the six realms of existence. [This is also discussed] in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

The verse says: "In those of good karma, cooling begins from below; in those of evil karma, cooling begins from above. In both cases, it reaches the heart, where they simultaneously relinquish their bodies at one place.

This clarifies the two paths of good and evil. The meaning is that when the sensation of cold arises in the eighth consciousness—which is non-appropriating—wherever warmth remains, the eighth consciousness persists.
By specifying "below the evolving consciousnesses," it distinguishes this from the evolving consciousnesses, which do not give rise to the sensation of cold.
"Each has its own distinct basis" refers to the first five consciousnesses, as they each rely on their own respective five sense organs and do not share a common basis.
"Or they do not function [at all times]" means that they arise in dependence upon various conditions and are therefore absent at certain times.

"They do not abide in the body" refers to the sixth consciousness, which relies on the mind-faculty (manas) and does not rely on the material sense organs, because it lacks the characteristic of being corporeal. "Its objects are not fixed" means that, like the five consciousnesses, it takes objects... [incomplete source text].

Because it is fixed on a single object and proceeds continuously throughout the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), it possesses the aforementioned characteristics and should not possess the sensation of cold.

Since the six consciousnesses arise [only occasionally], they are merely maturation (*vipāka*) and are inferior; thus, the eighth [consciousness] is concluded as being both constant and pervasive, continuously maintaining the appropriation (*upādāna*).
Therefore, when it relinquishes the appropriation, the sensation of cold arises, for consciousness and warmth are inseparable. Because of this...

When the sensation of cold arises, it is then the same as that which is non-sentient (*asattva*). Although it is a transformation of the eighth consciousness, it can take that [cold] as its object while not being appropriated (*anupātta*), because it is not sentient.
For the reasons stated above, one should know that the substance of the eighth consciousness definitely exists.
[Section Two: Specifically Clarifying Birth and Death is Concluded. [The preceding six sections on the Mind at the Time of Birth and Death are Concluded.]
The following seven [points] cite the basis for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, a sutra states: "Consciousness conditions name-and-form" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*), and so forth; thus, the term "consciousness" therein refers to the eighth consciousness.

By citing the sutra and inferring its meaning, it is proven that there exists an eighth consciousness which serves as the condition for name-and-form. Regarding "consciousness conditions name-and-form," consciousness...

This refers to the eighth consciousness. "Name" (*nāma*) consists of the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; "form" (*rūpa*) is the aggregate of form. Regarding the "two dharmas":
consciousness is one dharma, and name-and-form together constitute the other dharma. The "bundle of reeds" is a metaphor for these two dharmas turning together simultaneously.
As stated below, the Master of the Treatise cites the etymological explanation from that sūtra: the Sanskrit term *kalala* [is explained as follows]. This...

The coagulation of clouds is the mark of the initial embryo; therefore, it is called the aggregate of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-skandha*). Regarding the phrase "the eyes and so forth," this distinguishes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which are not the basis for name-and-form.

Fearing that one might argue: "Within 'name,' the aggregate of consciousness is the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) consisting of the five sensory consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness," [the text clarifies].

This is the sixth consciousness. The Master of the Treatise suppresses [the opposing view] by stating that it also cannot be called the "consciousness aggregate" (*vijñāna-skandha*) within the context of the names [of the members].

That is to say, the five bodies of consciousness are the member of "consciousness" external to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), whereas the sixth consciousness is the "consciousness aggregate" within the names.

At the stage of the *kalala*, the five consciousnesses do not exist because the five sense organs are absent and thus lack the capacity to produce them; therefore, one should know that the "consciousness aggregate" within the names is exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, all...

[The above] concludes [the section on] the lack of constancy in the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and establishes that only the eighth [consciousness] possesses the meaning of "consciousness" as explained in that sūtra.

In the previously cited "Chapter on Reasoning," the formal explanation of the citations of reasoning is divided into ten sections: (1) the mind that sustains the seeds; (2) the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*);
(3) the substance of the realms of existence and modes of birth; (4) the physical body with its material sense organs; (5) the triad of life-force, warmth, and consciousness;
(6) the mind at the time of birth and death; and (7) the basis for dependent origination. These seven categories have been fully explained in the third fascicle. Within this [section]:
The eighth [section], the analysis of the substance of the consciousness-sustenance (*vijñānāhāra*), has two parts. First, the formal explanation of the consciousness-sustenance:
Furthermore, a sūtra states that for all sentient beings... [omitted] ...because when [the body] undergoes transformation and decay, form (*rūpa*) is of no use.

Citing scriptures and inferring their meaning, it is proven that the eighth consciousness constitutes the essence of *vijñānāhāra* (consciousness-food). Regarding *vijñānāhāra*, consciousness itself is the food;

"food" here carries the sense of providing nourishment and sustenance. That is to say, the eighth consciousness provides nourishment and sustains the physical body with its material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*).
Within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it sustains the seeds. Furthermore, citing the scripture that speaks of four kinds of food, food possesses...

Morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). Because it is eaten in morsels, it is called "morsel food. It exists only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), as its essence consists of the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility.
This is because these three do not exist in the two higher realms. At the time of transformation and decay, it performs the function of providing nourishment and maintenance;
therefore, this morsel food has "transformation" as its characteristic. Question: Why do the two objects—visible form and sound—not [function as morsel food]?
[Question: They serve as the [sensory] bases (*āśraya*). [Answer: The two consciousnesses of the eye and ear apprehend their objects through contact at a distance (*viprakṛṣṭa-grahaṇa*).

Since the two objects—visible form and sound—do not come into contact with the sense organs, they cannot nourish the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the organs; therefore, they do not serve as the bases. As for the three organs of the nose, tongue, and body, they apprehend their objects through contact (*saṃnikarṣa-grahaṇa*).
Because the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangibility—come into contact with the organs, they are able to nourish the primary elements of the organs. For this reason...
Only the three objects [of smell, taste, and touch] are taken as the substance of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"This edible food should be said to be comprised within the spheres (*āyatana*) of odor, taste, and tangibility. Through odor, taste, and tangibility, when they are properly digested and transformed, they are able to nourish and sustain;

when they are not properly digested and transformed, they cause depletion and decay. Since other phenomena such as visible form (*rūpa*) lack both nourishment and depletion through digestion and transformation, for this reason..."

It is said that those things which are not of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), yet cause the mind to rejoice and the sense faculties to be gladdened at the time of swallowing, are merely called the nutriment of contact (*sparśa-āhāra*).
If, after being consumed, they increase joy and happiness and are digested with ease, [they are so designated].
This is what is called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*). If various material objects lack the two aforementioned characteristics at the time of swallowing, they are not called "food" at all.

Thus, the "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*)—which is one of the twelve bases (*āyatana*)—is explained here as representing the category of "form" (*rūpa*) among the three aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*);
it does not include the meaning of edible food, because the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are identical to the base of form.

Second is the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*), which has the characteristic of contacting objects. This extends to its capacity for providing benefit through equanimity (*upekṣā*) as a superior form of sustenance.
"Contact" refers to the act of touching; it is the mental factor of contact (*sparśa-skandha*) associated with the six consciousnesses.

When it encounters external objects such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and other sense-fields—whether they be soft, smooth, slippery, cold, warm, or other tactile sensations—it gives rise to joy and pleasure. Together, these are able to nourish and sustain the sense faculties.
When the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are being correctly experienced, it is termed "nutriment of contact" (*sparśāhāra*). Suppose someone were to ask:

"Since contact (*sparśa*) is present in all eight consciousnesses, why is the nutriment of contact restricted only to the first six? The answer would be: "Although this contact is associated with all eight consciousnesses, we now take its aspect as 'nutriment' (*āhāra-artha*) as the predominant factor.
This is because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the contact associated with the first six consciousnesses is coarse and manifest, and thus it is capable of [appropriating and] sustaining."
Because it experiences pleasant and joyful sensations, it can produce a bodily equanimity (*upekṣā*) that is conducive to benefit; this is the sense of "predominance.
In the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, contact occurs simultaneously with the object because the object is subtle; thus, they are entirely unable to produce pleasant or joyful sensations.

Although they do produce the sensation of equanimity, it serves neither to harm nor to benefit; therefore, contact in the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, as well as contact associated with other consciousnesses accompanied by sorrowful or painful sensations, [are not predominant].
Equanimity that is not conducive to benefit is not the essence of nutriment, because it does not provide sustenance.
For example, when a man and a woman come together in touch, that touch can sustain the body and thus receives the name of "nutriment."

The third is the nutriment of mental volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*), which has aspiration as its characteristic. This is because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses a predominant aspiration toward its objects.

Volition is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-caitta*); when in a state of outflow (*sāsrava*), it functions together with the object-specific factor of desire (*chanda*) to give rise to craving for the object.

Because it is capable of providing nourishment and sustaining the function of eating, it is called the food of volition (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*). Its characteristic is aspiration, as in the sayings: "suspended sand satisfies hunger" and "longing for plums quenches thirst"—this is what is meant by the food of volition.

Question: Since it operates in conjunction with desire (*chanda*), [how is it distinct from the food of desire?]* *Note: The final sentence fragment in the source text appears to be the beginning of a question regarding the distinction between the food of volition and the food of desire.*
"What is it that desire does not nourish? Answer: "Volition (*cetanā*) benefits the faculties; it is not desire that has this capacity. Question: "Volition is common to all consciousnesses;
why is it attributed only to the sixth [consciousness]? Answer: "Only when volition is conjoined with desire does it possess the meaning of 'nourishment.
Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has a superior aspiration toward its objects, this 'volition-nourishment' belongs exclusively to the mental consciousness."

Fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) has the characteristic of sustaining (*dhṛti*). This is because it possesses the excellence of sustaining a continuous stream of a single category [of existence].

Consciousness is the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*). Within the state of outflow (*sāsrava*), by the power of either edible food, contact, or volition, it is able to perform the functions of nourishment and maintenance;
therefore, it is called the nutriment of consciousness, characterized by sustaining. Question: Since the meaning of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) applies to all cognitions...

The same applies [to the other three]. Why then is only the eighth consciousness designated as the "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*)? The answer is: because this eighth consciousness has a superior sense of "maintaining and upholding" (*dhṛti*), it alone is called the consciousness-food.
Accordingly, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that these four foods [are so called] because they sustain the body and life, yet they are neither universal nor constant.

This citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* establishes that there are four nutriments (*āhāra*). They are subsumed within three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*). Regarding the inclusion of the four nutriments within three aggregates:

this refers to excluding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). As for the nutriment of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), form is of no use once it has been transformed [by digestion].

Furthermore, because the objects of perception (*saṃjñā*) in contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*) are distinct in meaning, the nutriments of edible food and contact are subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*). This concerns the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*).

They are also included within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Since the treatise states that the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*) belongs to the six consciousnesses, the nutriment of volition (*cetanāhāra*) should be subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and the aggregate of consciousness;
for volition is the primary and most eminent factor among formations. Furthermore, the treatise states that the nutriment of volition belongs to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it includes the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*); this is because the meaning of "consciousness" is the same for both.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the four nutriments are subsumed within the five bases (*pañcāyatana*): among the twelve bases, seven are excluded—the five sense-faculty bases and the bases of visible form and sound—because they lack the nature of nutriment.

Only odor, taste, and tangibles subsume the nutriments of edible food and contact-food; as for the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it subsumes the nutriment of consciousness. The mind-base (*manāyatana*)... [is excluded].

Because of the nutriment of volition (*manosaṃcetanāhāra*). Furthermore, the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*) is the seventh consciousness; it is appropriate that it be associated with the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*), as they are invariably connected.
Regarding the inclusion of the four kinds of nutriment within the eleven elements (*dhātu*), one likewise excludes seven elements, identical to the previous seven bases.

As for the two nutriments of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and contact (*sparśāhāra*), these consist of odor, taste, and tangibility, and are thus subsumed under three elements. Moreover, the nutriment of contact can also pervade the six consciousness-elements, according to the treatise.

This is because it is explicitly stated that [the other three nutriments] belong to the six consciousnesses. The nutriment of volition (*manasikāra-āhāra*) is likewise subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) and the sphere of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), for the treatise states that the nutriment of volition belongs to the mental consciousness.
The nutriment of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*) subsumes all seven types of mind-spheres (*cittadhātu*), namely, the sphere of the mind-faculty (*manaindriyadhātu*).

And the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*): because the self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of these various consciousnesses share the same substance as the eighth [consciousness]. From "These four" below, the meaning of nutriment (*āhāra*) is established.

From "Edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) below, the previous three nutriments are distinguished; they cannot encompass all sentient beings, and thus within the three realms (*traidhātuka*), there are those that are pervasive and those that are not.
From "The eye and so forth" below, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are distinguished regarding the states with mind and without mind.
In the middle [of the body], it functions intermittently; regarding the maintenance of the physical body and life-force, it is neither universal nor constant, and thus cannot serve as nutriment.
△ The first section, the formal explanation of consciousness as nutriment, is concluded. Below, the second section consists of restating the opponent’s position and refuting it.
Regarding those who maintain that there is no eighth consciousness (up to): "Because non-associated dharmas are not substantially real.

This refutes the externalist attachment and reveals that only the eighth consciousness is the substance of the *vijñānāhāra* (consciousness-nutriment). "The past" refers to the time before entering meditative absorption;
"the future" refers to the time after emerging from absorption. They [the opponents] maintain that in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), there is [nutriment] at both ends.
[The opponent claims: "The mind itself is the food for one in the state of no-mind. [The author] refutes this: "The past has already ceased and is not permanent;

the future has not yet arisen and is not present. It is like a flower in the sky—how could it possess the nature of food? Furthermore, fearing that [the opponent] might resort to another argument, [they claim] that the 'mind capable of inducing concentration' acts as the food that sustains the body for the one who has entered meditative absorption.
[The author] refutes this: "At the time of abiding in the state of no-mind, the mind capable of inducing concentration..."
That which has already ceased does not exist; what, then, could serve as nutriment? Since it belongs to the past, it has already been refuted.

Furthermore, we fear you might resort to a further argument, claiming that the two attainments—non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—which are formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), constitute the nutriment for those who have entered these two attainments.

This is refuted as follows: the four nutriments, such as edible food and so forth, do not include the nutriments of non-conceptualization and the like. Since formations dissociated from mind are not... [the text continues].
It truly exists, yet it lacks the functional capacity to serve as sustenance.

Some maintain that even in states such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the sixth consciousness still persists; however, this is because [the opponent's position] holds that the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous character) and so forth lack substantial reality.

Citing their argumentative words, [the author] generally refutes them as irrational; that which shall be extensively refuted later is explained in detail in the ninth chapter, where the definition of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is clarified.
Regarding "the two upper realms," these are the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

Since the bodies in those two realms are both contaminated (*sāsrava*), if one maintains that there is no eighth consciousness and only the sixth exists, then when the sixth arises as uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), [it would have no support].

Because contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) maintains a contaminated body, it is said that uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) and the like cannot serve as food, as they destroy existence (*bhava*).

Fearing that the opponent might further argue that the six uncontaminated consciousnesses possess contaminated seeds (*bīja*), and that these contaminated seeds can serve as their food, [the author] refutes this, saying:
"The uncontaminated is like *nirvāṇa*; it does not maintain contaminated seeds. Therefore, it maintains [existence]."
Regarding the seeds of outflows (*sāsrava-bīja*), we maintain that they reside solely in the eighth consciousness.

Furthermore, fearing that others might argue that sentient beings in the higher realms sustain their bodies with life-force (*jīvita*) and sustain their life-force with the body—thereby taking each other as food—we refute this by stating: among the four types of nutriment (*āhāra*), the "nutriment of the body" (*kāyāhāra*) is not mentioned therein.

Furthermore, regarding the nutriment of life-force (*jīvitāhāra*): since there is no material body in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and life-force has nothing to sustain it, what could serve as its nutriment?

As for the "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāyasabhāga*) and so forth, since they lack substantial reality, they are collectively refuted as being among the dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*), and thus neither can fulfill the definition of nutriment.
From this, it is known with certainty that [the consciousness] distinct from the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas)—that very consciousness—is precisely this eighth consciousness.
This concludes the demonstration that the eighth consciousness possesses the function of constant maintenance and is therefore able to serve as nutriment (*āhāra*). Fearing that one might object:

"If the Buddha also relies on nutriment, he too should be a sentient being (*sattva*)," the text explains: "Only by relying on the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) that are tainted (*sāsrava*) is one established as a sentient being."

The Buddha is without outflows and is not subsumed within the category of sentient beings. When the Buddha says that sentient beings abide by means of nutriment, he speaks by way of conventional manifestation;
it is not that the Buddha abides by means of nutriment. Furthermore, he is indeed a sentient being, as previously stated, yet he is distinct from the various evolving consciousnesses.

There is a maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that constantly sustains the body and life; this consciousness has the nature of nutriment (*āhāra*) and is superior to the three preceding nutriments.

One should know that this consciousness is the eighth consciousness. [The second section,] the refutation by restating the opponent’s position, is concluded. [The above eight points conclude] the citation of the substance of the nutriment of consciousness.
Below, the ninth point, citing the state of mind in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), is divided into two parts: first, citing the sūtra to provide a formal refutation.

Furthermore, a sūtra states that for one who abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), [the question arises] based on what it is said that "consciousness does not depart from the body.
By citing this sūtra and inferring its meaning, one proves the existence of the eighth consciousness, which certainly does not depart from the body.

This is because for a person who has entered the attainment of cessation, the activities of body, speech, and mind are all entirely extinguished. Respiration is the preparatory activity of the body; vitarka and vicāra are the preparatory activities of speech.
Feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are mental applications that correspond with the first six consciousnesses;

because they are all extinguished within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), yet life-force (*āyus*) does not cease, it is the eighth consciousness. That which possesses upon its seeds the uninterrupted capacity to maintain the continuity of the resultant form and mind is called "life-force.
Furthermore, it is not separate from warmth (*uṣman*); warmth is the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the eighth consciousness.

These two factors are both not separate from the eighth consciousness. Since one is within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the six groups of consciousness, as well as the preparatory applications of body, speech, and mind, are all inactive;
yet, because vitality (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*) still persist, it is clearly known that this is indeed the eighth consciousness, which serves as the support for vitality and warmth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the eye and so forth," it explains that one who enters the meditative absorption of cessation does so in order to cease the eye [and the other faculties].
Because they are equal in terms of consciousness, within this state all evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are extinguished.

If one does not admit [the existence of the eighth consciousness], that is to say, for those who maintain that there is no eighth consciousness, upon what basis does that sūtra state: "consciousness does not depart from the body"?

[The first section, citing the sūtra to directly refute [the opponent's view], is concluded. Below, the second part—reiterating their position and analyzing the refutation—is divided into three sections. First, reiterating their position and providing a general refutation.

If it is argued that at a later time that consciousness arises again—[up to] because there is no rebirth apart from relying on another body—even if they further maintain this counter-argument, namely:
"When entering meditative absorption, the sixth consciousness is extinguished; when subsequently emerging from absorption, the sixth consciousness arises.
Just as malaria temporarily subsides yet the disease does not leave the body, so too is this consciousness; thus it is said to 'not leave the body,'" [we] refute this as follows:

If they were to arise again later, they would be called "not separated from the body. This would contradict the sūtra’s statement that mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased, because the mind and mental formations would then share the same arising and ceasing.
Since it has already been stated that [the formations] have ceased, how could they not be separated?

If vitality (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and the sense faculties (*indriya*)—which have ceased and do not arise again—were to arise like consciousness (*vijñāna*), it would lead to a great error. Therefore, vitality, warmth, and the rest, while in the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), are all...

It does not depart from the body. Consciousness is also like vitality and warmth; it truly does not depart from the body. It is not like the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), which, having ceased, arise again.

Furthermore, below this [passage], even granting their counter-argument that there is no consciousness in this state—since if consciousness were entirely absent, one would not be a sentient being—what does that sutra say?
It says that those who dwell in the meditative attainment of cessation are "dwelling in the attainment of cessation," because they must necessarily be sentient beings. Moreover, it is different...

"Regarding 'familiar with the inferior' below: this refers to the previous adherence to the non-existence of consciousness, whereby one claims that all consciousnesses are absent; thus, [the text] uses rubble and debris as a refutation.

This adherence to the non-existence of consciousness merely denies the existence of the *vipāka* (maturation) consciousness, while it is evident that the sixth consciousness exists, as it arises again upon emerging from meditative absorption.

Furthermore, [the text] refutes [this view] by stating that if there were no consciousness to maintain the sense faculties, vitality, and warmth, one would be like a corpse, and consciousness would not arise again. If one were to claim this..."

If the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) were to cease and then arise again, there would be an interruption. What does that sūtra say? It states that "consciousness does not depart from the body.

However, when the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna) abandons this body and transfers to another body, it never returns again; thus, there is no logical basis for its being born in this body once more.

Furthermore, if in this state there were no consciousness that maintains the seeds (up to the point where it is established that) there must certainly be a real consciousness that does not depart from the body, then [the opponent’s argument] would again refute their own position that [consciousness] arises again after having been extinguished; therefore, it is said that there is no consciousness maintaining the seeds, and subsequent consciousness would not arise.

Regarding the phrase "past and future" below, this generally excludes all dharmas that have already ceased or have not yet arisen, which lack the maintenance of life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*), and thus do not depart from the body.

[This is] the meaning. However, the statement that "in the attainment of cessation and so forth, consciousness does not depart from the body" serves to clarify that the entity of the eighth consciousness must necessarily be present within this state.
If it is argued that the sixth consciousness exists in this state because one can cognize that consciousness has entered this meditative attainment—[this is refuted as follows:]...

Even if they were to argue that the sixth consciousness exists within the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and therefore it is called "not separated from the body" in that sutra, this is refuted as being illogical:
this meditative attainment is designated as the "mindless attainment" precisely because the sixth consciousness is absent.

How could there be a sixth consciousness? Furthermore, it is called "mindless" (*acittaka*). They further argue: "That which is called 'mindless' refers only to the absence of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), not the absence of the sixth.
To this, the objection is raised: "Then all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) should be called 'mindless. Why?

Because whenever one enters meditative absorption, the five consciousnesses—eye and the rest—necessarily do not arise. As for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is included among the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ vijñānakāya*)."

Successively refuting the sixth [consciousness]: that is to say, if the five consciousnesses do not exist, then the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) also does not exist, because the sixth consciousness is likewise a *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness).

Alternatively, it is because this state is inferior; that is to say, the mental states (*ākāra*) of consciousness in this state are subtle and hidden, and thus cannot be known, just as vitality (*āyuḥ*) and warmth (*uṣman*), though inseparable from the body, are not perceived.
Such is not the case for the sixth consciousness. If there were a sixth consciousness, [it would be perceivable].

Since the mental aspects (*ākāra*) and objects (*ālambana*) would be cognizable, there is further concern that one might argue that consciousness exists in this state because its aspects are knowable.
This is refuted as follows: it would then follow that, like other states, this is not included within the meditative absorption of the mindless state (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
Why? Because one enters this absorption precisely to cease coarse and agitated thought and mind; how could such a mind still exist after having entered the absorption?
△ First, the refutation of the overall thesis is concluded. Below, [it is argued that] there is consciousness and an object.
Furthermore, if the sixth consciousness exists at this stage (until: how can it be said that the mind has ceased and yet persists)?
Question: Within this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), do mental factors (*caitta*) exist or not? Only after this is established can one then refute the activity of the mind (*cittacāra*).

Since "activity of the mind" refers to feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), and these are mental factors, and since the Sūtra states that they have ceased, why do you insist that they exist? If mental factors were present, would this not contradict the Sūtra?

Regarding the objection raised below concerning the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of this meditative absorption, the proponent offers a defense: "Among the mental factors (*caitta*), only feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are specifically designated as 'mental formations' (*citta-saṃskāra*);
therefore, in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it is only feeling and perception that are ceased, while other mental factors remain, as there is no contradiction.

The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this by analogy: "If one were to name this attainment 'cessation' merely because of an aversion to feeling and perception, then in the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti'), only..."
When one is weary of coarse perception (*audārikasaṃjñā*), only that perception should cease; yet the six consciousnesses would still remain, which you do not admit.

Furthermore, since the mental factors (*caitta*) that provide support have ceased, the mind (*citta*) that is supported by them should also cease. Why then do you maintain that the sixth consciousness exists in this state?
[The opponent] offers a further defense, saying: "It is like the body; although inhalation and exhalation have ceased within the body, the body..."
It is not extinguished. How can one then demand that the mind-king (citta-rāja) be extinguished along with its mental concomitants? To raise an objection by analogy:

if it is claimed that when bodily formations (kāya-saṃskāra) are extinguished, the body itself is not extinguished, then by analogy, when mental formations (citta-saṃskāra) are extinguished, the mind itself should likewise not be extinguished.

Furthermore, when vocal formations (vāk-saṃskāra)—namely vitarka and vicāra—are extinguished, speech itself should also not be extinguished; for there has never been anyone who could speak without giving rise to vitarka and vicāra. Therefore, it is said: "But it is not..."

This is accepted. However, regarding the discussion below on the "factors of action" (*carita*), the Master [Vasubandhu] is precisely clarifying that among the preparatory applications (*prayoga*), there are those that are pervasive and those that are not pervasive;

one must not take them as mutual analogies, for that would contradict and undermine correct reasoning. Among the three types of action, bodily action is not pervasive, whereas vocal and mental actions are both termed pervasive actions.
Therefore, it is said: when seeing ceases, the body still remains; when vitarka and vicāra cease, speech [ceases].
Because there is no [separate] cause: when sensation and perception cease, the mind necessarily ceases along with them. How, then, can it be said that "the mind remains" while they have ceased?
This is intended to show that in their absence, both are absent; for since these [mental factors] are universal, they ought to perish together.

Furthermore, since it is admitted that volition (*cetanā*) and the other [mental factors] are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), then perception (*saṃjñā*) should also arise inseparably from them.
