To clarify that they are successively absent, he refutes the remaining views regarding mental factors. Regarding "volition and the others": volition is associated with desire;
"and the others" refers to the five [factors] beginning with desire. By the mention of "other places," the ten [factors] consisting of the universal and the object-specific ones are indicated.

The universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) consist of eleven [factors] such as faith (*śraddhā*). The great wholesome ground factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) consist of twenty-six [factors] such as greed (*lobha*).

Therefore, the refutation is difficult to overcome: "Furthermore, if it is admitted that volition (*cetanā*) and the others are universal mental factors, then when the two factors of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease, the remaining universal mental factors should also cease.
Since the universal mental factors have ceased, [the great wholesome ground factors] such as faith would also cease."

The dharmas also do not exist [therein], for it is not the case that the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) have ceased, as others remain present. How, then, can it be said that only sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) cease?
Since other mental factors are admitted to exist below [this level], one may further raise the objection that they must coexist. Furthermore, this is stated below.

This explains the principle that "if there is existence, there must be co-existence. Since contact (*sparśa*) serves as a condition for all dharmas, if volition (*cetanā*) and so forth exist, there must necessarily be contact.
Since contact conditions feeling (*vedanā*), feeling must arise. Feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*) are inseparable;
thus, perception should not cease. How could any other dharma remain while feeling and perception cease?

If it were the case that craving is conditioned by feeling, yet not all feelings [lead to it], then the meditative attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*) could not be established.
The proponent offers a rebuttal: "Craving is conditioned by feeling because it arises from pleasant feeling; if one experiences painful feeling, craving does not arise. He provides an analogy:

"It is like contact being the condition for feeling, where some [contacts] do not give rise to feeling. The Master of the Treatise challenges this: "Because there is a distinction [between the cases]."
This means that from the passage "The Buddha... onwards, the text explains the meaning of the distinction. That is to say, within the Buddha’s sūtras, there are inherent distinctions;

specifically, while it is sometimes distinguished that craving arises conditioned by sensation, there is no instance where it is distinguished that sensation arises from contact without being experienced.
Furthermore, it is said that ignorance-contact (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*) is the condition for the arising of feeling (*vedanā*). Therefore, wherever there is contact, feeling must necessarily arise;
it is a settled principle that feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*) are inseparable.

Alternatively, they may argue in turn that in other states of mind where consciousness exists, feeling and perception do not cease, because even in the state of cessation (*nirodha*), mental factors such as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth still exist. To refute this, it is said: "Even if you grant that mental factors exist..."

This contradicts the scriptural teachings. Furthermore, the statement that "mental formations have ceased" could not establish it as the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).
△ Second, the section on "consciousness having an object" is concluded. Below follows the three sections on "consciousness without an object."
If there were no mental factors (*caitta*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) would likewise not exist; how could there be consciousness without mental factors?

If you admit that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) lacks mental factors, do not maintain that the sixth consciousness exists therein, for mind (*citta*) and mental factors are inseparable.
Since the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-caitta*) have ceased, the mental phenomena (*caitasika-dharma*) must also cease accordingly. If you claim that mind does exist [therein]...
If there were no feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, then feeling and the others would not be universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).
This is because the universal mental factors comprise ten mental concomitants (*caitta*); if there were no mental concomitants, the universal factors such as feeling would not exist.

Furthermore, this consciousness would not be an associated phenomenon (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), because without mental concomitants, there can be no association. If one were to admit the existence of consciousness while denying the existence of mental concomitants, [it would follow that they are dissociated].
This consciousness would then lack its basis, object, and so forth. At the time of the conjunction of the three, contact (*sparśa*) is necessarily the basis;

if there were no locus for contact, the three would not be in conjunction. Furthermore, when the mind arises, attention (*manasikāra*) serves as its condition; if there were no attention, consciousness would not arise.
If one were to allow that this mind lacks a basis and an object, it would follow that it is not a mental state, just like material phenomena (*rūpadharma*). Moreover...

Citing scripture as proof: "In states where mind exists, mental factors must necessarily exist. From "If this... below, the intention of the scripture is explained and their false attachments are refuted.

If it is argued that at other times the triadic conjunction possesses power [to produce consciousness], [the response is: no; otherwise, how could it be called a "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?

Even if one were to propose an alternative argument—that at other times the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness possesses the power to conjoin, thereby producing contact (*sparśa*), which in turn gives rise to sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth—this is not the case within meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Why? Because prior to this absorption, through the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one cultivates a state of aversion toward coarse and restless mental factors (*caitta*).
While in the state of absorption, these three factors lack such capacity; they do not produce contact, nor do they give rise to sensation and the rest. Therefore, [the objection does not apply].
In this meditative absorption, there are no mental factors (*caitta*). The Master of the Treatise raises an objection:

"If it is because one feels aversion toward mental factors prior to the absorption that there are no mental factors within it, then this absorption should be called 'the absorption that extinguishes mental factors.

Why does the Sūtra state only that this absorption extinguishes feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)? Furthermore, even if one were to argue that at the time of feeling aversion prior to the absorption, one only felt aversion toward feeling and perception...

Therefore, it is given the name "attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception" (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). As for the other mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), they are not so named because they cease only in accordance with that [attainment].
Furthermore, an objection is raised: "Since one has become weary of sensation and perception, and the other factors cease in accordance with them, the mind (*citta*) should also cease.

For the other mental factors follow the cessation of sensation and perception; since the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is like those other factors, it too should cease in accordance with sensation and perception. If the mind does not cease..."
How is this state called "mindless absorption" (*acittaka-samāpatti*)?

Furthermore, what is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in this state of concentration? [If it were absent,] why would there be no mental factors (*caitta*), and the mind (*citta*) itself should also be non-existent.
First, one asks whether the mental consciousness within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to one of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Then, restating the point, it is refuted as follows:

The mental consciousness within meditative concentration cannot be of a defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, because within various wholesome concentrations, such defilement and indeterminate states do not exist.
Furthermore, a defiled or indeterminate mind must necessarily be accompanied by mental factors (*caitta*), which contradicts your prior tenet that [this state] is without mental factors.

Furthermore, since one develops a sense of revulsion toward defiled distraction prior to entering meditative concentration, how could one instead give rise to unwholesome or defiled mental factors while within that concentration?
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Moreover, in this concentration, consciousness is not separated from the body;

it is certainly not mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because [mental consciousness] cannot be established as being wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. If the mind of this concentration were a wholesome mind, it should..."
It is associated with mental factors of the wholesome state; furthermore, this also contradicts your tenet that there are no mental factors [in such states]. Moreover, it is said:

"If the roots of goodness already exist, why do the two types—perception and feeling—not manifest? If perception and feeling were present, one could not call it the 'attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

This was stated beforehand to suppress the opponent's potential counter-argument that the mind might be of an inferior nature; [the point is that] its intrinsic nature is wholesome, which is faith (*śraddhā*).
These eleven dharmas are ultimately wholesome (*paramārtha-kuśala*). According to our own school, this refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Nirvāṇa.

As for that which they grasp as a wholesome mind devoid of mental factors (*caitta*), since one has cultivated the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it would lack mental factors such as the wholesome roots;

thus, it could not be associated with them. Furthermore, because it still belongs to the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*), it is not Nirvāṇa. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explains: "Moreover, this mind is not..."

It is virtuous by its own nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*), because only the roots of virtue and so forth are included within that category. Furthermore, this virtuous mind is not ultimately virtuous (*paramārtha-kuśala*);
only liberation is definitively so. Since it remains at the stage of a cause, it is not called liberation.

If one were to claim that this mind is virtuous through origination (*samutthāna-kuśala*), then for a noble being (*ārya*) in the state of fruition, it would have to be considered virtuous through application (*prayoga-kuśala*).
The roots that initiate activities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are called "virtuous by way of origination" (*samutthāna-kuśala*).
As for those who contradict our own school, they maintain the thesis that the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) possesses mind but lacks mental factors (*caitta*).

Since they admit the presence of mind, just as in other virtuous minds, it would arise immediately after [a preceding state] with the three types of virtuous roots—non-greed and so forth. How then could there be a virtuous mind without mental factors, given its origination from what precedes?
Therefore, the mind is virtuous, and this is also due to the power of the roots of virtue. How could there be a mind existing alone without mental factors?
One should understand that when examining the evolving consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness and so forth—even in states such as the attainment of non-conception—the same principle applies.

Establishing this stage, there are no evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); there is only the eighth consciousness. This accords with that sūtra’s statement that "consciousness does not depart from the body.

Regarding the entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), it is explained that this absorption merely ceases those evolving consciousnesses characterized by distraction and movement;

it does not cease the underlying consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which possesses subtle and hidden modes of activity, maintains extreme tranquility, and acts as the sustaining consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*). Since this is the case for the absorption of cessation, [it follows that... there is none.

The stages of perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth should be understood by analogy with this. △ Third, the conclusion of the section on "consciousness existing without objects. This concludes the nine preceding citations concerning the mind in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Below, ten citations concerning defiled and pure minds follow.
Furthermore, a sūtra states that because the mind is defiled (up to) "all those who have already severed [defilements] should [still] give rise to it.
By citing this sūtra and inferring its meaning, it is proven that there exists an eighth consciousness called the "defiled-pure mind" (*kliṣṭa-śuddha-citta*).
Regarding the phrase "defiled-pure phenomena": this refers to all mundane conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, as well as those that are wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth. All of these...
Taking the eighth consciousness as the basis, it arises because of the eighth; the active manifestations of the preceding seven consciousnesses abide in dependence upon the eighth.

The substance of the eighth consciousness itself receives their perfuming and maintains the seeds of those preceding seven consciousnesses across the three natures. Therefore, this eighth [consciousness]...
This is called the "defiled and pure mind. To further illustrate defilement, three types are briefly opened up:

namely, affliction (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Affliction refers to the delusions; these are the three branches of ignorance, craving, and grasping within the twelve links of dependent origination. Karma refers to the actions; these are the two branches of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
Suffering refers to the results; these are the five branches beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the two branches beginning with birth (*jāti*). Through affliction...

Karma is initiated. Because fruit is induced by karma, there are the categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*). Since these categories are distinct, the seeds serve as the cause for the active manifestations (*samudācāra*), and the active manifestations serve as the fruit of the seeds.

If the eighth consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds of the afflictions, then when the active manifestations of the afflictions have ceased while sentient beings transmigrate through the nine stages of the three realms, the subsequent arising of afflictions would all be without a cause. It would be like...
Udraka Rāmaputra was born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception;

though he was free from defiled thoughts, after his life ended, he fell into the body of a flying wildcat, preying on forest birds above and spying on fish in the deep waters below. How could such active afflictions have arisen without causes and seeds?
Regarding other dharmas that do not maintain seeds: past and future minds and so forth lack a substantially real essence and thus have no capacity to maintain seeds.

As for "if [it were] the various..."—this refers to the fruits of the three vehicles, which are realized only after one has permanently severed the afflictions (*kleśa*). As for "if the various afflictions... [the text continues].
If [the fruit] were produced without a cause, the noble fruits would be eternally severed.

Since those afflictions would be produced without a cause, if this consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds of karmic results, [the attainment of the fruits] would not be established here, and consequently, it would not be established later either.
Regarding "the fruits of various karmas": this refers to the ripening fruits (*vipāka-phala*) induced by wholesome and unwholesome karma within the three realms and nine stages.

If this consciousness did not exist to sustain the seeds of karmic fruits, then when the fruits of prior karma are exhausted and the fruits of subsequent karma arise, they would likewise be without cause;

for other dharmas have already been refuted as being the causal seeds. Regarding "dharmas of different categories": this refers to the wholesome and unwholesome fruits of the six destinies and the three miserable paths. Three...
When the realms, karma, and its fruits are exhausted without remainder, it is called "nirvana without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*).

Since you admit that karma and its fruits [arise] without cause and yet persist eternally, it would likewise follow that afflictions should also arise eternally without cause; furthermore, the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles would never exist at all.

Moreover, regarding the downward progression of conditioned activities, this is refuted by means of the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). That is to say: if ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth—if these were non-existent...
This consciousness does not have formations as its condition; rather, formations are karma, which are established through perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Since consciousness is that which is perfumed, it is said to be the condition. If this consciousness did not exist, what would receive the perfuming? It cannot be the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), for they were previously refuted [as being so].

The defiled consciousness that is produced by the fetters and afflictions as it leads to rebirth in the eighth realm of existence is called "rebirth-linking defiled consciousness" (*pratisandhi-saṃkliṣṭa-vijñāna*) and is also termed "consciousness induced by formative forces" (*saṃskāra-ākṣipta-vijñāna*).

If this consciousness were absent, it would not be induced by formative forces either; for consciousness is conditioned by formative forces, and name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness. If this consciousness were absent, [the subsequent stages would not arise].

It should be stated that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) has volitional formations (saṃskāra) as its condition. To this, an objection is raised: "Because there is a vast temporal gap, the sense of being a condition does not exist.
Since the sense of being a condition is absent, it does not constitute a causal condition (hetupratyaya). Because this is not established, subsequent causal conditions also cannot be established."
All pure dharmas (*viśuddha-dharma*) are likewise of three kinds; [if it were otherwise], there would consequently be no fruits of the path of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

By citing pure dharmas, he also opens up these three types: namely, the mundane path of purity (*laukika-viśuddhi-mārga*), the supramundane path of purity (*lokottara-viśuddhi-mārga*), and the fruit of abandonment through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti-prahāṇaphala*).
These are distinct because of these three types. This is because one who cultivates the path comes from a different category and extinguishes the mind of that different category.
Only then can the pure dharmas arise. If this consciousness did not exist to sustain the seeds of these two paths, those two pure dharmas would have no cause for their arising.
Furthermore, the possibility of other dharmas sustaining the seeds has already been refuted previously. The pure path is the cause and nirvāṇa is the fruit;

when the causal practice is forever exhausted, the resultant virtue becomes perfected. If they were produced without a cause, then once the two paths had been exhausted, they would necessarily arise again. [The capacity...]
If [the path] were to arise without a cause based on the pure path (*viśuddha-mārga*), then its basis—the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth—would likewise have to arise without a cause.
Since afflictions do exist, how could it be called *nirvāṇa*? For *nirvāṇa* is realized precisely because there are no afflictions.

The supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*) must necessarily arise from originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). If this consciousness did not exist to maintain these seeds of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), then the supramundane path...
Initially, it should not arise, whether it be contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), because these two categories are distinct and [the former] is not its cause.

It cannot arise without a cause, for it is not of the nature of a seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*). Since supramundane paths (*lokottara-mārga*) necessarily arise from seeds, and the seeds of uncontaminated phenomena must certainly be sustained by consciousness, how could one maintain that the supramundane path arises without a cause?
If the cause of the supramundane path does not arise initially, it likewise [does not arise] subsequently.
The fruits realized [through practice] would likewise not arise; thus, the fruits of the paths of the three vehicles would be non-existent.

This is because, if this consciousness did not exist, it could not maintain the seeds of affliction—[and so forth]—since only this [consciousness] is capable of maintaining the seeds of both the defiled and the pure.

The fruit of abandonment through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is only fully accomplished by means of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*). If this consciousness did not maintain the seeds of the afflictions, there would be no cause for the fruit of abandonment;
how then could it be achieved? This refers to the section below explaining that if there were no consciousness maintaining the seeds, the afflictions would not manifest.
The meaning is that when the path of antidotes arises, both the seeds and the manifestations of the afflictions are forever and utterly severed.

Only then can one attain the fruit of transformation and severance. Since there would be no afflictions, the fruit of severance could not be established. Regarding the distinction between the defiled and the pure:

it excludes the possibility that any other dharma possesses the capacity to maintain seeds. That is to say, when the sixth consciousness is associated with the Path during the stage of cultivation, it is itself termed "pure";
it cannot be defiled, nor can it maintain the seeds of affliction, as the pure mind is tranquil and still.
It would be like *nirvāṇa*. How could the agitation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) not be contradictory [to such a state]?

Since the minds of the past and future and the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are not substantially real, it is also logically untenable for other dharmas to maintain the seeds.

That which is abandoned is the affliction, and that which abandons is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). If this consciousness did not exist to maintain the seeds of the afflictions, there would be nothing to be abandoned; and if there is nothing to be abandoned...

Therefore, even the act of severing does not exist. Upon what could "severance" depend, and by means of what could it be severed, such that one establishes the fruit of purification as the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*)?
If they were to counter-argue that the fruit of severance is established because subsequent afflictions do not arise due to the power of the path of antidotes (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), we refute this:

in that case, at the moment the first path arises, one would have to be considered an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*). Furthermore, at the time of the initial Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is called the "first... [of the noble ones].
When the Path arises, at this stage one merely severs the seeds and manifestations of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). One has just entered the stream of the Noble Ones (*ārya-srotas*).

Only when the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) are completely exhausted up to the ninth stage does one become an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*). How could the fruit of severance be established immediately upon entering the stream of the Noble Ones?

If one were to realize the state of an Arhat at the first fruit (*prathamaphala*), there would be no ālayavijñāna to contain the latent defilements; yet, throughout the subsequent nine stages, various afflictions [would still persist].
All seeds have already become causeless, for they will never arise again. Since they will never arise, how can the Sūtras state that the afflictions of the nine stages each consist of nine grades?
If one admits the existence of this eighth consciousness, then all causes and effects are fully established, for it is only this eighth consciousness that is capable of sustaining the seeds.
△ This concludes the citation regarding defiled and pure minds. General Conclusion.
The preceding two sections have concluded the citation of correct reasoning; the following three sections exhort faith and acceptance.
To prove that this consciousness possesses infinite logical principles, all wise persons should believe and accept it with deep conviction.

△ This is the third section, concluding with an exhortation to believe and accept. This concludes the first transformation (*pariṇāma*). Below, the second and third transformations are divided into three parts.
First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the formulation of the inquiry.

Having thus explained the characteristics of the first transformation, what are the characteristics of the second transformation? The characteristics of the first transformation are as previously stated:

the characteristic of containing the seeds (*ālaya*), the characteristic of the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), the characteristic of being the cause that sustains the seeds, the subtle characteristic of cognizing objects, the characteristic of being associated with and characterized by [mental factors], the characteristic of spontaneous relinquishment, and the characteristic of being non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*). And so forth...
Like a violent torrent and so forth, it is neither annihilated nor permanent; its various characteristics have already been explained as before. Furthermore, the second transformation is asked about:
how are its characteristics revealed? △ First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the formulation of the question are completed.
Below, the second part provides the general answer by citing a verse.
The verse says: "Next, the second transformative consciousness... [omitted] ...is absent in Arhats, in the meditative attainment of cessation, and on the supramundane path.
Regarding "the next, the second transformative consciousness": this name *manas* for consciousness is a single term in the verse; in the Sanskrit language, *manas* is translated as "mind" (*yi*).
Because it possesses the sense of constant and thorough deliberation, it is called "mind. "Dependent upon that and evolving" refers to what is stated in the verse.

Regarding the basis (*āśraya*): because the seventh consciousness arises depending upon that eighth consciousness. Regarding its object (*ālambana*): this refers to the objective sphere mentioned in the verse;
for the seventh consciousness constantly takes the eighth as its object, grasping it as the self. Regarding "having reflection as its nature and characteristic" (*mananā-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*):
this refers to the verse’s description of its intrinsic nature and mode of activity (*ākāra*); for both the intrinsic nature of the seventh and its mode of apprehending objects consist of reflection.
Regarding the "four afflictions that are always concomitant," the verse states they are associated with the four fundamental afflictions:

namely, self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), as well as self-pride (*ātma-māna*) and self-love (*ātma-sneha*). The names of these four are given in the verse, while their meanings are explained in the commentary itself.

Regarding "concomitant with the others, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth," the verse states they are associated with the other fourteen mental factors (*caitta*). The names of these "others" and their meanings are [explained] in the commentary.
The middle section provides its own explanation. Regarding "subsumed under obscured-neutral": among the four natures mentioned in the verse, it is exclusively of the obscured-neutral nature.

Regarding "according to where it is produced and to what it is bound": this refers to the realms and stages; according to whichever realm the eighth consciousness is produced in, it is bound to that very realm.
"Bound" (saṃyukta) has the meaning of not being separated, because it clings to [the self] as "I" at every moment. [This applies to those who are not yet] Arhats.

Regarding the statement that the manas does not exist in the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), or the stage of an Arhat: these three states are summarized in the verse as being devoid of manas. In the stage of an Arhat, it is because one no longer clings to a self.

In the state of cessation, it is because the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) has been suppressed. In the supramundane path, it is because of the initial turning of wisdom (*prathamavivartajñāna*).

For these reasons, the manas is absent in all three of these states. The second section, the general response by means of the verse, is concluded. Below follows the third section: the detailed explanation.

The explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into three parts. First, the general explanation of the meaning of the verse is divided into eight sections. First, the general explanation of the name.

The Treatise says: Following the first [of the eight consciousnesses], the ripening-result (*vipāka*) transformative consciousness, up until [the point where it] serves as the immediate support (*āsraya*), it is therefore named simply "mind" (*manas*).

This explains the first two lines of the verse. Following the initial transformation of consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), one should logically proceed to analyze the characteristics of the second transformation of consciousness.

As for this second transformation of consciousness, it is given the specific name *manas* in the sacred teachings because its functional activity of constant and thorough deliberation (*santatam parīkṣaka-manana*) is superior to that of the other seven types of consciousness. The eighth consciousness is constant but not thorough; the sixth...

It is discerning (*samanvāhāra*) but not constant (*nitya*). The first five [consciousnesses] are neither constant nor discerning, because they are interrupted and lack conceptual discrimination (*nirvikalpa*).

Only this seventh [consciousness] is both constant and discerning; therefore, it excels the other consciousnesses. This is called "below. Question: This is termed the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The sixth is also called "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*). What is its distinction? The answer is:

this seventh [consciousness] is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound), because it directly maintains the function of constant and thorough deliberation (*santīraṇa*) within the essence of consciousness. This is like the name "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*), which refers to the eighth consciousness;

it directly maintains the karmic function of containing the three types [of seeds], and is thus called "maintaining the essence" (*svabhāvadhāraṇa*) and "maintaining the karmic function" (*karmadhāraṇa*).
[The author] explains: Therefore, because the substance of this consciousness is itself the *manas*, that sixth consciousness is designated by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Here, the mental faculty (*manas*) is the primary element, serving as the support for this consciousness—just as the eye is the primary element, serving as the support for visual consciousness. In both cases, the terms "support" and "supported" are employed to manifest the *tatpuruṣa* compound.
Consequently, the substance of that consciousness is distinct from the *manas*. [The phrase] "However, all [the following]" explains the establishment [of these terms] in the sacred teachings.
This is the name. It serves to prevent confusion with other meanings. Furthermore, the explanation provided below establishes that the designation has the sense of differentiation:

namely, the eighth consciousness is called "citta" (mind) because it possesses the sense of accumulation; the first six are called "vijñāna" (consciousness) because they possess the sense of discernment;

and this seventh alone is inferior to those preceding and following it, and is therefore merely called "manas" (intellect). Alternatively, it reveals that this consciousness serves as the immediate supporting faculty (*āśraya*) for the sixth consciousness. This...

It is merely called "mind" (manas); that [consciousness] is called "mental consciousness" (mano-vijñāna). △ The first section, the general explanation of the name, is concluded. Below, the second section explains the basis (āśraya), which is divided into three parts.
First, the formal explanation of the basis.
The phrase "depending on that" (*tad-āśrita*) indicates its basis (*āśraya*), because this [seventh consciousness] constantly depends on that consciousness to apprehend its objects.
The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the eighth [consciousness], for the sacred teachings state that the seventh depends on that storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

The view that it depends solely on the seeds of consciousness is not correct; rather, this seventh [consciousness] takes the seeds of that eighth consciousness as its basis, and does not depend [on them].

Regarding its manifestation: this [seventh consciousness] occurs without interruption, for it can arise even without depending on the manifestation of that [eighth consciousness]. One interpretation holds that it is correct reasoning that both the seeds and the manifestations depend [on the eighth];
that is, this seventh [consciousness] takes both the seeds and the manifestations of the eighth as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

Since it is called a "transforming consciousness" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and thus involves transformation, it must depend upon the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) in order to arise. Thus, it flows forth.
This refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which flows through the various realms of existence (*gati*) according to wholesome and unwholesome karma.

This seventh consciousness constantly relies upon the eighth, taking it as its objective referent (*ālambana*) and grasping it as the internal self. △ The first section, the formal explanation of the basis, is concluded.
The lower two [sections] extend laterally to other treatises and are divided into two parts. First, a brief explanation of the three types:
"All minds and mental factors have a basis" (up to) "is called having a basis, not other phenomena."

This refers to the eight types of consciousness and their associated mental factors (*citta-samprayukta-dharma*). Their arising necessarily requires a basis (*āśraya*). However, because the meaning of "basis" is distinct, it is divided into three kinds. The cause itself is the condition;
because the cause functions as the condition, it is called the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). The cause is the seed, while the condition has the sense of "arising.
It is called a "cause" in relation to the manifest fruit (*pravṛtti-phala*), and it is further called a "condition" because it is capable of producing the manifest. That is to say:

Because the actualized manifestation (*samudācāra*) arises from seeds, the actualized manifestation possesses the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to its own direct seed.
Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), namely those such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) that possess functional activity, necessarily depend upon causes and conditions to arise.

Question: What is the difference between the "basis of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*) and "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) themselves? Answer: The basis is narrow while the conditions are broad; conditions consist of the presence of the seed for arising.

The former is broad because it encompasses three meanings: the manifestation of various [phenomena], the manifestation [of phenomena] perfuming seeds, and the seeds themselves. The latter is narrow because it relies on only one meaning: that manifestation arises from seeds alone.
This single meaning of seeds giving rise to manifestation represents the cause being latent while the fruit is manifest;

this differs from the perfuming of seeds by active mental states (*pravṛtti*), because the cause of an active state is not latent, and the fruit produced by such perfuming is not manifest. Furthermore, regarding the basis of causal conditions, the cause and fruit are identical [in their locus].
At that time, seeds of different types do not produce one another; cause and effect are distinct.

As for the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it has the sense of assisting and promoting growth, or the sense of not causing harm. Whether favorable or adverse, powerful or weak, all are dominant conditions.

Because of these dominant conditions, there are those that are proximate and those that are remote; thus, the dominant condition is broad rather than narrow. This is the basis of the dominant condition.
It is narrow and not broad; it takes only that which possesses power and is capable of directly inducing [the subsequent state], namely the six internal bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmika-āyatana*).

These six internal bases are the co-existent faculties (*sahabhū-indriya*), because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) function in dependence upon them. As for the "equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*):

"equal" (*sama*) means uniform, because the preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness arise with identical modes of activity (*ākāra*). Because there is no interval between them, it is called "immediate" (*anantara*).
When the preceding consciousness ceases, it is able to induce the subsequent consciousness; therefore, it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*).

It is also called "mind" (*manas*) because the seventh mind constantly engages in deliberation from moment to moment without interruption; thus, it is the "equal and immediate" (*samanantara*) condition. The preceding consciousness that has ceased is termed the "mind.
It is also called "opening and guiding" because it possesses the sense of opening up and leading forth. Question: What is the relationship between the equal and immediate condition and its basis?
[Question: Different. [Answer: If one discusses the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*), it is broad because it encompasses both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*).

If one discusses the basis of their substance, it is narrow because it refers only to the mind-king. This constitutes the meaning of their distinction. [Question: Among these three bases, what are the distinct characteristics of "arising" (*utpāda*), "transforming" (*vartana*), and "originating" (*pravṛtti*)?

[Answer: "Arising" refers to the dependence on seeds; it is when the manifest fruit (*phala*) actually arises. "Transforming" refers to the conformity and the providing of power that causes [the fruit] to...
Transformation (*parāvṛtti*). Regarding "arising," it refers to opening up what precedes so that what follows may arise. These are the three distinct characteristics. Question:
Why are the other three conditions established separately as "supports" (*āśraya*), while the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) alone is not established as a support? Answer:

Each of the three [other] conditions possesses both the sense of being "constant" (*nitya*) as a condition and the sense of being "dominant" (*pradhāna*) as a support. As for the object-condition, it possesses only the sense of being constant and lacks the sense of being dominant; therefore, it is only mind (*citta*).

Below "mental factors" (*caitta*), the three types of bases are summarized and revealed. These exist only in mental phenomena and not in other material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), because they possess all three [bases] in their entirety.
△ The brief explanation of the three types is concluded. Below, the extensive explanation of the three types is divided into three parts.
First, the explanation of the seed-base (*bīja-āśraya*).
Regarding the initial basis for seeds, some have said (up to): "It is certain that there is a distinct basis for each seed.
This statement is not correct. It means that only after the seed has ceased does the manifest resultant dharma arise.
In the second fascicle of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, twenty-four types of "already arisen" are listed: twelve are "already arisen with seeds," and thirteen are "already arisen without seeds."
Regarding "arising," the proponent takes the thirteen [factors] that have already arisen as proof for the extinction of the seed and the manifestation of the arising.
As for the claim that the seed and the sprout do not arise simultaneously, they also cite external seeds as proof for their established thesis.

The following section of the *Nyāyānusāra* refutes the aforementioned position, stating that the citation from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* does not constitute valid proof; for that *Samuccaya* speaks of "arising without a seed."
This is because it is explained in reference to the production of subsequent seeds; for a seed producing a seed does not occur simultaneously.

Furthermore, when speaking of seeds producing sprouts and so forth, one refers to rice, wheat, and the like, which are external seeds and not internal ones. Below the section on "flame and wick," the Master of the Treatise clarifies the correct meaning:

the flame is a metaphor for the manifest (pravṛtti), and the wick is a metaphor for the seed. Just as the wick can produce the flame, and the flame burns and consumes the wick, this serves as a metaphor for the seed producing the manifest.

[The seeds and] active manifestations function as mutual causes: active manifestations infuse the seeds, and [the seeds produce] active manifestations. However, when a seed gives rise to a subsequent seed of its own kind, cause and effect do not coexist.

When seeds and active manifestations mutually produce one another, they are necessarily coexistent. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (lower section) cites scriptural evidence for the aforementioned principle:

"That which is impermanent is precisely the seed, because it undergoes transformation. Although both self-referential and other-referential meanings are cited, [it is established that the seed is the impermanent entity].
In this context, only the seeds and manifestations of other-nature (*parabhāva*) are taken as the evidence for the dependence on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*).
In the lower section of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it further cites evidence for the principle that seeds and manifestations are simultaneous.

Defiled phenomena—namely, the preceding seven consciousnesses—act as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed object (*vāsya*) in relation to the eighth consciousness, serving as mutual causes and conditions. Furthermore, it states that seeds and their manifesting fruits are inseparable. Even if...

There is a lower section. Regarding the explanation elsewhere that seeds and their fruits have a temporal sequence, this follows the principle of conventional flow (*saṃvṛti-pravṛtti*) and is not an ultimate (*paramārtha*) teaching.
Therefore, it is established that each mind and mental factor (*citta-caitta-dharma*) definitely possesses its own seed as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
[End of Section One: Explanation of the Seed-Support. The following two sections explain the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), divided into two parts. Part One: Three [points].
The Master refutes this.
Next, regarding the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), some say: (up to) "it must depend upon the *manas* in order to arise.

As for the simultaneous support: consciousness is the dependent (*āśrita*), and the sense organ is the supported (*āśraya*). Because they exist at the same time, it is called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*).

Furthermore, there is a passage below [in the text] which states: "This explanation is not yet correct. It means that the first five consciousnesses take only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), and have no separate supports such as the eye and so forth. This is because the sense organs, such as the eye, are the seeds of those consciousnesses.

Regarding the verse cited here, there is an explanation in the sixty-third fascicle of the *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source). The first two lines refer to the master of the treatise provisionally taking the five [consciousnesses]...
"Consciousness takes the seeds as its support. [This is] the answer of the Sautrāntika masters, because they admit the existence of seeds.
Furthermore, it is said that the eye-consciousness and so forth arise and evolve appearing as the semblance of objects such as form.

The latter two phrases represent the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) for the purpose of refuting the non-Buddhist attachment to the body as a unified self (*ekatva-saṃjñin ātman*). Thus, regarding a reality beyond words, they have forcibly applied verbal conceptualization.
The teaching that there are ten bases consisting of sense faculties and objects was intended to lead each person to observe them individually and thereby realize the emptiness of the self.
Now, these [opponents], unaware of the master’s provisional teaching and the Buddha’s intentional meaning, cite this to prove their own dogmatic positions.
How could one take the seeds of consciousness to be the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*)? The meaning of that verse is as follows:

the proponent himself explains the intent of the verse, asserting that the seeds of consciousness constitute the faculties and the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) constitutes the objects. This serves to prove that there are no separate [material] eyes and so forth that function as faculties.
In the *Ālambanaparīkṣā*, the Bodhisattva Dignāga himself explains: "The existence of the faculties is inferred from their capacity to produce consciousness. This...

However, it is merely a functional capacity (*śakti*), not something produced externally. Therefore, the fivefold functional capacities for color-form upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are termed the "eye-faculties" and so forth;
this does not contradict reason. These faculties, as functional capacities, and their corresponding external objects of color-form have served as reciprocal causes since beginningless time.
That is to say, when these capacities reach a state of maturation, they produce the five internal objective colors upon the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*). These internal...

Below, the scripture is cited to prove the meaning of relying upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*). In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is further cited to prove that the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) definitely relies upon a body possessing material sense faculties.
Alternatively, regarding the charge that the reason (*hetu*) established is subject to the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:
The maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is an existent entity. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it definitely appropriates the material sense-faculties.
The reason (*hetu*) is "because it does not depend [on them] universally. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is like the six consciousnesses.

If the maturation-consciousness did not depend on the material sense-faculties universally, then the reason would not be present in the locus of the thesis (*asiddha*), and the example would be inconsistent; thus, there would be the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Thus, the third master’s formulation of the thesis below remains incomplete in its reasoning. △ The refutation of the three masters is concluded above.
Below follows the correct doctrine’s refutation of the preceding views.

There is an interpretation that all the preceding explanations are unreasonable (up to the point where it says): "Alternatively, taking the support as the support is merely a conventional designation made according to circumstances;
this is the correct principle. This refutes the previous [view] because it fails to recognize the distinction between the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*).

"Support" refers generally to the meaning of both the supported and the support, which is why the analogy of king and minister is used: the king represents the support, and the minister represents the supported.
Regarding the basis (*āśraya*): if the dharmas are "lower," they clarify the basis alone because it possesses four meanings. First is definiteness (*niyata*):

this correctly distinguishes [the sixth consciousness] from the first five consciousnesses as its basis. That which serves as a basis must exist with certainty; however, at the time when the sixth [consciousness] exists, the first five do not necessarily exist.
This also excludes the five material sense organs (*pañca-rūpīndriya*) as being the basis for the eighth [consciousness], and likewise...
This is not determinate. For example, as in the case of those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they lack the physical sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*).

Furthermore, to distinguish the seven manifest [consciousnesses] capable of perfuming from the seeds that serve as the basis for their growth and persistence, one must note that these manifest perfuming consciousnesses necessarily undergo interruption;
how, then, could there be any sense of determinacy? Second, regarding "possessing an object": what is called "possessing an object" refers to the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-ṣaḍāyatana*).

This refers to the sense of being an object-possessor (viṣayin). [In this context,] the faculties are the illuminators and the objects are the illuminated; therefore, it is said that the illuminator possesses an illuminated object.

This excludes the four great elements, the life-faculty, the five sensory objects, and all seeds, for although they possess the sense of being determinate, they lack the sense of being an object-possessor and thus cannot serve as the support (*āśraya*).
[This is because] they are not illuminators and therefore have no illuminated objects. Third is "being primary. To say "being primary" is also...

The mind-king (citta-rāja) and the five material sense-faculties definitely possess objects and function as sovereigns; therefore, these distinguish them from the five omnipresent mental factors (sarvatraga-caitta).
Although the latter possess both the qualities of definitely having objects and being determinate, they lack the quality of sovereignty and thus are not the supports (āśraya).

Fourth, it causes the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects. To say they "apprehend their respective objects" means that they take the basis (the support) and the supported (the dharma) as their objects.

This excludes the eighth consciousness in its active state, which cannot serve as a simultaneous support for the seeds within the consciousness, because those seeds lack the capacity for cognitive engagement (*ālambana*) and thus cannot apprehend themselves.

The eighth [consciousness], the present manifestation, serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*). This eighth present manifestation alone possesses the three characteristics of being determinate, having an object, and being predominant.

It serves exclusively as the support (*āśraya*) for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), because the mind and mental factors are that which possess the capacity for objective apprehension (*ālambaka*).

Therefore, it takes the eight present manifestations as its object-condition. Thus, the passage beginning with "Therefore, all... cites evidence that those which depend [upon it] are exclusively mental phenomena (*caitta-dharma*). Because...

Generally speaking, the primary mind (*citta*) functions interchangeably as both subject and object, whereas mental factors function only as subjects because they are not sovereign.

However, there are cases where other texts speak of "subjective support" and "objective support" without clarifying their distinction; all such instances are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

The basis of the immediate cause (*hetu-pratyaya*), the basis of the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and the basis of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The statement "it evolves depending on that" indicates only the former two. The intent of the verse is to speak only of the causal condition and the predominant condition, in order to show that for this consciousness, the basis and the condition are identical.
This explains the meaning revealed in the aforementioned verse: "basis" refers to the predominant condition, and "condition" refers to the causal condition.
Because the eighth consciousness is the true seed-condition, when struck by an object, it gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses;

therefore, it is said to be the "supporting condition" (ālambana-pratyaya), being identical to the eighth consciousness in this regard. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the first two supports possess superior functions:

this means that the supporting cause (hetu-pratyaya) possesses the superior function of directly producing [the result], while the supporting dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) possesses the superior function of inducing [the result]. Therefore, in the verse, these are explicitly revealed.

Regarding these two, they may be the "opening and guiding support" (*āśraya*). As for "easy to understand": because the principle of the preceding ceasing and the succeeding arising is easy for people to understand, the previous verse did not explicitly state that meaning.
△ This concludes the third section, the correct explanation of the verse’s intent. This also concludes the two preceding explanations regarding the "support.
Below follows the third explanation regarding the "object-condition" (*ālambana*), which is divided into two parts. First, the correct explanation by means of question and answer.

Thus, having already explained the support (*āśraya*) of this consciousness—up to the point where it is stated that the Sage taught this consciousness takes the *ālayavijñāna* as its object—the two conditions of the previously explained support, namely the sense organ (*indriya*) and the seeds (*bīja*), have been concluded. Furthermore, a question-and-answer session is presented again to clarify that the seventh consciousness takes that very *ālayavijñāna*, which is its support, as its object.
1. The direct explanation through question and answer is now complete. Below, two points are raised to refute misconceptions.
The refutation is divided into two parts. First, the three masters’ refutation:

there is an interpretation that this [consciousness] takes the substance of that [external object] as its object; thus, as in the statement of "mere consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*), there is no fault of contradicting the scriptures.

Nanda’s formulation of the thesis is not yet correct. He claims that this seventh [consciousness] takes that eighth [consciousness] and its mental factors as objects, and clings to them as "I" and "mine.
The treatise explains below the meaning of clinging to "I" and "mine" mentioned above:

it means that when taking the mind-king (citta-rāja) as an object, one clings to it as "I," and when taking the mental factors (caitta) as objects, one clings to them as "mine"; therefore, it is said "respectively. However, the passage beginning with "But all... provides the proof.
Mental factors do not exist apart from the mind-king; therefore, whenever one speaks of the mind-king, mental factors necessarily accompany it.
Just as when one speaks of "consciousness-only," all phenomena are necessarily included, there is no contradiction or error within the sacred teachings.

There is an interpretation that their explanation is not logically tenable (up to the point where it is stated that) because [the seventh consciousness] has consciousness as its essence, it does not contradict the teachings of the Sage.

This refutes Nanda’s adherence to the view that the mental factors are the objects of the [seventh] consciousness; for there has never been a place where it was taught that the seventh consciousness exists.

Regarding the statement that the five [factors] such as contact (*sparśa*) are "inferior" (*adhas*), the establishment of this position by the Fire-Debater (*Vaiśeṣika*) is still not exhaustive in its reasoning.

That is to say, when one takes the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part) as the self (*ātman*), and when taking the *nimitta-bhāga* (the image-part), one grasps it as "mine" (*mama*). [The text] below, concerning the *nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga*, explains that these two do not exist apart from the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*).
This is because when one takes consciousness as an object, one simultaneously takes its *nimitta* and *darśana* parts as the self and what belongs to the self; logically, this is not inconsistent.

This is incorrect. There is another interpretation which holds that this statement is also unreasonable [up to the point where it concludes] that it is not a substantially existent entity and thus does not contradict the Noble Teachings.

Regarding Anahbuddhi’s general refutation of the position that maintains the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*)—namely, that the five material sense faculties and their objects do not belong to the aggregate of consciousness—that...
If one maintains that the object-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) consists of the material sense-faculties and their objects, it would not be included within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
This is because the seventh consciousness, which takes mind as its object, is subsumed under the aggregate of consciousness; how could it then take a material aspect as its object?

If one maintains that the seventh consciousness takes an object-aspect as its object, it would be identical to the five consciousnesses taking external objective aspects, which contradicts the teaching of the Sage that the seventh consciousness internally cognizes. If one maintains...

The seventh [consciousness] takes the objective aspect (nimittabhāga) as its object; it should be the same as the sixth, which—like the first five consciousnesses—takes common characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) as its objects.
Why, then, is it called the "seventh"? Because it exclusively takes internal objects. If it were to take the objective aspect as "mine," then within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),...
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there would be no "mine" (*mama-kāra*). Suppose it is asked: "If one is born in the formless realm, why is there no form? The answer is:
"Because one is born there through aversion to form, and because form does not change [there]. This should be stated as follows. Furthermore, the position established by Sthiramati is also illogical;
namely, that one clings to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the self and clings to its seeds as "mine. For...

[The term] "planting" [is used]. This explains that the seed is the functional capacity of consciousness; since it is not separate from consciousness, when one takes consciousness as an object, one is simultaneously taking the seed as an object.
Thus, there is no fault of contradicting the teachings in asserting "self" and "what belongs to self. △ The refutation by the three masters is concluded above.
Below, the correct principle refutes the preceding [positions].
There is an interpretation that all the preceding explanations are unreasonable (up to the point where it is said that) the grasping at "I" and "mine" do not arise simultaneously.
The master Dharmapāla refutes the preceding views in their entirety. He further restates and refutes by means of a dilemma the position held by Sthiramati regarding the object-condition of seeds:
if the seeds of form were not subsumed within the aggregate of consciousness, then because the seventh consciousness only takes consciousness as its object, the seeds would be grasped as non-real.

Furthermore, this contradicts the treatises which state that seeds are substantially existent (*dravyasat*). If seeds were merely nominal (*prajñapti*), they would not be causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Therefore, what they have asserted is entirely unreasonable. Below this, there is a general critique of the three masters who equally maintain the doctrine of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).

The view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is precisely the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). This view of a self, associated with the seventh consciousness, spontaneously and constantly takes [the aggregates] as its object.
How could there be room for a separate grasping at the meaning of non-transformation? [The text] explains this by stating, "The self and what belongs to the self," and so forth.
This means that although the views of eternalism and nihilism arise based on the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they do not occur simultaneously;

therefore, there is no single moment of mind in which one separately grasps at an eternal self and a nihilistic "mine" while both proceed together. If it is argued that the former grasping is for the self and the latter for what belongs to the self, that too is not [the case].

This is logical. Because this seventh [consciousness] transforms as a single flavor at all times without succession, one should know that—following the phrase "below"—the Master of the Treatise establishes his own correct position:

it takes only the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing portion) as its object and clings to it as the self. This is not like the three previous masters, who cling to other mental factors (*caitta*), the *nimitta-bhāga* (image portion), or seeds (*bīja*) as being "mine.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Since that [consciousness] is beginningless," the eighth point—that it is beginningless—is explained and established.

The continuum constantly serves as the support and object-condition for all consciousnesses. This [passage] below, "only grasping that," explains that the seventh [consciousness] grasps only itself as the self (*ātman*), and does not grasp it as "mine" (*ātmīya*).
When the treatise speaks of "mine," it does so merely by following the momentum of the discourse. Alternatively, this [passage] below provides another interpretation:
namely, that the seventh [consciousness], which acts as the grasper, takes the eighth [consciousness]—which is the grasped—as the self; therefore, regarding...

First, regarding the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), two meanings are explained. If one were to conclude by establishing the thesis as stated below, it would not contradict either principle or scripture.

In the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), [the view of self] takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object. Since that [storehouse consciousness] is already established as such, what fault could there be in this?
This clarifies the seventh consciousness in terms of its distinct objects of perception regarding whether it has been transformed or not yet transformed.

Under the section "Equality," the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is established as the stage wherein it takes all phenomena as its object. Regarding the ten kinds of equality: first is the equality of supreme delight.
2. Equality in experiencing dependent origination; 3. Equality in being free from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics;

4. Equality in the great compassion that universally rescues; 5. Equality in the great compassion that is independent of conditions; 6. Equality in manifesting according to the inclinations of all sentient beings;
7. Equality in having all sentient beings respectfully receive one's teachings; 8. Equality in the tranquility of the world.
All are equal in a single flavor. Ninth, suffering and pleasure are equal in a single flavor. Tenth, merit is ultimately equal. This refers to the seventh consciousness.
Having realized these ten kinds of equality, it manifests in form and preaches the Dharma, being able to take all things as its objects.
Herein, the subsequent section explains the phrase "taking that as an object" from the verse; this is spoken in reference to the state prior to transformation. Therefore, it only...

Regarding the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), suppose one asks: "Since the manas is the same [in both states], why does it not transform its basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) while it takes only the storehouse consciousness as its object?

Once it has attained the transformation of the basis, how is it able to take other phenomena as its objects? The answer is: At the time of awakening, there is no self; being pervasive rather than restricted, it is therefore able to take all things as its objects.
At the time of delusion, one clings to a self; being restricted rather than pervasive, its objects of cognition are not universal. This principle must necessarily be so. It is like...

"What is this consciousness that takes its own support as its object? This asks about the seventh consciousness. Since it arises based on the eighth consciousness, why does it take the eighth consciousness as its objective condition (*ālambana*)?
To answer this, an analogy is provided below: namely, that the immediately preceding mind (*samanantara-manas*) serves as the object for the subsequent moment;

this case should be understood in the same way. The second section, "The Correct Doctrine Refuting the Previous [Views]," concludes. This completes the three explanations regarding the [object-condition].
The section on conditions concludes. The following four [verses] explain the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
The verse states that "reflection is its nature and characteristic" (up to "...because it also carefully reflects upon the characteristic of non-self").
This reiterates the wording of the preceding verse to set forth the correct meaning, clarifying that a single reflection explains the three names. Only...

First, the explanation of the nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), including that of the *manas*. Thus, it is known that the seventh consciousness is named "constant and deliberative reflection" (*nitya-parīkṣaka-manana*).

Furthermore, it clarifies that whether in its transformed state (*parāvṛtta*) or its untransformed state (*aparāvṛtta*), it always functions as reflection; because of this reflection, it constitutes both its nature and its characteristics. △ The explanation of the nature and characteristics is concluded.
Below, the fifth section explains the associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*), which is divided into three parts. First, the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).
This is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation through question and answer:
"How many mental factors (caitta) correspond to this [state of mind]? ... [up to] "... they are called afflictions (kleśa) because one cannot escape from them.

Regarding the phrase "for the time being" (tāvat): it is used because there are other mental factors present; therefore, for the time being, it is said that they are associated with the four root afflictions.
"Afflictions are always present. Herein, the following explains the meaning of the four types of afflictions that are always present within the response.

That is to say, when the seventh consciousness is in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), it is associated with those [afflictions], constantly taking the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object and grasping it as a self.
What are these four? Among the six fundamental [afflictions], which four are they? [The text] says "self," etc., and answers: the four types.
Regarding the name: it further explains four meanings. As for "delusion regarding self" (*ātma-moha*), this is ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because one does not clearly understand that the essence of the eighth consciousness is fundamentally without self, yet constantly clings to a self, being deluded regarding the principle of non-self—this is called delusion regarding self.

"View of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). "Grasping" (*grāha*) has the meaning of attachment and the meaning of false appropriation. It refers to the false appropriation of that which is not the self.
To act for the sake of the self is called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). As for "self-conceit" (*māna*), it refers to arrogance; being haughty and self-important—this is the meaning of conceit.
Because one relies upon the self, the mind becomes uplifted and elevated; this is called "self-conceit. As for "self-love" (*ātma-sneha*), it is simply craving for the self (*ātma-tṛṣṇā*).
Because one is constantly unable to relinquish attachment to a self, it is called "self-love" (*ātmasneha*).
Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse indicates that view (*dṛṣṭi*) and pride (*māna*) arise together with love;

this serves to refute the Sarvāstivāda position that view, pride, and love do not arise simultaneously. Regarding the phrase "these four," this explains the names of the four types of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the internal mind, which is the seventh consciousness (*manas*), and the external evolving consciousnesses, which are the first six consciousnesses.

Because the four types [of afflictions], such as self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), arise constantly, the internal and external minds are perpetually defiled; thus, they are designated as "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because one cannot escape from saṃsāra.
The first section, the direct explanation through question and answer, is concluded. Below, the second section provides a detailed distinction through question and answer.
There are ten [afflictions] there; why are there only four here? (Up to: Therefore, the text and meaning of both [passages] do not contradict one another.
Question: These afflictions originally consist of ten types, namely: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and the five remaining views.
Why are there only four types in this seventh consciousness? Answer: It is said that because this seventh [consciousness] possesses the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it lacks the other views.
Regarding "non-arising": because seeing is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no single mind; rather, multiple instances of wisdom arise simultaneously.

How can it be that this consciousness must necessarily involve the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)? This is a further question. The answer follows later. Second, from "the two graspings" onwards, the meaning of the non-arising of the remaining views mentioned above is explained.

The "two graspings" refer to the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Together with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), these three are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

Birth [defilements] are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). This seventh consciousness, which is associated with the affliction of self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), is exclusively innate (*sahaja*) and is therefore abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
This clarifies that birth and abandonment differ. All forms of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth belonging to self-view arise dependent upon self-view;
however, this self-view associated with the seventh consciousness does not arise dependent upon those extreme views. Therefore, [the two are distinct].
There is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*); other views do not arise because one constantly clings internally to a self.

Thus, it must necessarily involve the view of self. [This answers] the previous question: "How must there be the view of self? "By means of the view’s thorough determination," etc., answers the previous question:
"Why are there only these four? Regarding the question: "How can the three—view, pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—arise together? [The answer is: According to the Sarvāstivāda...

[The opponent] says: "Since the mental factors of clinging, views, pride, and craving do not arise simultaneously, this question is raised. As for the response, 'There is no contradiction in their modes of activity (*ākāra*);

what fault is there in their arising together?'—the explanation of 'no contradiction in their modes of activity' will follow later. Furthermore, the opponent cites a scriptural passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to raise a further objection:
'The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that greed causes the mind to sink, while pride causes the mind to uplift; how can these not be contradictory?'"

The Master of the Treatise explains that there is no contradiction regarding their modes of activity (*ākāra*), thereby answering both questions simultaneously. That is to say, views consist of both conceptualized and innate types;

craving consists of that directed toward internal objects and that directed toward external objects; pride consists of that which is haughty and that which is based upon something. These three possess distinctions in terms of both their coarse and subtle aspects.
This is because the mode of activity (*ākāra*) therein does not contradict this meaning. Therefore, that *yoga* and the meaning of this treatise are not in conflict.

△ Second, the question-and-answer section distinguishing [the categories] is concluded. This concludes the first part: the root afflictions. Below, the second part—concerning the remaining [afflictions] and those categorized as "contact" and so forth—is divided into two sections.
First, the question-and-answer section providing a general outline.
Does this mental faculty (manas) have only four associated mental factors? No; it is accompanied by others, such as contact (sparśa) and so forth.

This question and answer clarify that the mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness are not limited to the four—self-delusion (*ātma-moha*) and the rest—but also include others, such as contact and so forth.
△ The first section, the general introduction via question and answer, is concluded. Below, the second section concerns the mutual relationship between the specific and the universal.
The analysis consists of five parts. First, the refutation that there are only nine [mental factors]. Part two: the explicit explanation of the meaning of this position.

One interpretation holds that these mental factors associated with the manas are only nine (up to the point where it says) because they are a single class that clings to a self; therefore, they do not coexist with those [other factors].
This interpretation is not complete. For while eighteen mental factors (caitta) generally accompany the mind, here only nine are present, as the other nine are missing.
The passage beginning with "that is, contact" explains the names of the five factors starting with contact, demonstrating that they are invariably associated with the seventh [consciousness].

The passage beginning with "as previously stated" explains the meaning of the word "remainder" in the verse; however, this reasoning is also not correct. That is to say, these factors such as contact [are associated] with the ripening [consciousness]...

Both [of these] are of an unobscured nature (*anivṛta*). Now, both are the seventh [consciousness], which is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta*); therefore, the word "other" (*anya*) is placed to show that this differs from that.

Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) in the verse is explained as having the same meaning as "aggregation. The four preceding afflictions aggregate and correspond with the five factors beginning with contact; thus, there are only nine objects.
Why is it that this [seventh consciousness] has no other mental factors (*caitta*)? This is the question.
Furthermore, the statement "desire and so forth" (欲等) separately excludes the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata*), as none of them are associated with the seventh consciousness;

however, this merely excludes non-associated wisdom (*prajñā-aviprayukta*) and does not yet fully capture the principle. This is because the seventh consciousness must be accompanied by wisdom in order to give rise to self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).
Since wholesome states are pure (*śubha*), those [factors] that do not accompany this consciousness exclude all eleven wholesome mental factors (*caitta*) in their entirety.
Regarding association: below the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it excludes the small, medium, and great categories of secondary afflictions, as they are not associated with it.
This reasoning has not yet reached its conclusion, because the seventh consciousness must always be accompanied by the eight great secondary afflictions. Regarding remorse (*kaukṛtya*):

this generally excludes the four types of mental factors within the indeterminate state (*aniyata-bhūmika*), as they are not associated with it. △ First, the explicit explanation of the meaning of grasping is concluded. Below, two points are restated.
Refuting other interpretations:
There is an interpretation that his explanation of "other" (*anya*) as meaning something else is irrational; therefore, this term "other" indicates the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
This is the correct position here, which refutes the previous interpretation as irrational. That is to say, this term "other" does not serve to exclude the non-obscured (*anivṛta*).

Because the term "obscured" (*nivṛta*) is used in the verse to distinguish them specifically, these remaining terms indicate the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), since root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) necessarily possess secondary afflictions.
△ Second, the refutation of other interpretations is concluded. This concludes the first section above, which maintains that there are only nine objects;
the following two sections maintain that there are fifteen objects.
