The mind does not arise and perish as a single unit; rather, it arises sequentially. Therefore, there is no fault of contradiction between this [position] and that [scriptural passage].
According to one interpretation, the six consciousnesses can coexist with all three natures (tri-niḥsvabhāva), whereby the difficulties previously raised are rendered futile in this context.

This is the correct principle of the meaning: namely, that the first six consciousnesses arise together with all three moral natures (*tri-śīla*). "Sudden" (*saterila*) refers to arising in an instant;
"continuous flow" (*nisyanda*) refers to being of the same kind from moment to moment; "more or less" refers to instances where [the consciousness] has arisen or has not yet arisen.
This refers to these five consciousnesses: when they arise in a sudden flash, the eye may take a wholesome object, the ear an unwholesome one, and the others may be neutral.

These three arise simultaneously. There are five types of minds, including the "sudden" (sa-er) and the "continuous flow" (děng-liú). First is the sudden mind (*ābhoga-citta*), which arises immediately upon encountering an object at the very first moment of hearing the Dharma.
Second is the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), which occurs when one has not yet fully apprehended the object and is still in the process of searching for it.

Third is the determinative mind (*niścaya-citta*), which knows the existence of the essence of phenomena and gives rise to certainty. Fourth is the defiled-pure mind (*saṃkliṣṭa-viśuddha-citta*), which, through the expression of dharmas, gives rise to attachment or aversion and thus becomes defiled or pure.
Fifth is the mind of uniform outflow (*nisyanda-citta*), because its moments of thought take objects as their conditions and are equal in succession.

Furthermore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* state that the five consciousnesses must simultaneously be accompanied by a conceptualizing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
It arises at that time. Therefore, the mind associated with the eye is called the "sudden" (*sa-hattha*) mind, because it initially falls upon the object.

Since this is the first engagement with the object and its nature as wholesome or unwholesome is not yet known, a subsequent "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) mind arises for the sake of full comprehension, functioning in conjunction with desire (*chanda*).

Because it takes the object as its sphere of hope, once it has sought it out, it cognizes the previously perceived object and subsequently gives rise to certainty, thereby sealing its understanding of the object.
Once certainty has arisen, it discerns the distinctions of the realms and grasps the characteristics of the primary causes and so forth:

dwelling in aversion toward enemies, dwelling in kindness toward kin, and dwelling in equanimity toward those who are neutral. Thus, defiled and pure mental states arise; with this defiled and pure mental consciousness as the precursor, [the subsequent process unfolds].
The minds that induce visual consciousness—whether of the same nature as it, wholesome, or defiled—and which arise in accordance with their timing, are called "outflowing" (*niṣyanda*) minds.
Just as this occurs for visual consciousness, so it is for the arising of auditory and other consciousnesses.

Among these five types of mind within the eight consciousnesses, the first five consciousnesses possess four, excluding the "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) mind because they are non-conceptual. The sixth consciousness possesses all five; the seventh lacks the "sudden" (*ābhoga*) mind.

Regarding the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), there are three types: the determinative (*niyata*), the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), and the outflowing (*naiṣyandika*). Regarding the eighth [consciousness], there are likewise three types: the sudden (*ābhoga*), the determinative, and the outflowing.
Alternatively, it is said that the first five [consciousnesses] possess only two types: the sudden and the outflowing; however, this meaning remains incomplete.

Since the first five consciousnesses are already associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they ought to possess a determinate mind; furthermore, since they pertain to all three moral natures, they ought to possess both defiled and pure minds.
Therefore, it is said that there are four [types]. The passage "The five consciousnesses and the mental faculty... below explains their differing natures; the term "Tang" (唐) is redundant.

"Abandoned" means that although the fifth and sixth [consciousnesses] necessarily arise together, their natures—whether wholesome and so forth—are not necessarily the same as those of the [first] five.
Thus, your previous objection regarding a single consciousness having three natures is rendered futile.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states that when encountering the condition of sound (up to the point where it says) "it also takes the five objects as its conditions," it does not state that they are of the same nature (*sabhāga*).
This citation serves as proof that [the consciousnesses] do not share the same threefold moral quality (*trividha-svabhāva*) as the preceding five [consciousnesses].

That is to say, for one who emerges from meditative absorption, if the condition of sound is encountered and induces the arising of concentration, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the concentration and is thus universally of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*). As for the other ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) that arises, regarding its nature...
It is indeterminate; therefore, the sixth [consciousness] and the five [sensory consciousnesses] must necessarily differ in nature. It is not merely that the latter is fixed as being lower;

this explains that within the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the ear-consciousness perceives sound, whereas it is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This is because the five consciousnesses exist within the state of meditative concentration.
It is not that at the time of grasping sound, the mental consciousness induces the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within the state of equipoise (*samāhita*); this absorption is not...
The solitary mental consciousness (manovijñāna) leads the way, and it likewise gives rise to the mental factor of desire associated with joy; only then does one emerge from meditative absorption.

During the stage of the ear-consciousness within concentration, if one hears a sound with sudden clarity, the mind will necessarily become distracted. This is one of the great secondary afflictions (upakleśa), termed "unwholesome by nature" (akuśala-svabhāva).
For one who has not yet attained the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti)—that is, while still in the state of outflows (sāsrava)—this constitutes a momentary lapse of the mind.

They are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*). Because the mind is obscured during the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), the fifth and sixth [consciousnesses] do not share the same determinate nature.
From this point downward, the conclusion clarifies the meaning of how the fifth and sixth differ in their natures.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that within the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), the seeds of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) have been permanently eliminated.

The commentary explains that there are three stages: namely, entering, abiding, and emerging. "Abiding" is termed meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while the two stages of entering and emerging are termed meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).
The treatise further states that these primarily refer to the two phases of entering and emerging from concentration. This is the intended meaning.

It is evident that even within one part of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) exist. Therefore, the preceding text states that the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) in concentration hears sounds upon their sudden occurrence.
Furthermore, the subsequent treatise says: "Because it excludes *samāhita* (equipoise), it is said to be by nature distracted and mobile;

this does not exclude *samādhi* (concentration). Thus, concentration may indeed be present. Regarding the passage below concerning the five consciousnesses, which explains how the three natures arise together, the term "exclusive focus" (*ekotībhāva*) merely follows [the conventional usage].

It is of a single nature. Because it does not follow those [states] that are wholesome or defiled, but is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the six evolving consciousnesses may coexist with all three natures;
this concludes the demonstration of their being contaminated (*sāsrava*). In the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) state, the first six evolving consciousnesses arise simultaneously with all three natures.
It is exclusively of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*). If it is asked: "In the state of sovereignty (*vaśitā*), there are also both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

Since form and mind exist there, they ought to encompass all three natures; why then are they exclusively virtuous? The answer is: "The Buddha’s form, mind, and so forth, are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). To say they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path explains that they are exclusively virtuous.
This is because they are of a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and manifest as being devoid of the seeds of the unvirtuous (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Just as with "extreme bliss" (*parama-sukha*) downward, it provides an analogy for extreme suffering, showing that there is no faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*).
It concludes by clarifying that when the treatise mentions the "remaining three," these are definitively grief, joy, and pleasure.
Other sources state that those [realms] possess pleasure as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda-sukha*); however, for fear of making this work too voluminous, I shall not describe it in detail here.
To explain other points in general: other sources state that even in places where one experiences exclusively suffering, there is pleasure as a result of outflow.

For example, in the Hot Hells, when the fierce fires momentarily subside, or when one perceives objects such as clear springs or flowing streams, these are also termed "pleasure," though in reality...

It is not pleasure; therefore, it is called "outflow" (*niṣyanda*). This refers to the meaning of pleasure as taught in the context of worldly transmigration (*saṃsāra*), or it refers generally to other states of mixed sensation where there is outflow-pleasure.
It does not mean that there is no pleasure resulting from karmic maturation (*vipākaphala*);

for that which lacks maturation-pleasure is designated as "pure suffering. However, in various holy scriptures, the intent of the teachings cited by the former master is explained comprehensively as follows:

"Sadvedanā is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*). Regarding the phrase "based on the majority," this indicates that there is also a small portion that extends to the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Alternatively, because it is spoken in reliance upon the flow of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) characterized by grief and sorrow, there is no fault of contradiction.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, the lower section explains that the statement in the preceding treatise regarding the association with the faculty of grief is all spoken from the perspective of the mundane flow of cyclic existence, and does not refer to a real faculty of grief. Furthermore, in the same lower section, that treatise is explained.

It is taught that mental suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is of the same category as grief (*daurmanasya*); thus it is metaphorically termed "grief," though in reality it is suffering. Furthermore, the commentary explains the intent [of this teaching] by stating:

"Alternatively, because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) harms both body and mind, although it is subsumed under the faculty of suffering, it is designated here according to its specific relation to the mind."

Furthermore, what is called "sorrow" (*daurmanasya*) is in fact suffering (*duḥkha*). Just as the joy (*prīti*) of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), by virtue of its dependence on the body, is also called "pleasure" (*sukha*), yet is in fact joy.
Works such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* fully elucidate this meaning; this general conclusion from other treatises is also consistent with the above sense.

However, regarding the statement that pleasure exists in the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*), all such explanations of pleasure are merely figurative designations (*prajñapti*). This applies up to the third [dhyāna].
Regarding the dhyānas: because there is no faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), eleven faculties are spoken of in relation to the desire realm and the first two dhyānas.

In the first five [faculties] and the sixth [faculty], there are four each—excluding pleasure—which together constitute eight faculties. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses each possess only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), which together constitute ten faculties.
Because the body and mind in the hells are both the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), there are eleven; this is based solely on the presence of suffering and so forth.
This is the explanation of the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*). Alternatively, in the untainted state (*anāsrava*), there are twelve faculties:

namely, the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), the mental faculty (*manas*), joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which together constitute nine faculties; when combined with the three untainted faculties (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*, etc.), there are twelve. This occurs before reaching the stage of pleasure (*sukha-bhūmi*).
Therefore, excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), there are only eleven. Alternatively, in the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), there are also twelve faculties;

namely, the five faculties beginning with the eye, the two faculties of male and female, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and the three of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity—thus making twelve.
Since one has not yet reached the stage of pleasure (*sukhabhūmi*), the faculty of pleasure is excluded, leaving only eleven. This is the explanation based on the twenty-two faculties.
Since there is no authoritative basis for the meaning of the eleven faculties (*indriya*), all three interpretations remain valid; let them await further consultation.

From "By this" onwards, the conclusion clarifies that there is no fault in the treatise’s statement regarding the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) being associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). From "These [points]" onwards, the preceding meanings are summarized.
△ The section on the existence or non-existence of pleasure and suffering is concluded. Below, four points are raised to refute misconceptions.

There is an interpretation that the six consciousnesses and the three feelings do not coexist (up to the point where it says): "Because the Buddhas have already severed the causes of sorrow and suffering.
Herein, the argument refuting the position [of the opponent] is identical in intent to that in the chapter on the Three Natures;

therefore, it is not explained again. △ Fourth, the section on citing positions and refuting them through debate is concluded. This concludes the brief indication of the six stages mentioned above. Below follows the detailed exposition of their distinctions.

The detailed classification has five parts. First, the classification of the universal and specific-object mental factors, which is divided into three sections. First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the presentation of the inquiry:
Regarding the six categories of mental factors briefly indicated previously (up to), what are the characteristics of the first two categories?

In this section, the preceding summary of the meaning of the six stages has been concluded. Now follows the detailed exposition of the distinctions among these six stages, which will be explained in sequence;

therefore, the question is asked: "What are their characteristics? △ First, the conclusion of the preceding summary and the posing of the question are complete. Below, the second part provides a general answer by citing a verse.
The verse says: "First, the universal [factors] such as contact... up to... resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; their objects of focus differ.

This verse is cited to answer the intent of the preceding question. The first line praises the stage of the universal factors. The second and third lines praise the stage of the specific-object factors.
The fourth line explains the meaning of the specific-object factors. △ Second, the citation of the verse to provide a general response is complete. Below follows the detailed explanation.
The meaning of the verse is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitta*).
The treatise says: "Among the six stages, the first are the omnipresent mental factors... [up to] "...these scriptural authorities are numerous and manifold."

Regarding the first line of the verse, the five objects such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth are explained in detail—both their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and their specific functions (*karma*)—in the section on the "first transformative consciousness" in the third fascicle;
therefore, they are not reiterated here. Furthermore, questions and answers are presented to clarify the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

The scriptural authority can be established. It is stated in the three fascicles [of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*]: "Its universal characteristic shall be explained extensively later; the text appears here.

Below this, first the sacred teachings (*āgama*) are cited to prove that contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—these four—are universal (*sarvatraga*).

Because they arise from the transformation associated with the conjunction of the three [faculties, objects, and consciousness], these four factors possess the meaning of being universal. Furthermore, below the citation from the *Sūtra*...
The *manasikāra* (attention) that functions as realization is also omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), because consciousness arises only when there is attention.
In the passage following this sutra, another sutra is further cited to prove that this *manasikāra* has the meaning of being omnipresent.

Since *manasikāra* is a mental factor (*caitta*) and discernment (*vijñapti*) is the mental king (*cittarāja*), and because the mind and its factors are inseparable, this demonstrates that it is omnipresent. These scriptural authorities are indeed [authoritative].
Regarding the proof that [the universal factors] are not merely one: this concludes and clarifies the sacred teaching. The proofs for the five universal factors are indeed not of a single kind.

Having finished citing the scriptures, as for the reasoning—that the arising of consciousness necessarily involves the "threefold conjunction" (and so forth)—the meaning of why the others are not universal factors will be explained in due course.

In all cases of investigating phenomena (*vastu*), one must employ reasoning. Now, by analyzing the locus of contact (*sparśa*), it is established that this is a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

This means that when the three factors—sense organ, object, and consciousness—conjoin, contact necessarily arises; yet, since those three conjoinings themselves must also involve contact, the conjunction of mind and mental factors with their objects must necessarily depend on the power of contact.
This is the meaning of its being a universal factor, which causes the mind to contact its object according to principle.
One should attend to this: all minds and mental factors arise by means of attention (*manaskāra*); therefore, one knows that attention is also a universal factor (*sarvatraga*).

Feeling (*vedanā*) experiences favorable objects, causing the mind and its associates to become joyful; it experiences unfavorable objects, causing them to become sorrowful; and it experiences neutral objects, causing them to become equanimous.

If there were no feeling, when the mind and its associates arise, there would be no occurrence of their respective characteristics in accordance with the three types of objects. Since this [feeling] is able to cause these to arise, it is [a universal factor].

Universal: Regarding all minds, the apprehension of the specific characteristics of objects necessarily depends upon *saṃjñā* (perception); therefore, the mental factor of perception carries the meaning of being universal.
"Correct causes, etc. refers to [the inclusion of] "incorrect causes"; [through perception] one apprehends what is correct and performs wholesome deeds, as well as what is incorrect and unwholesome.
If there were no volition (*cetanā*), then at the stage when the mind arises, there would be no sense of conforming to what is deviant or correct, nor of performing wholesome deeds and so forth.

Since this [volition] enables such grasping, it is a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). This concludes the presentation of the reasoning. From here on, the following summarizes that these five aforementioned factors possess the characteristic of being universal.

The others are not universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), as they lack this characteristic; this clarifies the subsequent specific objects (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*). △ The explanation of the universal factors is concluded.
Below, the explanation of the specific objects is divided into three parts. First, the formal explanation of the five objects.

Next, regarding the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviṣaya*), these refer to the range from desire (*chanda*) to wisdom (*prajñā*). By this principle, desire is not a universal factor (*sarvatraga*).

This provides a general enumeration of the five objects and their sequential order, followed by a detailed explanation of their meanings to demonstrate that they do not function universally. The question "How [is it]?

introduces the response to clarify the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and functional activity (*karman*) of the mental factor of desire. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "With respect to an object that is desired..."
It has as its essence the aspiration for the performance of various [tasks] that it induces, and as its function, serving as the basis for right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*).

Regarding the first point, there is an interpretation that explains "the desirable" (*abhipreta*) by means of "the delightful" (*abhinandaniya*); thus, it asks: regarding objects that are loathsome, one desires their non-occurrence.

If one desires separation from that [object], there must also be desire; why then can it be claimed that only the former is called "desire for hope" (*āśāstichanda*)? The Master of the Treatise answers:
This desire for what is pleasing (*abhipreta-chanda*) exists only at the time when one seeks non-separation from that object;

it has the quality of being pleasant with respect to its own basis (*svabhāva*), and not with respect to an object that is loathsome. Since there is also desire for what is pleasing, the conclusion below clarifies that desire is not exclusively a pervasive mental factor (*sarvatraga*).
Because desire does not arise in the case of neutral objects (*upekṣā*) due to their being indifferent and not being desired;

and because the meaning of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is explained below as being "that which is sought," since desire exists in both the seeking of union with what is pleasant and the seeking of separation from what is loathsome. Regarding the phrase "in the case of the neutral":
this concludes by demonstrating that desire is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), because there is necessarily no desire for neutral objects or for that which is not desired.

Therefore, regarding the meaning of "subsequent existence" (*punarbhava*) below: it explains what is desired by means of the desire to observe, meaning that the desire to investigate is itself what is desired.

If [the text] does not say "not," it explains that it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*). As for the phrase "due to the power of the object": it takes as its objective support whatever object currently exists.
Because it is not characterized by aspiration, there is a complete absence of desire. From "By this" [the text] below concludes the explanation of the three preceding meanings of desire;
none of them are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*). Regarding these three meanings, although the terminology differs, their meaning is not contradictory.

Some say that because [the mind] reaches its object through the power of aspiration (*abhilāṣa*), the treatise states that this diligence (*vīrya*) has "taking [an object] as its basis" as its function.

That explanation is not correct. This is because they maintain that desire (*chanda*) is universal (*sarvatraga*) since it gives rise to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The Master refutes this, saying, "That is not so," and so forth.
That is to say, the various holy teachings state only that attention (*manasikāra*) is able to give rise to the various consciousnesses, and not...
It was previously stated that desire (*chanda*) gives rise to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). This is refuted by citing scriptural examples as explained below.

As the Sūtra says: "All phenomena have craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as their root. How, then, could craving itself give rise to the mind and mental factors? One should understand that desire is the root because it initiates all activities;
or, as it is said, wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*) can arouse right effort (*samyag-vīrya*), through which one diligently practices all [virtuous deeds].
Excellent. Because desire is the root, the treatise explains this desire as having diligence as its basis and activity. This is because all phenomena take desire as their root;
it is not that desire can produce the mind and mental factors.

What is the nature of resolute belief (*adhimokṣa*) regarding a determined object? [From "up to" this point: This would further require dependence on another, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress.
The question and answer explain the essential nature and function of the mental factor of resolute belief.

Its essence is to seal and maintain [the object]. Its function is that other conditions cannot lead it astray. That is to say, "false or correct, inferior or... explains the meaning of determination; namely, false or correct teachings.

Furthermore, regarding the power of evidence from both false and correct reasoning, that which is a definitive, firm apprehension of an object—unshakable by other conditions—is called "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*).

Therefore, below the section on "doubt," this resolute conviction is explained as not being a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), because at the time of doubt and when there is no definitive apprehension, there is no such firm holding.
Below the section stating "some say," they maintain it to be universal, asserting that it is the mind...
When a mental factor (*caitta*) grasps its own object, that which is unimpeded with respect to the focal object (*ālambana*) is termed "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*).

[The opponent claims] that because it pervades the mind and so forth, it has the meaning of being "omnipresent" (*sarvatraga*). The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: That statement is irrational.

For that which is "able to be unimpeded" refers to the various phenomena that constitute the focal objects, while that which is "not impeded" refers to the cognizing mind and mental factors themselves.

Regarding the arising of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*): its conditions are the faculties (*indriya*), the objects (*ālambana*), and mental attention (*manasikāra*). How could resolute conviction arise from the object alone?
If it were to arise from the object, one would have to restate that position and refute the difficulty as follows:

if that resolute conviction arises because of this object, then this object must in turn depend on another moment of mind to arise. This would entail the fallacy of mutual generation between mind and object. [And] mutual generation between mind and object...
As this process continues without ceasing, it is said to be "infinite.
Why is there mindfulness of objects previously experienced? [This continues] until: because it serves as the cause for recollection at a later time.

The question and answer explain the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and functional activity (*karma*) of the mental factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*). To clearly remember all phenomena is the nature of mindfulness.

Because of this clear recollection, concentration (*samādhi*) subsequently arises; this is the function of mindfulness. The phrase "repeatedly recollecting and maintaining" [in the root text] explains the aforementioned "clear recollection" as well as the meaning of concentration being its basis.
The phrase "regarding that which has never before been experienced" explains that the mental factor of mindfulness is not a universal (*sarvatraga*) factor.

Because mindfulness does not arise regarding objects not yet experienced or those not clearly registered, some claim that the mental factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) has the meaning of being omnipresent (*sarvatraga*), on the grounds that mindfulness must necessarily exist whenever the mind arises.
The Master [Vasubandhu] refutes this difficulty, saying: "That statement is irrational;

otherwise, there would be no delusion (*moha*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth at a later time, because they too would have existed previously, just as in the case of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses."
Regarding the argument concerning temporal priority (*pūrvakāla*): if there was no faith previously, yet faith can still arise, what is the use of its prior existence?

Furthermore, if the seven [mental factors] existed previously, they would certainly not arise later; how then could it be that they lacked a cause previously? Thus, establishing a prior cause becomes useless.

By examining both prior existence and prior non-existence, neither can serve as a cause. Therefore, since [the factors] exist both before and after, [the opponent’s] dual arguments are both refuted. Prior...

Below the section on "Mind and Mental Factors," it clarifies that the preceding cause does not reside in mindfulness (*smṛti*). Rather, the power of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) alone is sufficient to serve as the cause.

Furthermore, if a preceding moment of mind causes a subsequent moment of mind to arise, this constitutes the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This condition, in terms of its primary subject, is exclusively the mind-king (*citta-rāja*);
mindfulness, however, is a mental factor (*caitta*) and is not of the nature of the primary subject.
What is concentration (*samādhi*)? [It is that which] regarding the object of observation... because it does not arise in all states, it is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*).

The question and answer explain the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*) of the mental factor of concentration. Its essential nature is focused attention without distraction. Its function is the arising of wisdom (*prajñā*) through prolonged concentration.

This means that by observing the lower [levels], one explains the aforementioned "focused attention without distraction. Its function is to serve as the basis for knowledge (*jñāna*); this is the meaning of its being "concomitant" (*sahagata*).
"Non-... refers to neither attainment nor loss; it is the non-conceptual mind with respect to its object. Therefore, it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
Regarding the phrase "the mind is focused," this explains the aforementioned "focus. It does not mean being fixed upon a single object;

rather, because there is no second thought while abiding in an object, focusing on all objects is likewise termed "focused attention. This is because the objects come and go of their own accord, while the mind remains constantly concentrated.

Commentary: If it does not descend, it refers to the mental factors associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is also not a universal factor (*sarvatraga*), because concentration does not arise unless the mind is bound [to an object].
Some say that at that time concentration also arises—[as in the case of] mindfulness, wisdom, and so forth—which are not identical to the mind itself.
The mental factor of concentration (*samādhi*) has the status of being a universal (*sarvatraga*). This means that even when the mind is not bound [to an object], concentration still arises;
though it is subtle and difficult to perceive, one should speak with certainty because concentration truly exists.

Furthermore, if it were argued that its status as a universal consists in causing the mind to conjoin and proceed toward an object, the Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "This is also not logical, for that is the function of contact (*sparśa*). That is to say, it causes...
The mind contacts its object; this is the functional activity of contact (*sparśa*). Is it then necessarily so?

If you say [it is], you are again insisting that it is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), meaning it necessarily causes the mind, for the duration of a single moment, not to shift its object, and thus it must be universal.

To this, he further refutes: A single moment of mind is the shortest possible duration of time; it naturally does not shift. What mental factor could then be necessary to prevent it from shifting its object?

If it is argued that [concentration] is again held to be a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), it is further refuted as follows: "It would cause the mind's object of cognition (*ālambana*) to be exclusively attention (*manaskāra*);
how could it be a determinate mental factor? Regarding the statement "it is said to be," this means that concentration as a mental factor is provisional and not substantial;

therefore, it is said to be identical to the mind itself, because the Sūtra refers to concentration as the "training of the mind" (*citta-śikṣā*). As for the phrase "that is not," the Master [Vasubandhu] refutes it, meaning that...

Citing the sutras does not constitute a definitive proof; for it is by means of concentration (*samādhi*) that the mind is gathered and made one-pointed, and thus the sutras describe it as "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*).

The five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) are all subsumed within this concentration.

Just as mindfulness and wisdom each have their own distinct essence and are not identical to the mind itself, how could wisdom—regarding its observed object—be non-universal, like faith, greed, and so forth? It certainly is not universal.
The question-and-answer section explains the essence, nature, and function of wisdom (*prajñā*). To discern all phenomena is the nature of wisdom; to decisively sever doubt is its function.
The phrase "contemplating" (*vipaśyanā*) below explains the aforementioned "discernment" (*vibhāvanā*) and "severing doubt. "Investigating" (*vicaya*) explains discernment;

"ascertaining" (*niścaya*) explains the severing of delusion. Regarding the phrase "not an object of contemplation" below, it explains that [wisdom] is not a universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), because of ignorance (*moha*).
Because wisdom does not arise when the mind is obscured. Some say that the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) is also a universal (*mahābhūmika*).
This means that at times of delusion, the characteristics of wisdom are subtle and hidden; therefore, those with great faculties cannot perceive them.

Since contact (*sparśa*), desire (*chanda*), and so forth are called "mental factors of the universal ground" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), and since contact is a universal factor, desire should likewise be so. Thus, it is said in the Abhidharma: because they are mental factors of the universal ground.
The various schools [of thought] submit [their positions]. The Master refutes them using correct reasoning (*yukti*). "School" (*nikāya*) refers to their respective positions.

Regarding the *Abhidharma* (Dharma of Counter-position): each is categorized according to its class. Because factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and desire (*chanda*) are universal across all stages, they are called "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika-dharma*).

If one discusses the "universals" (*sarvatraga*), those such as desire are excluded; if one discusses the "object-specific" (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, those such as contact are excluded. Thus, the *Abhidharma* is said to involve mutual contradictions.

The remaining meanings are as stated in the text; they need not be elaborated upon here. △ The first section, the formal explanation of the five objects, is concluded. Below follows the second section, the extensive analysis of their manifestation.
According to one interpretation, these five are necessarily mutually supportive (until): that is to say, when there is no focused concentration, but rather a state of distracted searching.

The first interpretation is not correct, because it implies mutual dependence, which necessitates simultaneous arising. The second interpretation accords with correct reasoning: namely, that the five mental factors do not necessarily arise together.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (lower section) cites scriptural evidence stating that among the four "all-s" (*sarva*), the latter two are absent;
these refer to "at all times" and "always together," meaning there is no sense of being simultaneous or co-arising. Furthermore, it speaks of the "object-condition" (*ālambana*).
There are four objects and five types of cognizing minds; they do not necessarily arise together. This should be explained as follows. The author of the treatise establishes his own correct position:
that at times one [mental factor] arises, up to and including at times when all five arise, or there may be times when none of the five arise simultaneously;
therefore, it is said to be "indeterminate. Regarding an object of desire, when only aspiration arises, there is no second...
The same should be understood for the two factors of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*). Regarding the first [concentration], it may be explained as follows:
at the initial stage of the object of observation, one merely gives rise to focused attention (*ekāgratā*). By the term "focused attention," the definition is established;

that is to say, because the mind of a deluded person is largely distracted, one focuses on the object of observation in order to stop that distraction. Because of their delusion, they are unable to exercise discernment (*pravicaya*).

It is the same as that of the sages and worthies. Because concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are observed in equal measure, one gives rise to focused attention solely toward the object of observation.
Suppose someone were to ask: "If there is no discernment (*vīkṣaṇa*), how can there be an object of observation? The author of the treatise answers:

When one applies effort toward that concentration, distraction is first ceased by following a small amount of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*); this is what is called "equipoise" (*samāhita*), which takes the object of observation as its focal point. This is what is meant by "equal."

"Maintaining" refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Or depending on the majority" does not mean a single object of focus. When these words are spoken, they refer to the terminology of concentration.
As for the "Heaven of Forgetfulness through Play," it is a heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); because at times of sensual pleasure, one forgets the east while playing in the west.
[The practitioner] forgets what follows while focused on what precedes. Although this is called "focusing on a single object," one nevertheless gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed arises toward a favorable object; hatred arises toward an unfavorable object; and delusion does not arise from either. How can one focus on a single object and yet give rise to these three?

By analogy, while the name "concentration" (samādhi) implies focusing on a single object, the actual objects are not necessarily one. Next, regarding the passage "or else, with respect to the object of observation... and below, it explains that only wisdom (prajñā) arises. Regarding...

The object of observation is pursued through mental dispersion; this is the meaning of "discrimination" (*pravicaya*). Because it differs from the preceding meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no single-pointed focus.

At times, two [mental states] arise simultaneously—namely, that which pertains to what is desired and that which coexists with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—and instances of this kind are not limited to one.
"Sometimes two arise, up to a total of twelve" means that with respect to the four objects, there are ten pairs that arise in succession:
first, desire and understanding; second, desire and mindfulness; third, desire and concentration; fourth, desire and wisdom; fifth, understanding and mindfulness.

Sixth is the liberation of concentration (*samādhi-vimukti*); seventh is the liberation of wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*); eighth is mindfulness of concentration (*samādhi-smṛti*); ninth is mindfulness of wisdom (*prajñā-smṛti*); tenth is the union of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).

These occur simultaneously with respect to four objects. There are ten categories of concentration. The verse says: In the desire realm, there are four [categories] including liberation, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;

In the [upper realms], there are three including liberation, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; In the [upper realms], there are nine including mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; The tenth, the union of concentration and wisdom, exists in all twelve [realms].
"Sometimes three arise, up to a total of thirteen": this means that with respect to the four objects, ten sets of three arise in succession.
These are: (1) desire, resolve, and mindfulness; (2) desire, resolve, and concentration; (3) desire, resolve, and wisdom; (4) desire, mindfulness, and concentration;
(5) desire, mindfulness, and wisdom; (6) desire, concentration, and wisdom; (7) resolve, mindfulness, and concentration; (8) resolve, mindfulness, and wisdom; (9) resolve... [and so forth].

Concentration and Wisdom. Ten recitations of concentration and wisdom arise simultaneously with respect to four objects; there are likewise ten numerical instances. The verse says: When desire, understanding, and mindfulness encounter concentration and wisdom, there are three.
When desire and mindfulness further encounter concentration and wisdom, they are combined. When desire and concentration encounter wisdom, the count should be six.

When understanding and mindfulness add concentration and wisdom, the count is eight. Understanding and concentration, wisdom and mindfulness, and concentration and wisdom—when combined, there are... [The text ends here.]
The thirteen [mental factors] are now complete. At times, four [factors] arise; up to a total of five sets of four.

These five sets of four refer to the sequential arising [of factors] in relation to the four objects: (1) desire, resolve, mindfulness, and concentration; and (2) desire, resolve, mindfulness, and wisdom.
1. Desire, understanding, concentration, and wisdom; 2. Desire, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; 3. Understanding, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

These four arise simultaneously with respect to the four objects, and there are only five [categories] in total. The verse says: One arises first; the preceding four arise together. Two exclude concentration.

Three are mindfulness; four are understanding; The fifth is the exhaustion of desire through wisdom. Reversing from wisdom, one excludes [the others] to reach four, then five, then four. The preceding and succeeding treatises can truly serve as proof.
At times, five lower [factors] arise; that is to say, when five types arise simultaneously with respect to four objects, they are counted as one total.
In this way, the lower [factors] form a total and specific enumeration of phrases: there are five phrases for the single arising of desire and so forth;
ten phrases each for the simultaneous arising of two and three; five phrases for the arising of four; and one phrase for the arising of five. Altogether, there are thirty-one.
[This is] a phrase. Alternatively, there is the interpretation that below the mind [it] explains how all five [consciousnesses] do not arise.
That is to say, in the state of having a mind, just as with the four objects, all five do not arise. Or at times, when the four objects suddenly fall upon the mind, the five also do not arise;
because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is not associated with the five, they do not arise simultaneously. Thus, the five do not arise. Instances of this kind are not limited to one.
△ The detailed explanation of their manifestation is concluded. The following three sections pertain to various categories.
Regarding the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, these five object-specific mental factors (cannot infer, because they lack discernment).

Regarding these five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa-viṣaya-ka-citta*), they do not exist within the eighth consciousness during its contaminated state (*sāsrava*). In the seventh consciousness, when it is contaminated, there is only wisdom (*prajñā*).

Because the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) of these two consciousnesses involves association with all five [mental factors], this has already been explained in detail in the previous section on the second transformative consciousness.
As for the sixth consciousness, it is associated with the five object-specific factors in both their contaminated and uncontaminated states; therefore, they exist [there].

The interpretation is not yet correct. This means that there is no logical basis for the five sensory consciousnesses to be associated with the five object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-ka*).

The passage beginning with "because they take what has already been obtained as their object" explains why these five [sensory consciousnesses] lack the quality of association; this should be understood according to the sequence.

There is an interpretation that the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) may possess these five [wisdoms], because all five sensory consciousnesses include the wisdom of accomplishing tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

This is the correct position of the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*), who maintains that the first five consciousnesses may be associated with all five [wisdoms]. Although there is no explicit mention [of this] below, it is explained that the first five consciousnesses [possess them].
There are also subtle desires, inclinations, and mindfulness; these should be understood respectively.

Although it does not explicitly explain that the first five consciousnesses possess the quality of focused attention (*ekāgratā*), if one were to ask: "The five consciousnesses are distracted and mobile; how can they have concentration? it is therefore explained as follows:
Because it excludes *samāhita* (equipoise), its nature is said to be distracted; it does not exclude *samādhi* (concentration), and thus concentration may still be present.

"Equipoise" (*samāhita*) refers to the moments of entering and emerging from meditative absorption; at these times, the five sensory consciousnesses cannot possibly exist. "Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to the moment of abiding in absorption;
because during the time one is in absorption, the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of objects is the same as that of the five sensory consciousnesses, concentration may indeed be present. Although...

Below, the first five consciousnesses are explained. Regarding the statement that they possess the sense of discernment (*pravicaya*) and that the two—eye and ear—are associated with the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*):

this establishes that eye- and ear-consciousness are associated with discerning wisdom (*prajñā*). Since these two possess wisdom, it follows by analogy that the other three—nose, tongue, and body consciousness—likewise possess wisdom without error.
"Not yet masterful" concludes the preceding discussion on the impure (*sāsrava*) states; the five objects may or may not arise subsequently.
The untainted [consciousnesses] (anāsrava) and the five objects are necessarily present. Regarding the observation of the lower [realms], this explains the state of mastery.
There are necessarily five objects associated with the five consciousnesses, each corresponding respectively.

Regarding these five object-specific mental factors (*viṣaya-viniyata-kausalā*), with which feelings (*vedanā*) are they associated? [The answer continues] through various analytical categories as should be considered according to reason.
The questions and answers clarify the association of the object-specific factors with the five feelings. At first, there is an interpretation that is not yet correct, which states:

"Desire (*chanda*), one of the mental factors, is concomitant with three feelings, excluding the two feelings of grief (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), because the objects of grief and suffering are not what is desired. The remainder...

The mental factors of resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are associated with the other four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*). "Resolution" refers to resolve;
"and so forth" includes mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Regarding the phrase "because resolution and so forth are absent in the five consciousnesses":

since the first five evolving consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*) are consciousnesses associated with the feeling of suffering, and these consciousnesses do not correspond with those four mental factors, the feeling of suffering likewise does not correspond with them.

Regarding the fourth [point], the association with mental factors (*caitta*), there is another interpretation based on correct reasoning (*yukti*). It is accepted that the five [mental factors] beginning with desire (*chanda*) are associated with the five types of feeling (*vedanā*).

This is because the former masters maintained that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) does not coexist with the mental factor of desire; however, the present [author] cites a treatise (*śāstra*) to prove that it does indeed arise together with desire.
Because it is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) at the time of sorrowful distress; because that which seeks to realize [the goal] is a mental factor of desire (*chanda*).

Previously, it was maintained that the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) does not coexist with desire; now, by citing the case of one who intensely craves liberation from pure suffering, it is shown that desire arises together [with it].

Furthermore, the mental factor of desire necessarily pervades the sixth consciousness (the mental consciousness), for it has already been stated that there is suffering on the level of the mind. This also demonstrates desire.

It is associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*). The treatise states that craving is "below" [the realm of form]. This again cites the treatise to prove the point that desire is associated with both sorrow and suffering.
Previously, it was held that the faculty of suffering lacks discernment and so forth; now, it is cited as being associated with the mental faculty (*manas*).

Furthermore, because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is associated with the four [mental factors] such as investigation (*vitarka*) and decision (*vicāra*), there is no error in [asserting that] suffering is associated with these four.

Moreover, from "the five consciousnesses below" onwards, the preceding arguments regarding investigation and decision are successively refuted. From "by this, below" onwards, the conclusion is drawn that the five feelings, such as desire, are associated [with the mental consciousness].
From "these five below" onwards, the conclusion is drawn to clarify the distinctions among the three natures, the three realms, the three trainings (*śikṣā*), and other categories. (1)

The reasoning is as before; the wording does not appear again. △ The third section, concerning the various categories, is concluded. This completes the preceding discussion on the universal and object-specific mental factors.
*Vyākhyāyukti* (A Vernacular Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*), Fascicle Five.
The Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Six.
Composed in verse by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu;
composed as a treatise by Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others.

Part Three: The Section on the Third Transforming Consciousness. This section is divided into two parts: first, citing the headings and posing the questions; second, providing the general answer by quoting the verses, which is further divided into three parts.
First, the fundamental consciousness that undergoes transformation; second, the mental factors associated with it, which are divided into three parts.

First, a brief indication of the six categories. Second, a detailed exposition of their distinctions, divided into five parts. The first two—the universal and the object-specific categories—have already been completed in the fifth fascicle.
This second part, the category of the wholesome, is divided into three sections. First, concluding the preceding section and posing the question.
Having already explained the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) categories, what are the characteristics of the wholesome (*kuśala*) mental factors?
Regarding wholesome mental factors, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* lists thirteen kinds of wholesomeness; this is the first of them, which constitutes the essence among those thirteen.
What are the thirteen? First, natural wholesomeness (*svabhāva-kuśala*), because they are mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*). Second, [wholesomeness by] association...

1. Wholesome by nature (*svabhāva-kuśala*): because it is the associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) themselves. 2. Wholesome by association (*samprayoga-kuśala*): because they are the concomitants of those [associated phenomena]. 3. Wholesome by following (*anubandha-kuśala*):

because they are the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those [wholesome states]. 4. Wholesome by initiation (*samutthāna-kuśala*): because they initiate bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*). 5. Wholesome in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-kuśala*): because it is suchness (*tathatā*). 6. Wholesome by birthright (*upapatti-labdha-kuśala*):

because it is innate (*sahaja*) wholesomeness. 7. Wholesome by application (*prāyogika-kuśala*): because it is cultivated through skillful means (*upāya*). 8. Wholesome by manifest worship (*abhimukha-pūjā-kuśala*): [referring to] the drawing of... [text truncated]

1. It is the excellence of recording the venerable countenance, because it transcribes the treasury of the Dharma. 2. It is the excellence of benefiting others, by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). 3.

It is the excellence of inducing [others] to practice, because cause and effect mutually induce one another. 4. It is the excellence of antidotes, because it employs various antidotes such as revulsion and destruction.

12. Wholesome by tranquility (*śamatha*), because it eternally severs the defilements that constitute obstacles. 13. Wholesome by natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), because it consists of the causes and effects of superior supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
△ The first section, concluding the preceding and posing the question, is finished. Below, the second section provides the general answer in verse.
The verse says: "Wholesome [states] are faith, shame, and dread, (up to) diligence, serenity, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming.
This verse summarizes the eleven mental factors belonging to the wholesome category in order to answer the question.

There are three phrases in the first line of the verse: namely, faith, shame, and dread. There are three [factors] in the second line of the verse: namely, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Three.

Regarding the term "roots" (*mūla*): because they give rise to what is wholesome in a superior manner, they are called "wholesome roots. The third line of the verse contains three factors: diligence (*vīrya*), which is the same as vigor;
tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), which is the same as pliancy; and non-negligence (*apramāda*). The fourth line of the verse contains two factors:

equanimity in action (*upekṣā*) and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*). This concludes the second section, the summary response by citing the verse. Below follows the third section, the explanation of the meaning of the verse, which is divided into three parts. First:
The formal explanation of the mental factors (*caitasika*) consists of eleven chapters.

The treatise states: "Only those that coexist with a wholesome mind are called wholesome mental factors" (extending to) "delighting in and realizing the cultivation of mundane and supramundane virtues."
General Explanation of the Wholesome Factors: These are associated exclusively with wholesome minds and are fixed at eleven in number. Regarding "What is faith? and so forth:
first, an explanation of the essence, nature, and function of the mental factor of faith. It causes the mind and its concomitants to attain purity; this is the self-nature of faith.
To delight in performing various virtues is the function of faith. Furthermore, there are briefly three types of distinctions regarding faith.
The treatise summarizes the three aspects of reality, virtue, and capacity by means of the meanings of profound patience (*adhimukti*), profound delight (*ruci*), and profound desire (*chanda*).

First, regarding "faith that [things] truly exist" and below, this explains profound patience. All phenomena—namely, the internal body, external objects, and so forth—each possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

these are called the principles of real entities (*vastu-tattva*). Because the specific characteristics of all phenomena cannot be augmented by verbal expressions and cannot be reached by the consciousness (*vijñāna*), one can only have faith in them.

To "accept" means to believe in their actual existence. Second, regarding the phrase "believing in their virtues," this explains "profound delight. As for the virtues of the Three Jewels: the Buddha has the *dharmakāya* as his virtue;
the Dharma has *prajñā* as its virtue; and the Saṃgha has liberation as its virtue.

Because these three factors remain eternally pure even while amidst defilement, they are called "truly pure. By believing in these three virtues, one gives rise to a sense of fondness and delight; this is what is meant by [the term].
Deep faith and delight. Third, believing that there is the capacity to descend. This explains deep aspiration. Worldly wholesome states with outflows can induce the uncontaminated;
supramundane wholesome states without outflows can induce the unconditioned. Therefore it is said: "Deep faith possesses power; its attainment lies in the mind, and its fulfillment lies in action.
That which is conditioned is called "fulfillment" (*cheng*); that which is unconditioned is called "attainment" (*de*). One believes in the aforementioned various virtues and gives rise to them.
Because of this hope, it is called "deep desire. Through these three types of faith, one is able to counteract that lack of faith;
for by means of this faith, one loves the cultivation of all virtues, whereas that lack of faith obstructs all virtues.
"Patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), which is the cause of faith; since faith is its direct opposite, [patience] has purity as its characteristic.

Through this question and answer, the essential nature of the mental factor of faith—its cause, fruit, and intrinsic nature—is clarified. Question: As previously stated, patience and aspiration are the cause and fruit of faith;
why then are they called its "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*)? The Master of the Treatise answers: It was just stated that its nature is the purity of mind.
This is its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The questioner again presents a challenge, saying: "I have not yet understood the meaning of the term 'purity of mind.
If purity is identical to the mind, then since the mind has no [separate] object, it should not be a mental factor (*caitta*). If one were to provide an explanation:
it is a *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound, because the essence of the mind possesses the function of purity. If one intends for the mind to become pure, the mind—
The same applies to shame (*hrī*) and the other [virtuous mental factors] that cause the mind to be so. Therefore, it is asked: "What is the distinction between shame and the others?

Since these factors such as shame also cause the mind to be pure, if one were to provide an explanation, the compound would be analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) rule—specifically the *śeṣa-tatpuruṣa*—where the mind-factor is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) that brings about this state.

The mind-king (*cittarāja*) is that which is governed. Regarding "the pure factors associated with the mind": these are the mental concomitants (*caitta*) that are associated with the mind, as well as those such as shame (*hrī*) and so forth;

thus it is said, "it is likewise difficult [to distinguish]. If one were to provide an explanation, it would be like the analogy of a neighbor living near a powerful neighbor, because those mental concomitants are close to the mind-king.
The Master of the Treatise replies: "This factor of faith (*śraddhā*) is by its very nature (*svabhāva*) clear and limpid."
It is able to purify the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) of others; because the mind is preeminent, it is simply said that "the mind is purified," though the mind is present therein.
This is like the analogy of water below: faith is compared to a pearl, while the other mental factors are compared to turbid water. An objection was raised above:
"If purity is the defining characteristic, how does it differ from shame (*hrī*) and the rest? Therefore, this commentary explains: although shame and the others are wholesome, they are not...

Purity is its characteristic. This purity as a characteristic avoids the fault of being confused with other things. Furthermore, following the various defiled phenomena, the characteristics of the defiled and the pure are again presented in contrast;
through this symmetry of meaning and force, the purity of others' minds and so forth is clarified as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of faith.
Some say that the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā*) is "delight" (*abhirati*). [This continues until: "By this, one should know that the purity of the mind is faith.
The Sthavira school of the Hīnayāna states: "The characteristic of faith is delight. The Master of the Treatise refutes this, saying: "It would then have to apply to all three natures (*trividha*).

Faith is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*); delight is of a defiled nature (*kliṣṭa*); and "pleasure" (*sukha*) applies to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Since it would thus apply to all three natures, its essence [would be inconsistent].

This refers to desire (*chanda*). What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of faith? It is exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*). Furthermore, the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and its origin (*samudaya-satya*) are the objects of faith (*ālambana*).
If one were to claim that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of faith is "delight" (*abhirati*), then who would delight in these two truths of suffering and origin?

Therefore, it is said: furthermore, suffering and origin should not be the objects of faith. This refutes the position of certain Mahāyāna teachers who maintain that the characteristic of faith is "conformity" (*anuloma*).

[The opponent] asks: "If the three natures (trisvabhāva) all pertain [to this state], why is it designated as exclusively wholesome? Furthermore, according to the meaning of 'conformity' (*anukūla*), there are two distinct types:

first, conformity through conviction (*adhimukti*), which is precisely resolve; second, conformity through inclination (*chanda*), which is precisely desire. Apart from conviction and inclination, there is no meaning of the characteristic of conformity.
Since this resolve and desire already belong to the category of 'particular objects' (*viśeṣālambana*), how can they serve as characteristics for the mental factors in a wholesome state?"
The conclusion states: From this, it should be understood that the purity of mind is faith.
What is shame (*hrī*)? It relies upon the power of oneself and the Dharma (and so forth), serving as the antidote to shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and bringing all evil conduct to rest.
Second, the explanation of the essential nature and function of the mental factor of *hrī* (moral shame). "Self" refers to one's own person; "Dharma" refers to the teaching. That is to say:

"With such a body as mine, having understood such a Dharma, how could I dare to commit various evils? Thus, its essential nature consists in revering the worthy and honoring the good, while its function is the cessation of unwholesome conduct.
This means that based on the following [text], the preceding [terms] "self" and "Dharma," as well as the meaning of "revering" and "honoring," are explained. Specifically:
Relying on one's own noble self, one takes the Dharma as supreme; one admires the virtuous and respects the good.
Regarding faults and evil deeds, one feels natural shame; through this sense of shame (*hrī*), one subdues the lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and all evils naturally cease.
What is the reliance on worldly power (*loka-vaśa*) as shame (*apatrāpya*)? It serves as the antidote to non-shame (*anapatrāpya*) and brings all evil deeds to rest.
Third, the explanation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*) of the mental factor of shame: "Worldly censure" refers to the power of the world.

To feel aversion toward those who possess evil and refuse to associate with them, and to reject evil dharmas and actions so as not to perform them—this is the essence of shame. It acts as the antidote to non-shame.
Shame (*hrī*). To cease unwholesome conduct is the function of shame. "Relying on the inferior" explains the worldly power;
the meanings of "light rejection" and "shameful embarrassment" are the same as above.

The sense of shame regarding faults and evils is the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of these two; [this extends] up to the point where "self" and "other" are defined by what is beneficial or detrimental to oneself.
This passage distinguishes that *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread of blame) have the sense of shame regarding faults and evils as their common essence.

Based on the statements in other passages, the single dharma of "shame" (*lajjā*) constitutes the two distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The Master of the Treatise restates this distinction: if the single dharma of shame constitutes the two distinct characteristics, [they are] *hrī* and *apatrāpya*.
The two dharmas should be one entity, because that sense of shame (*hrī*) is itself a single entity.
If they were a single dharma with respect to these two dharmas, then these two dharmas would necessarily be incompatible; for what applies to *hrī* would not apply to *apatrāpya*.
Regarding *hrī* (shame), it should not be [identified with] *apatrāpya* (dread of blame). These two are not mutually exclusive in the way that *vedanā* (feeling) and *saṃjñā* (perception) are;

for they both possess the meaning of "modesty. If one were to argue that *hrī* and *apatrāpya* are distinct because *hrī* depends on oneself while *apatrāpya* depends on others—the former being the power of the self and the latter being the power of the world—one might fear such a counter-argument.
To refute this, [the text] says: they should not be substantially real (*dravyasat*), because they depend upon...

Self and other are provisional and not real. Furthermore, the holy teachings state that the essence of shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*) is real; [if one holds they are merely self and other], this contradicts those teachings.

If one were to allow that shame and modesty are a single real entity arising as two distinct [mental factors], this would further contradict the treatise which states that these ten [factors] pervade all wholesome minds.
According to what is stated in the treatise (*śāstra*), among the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not universal, whereas the remaining ten are all universal.
If shame (*hrī*) and dread (*apatrāpya*) were one, the number [of wholesome factors] would be only nine; thus, it would contradict the statement in the treatise. The opponent objects:

"Veneration (*gaurava*) has the wholesome as its object, while disdain (*anādara*) has the unwholesome as its object. When they take a single object, veneration and disdain should not arise simultaneously."

Regarding the two mental states: when shame (*hrī*) arises in relation to a wholesome object and shame (*apatrāpya*) arises in relation to an unwholesome object toward the same object, these two states—shame and remorse (*kaukṛtya*)—should not arise simultaneously.

For while their capacity to cause shame is the same, and their characteristics such as reverence (*gaurava*) and modesty (*lajjā*) are likewise identical, they differ in their specific natures. Furthermore, since the faults [of the opposing states] are the same, [the two should not coexist].
"Why do you single out shame (*hrī*) and so forth for criticism? Who said that these two dharmas have different objects?"—this is the Master of the Treatise’s (the author) cross-examination.
"If not so, how [could it be]?"—this is the question posed again by the opponent. "When a wholesome mind arises... and so forth; this is the Master of the Treatise’s explanation.
This means that within the context of wholesome and unwholesome objects, whichever object one encounters, whenever there is a state of reverence, there must necessarily be a state of rejection;

thus, shame (*hrī*) and embarrassment (*apatrāpya*) arise together. Since the focal object (*ālambana*) is no different, does this not accord with what was stated previously—that these two share the common characteristic of feeling ashamed of faults and evils?
"Your adherence to the lower [position]"—this rebukes and refutes the previous adherence to the identity of the essence of shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*).

By what reasoning can you block the difficulty previously cited regarding the ten universal wholesome mental factors? "However, the Holy Teaching says 'lower'"—this explains the meaning of "self" and "other.
Alternatively, "or rather, 'lower'"—it further takes the wholesome and unwholesome as "other," and benefit and harm as "self."
The phrase "non-attachment and so forth" includes non-hatred and non-delusion, [extending] to having the function of counteracting delusion and performing wholesome deeds.
This is a general explanation of the verse's statement: the three types of wholesome roots, beginning with non-attachment, and the three unwholesome roots, namely greed, hatred, and delusion.
Because non-greed and so forth counteract greed and so forth, the first section—beginning with "What is [non-greed]?"—explains the essence, nature, and function of non-greed.

"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three types of existence: namely, existence in the desire realm (*kāma-bhava*), existence in the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*), and existence in the formless realm (*ārūpya-bhava*).

These are the results; the "factors of existence" (*bhavāṅga*) are the causes. Within the three realms, being entirely free from greedy attachment toward both cause and result constitutes the nature of non-greed. Itself...

Its nature is non-attachment (*alobha*). It counteracts craving and attachment; its constant engagement in wholesome deeds constitutes its function as non-attachment. Next, regarding the passage "How so...

and below, there are five explanations concerning the essential nature and function of non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Suffering refers to the Truth of Suffering, which is the fruit. The instruments of suffering refer to the cause, which is the Truth of Origination.
To be free from hatred toward both the Truths of Suffering and Origination constitutes the nature of non-hatred; thus, its intrinsic nature is the absence of hatred.

It serves as the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and constantly performs wholesome deeds for the purpose of non-ill-will. Regarding the passage "when a wholesome mind arises," the following explains the two preceding types [of minds].

There is the sense of their arising together. As for the phrase "regarding existence and so forth," this refers to both existence (*bhava*) and the instruments of existence, as well as suffering (*duḥkha*) and the instruments of suffering;

therefore, it says "without attachment and without ill-will. As for the statement "established by contemplating existence and so forth," this refers to contemplating solely by means of wisdom (*jñāna*), rather than focusing exclusively on the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

When non-attachment is present, non-hatred must necessarily be present; therefore, as with the two dharmas of shame (*hrī*) and dread-of-blame (*apatrāpya*) mentioned previously, these are observed only in relation to what is wholesome or unwholesome and do not reside in the objective field itself, because both are omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
Below the phrase "How then... (the text) provides a sixfold explanation of the essence, nature, and function of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the state of being confused and obscured regarding phenomena and principles. What is now called "non-delusion" is the absence of this ignorance.

It is capable of clear understanding and thus has non-delusion as its nature. Its intrinsic nature is non-delusion; it counteracts ignorance and constantly performs wholesome deeds, serving as the function of non-delusion.
According to one interpretation, non-delusion has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its nature. [This continues until: "From this, non-delusion must necessarily exist as a distinct entity."

The first interpretation is one-sided and dogmatic. It claims that this non-delusion is a provisional designation based upon wisdom (*prajñā*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* cites scriptural evidence for this:

"Report" refers to what is heard; "teaching" refers to what is contemplated; "realization" refers to what is cultivated; and "knowledge" is itself wisdom. These are termed the "capable of hearing," the "capable of contemplating," and so forth.

Because it is capable of cultivation, it is said that, in order, all of these have the nature of *pratisaṃkhyāna-prajñā* (discriminative wisdom). Question: Since this is already wisdom (*prajñā*), why is it called "non-delusion" (*amoha*)? Answer:

Although this is indeed wisdom, within the category of wholesome factors (*kuśala-pakṣa*), it belongs to the three wholesome roots (*trīṇi kuśalamūlāni*). Because its functional capacity (*vṛtti*) is superior, non-delusion is exclusively wholesome.

Wisdom, however, extends to both the wholesome and the defiled (*kliṣṭa*). Just as afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are exclusively of a defiled nature, so too [is non-delusion exclusively wholesome]. Therefore, furthermore...
A separate opening. Next, the correct principle of the meaning: namely, that this non-delusion (*amoha*) has a distinct intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The Master himself establishes the correct principle regarding what is pervasive and what is not pervasive; this should be understood according to the text.

In the section on "Determination," it is cited as proof that pliancy does not pervade other states, but exists only in the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*). The interpretation [presented] below is incorrect; namely:

Through the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the application of effort (*prayoga*), one attains the stage of concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*); there is a subtle degree of flexibility and pliancy, which is the meaning of *praśrabdhi*.
Furthermore, citing the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is proven that this [state of] *praśrabdhi* exists within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

There is an interpretation that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) exists only in meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*). [This view is incorrect because] it is present throughout all three stages, including those with vitarka and vicāra.
This [latter] interpretation is the correct principle. That is to say, this pliancy exists only in the stages of meditative concentration and possesses the sense of "nourishment" (*upastambha*).

Furthermore, citing a scriptural statement, [the author] refutes the attachment that pliancy also exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). By stating "all lower [stages]," he explains the meaning within the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section).

Regarding the three stages beginning with "with vitarka and vicāra": this refers to the first dhyāna. When one has not yet entered meditative absorption, it is called the stage with vitarka and vicāra;

when one has already entered meditative absorption, it is called the stage without vitarka and with only vicāra. From the second dhyāna upward, there are seven stages collectively termed the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
When the treatise speaks of "all stages," it refers exclusively to those with vitarka and vicāra.

[This applies to] the three [higher] stages. Because the Stage of Mixed Dwelling in the Five Destinies (*pañcagati-saṃsṛṣṭā bhūmi*) is not mentioned, we know that there is no pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
These eleven types have already been explained in detail [above], because pliancy must necessarily accompany the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

38.
