Regarding the presence or absence [of factors] according to their respective stages within the gateway of the eight consciousnesses: the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are absent during the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), yet both are present within the stage of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
As for the sixth consciousness, if it is in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-avasthā*), all eleven [factors] are present;

otherwise, it lacks *praśrabdhi* (pliancy). One interpretation holds that it is incorrect to say the five sensory consciousnesses lack *praśrabdhi*; another interpretation maintains that they do possess *praśrabdhi*.
Regarding the principle: "Virtue induced by meditative concentration" refers to the fact that when the five consciousnesses are induced by a concentrated mind, they too become harmonious and refined;
furthermore, within the state of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), being associated with wisdom, there must necessarily be pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
Regarding these eleven wholesome [factors], with which feelings (*vedanā*) are they associated? (Up to: The analysis according to other categories should be considered as appropriate.
Regarding the four or five doors of feeling: "These wholesome [factors] below" is the question. In the answer, it is said that the ten wholesome factors are associated with the five feelings.
The single factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) eliminates the feelings of sorrow and suffering, because those [feelings] involve oppression and lack pliancy.

This belongs to the fifth category below, the "Specific Objects" (*viṣayaviśeṣa*). Faith and the others are exclusively wholesome in nature, whereas the specific objects are common to both the wholesome and the defiled, as they possess a wholesome nature.

This is also not contradictory. The statement that "eleven are exclusively wholesome" refers to the sixth gate, the classification by the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); among the three natures, these are exclusively of the wholesome nature.
The statement that "pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not in the desire realm, while the others pervade all three realms" refers to the seventh gate, the classification by the three realms;
pliancy alone does not exist in the desire realm, whereas the other ten wholesome factors pervade all three realms. All are [further classified] as the three types of training (*śaikṣa*, etc.).

This is the eighth section on the Three Trainings (*tri-śikṣā*): first, those in training (*śaikṣa*); second, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); third, neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*).

All eleven [categories] possess these, because they share the same nature of wholesomeness (*kuśala*). This concludes the ninth section on Seeing and Cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā*), which states that the eleven wholesome factors are not abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), but are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding the "six faculties" (*ṣad-indriya*), these refer to the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

[This refers to] the faculties (*indriya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* states that the six faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). This is because the two faculties—“one who has already known” (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and “one who possesses complete knowledge” (*ājñendriya*)—are not subject to abandonment.

Regarding the section on "other categories," the concluding summary clarifies that the distinctions of the other categories should be understood according to reason; the specific terminology is not repeated here.

△ The three divisions belonging to the various gates are concluded. This concludes the two preceding wholesome states. Below, the states of the three faculties and the afflictions are divided into three parts.
First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the posing of the question:
Having thus explained the mental factors of the wholesome states, what are the characteristics of the mental factors of the afflictions?
Afflictions are like a dense forest; thus, there is the teaching of roots and branches. They are established as two categories of afflictions: the root and the derivative.
Because the roots exist, the branches and leaves grow accordingly. There are six kinds of roots, which may further be expanded into ten.
There are twenty [mental factors] in total, which are further divided into three groups. Regarding the six faculties (*indriya*): first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, pride;

fifth, doubt—these are called the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mūḍha-āsrava*). The sixth is evil view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). If this one is expanded, there are another five names: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and fifth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). These...

These are called the five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*). Those previously mentioned are called "dull" because, regarding their objects of perception (*ālambana*), they are stubborn, ignorant, and lack decisiveness.

These are called "sharp" because, regarding their objects of perception, they are decisive and severing. All ten are called "afflictions" (*paryavasthāna*) because they are employed by the sovereign mind-king;
thus they are named "mental concomitants" (*caitta*). The three divisions of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) will be explained in the following text. Above.
The roots and their concomitants disturb the King of the Mind (cittarāja), rendering it lack of mastery; therefore, they receive the name "afflictions" (*kleśa*).

To explain extensively the characteristics (*ākāra*) of these afflictions, the preceding section on the wholesome state has already been concluded. Furthermore, one asks: what are the characteristics of the mental factors (*caitta*) that constitute affliction?
△ First, the preceding summary and the posing of the question are concluded. Below, the second section provides a general answer by citing a verse.
The verse states: "The afflictions are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views.
This verse enumerates the six types of root afflictions as a general response to the intent of the question. In the treatise, each of these is explained individually.
Meaning. △ Second, the general response by citing the verse is concluded. Below, the third section explains the intent of the verse and is divided into two parts.
First, the formal explanation of the mental factors (*caitasika*) is divided into two parts. First, the five dull afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).

The Treatise says: These six natures, beginning with greed, are the roots because they are able to summon the defiled phenomena of future births. The Treatise says: "Below" [this section] provides a general explanation of the six types of mental factors;

they collectively receive the name "defilements" (*kleśa*) because they all share the meaning of being fundamental. Regarding the first [point], "How is it? and so forth, this explains the essential nature and functional activity of greed. As for the phrase "possessing the means of existence":

*kleśo mūlam bhavasya hi |* *tasmāt teṣāṃ vyavasthānaṃ yathāvad upavarṇyate ||* *lobho dveṣaś ca mohaś ca ete trayaḥ kleśā ucyante |* *mūla-hetutvād eṣām eva pṛthagvyavasthānam ||* *te punar lobhādayaḥ ṣaḍvidhāḥ svabhāvataḥ karmaṇaś ca nirdeśyāḥ |* *tatra lobhasya tāvat svabhāvo 'bhiṣvaṅga-lakṣaṇaḥ |* *karma tu saṃsāra-pratisaṃdhāna-hetur bhavati ||* The Treatise says: "Possessing the means of existence" refers to those who possess the instruments for the production of further existence.

The state of the wholesome has already been explained. As for the statement, "Because the aggregates of clinging arise through the power of craving," this explains the meaning of the aforementioned suffering of birth.
Craving is precisely *rāga* (greed); the aggregates of clinging are suffering. Because greed exists, its function is to produce suffering. Furthermore, as for the "aggregates of clinging":
Because one grasps at the five aggregates as a self, the following section beginning with "How so... explains the essential nature and function of hatred (*dveṣa*).
Suffering and the instruments of suffering have already been explained in the section on the wholesome state. "Bodily and mental feverish affliction" explains lack of peace and security.

"Arising of various unwholesome karmas" explains the basis for misconduct (*duścarita*). The subsequent section beginning with "How so... explains the essential nature and function of delusion (*moha*). Delusion is...

Ignorance (*avidyā*) that does not arise in dependence upon an object is called "solitary ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). Its primary characteristic is delusion regarding the principles of the truths (*satya*), which is the meaning of "discriminative.

That which arises in dependence upon an object is called "associated ignorance" (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*); its primary characteristic is spontaneous delusion regarding phenomena, which is the meaning of "innate.

Because it is characterized by the darkness of delusion, it is termed "delusion" (*moha*). This explains, from below, the basis for the aforementioned defilements (*saṃkleśa*), namely doubt (*vicikitsā*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The root afflictions and secondary afflictions collectively manifest both innate and discriminative [afflictions].
All defiled phenomena depend upon ignorance, because this ignorance pervades all defiled states.
What is pride (*māna*)? It is relying upon oneself in relation to others... [omitted] ...from which the various types of pride arise; thus there is no fault.

This explains the mental factor of pride (*māna-cetasika*), its essential nature (*svabhāva*) and its function (*karma*). That is to say, if one is inferior... [omitted] ...it explains that for those who give rise to suffering through pride, there is one who possesses pride.

Toward those who possess neither virtue nor virtue, one fails to show humility in either case. Through the mutual disparagement of self and others, karmic actions accumulate and one revolves in saṃsāra;

from this, all manner of suffering arises. As for the seven types of pride (*māna*), they are: pride of superiority (*māna*), pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*), pride (*māna*), pride of excellence (*adhimāna*), false pride (*mithyāmāna*), pride of self (*asmimāna*), and pride of meanness (*ūnamāna*). These constitute the seven kinds.

**Māna (Pride):** To consider oneself superior to those who are inferior, or equal to those who are one's equals, is termed *māna* because it accords with the object; it is pride because it consists of a lack of respect.

Although the principle [of comparison] may be similar, it involves evaluating others in relation to oneself; thus, it constitutes pride. **Adhimāna (Excessive Pride):** To consider oneself equal to those who are superior, or superior to those who are one's equals, is called *adhimāna*.
Because it adds one degree to *māna*, it becomes excessive pride. This is *mānātimāna* (pride beyond pride).
One who considers oneself superior to those who are actually superior is called *mānātimāna* (conceit exceeding conceit), as it involves adding two degrees of superiority.

One who possesses *adhimāna* (overweening conceit) considers oneself superior, equal, or even inferior to others because one falsely imagines that one has attained a progressively higher state of excellence.

One who possesses *mithyāmāna* (false conceit) falsely imagines oneself to possess virtues when one lacks them, or claims that others who possess virtues do not. One who possesses *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am") clings to a self...
Because one weighs oneself, exalts oneself, and treats others with contempt, the "inferiority pride" (ūnamāna) consists of regarding oneself as slightly inferior when others are far superior;
although the sentiment appears to be humble, it is called pride because one does not respect them. Regarding the nine types of pride:

since there are three grades for each of the three factors—self, qualities, and status—they constitute nine types. First, [pride] regarding whether the self is superior, equal, or inferior [to others]; second, [pride] regarding existence...

"I am superior," "equal," or "inferior. Regarding these three—superiority, equality, and inferiority—there is no self. "Superior" means being powerful; it refers to the thought, "I am superior to that [other].

"Equal" means being on the same level; it refers to being equal to others. "Inferior" means being base; it refers to the thought, "I am inferior to that [other]. Since the self is thus [non-existent]...

The same applies to the basis of virtue (*guṇa-adhiṣṭhāna*). "Self" refers to the self as it is grasped; "virtue" refers to the virtues that have been cultivated; and "basis" refers to the sphere of experience.
These seven types of pride, in their nine varieties, are all generally abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Below this, the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*) is summarized and clarified: it is possessed by both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*) at all times, and must not fail to be examined. However, regarding...

Regarding the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), there is likewise no fault in its arising. Since the Bodhisattva vehicle takes the benefit of sentient beings as its primary aim, the arising of respect or pride is necessarily conditioned by purposeful action;

because it functions with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) according to what is appropriate for others, it does not constitute a fault. As for the category of pride (*māna*): [...]* *Note: The original text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, specifically concerning the section on the "Perfections" (pāramitās), where the specific context of "pride" is discussed in relation to the bodhisattva's skillful means.*
Regarding the existence or non-existence of my virtuous qualities, as well as their superiority, equality, or inferiority, there are three types of views similar to the preceding seven:

first, regarding superiority, equality, or inferiority, one respectively conceives of oneself as superior, equal, or inferior; second, regarding superiority, equality, or inferiority, one respectively conceives that [the self] possesses superiority, equality, or inferiority.

Third, regarding those who are superior, equal, or inferior, one respectively conceives that there is no superiority, equality, or inferiority. Now, among these, one who conceives of themselves as "I" [in relation to others] conceives themselves as superior to the superior;
this is a type of *mānātimāna* (conceit beyond pride). One who conceives themselves as equal to the superior is a type of *atimāna* (excessive pride).

One who conceives themselves as inferior to the superior is a type of *māna* (pride) alone. These arise from conceiving oneself in relation to another who is superior. One who conceives themselves as superior to an equal is *atimāna*.
Regarding those who are equal, conceiving oneself as equal is a type of simple pride (*māna*). Regarding those who are equal, conceiving oneself as inferior is a type of simple pride;
this arises from conceiving oneself as equal to others who are equal. Regarding those who are inferior, conceiving oneself as superior is a type of simple pride.

Regarding those who are inferior, conceiving oneself as equal, and regarding those who are inferior, conceiving oneself as inferior—both are types of simple pride; these arise from conceiving oneself as superior to others who are inferior. These two conceptions exist.

One who, regarding what is superior, conceives it to be superior, belongs to the class of *māna* (pride) and *atimāna* (excessive pride). One who, regarding what is superior, conceives it to be equal, belongs to the class of *adhimāna* (overweening pride).

One who, regarding what is superior, conceives it to be inferior, belongs to the class of simple *māna*. This [latter] arises from conceiving oneself as superior to that which is actually superior. One who, regarding what is equal, conceives it to be superior...
The type of *atimāna* (conceit): regarding an equal, one conceives oneself to be equal. The type of *māna* (pride) alone: regarding an equal, one conceives oneself to be inferior;

this [conception] arises from that [equal] by conceiving oneself to be superior. The type of *māna* alone: regarding an inferior, one conceives oneself to be superior; regarding an inferior, one conceives oneself to be equal;
regarding an inferior, one conceives oneself to be inferior—all of these are types of *māna* alone. These arise from that [inferior] by conceiving oneself to be superior. Three.

Regarding "reckoning as inferior" (*hīnādhimokṣa*): reckoning oneself as inferior to one who is superior, and reckoning oneself as equal to one who is superior, both belong to the category of simple pride (*māna*).

Regarding the statement "reckoning oneself as inferior to one who is superior": since there is no one inferior, it follows that [the other] is either superior or equal; thus, there are two categories. Reckoning oneself as equal to one who is superior belongs to the category of excessive pride (*adhimāna*).

Reckoning oneself as superior to one who is superior belongs to the category of pride beyond pride (*atimāna*). This [reckoning as inferior] arises from reckoning oneself as inferior to another who is superior.

Regarding the estimation of oneself as being no superior among equals, there are two types of simple pride (*māna*): the estimation of oneself as being no equal among equals, and the estimation of oneself as being inferior among equals.

As for the term "no equal," this does not mean being superior; rather, it refers to the estimation of oneself as superior among equals, which is the type of pride known as overweening pride (*adhimāna*). Conversely, the estimation of oneself as inferior among equals [is the other type].

This is the category of *ūnamāna* (inferiority-pride). Regarding the estimation of oneself as not inferior when one is equal, there are also two types. To say "not inferior" means that one is neither superior nor equal;
to estimate oneself as superior when one is equal is the category of *atimāna* (excessive pride). To estimate oneself as equal when one is equal is the category of *māna* (pride) alone.

This [latter] arises from estimating oneself as not [inferior] in relation to others who are equal. To estimate oneself as not superior when one is inferior is the category of *ūnamāna*. To estimate oneself as not [superior] when one is inferior... [text ends].
These also consist of two types. Regarding the term "equal" (*sama*): it is neither superior nor inferior;

to conceive of the inferior as superior is the category of simple pride (*māna*), while to conceive of the inferior as inferior is the category of inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*). Regarding the term "not inferior" (*anavamana*): it is also of two types.
To conceive of the inferior as superior is the category of simple pride, while to conceive of the inferior as equal is [the category of] inferiority-pride.
Regarding the category of pride (*māna*): this consists in conceiving oneself as inferior to others while [actually] being superior.
What is doubt? It concerns the principles of the truths (*satya*). Since the meanings of *mati* and *prajñā* are not different... [the text continues].
This explains the essential nature and function of the mental factor of non-doubt (*a-vicikitsā*). Non-doubt refers to other wholesome mental factors;

because doubt exists, it acts as an obstacle to non-doubt within the category of wholesome qualities. What does it obstruct in the wholesome qualities? It means that for one who is hesitant, the wholesome does not arise.

According to one interpretation, [the Vaibhāṣikas] maintain that doubt has no substantial reality and is merely a provisional designation based upon wisdom (*prajñā*); hesitation is doubt, while discernment is [wisdom].

*Prajñā* (wisdom) refers to the discernment (*viveka*) that exists at the time of correct investigation; therefore, it is said to be its essential nature (*svabhāva*). *Vi* means "to benefit" or "to assist," signifying that which assists wisdom.

The Sanskrit term *mati* is translated as "wisdom" (*hui*) in the language of Qin; thus, it is called "discernment. This citation of the Sanskrit etymology serves to prove that wisdom is its essential nature.
The term *prajñā* is translated as "knowledge" (*zhi*), which follows the same principle.
There is an interpretation that this doubt has a distinct intrinsic nature (of its own), and therefore this doubt does not have wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.
This is the correct principle. That is to say, doubt has a real entity which prevents wisdom from reaching a decision. Furthermore, he cites a treatise as proof:
among the six fundamental [afflictions], wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is nominal and has wisdom as its essence; the remaining five—greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt—are all substantially real.

Because [the category] exists, why this partial attachment and doubt? It takes wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. The term *vyava* is appended at the end. The Master of the Treatise raises an objection by analogy: in the Sanskrit, if it were *yan*, the syllable *ya* is pronounced as *jña*;
in the language of Qin (Chinese), this means "wisdom" (*jñāna*). That is to say, if one holds that wisdom is doubt, then one might as well hold that wisdom is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As for the statement that "the category (*dhātu*) changes its meaning through the power of assistance," this conversely demonstrates that the category itself does not change in meaning.

This refers to the meaning of "cause. That is to say, by means of the assistance of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the causal nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) is transformed; the same applies to the transformation of discernment (*prajñā*) into doubt.

Therefore, this doubt does not have discernment as its essence, thereby demonstrating that discernment does not transform into doubt. △ The first section on the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-kleśa*) is concluded.
The latter two [categories] comprise five types of *kleśa* (afflictions) and five types of *drṣṭi* (views).

What is meant by "evil views" (*pāpadṛṣṭi*) regarding the principles of the various truths? [They range from] sixty-five [types] and so forth, which are subsumed under those arising through discrimination (*vikalpaja*).
This explains the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and function (*karman*) of evil views: to seek erroneously is the essence of evil views; to bring about suffering is their function.
Karma is the function of wrong views. This single wrong view is divided into five because their respective karmic functions are distinct;
they all involve inverted investigation of the principles of truth and have defiled wisdom as their nature, and are thus called the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
Therefore, while these five views are identical in their essential nature, their karmic functions are distinct. *Satkāya-dṛṣṭi* is here translated as the "view of a self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

Because one clings to the body as "self," all other views arise based on this body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for all modes of view (*dṛṣṭi-gati*).
Below, regarding the distinctions of this view, the meaning of the specific variations of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is clarified. As for the twenty phrases:
for example, calculating that "form (*rūpa*) is the self," "the self possesses form," "form belongs to the self," or "the self is within form. There are four such [assertions] for each aggregate.

The five aggregates comprise twenty phrases. Regarding the sixty-five [instances]: for example, if one reckons form (*rūpa*) as the self, then for each of the remaining four aggregates there are three types of "mine" (*mamakāra*):
namely, "my ornament," "my servant," and "my vessel. This amounts to twelve [instances].
Form is the single self, making thirteen in total. Across the five aggregates, there are thus sixty instances of "mine" and five instances of the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Together, they constitute sixty-five categories.
The two types of extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—namely, the seven theories of annihilationism and so forth—are subsumed within the category of speculative views (*vibhajyavāda*).

That is to say, these extreme views are based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); by clinging to either annihilation or permanence, one clings to annihilation or permanence for oneself and is unable to transcend [samsara].

"Detachment" (*niḥsaraṇa*) refers to the function of obstructing the practice of the conduct of renunciation. Below this, the distinctions among the views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are clarified;
that is, the sixty-two [views] of the various non-Buddhists all arise from the false conceptualizations of the distinctions among the five views. Master Qingliang stated:

"These sixty-two [views] take the view of extremes and wrong view as their essential nature. [They also include] the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)."
They take these as their retinue; because they rely on the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their foundation, they are called the various divergent paths of views.
Among them, there are those who cling to the four types of universal permanence regarding the past: first, observing the mind and its objects; second, observing the four great elements;

third, observing the eight consciousnesses; and fourth, observing the principle of the aggregates (*skandha*). They collectively reckon these to be permanent, maintaining that since the conceptualizing mind of arising and ceasing has already ceased, within the [true] principle...

Nevertheless, they establish [a state of] non-arising and non-ceasing. Those who propound a partial eternalism also have four types: first, observing the mind in relation to the arising and ceasing of sentient beings;
second, observing the environment to see whether it is subject to destruction or not; third, observing the self-mind in relation to the arising and ceasing of the body;

and fourth, observing that while the four aggregates (skandhas) perish previously, they are now eternal. Each of these calculates one part as eternal and one part as impermanent, and further calculates the subsequent...
Regarding the "sixteen views with perception": these consist of four permutations—such as "form is the self"—each of which is combined with the four aggregates, resulting in sixteen aspects.
These are considered ultimate afflictions, extending even to the view that they do not mutually contact one another.

Regarding the "eight theories each for the non-percipient and the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient," this means there are eight theories concerning the non-percipient state, which calculate that there is no perception after death; these are collectively observed across the four [permutations].
The aggregates (*skandha*): the present cause perishes, and the future fruit ceases. Because cause and effect are discussed in conjunction, there are eight characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding those who maintain the "eightfold neither-existence-nor-non-existence" discourse: within form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and perception (*saṃjñā*), one sees both existence and non-existence; in the sphere of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), one contemplates both non-existence and not-non-existence.

When these four aggregates are explained together, each possesses both existence and non-existence, and each possesses both non-existence and not-non-existence; this is called the "eightfold coexistence."

No. Regarding the seven types of annihilationism: the two realms of humans and devas within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) taken as a single location—observing these seven locations, one calculates that they are extinguished before one's eyes and no longer exist after death; this is what constitutes annihilationism.
The three types of wrong view refer to the denial of cause and effect, function, and real entities (up to) all such categories as these, which are all subsumed under wrong view.
That is to say, wrong view consists of the repudiation of cause and effect, as well as all other erroneous attachments outside of the four [wrong] views; this is the meaning.

Just as with the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), because its name and meaning are all-encompassing, whatever other conditions are not included elsewhere are all subsumed by this condition. This is because...

This illustrates the four views. Those not included [in these four] are all subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Below this, it clarifies the distinctions among wrong views. Regarding the two types of "no cause" (*ahetuka*):
first, observing that eighty thousand *kalpas* ago there was no cause yet things existed of themselves, this constitutes the "original no-cause.

Second, observing that the nature of things within a *kalpa* does not undergo change or transformation, this constitutes the "subsequent no-cause. Regarding the four views such as "having an end" (*antavān*) and so forth: first, one observes the three periods of time by means of the present...
First, regarding existence as finite: the past and future are infinite. Second, regarding observation through seeing and hearing:
that which is seen and heard is finite, while that which is not seen or heard is infinite. Third, regarding observation through universal knowledge: that knowledge which is boundless is infinite.
Their realm has extremes and has limits. They contemplate the arising and ceasing within a single body;
taking this single body as finite, they regard arising and ceasing as infinite. Regarding those who evade with "neither-dying-nor-chaos," there are also four types.

First, they contemplate the source of transformation, which is divided into eight meanings: namely, transformation, permanence, arising, ceasing, increase, decrease, existence, and non-existence. Therefore, they answer the person before them as follows:

1. Regarding the view that both arising and ceasing exist, he answers with the single character "no" (wu). 2. Regarding the view that neither arising nor ceasing exists, he answers with the single character "yes" (yi).
3. Regarding the view that both exist, he answers the former person by saying: "That which is 'also existing' is precisely 'also non-existing';
within 'also non-existence,' it is not 'also existing. Thus, all such sophistry and confusion cannot be subjected to further interrogation; this reveals [the truth].
This is an erroneous answer. One may attain birth in the Heaven of the Deathless (*Amara*). As for the five [types of] nirvāṇa: they consist of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas.

Calculating these five locations as secure and peaceful, they are established as nirvāṇa as a supreme, pure refuge. Alternatively, one may calculate "lower mastery" (*adhaḥ-vaśitva*) to refer to the Peak of the Desire Realm (*bhavāgra*).
Regarding the World-Lords Śakra and Brahmā: Śakra is Śakradevendra, the Lord of the Heaven of the Desire Realm; Brahmā is...
Mahābrahmā is the lord of the great trichiliocosm; therefore, he is collectively designated as the "Lord of the World.
He reckons that this deity, as well as other categories of things, are substantial, eternal, and unchanging. Alternatively, he reckons that [deities] such as Īśvara are the cause of all things.

This is precisely reckoning that [the self] is real and eternal, capable of producing all phenomena. Alternatively, there are those who recklessly calculate various false liberations and falsely grasp them as the fruit;
or those who take what is not the Path to be the Path and falsely grasp it as the cause. All such cases as these [are included].
All are subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the four types of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): it is said that [adherence] toward the various views and the aggregates upon which they depend constitutes wrong view, and is not subsumed under the other two types of adherence (*parāmarśa*).
As for "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), it means taking up the views of others as one's own views. These "various views" refer to the three preceding views; that is to say, this—

The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in clinging to those three views, as well as the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) which serve as their basis, and regarding them all as supreme, capable of attaining and realizing pure *nirvāṇa*.
Because of this clinging, each [view] contends with the others; therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as the basis for all strife and contention.
As for the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it consists in adopting the practices of others and taking them to be one’s own precepts. All...
The observation is as before. Because of this precept, all non-Buddhists undertake ascetic practices such as plucking out their hair or smearing themselves with ashes;

therefore, it is said that its function is to serve as a basis for fruitless exertion and suffering. However, the following explains the distinctions in the meanings held by other schools. Specifically, regarding the adherence to what is supreme:
to regard what is not a result as a result is called the "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). To adhere to [a path] as being able to bring about purification...

This refers to regarding what is not a cause as a cause, which is termed *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances). The Master of the Treatise explains that this is an elliptical statement (*saṃkṣepokti*), or a "door of conformity" (*anuvartanamukha*).
That is to say, when stating "the most excellent," it elliptically implies "purity"; and when stating "purity," it elliptically implies "the most excellent."

In reality, both meanings of cause and effect are fully present. "Otherwise" (below) means that if it were not a case of abbreviated inclusion, and one were to separately calculate [them] as cause and effect, this should be called a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) rather than being subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). This is because one who holds a false view...
Because cause and effect are distinct. △ Second, the five views and five afflictions are concluded. Together with the above, the primary explanation of the mental factors (cetasika) is finished.
Below, the [factors] are categorized according to various gates, comprising ten chapters.
Thus, among these ten afflictions—both general and specific—they arise only after one has personally examined and reflected upon them.

First is the gate of innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) [afflictions]. Regarding "general and specific": "general" refers to the six root afflictions, while "specific" opens those into ten afflictions, because one wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is divided into five.
As for the six that are both innate and conceptual, they are: greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and... [and so forth].

Delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—these are explained as being "innate" (*sahaja*) when they arise spontaneously, and "conceptual" (*vikalpita*) when they arise through deliberation.

Since both meanings are present, it is said that they "arise together. Regarding doubt and the latter three views, these consist of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*), and the [view of] self-identity;
thus, they constitute the three views. These four exist only as conceptual and lack the quality of being innate. Bad friends and false teachings are external conditions. From oneself...
Careful reflection and investigation [reveal] that internal causes are primary; for it is only through the combination of internal causes and external conditions that [phenomena] can arise.

Among the views of extreme adherence (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), those that are innate (*sahaja*)—up to and including [the view that the self is eternal]—all give rise to terror and fear, apprehending that the self will be annihilated.

This interpretation is not correct. It is said that innate (*sahaja*) extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) consist solely of the view of non-existence (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), whereas the speculative (*vikalpita*) view of permanence lacks the quality of being innate.
The passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi* cited as proof—"Which extreme views are innate?"—is the question posed by that treatise.

The response, "Those subsumed under the view of non-existence," is the answer provided by that same treatise. This citation is used to prove that the innate [extreme view] consists exclusively of the view of non-existence.
[The text] says: "Seeing. Regarding the 'learning of the present realization' (*śaikṣābhisamaya*) below, it is extended to show that the innate [afflictions] are exclusively views of annihilation.

As for the 'learning of the present realization,' this refers to the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*). Therein, there are only innate afflictions without conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Now, where is this 'I' and 'mine'?"
This demonstrates that it is a view of annihilationism. Even among birds and beasts, this [view] arises only as innate (*sahaja*) and not through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
since they all fear the annihilation of the self, this also proves that the innate [view] is exclusively the view of annihilationism.

There is an interpretation that this treatise explains [the view of permanence] based on coarse characteristics, stating that it is "either innate (*sahaja*) or conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*).
This is the correct principle. That is to say, this innate [view] also commonly refers to what is generally observed.

Furthermore, birds and beasts are cited as evidence for innate eternalism: they build nests to dwell in and stockpile grain in burrows, intending to preserve them permanently. Is this not indeed innate?
Birth also possesses the view of eternalism. Furthermore, citing various treatises, it is proven that both innate and conceptual [views] equally grasp at annihilationism and eternalism.
Why then do you maintain that the innate [view] is subsumed solely under the view of annihilationism?
Regarding these ten afflictions, which ones are associated with how many others? (Up to: There is no fault in [stating that] greed is associated with the five views.
Second, the section on mutual association is divided into six parts. The first part distinguishes the associations of greed with the various [afflictions].
[This discussion] excludes delusion, which is treated in the final sixth section. Regarding the two objects of love and hatred, they must necessarily not be the same; this explains greed and...
Hatred (*dveṣa*) does not arise simultaneously [with greed]. Since "love" (*anunaya*) explains greed and "aversion" (*pratigha*) explains hatred, there is no simultaneous arising.

Regarding the lack of decisiveness toward an object, the absence of defiled attachment explains both greed and doubt; they do not arise together. Lack of decisiveness explains doubt, while greed itself is defilement.

Alternatively, although there is the sense of being associated (*saṃprayukta*), there is also the sense of being dissociated (*viprayukta*). That which is beloved is greed; it is intimacy toward the object. That which is despised... [is hatred].

Pride (*māna*) is distant from its object because that object is not unitary; therefore, it is said not to arise simultaneously [with other afflictions]. Greed (*lobha*) is directed toward what is defiled, whereas pride is directed toward what is relied upon;
since both are proximate to their respective objects, they are said to attain association (*saṃprayoga*). As for the five views and craving, they share the same objects as greed;
therefore, there is no fault in greed being associated with the five views.
Hatred (*dveṣa*) and pride (*māna*), as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*), may arise together; [this is] as explained in sequence, where hatred either exists or does not exist.

Regarding the second point, the examination of hatred in relation to its associated factors—with the exception of greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*)—there is also the sense that they do not necessarily arise together.
This is because the object of hatred is distant, whereas the object of pride is intimate; therefore, it is said that hatred and pride are not mutually concomitant.
Pride arises toward those one looks down upon; hatred arises toward those one dislikes. Since these two objects are equally remote [from the mind], they can arise simultaneously.
At the initial stage of doubt, one is hesitant and has not yet come to dislike the object; therefore, it is said that there is no possibility of hatred and doubt arising together.

However, when doubt persists without resolution, hatred then gives rise to indignation; thus, it is said that hatred and doubt can be associated. Conversely, because doubt is conducive to non-hatred, it is said that they are not associated.

Doubt, opposition, and resentment arise together; therefore, it is said that they likewise function accordingly. The two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) involve attachment and lack the quality of hatred toward others;

thus, they are not associated with hatred (*dveṣa*). Regarding "this [hatred] and the three views": the word "this" refers to hatred, while the "three views" refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Below the section on "those who delight in existence," the view of extremes—the eternalist view—is explained as not arising together with hatred.

Regarding the phrase "in the presence of suffering," this explains the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). It is associated with hatred (*dveṣa*). The view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is the reverse of this;

regarding the mention of the presence or absence of hatred, it refers to the reversal between the aggregates of suffering and pleasure. The arising of the view of annihilation from the aggregate of suffering is not associated with hatred.

The arising of the view of annihilation from the aggregate of pleasure occurs together with hatred. The arising of the view of extremes—namely, eternalism and annihilationism—necessarily depends upon the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Therefore, [it is said] "the body."

[The text] observes that the shadow [of the meaning] is abbreviated and not explicitly stated. Regarding "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and below, it explains wrong view and hatred (*dveṣa*). When one denies or slanders an evil thing—whether it exists or does not exist—that is dissociated from hatred.
When one denies or slanders a good thing, it arises concomitantly with hatred.
Pride is fixed toward its object, whereas doubt is not; this also applies to a portion of the view of self and the view of extremes.
Third, regarding the association of pride with other mental factors: excluding greed, hatred, and delusion, pride is fixed toward its object because it is an unshakable state of contempt;
doubt is not so, as it wavers and fluctuates, and thus they are not associated. The five views involve grasping at their objects.

It does not shift. Therefore, it successively associates with pride (*māna*). However, it does not arise simultaneously with the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), because when one clings to the self as being annihilated, pride lacks its characteristic of haughty reliance.

Regarding the statement that "pride shares a portion with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*")—annihilation arises from the view of a self-identity and is thus called a "portion" of the view of a self-identity.

Regarding the statement that "pride shares a portion with false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*)": both [the view of a self-identity and false view] involve the absence of causes, and so forth; thus, they are false views.
That which is comprised by views includes a portion of false view; therefore, the body [view] and false view each have a portion that does not coexist with pride.
All others arise together.
Because doubt is characterized by a lack of definitive resolution and is thus contrary to views, doubt and views certainly do not arise together.

The fourth, doubt (*vicikitsā*), is associated only with the five views (*dṛṣṭi*). Excluding the previously mentioned greed, hatred, delusion, and pride, it is said here that they do not arise together because doubt lacks definitive resolution, whereas views do not involve hesitation; thus, their association is naturally impossible.
The five views do not correspond with one another; this is because there cannot be multiple instances of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind.

Regarding the five views, they do not correspond with their own kind, nor with the aforementioned [afflictions] of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. This is what is meant by "non-correspondence."
The five views have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said that there is no single moment of mind in which multiple instances of wisdom coexist.
Delusion (*moha*), however, is invariably associated with all nine types [of afflictions], because the arising of all defilements necessarily depends upon delusion.
Sixth, regarding the explanation that delusion (*moha*) and greed (*lobha*), etc., are all associated [with one another]:

because this ignorance (*avidyā*) pervades all defiled states, these ten afflictions are associated with which consciousnesses? ... up to: because pride (*māna*), etc., arise through deliberation (*tulanā*).

38. The Section on the Gates of the Consciousnesses. The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) lacks [the secondary afflictions] because it is pure and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); since it is neither wholesome nor defiled, these do not exist there. The manas possesses four:
greed, delusion, pride, and views, because it is constantly associated with them. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses all ten, because it lacks no distinction.

The five sensory consciousnesses possess only three; for those [three], namely greed, hatred, and delusion, are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). Question: Why do the five sensory consciousnesses lack pride and the others?
Answer: Because pride (*māna*) and so forth arise from weighing (*tulana*) and the like. Weighing and the like are equivalent to deliberation (*vimarśa*).

Pride and so forth arise from investigation (*parīkṣā*); that is, pride arises from weighing, doubt (*vicikitsā*) arises from deliberation, and the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) arise from investigation.
Therefore, those [states of] pride, doubt, and the five views are conceptual (*savikalpa*) and do not coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

With which feelings (*vedanā*) are these ten afflictions (*kleśa*) associated? [This section] up to the point where it says "hatred (*dveṣa*) is accompanied by joy and pleasure when encountering favorable objects" consists of five sections concerning the four or five doors of feeling.

First, it distinguishes how the three roots (*mūla*) are associated with the five feelings, without differentiating between those that are innate (*sahaja*) and those that are conceptual (*vikalpika*), because they are associated with both.
Question: Since greed (*lobha*) coexists with desire (*kāma*), how can it be associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*)? Hatred (*dveṣa*) is always characterized by aversion.

[Question: How can hatred (*dveṣa*) be associated with joy (*prīti*) and pleasure (*sukha*)? [Answer: Greed (*lobha*), when encountering adverse conditions, results in sorrow and suffering; hatred, when meeting favorable objects, results in joy and pleasure.
According to one interpretation, both innate (*sahaja*) and intellectually acquired (*vikalpita*) pride (*māna*) must be intellectually acquired to be able to give rise to those [afflictions].

Second, the analysis of pride (*māna*) shows that it is associated with the five feelings (*vedanā*). According to the first interpretation, suffering (*duḥkha*) is excluded; however, this does not yet fully capture the principle regarding innate pride (*sahaja-māna*). Question:

Since pride excludes suffering and its nature is one of loftiness (*abhyunnati*), how can it be associated with grief (*daurmanasya*)? Answer: It relies upon the inferior aggregates (*skandha*) characterized by suffering.

Because it is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*), the latter meaning is logically correct. That is to say, co-nascent pride (*sahaja-māna*) also arises together with suffering; since the mind already possesses suffering, [pride] must be associated with it.

Furthermore, discriminative pride (*vikalpa-māna*) does not exist in the purely miserable realms (*ekānta-duḥkha-gati*). This indicates that [pride] is associated with mixed sensations (*miśra-vedanā*) as well as suffering.

That is to say, in places of pure suffering, there is no instruction from false teachers, and thus discriminative [pride] does not exist of its own accord. However, in those purely miserable states, it is only...

It belongs to that which is co-nascent (*sahaja*). Therefore, one does not further create karma that leads to the evil destinies (*apāya*), because the volition (*cetanā*) capable of creating such karma arises solely from the discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
thus it is said that it must arise through discrimination, as it is able to incite that [karma].
It is held that the latter three views may be associated with four feelings (up to the point where they can be associated with the feeling of sorrow).

Third, regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the two types of grasping (*parāmarśa*), as well as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): these are associated with four feelings, excluding only the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

Question: Since doubt is accompanied by desire (*kāma*), it should not have sorrow or suffering; why then is only the feeling of suffering excluded? Answer: Desire and doubt lack suffering and so forth; they are also associated with joy (*prīti*).

Because they are associated with sensation (*vedanā*), one wavers and cannot reach a decision; through this process, anxiety arises. Therefore, [the sūtra] excludes only suffering (*duḥkha*). Furthermore, it is asked:

"Since the two types of grasping (*upādāna*) are clung to as supreme and pure, how could there be anxiety? Hence, the answer states: "The two types of grasping, etc. (referring to the fact that they are associated with the three sensations).
There is an interpretation that the innate views of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—up to what was previously stated regarding the rest—is based on the actual meaning.

This explains that the two views of self and extremes are associated with the five feelings; the first interpretation is not correct. That is to say, the view of self and the view of extremes [are as follows].

If it is co-nascent (*sahaja*), it is associated only with joy, pleasure, and equanimity; it differs from the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) which are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and do not admit the feeling of joy.
If it is conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*), it may be associated with four feelings, excluding only painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*). Question:

Since painful feeling has already been excluded, why is it also associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*)? Answer: For one who clings to the aggregates associated with suffering as "self" (*ātman*) or "mine" (*ātmīya*), [the mind] interprets the body...

The view associated with sorrow is the view of eternalism; the view of annihilationism is its opposite. Regarding "associated with sorrow," this explains that the extreme views (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) are accompanied by sorrow:

namely, one feels sorrow toward the aggregate of suffering when it is viewed as eternal, and likewise feels sorrow toward the aggregate of pleasure when it is viewed as annihilated. Thus, "its opposite" refers to the reversal of the aggregates of suffering and pleasure.

According to the correct principle of the latter meaning, both the view of self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes, if they are innate (*sahaja*), are also associated with the sensation of suffering.

“Both” (俱) clarifies that this refers specifically to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Excluding only the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), the phrase “purely experiencing the lower [realms]” explains innate view (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*), because in places of pure suffering, only innate [afflictions] exist.
He further cites a treatise to prove this. The rest is as explained below, concluding the actual meaning of the preceding section.

Regarding the coarse characteristics (*sthūla-nimitta*), greed, pride, and the four views (up to the remaining [afflictions]) arise together with the various feelings; this should be understood according to the principle.

These five groups and ten afflictions are correlated with the five feelings by assigning them according to their coarse characteristics; this is precisely the interpretation established in the aforementioned treatise.
Furthermore, regarding the intent behind the questions posed in the commentary: because they follow along with worldly transmigration, they are called "coarse characteristics.

As for greed, pride, and the four views—the four views consist of the two grasps of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). These six afflictions are associated with the three feelings of pleasure, joy, and equanimity, as they lack sorrow and suffering.
Hatred arises only in association with the three feelings of suffering, sorrow, and equanimity, as it lacks joy and pleasure. Ignorance is associated with all five feelings.
[They] are associated [with them]. Wrong view and doubt are associated with four [feelings], excluding suffering. The above is explained according to their coarse characteristics.

Greed and delusion are associated with the lower [feelings]. This explains the realms and stages through which the pleasant feeling associated with afflictions passes. Because greed and delusion are both innate to pleasure, they pervade the four lower stages:
the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), specifically the stage of the five destinies in mixed habitation, and the first three dhyānas of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).

It belongs to four stages. This is because, among the nine stages, four are situated in the lower levels. It does not extend to the higher stages because there is no pleasure (*sukha*) in those higher levels.
Regarding the "remaining seven" which possess pleasure: the five views, pride, and doubt are called the remaining seven.
Anger (*dveṣa*) is not mentioned because anger is devoid of pleasure. Excluding the desire realm, it extends through the three [upper] dhyānas, as analyzed below.

It arises with pleasure (*sukha*). This is because it does not exist in the lowest stage (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, regarding the mental factor of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and independent ignorance (*avidyā*), in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are associated only with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
It should be understood accordingly that other afflictions (*kleśa*) arise together with the remaining sensations in their respective realms and stages.

How many of these [afflictions] are mutually associated with the object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyataviśeṣa*)? Up to: "Because views are not distinct from wisdom when they coexist with it.

Regarding the five object-specific factors—namely, the four beginning with greed—they are all associated with the five object-specific factors. Question: How can afflictions possess concentration (*samādhi*)? Answer:
Because they all possess concentration when focused one-pointedly on an object. As for doubt and the five views, each may be associated with four [object-specific factors].

Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is characterized by excessive hesitation; therefore, it lacks resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*). Since view (*dṛṣṭi*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no logical reason for it to be listed twice [as a separate affliction].
As for which nature these ten afflictions are subsumed under: although they frequently arise, they do not obstruct the wholesome.

Sixth, the gate of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): This refers to the ten afflictions (*kleśa*). Hatred (*pratigha*) is exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*). The remaining nine are also associated with both the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unwholesome; thus it is said they "pervade both.
Furthermore, the afflictions of the two realms of form and formlessness are suppressed by the power of meditative concentration and are therefore exclusively of an unspecified nature (*avyākṛta*).
If, within the desire realm, these ten types of afflictions arise through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), they are of an unwholesome nature. If...

Regarding those that are innate (*sahaja*): they are capable of inciting unwholesome conduct and are themselves of an unwholesome nature, because that which is unwholesome harms both oneself and others.

The remainder are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Those that are subtle and do not obstruct the wholesome are also indeterminate, as they neither excessively afflict oneself nor others, and thus do not incite unwholesome conduct.
One should know that the following [passage] intends to refute the positions held in the previous chapter on the five feelings.

They maintain that the innate views of self and extremes are associated only with the feelings of joy, pleasure, and equanimity, because they are not associated with the five sensory consciousnesses and are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, this [text] refutes them to demonstrate that these [views] are indeed indeterminate.
To which realms (*dhātu*) are these ten afflictions (*kleśa*) bound? (Up to: This is stated according to the majority, or as a conventional door of exposition (*anuvartana-mukha*).

Regarding the seven [afflictions] belonging to the three realms—meaning that hatred (*pratigha*) exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the other nine pervade all three realms—this is a general answer concerning their binding to a realm and their mode of abiding.

As for the principle that one who has not abandoned the defilements of a lower level cannot bring forth the afflictions of a higher stage (*bhūmi*) into manifestation: this is because the afflictions of a higher stage do not arise until the defilements of the lower level have been relinquished.
Because the meditative absorptions of the higher stages are capable of manifesting. Question: Are the afflictions of the three realms identical or distinct? Answer:
Although all afflictions pervade the three realms, they each belong to their respective realm-attachments (*dhātu-bandhana*), just as with non-hatred (*avyāpāda*) mentioned above.
Furthermore, there is no unwholesome [state]. Although the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed unwholesome, they exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

When one reaches the higher stages, they are suppressed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are consequently reclassified as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), rather than being called unwholesome.

Moreover, within the higher stages, among the five faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*), there are only joy, pleasure, and equanimity; since sorrow and suffering are absent, hatred does not arise. Question: By what means is one detached from the defilements of the lower realms?

Question: Why do the afflictions of the higher realms manifest? Answer: Because one cultivates the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of the higher realms. Question: Why is it necessary to cultivate the meditative concentrations of the higher realms? Answer:

The treatises state that the various minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the desire realm are called "unstable stages" (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) because they lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Since there is no concentration in the lower realm, [the afflictions arise].

Because one cannot abandon defilement, one cultivates the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in order to sever the defilements of the lower levels. Furthermore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages become manifest.
This explains the attainment of the fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*) of those stages. The seventh [mental factor], which is innate (*sahaja*), is called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*);
because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is difficult to sever. One can only suppress the coarse innate afflictions of the sixth [consciousness] and gradually realize the higher [stages].

Fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*). That [concentration] is merely inferior; it explains that the coarse afflictions (*audārika-kleśa*) are severed, and because it arises only spontaneously (*svarasa-vāhin*), it is confused only regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

Since phenomena depend on the external gate, it is called "distraction" (*vikṣepa*). Due to this distraction, it directly obstructs concentration. "Attaining that inferior [state]" explains the accomplishment of attaining concentration.
Only when the afflictions manifest do they arise from the higher [realm] toward the lower. Regarding the phrase "the meditative mind of a higher stage": the fundamental...
Because it is clear and tranquil, all underlying afflictions are permitted to manifest therein. The concentrated mind is like water: if turbid, its appearance becomes muddled;
if pure, impurities naturally reveal themselves. The "fourth dhyāna" refers to the fourth meditative absorption. Within it lies the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (Asaṃjñisattva-deva).
When the celestial retribution of those beings in that heaven is exhausted, they depart from their celestial forms and manifest an intermediate state body (*antarābhava*).
Because one slanders an Arhat at the moment of emerging from meditative absorption, one falls directly into hell;

therefore, when descending, one gives rise to the innate craving that moistens rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the lower realm. These are all cases of giving rise to a lower [state] from a higher stage.

As for the term "lower," it is used to explain what is taught in other passages; this is based on the majority of cases, for there are not a few instances where one also gives rise to a lower [state].

The afflictions (*kleśa*) of lower stages also take higher stages as their objects; this is explained based on the majority of cases or specific instances. This clarifies that [afflictions] of lower stages take higher stages as objects.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is cited as proof that attachment (*rāga*) takes higher stages as its object. Since it has already been stated regarding attachment, one may infer by logic that aversion (*dveṣa*) likewise takes higher stages as its object.
Both the upper two realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*) are termed "detached from desire" (*vītarāga*); they collectively take all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as their objects.

"Lower" refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) that takes as its object the body, etc., of a higher stage (*ūrdhva-bhūmi*), grasping it as "I" or "mine," or as either annihilated or eternal, and giving rise to the conceit "I am.

Therefore, the views of a self-body, extremes, and conceit can also take a higher stage as their object. As for the fact that the remaining five [afflictions] taking a higher stage as their object is logically established:

since the five beginning with attachment (*rāga*) have already been shown to be able to take a higher stage as their object, the same applies to the remaining two—doubt (*vicikitsā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

The false view and the two types of grasping can also take higher [realms] as their objects. As for those who say that craving and so forth do not take higher [realms] as their objects, this is said based on coarse characteristics or according to a specific sense;
it is intended to show that, in reality, all of them can take higher realms as their objects, whereas none see lower ones.

Regarding the statement that "taking the phenomena of another stage as self and so forth" refers to taking other characteristics as objects: this means that the view of extremes necessarily arises dependent upon the view of a self-identity. This refers to...
It also arises [from a lower level]. In all cases, when the lower levels take the upper levels as their object, those born in the upper levels are said to be "lower.

This citation proves that pride (*māna*) also takes the lower as its object. Taking all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as the lower collectively: these conditioned phenomena are the same as previously mentioned, namely, the two views of self and extremes (*satkāya- and antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), as well as the affliction of craving (*rāga*).
Because they can take the lower as their object, one should reflect according to reason regarding the doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the latter three views; these four types are also subsumed therein.

It is obtained by taking the lower as its object. The term "hatred" is not mentioned because there is no hatred in the higher realms; the term "delusion" is not mentioned because it has already been explained as being pervasive.

Thus, the lower realm is mentioned. This explanation from another source is stated according to the majority of cases, yet it also reveals that [the afflictions] are obtained by taking the lower as their object in some instances.

Regarding these ten afflictions, by which of the categories of "in training" (*śaikṣa*) and so forth are they subsumed? They are neither "in training" nor "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), because they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).

As for the eightfold gate of the three trainings: that which is "in training" and "beyond training" is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*), whereas the afflictions are unwholesome; therefore, they are not mutually subsumed.
Regarding these ten afflictions, by what are they abandoned? (Up to: Because the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*) takes the truths as its collective object.
There are nine categories of abandonment; that is, among the three types of abandonment, these [ten] are not included in "that which is not to be abandoned" (*apraheya*).

This is because that which is not to be abandoned consists of the supramundane path, subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), none of which are defiled. This is intended to clarify that these are [abandoned] by vision.
These ten afflictions are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Of these, four are exclusively conceptual (*vikalpa-mātra*), while six are both conceptual and innate (*sahaja*).

Therefore, they are divided into two types of abandonment: those abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned by cultivation. Furthermore, as for the conceptual ones, they have already been suppressed prior to the [first] stage; upon attaining the true path of insight (*darśana-mārga*), both their seeds and manifestations are completely exhausted.
Thus, they are coarse and easy to abandon. As for the innate ones, they still arise intermittently during the first seven stages; however, in the eighth stage...

Only upon attaining the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) are they finally exhausted; therefore, these subtle [afflictions] are difficult to sever. As for the ten [afflictions] to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), through the attainment of true knowledge, one takes the four truths as a collective object, whereby they are severed once and for all.

However, regarding the delusion concerning the characteristics of the truths (*satya*), there are both general and specific types. (Up to: two [delusions] are exclusively deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), while eight are deluded regarding all four [truths].

This clarifies the general and specific delusions regarding the truths. General delusion is abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because the true path of seeing takes the truths as its object in their totality.

Specific delusion is abandoned by both the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and the path of seeing; alternatively, it is subtle and difficult to sever, and is severed only through cultivation. [This applies to] the two truths of suffering and origin (*samudaya*).

The causes and effects of the mundane world: these ten afflictions do not depart from the mundane world; therefore, they are called the "causal basis. The two truths of cessation and the path are the supramundane causes and effects.
Since one must sever the afflictions in order to cultivate the path and realize cessation, they are described as "fearsome.

How are they individually delusive? Two are exclusively delusive regarding suffering, while eight pertain to delusions regarding all four [truths]. This section provides a general indication; the following provides a detailed explanation of their characteristics.

The two views associated with the self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise only with respect to the fruit; [this continues] up to: "the coarse characteristics of being proximate or remote regarding the truths are thus.

First, it is explained that these two views are exclusively deluded regarding suffering (*duḥkha*). Regarding the statement that the view of a self and the view of extremes arise only with respect to the fruit: the fruit is precisely suffering.
Suffering is precisely the body. Because the body is in reality suffering, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Regarding the phrase "separate from emptiness and non-self":

this refers to various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who, failing to comprehend the principle of emptiness and non-self, give rise to two views concerning the body—namely, the view that the body is permanent, thereby separating it from the principle of emptiness, and the view that the body possesses a self, thereby separating it from the principle of non-self.
Now, when it says "separate from emptiness and non-self," it means...

This [ignorance] is the spontaneous, beginningless clinging to the body as being real, permanent, and a self; therefore, it belongs to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This refers to the meaning of "remote delusion.

That is to say, the subsequent explanation shows that the eight [afflictions] generally delude with respect to the four [truths]. Regarding "doubt and the three views": this means that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the two graspings (*parāmarśa*) constitute the "three";

these four are indicated in summary. They are the "direct delusions" regarding the principle of suffering. Below, the meaning is explained specifically. "The two graspings," etc., explains the two specifically.

Regarding those three views—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—one clings to those ascetic rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as well as the aggregates (*skandha*) upon which they depend, regarding them as supreme and capable of bringing about purification.
Due to this clinging, one gives rise to attachment toward oneself and aversion toward others.
The retinue gives rise to pride; this section should also connect with doubt (*vicikitsā*) and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), as the meaning follows accordingly.

The preceding was a general indication, namely, that doubt and the three views are directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering (*duḥkha*). Regarding "associated with" (*saṃprayukta*) below: this ignorance (*avidyā*), since it co-exists with craving (*rāga*) and the other afflictions...
It cannot serve as the primary [object]. It does not arise from conceptual discrimination; rather, it is a spontaneous delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

It is abandoned solely through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), being the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) because it functions independently. Conceptual delusion regarding principles (*tattva*) is abandoned solely through seeing (*darśana-heya*), such as doubt and false view.
Those that directly delude one regarding the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth either give rise to hesitation or deny them as non-existent; they differ from the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).

Furthermore, those [afflictions] such as greed are deluded only regarding the principle of suffering; therefore, it concludes: "The two types of grasping, greed, and so forth, should be known as pertaining only to suffering.

However, below the section on hatred, it explains that hatred also directly deludes the truths. Regarding the directness or indirectness of this delusion regarding the truths, the coarse characteristics are thus summarized:

the aforementioned two [types of grasping] are deluded only regarding suffering and represent only indirect delusion, whereas the eight [other afflictions] pertain to all four truths and possess both direct and indirect delusion.

To explain in detail: greed, hatred, pride, and the three views [of self-identity, extreme views, and wrong views] are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) because they do not contradict the contemplation of the truths.
This explains that among the specific delusions, those abandoned through cultivation are included; this refers to the meaning of "distant delusion.

Greed, hatred, pride, doubt, wrong view, and the two types of grasping—these seven afflictions possess the quality of arising together; therefore, they are called "co-emergent" (*sahaja*), which is distinct from those abandoned through cultivation.

These are also innate (*sahaja*). As previously explained, those that directly delude regarding the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth, as well as those that directly delude regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
The view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) arise simultaneously and are likewise termed innate.

Furthermore, the ignorance associated with these nine [afflictions] that shares their same object of delusion, as previously mentioned—these three afflictions, although they delude regarding the truth of suffering, are not abandoned by insight; they arise solely through spontaneous functioning (*svarasavāhin*).
This refers to the meaning of being "distant" and "deluded"; therefore, it is subtle and difficult to sever, and is only abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding "hatred, remaining attachment, and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes pride (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). Another source states: "Hostility exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); craving, pride, and ignorance pertain to all three realms.
These four afflictions operate spontaneously toward contaminated objects (*sāsrava-vastu*); they persist for a long time and are firm, making them difficult to liberate from. Therefore...
These are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Although all afflictions possess objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), the distinctions according to other categories should be considered as appropriate.
Tenth is the gate of establishing names according to their specific objects. Regarding the objective aspects of the afflictions: craving has the beloved object as its aspect, and so on, up to...
Ignorance (*avidyā*) has delusion regarding objects as its characteristic. Although it possesses an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), this is not used as its designation;

rather, it is named "affliction with an object" or "affliction without an object" based on whether or not it relies upon a substantial basis. Regarding the phrase "its direct objective support" (*sākṣāt-ālambana*):

two types of names are established based on whether they are contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). For example, when taking *nirvāṇa* or the Path (*mārga*) as an object, this is the meaning of being uncontaminated. When taking one's own level (*svabhūmi*) as an object, it directly grasps [it].

Because its objects and their characteristics are similar, it is called the "objective sphere" (*vastv-ālambana*). As for the [Truths of] Cessation and the Path, or those belonging to other stages, they have never been personally realized;

they arise merely as conceptual images and do not consist of the actual presence of the object. Therefore, because they are not similar, they are called the "sphere of names" (*nāmālambana*). This is the analysis according to other categories.

"Reflecting according to principle" summarizes the specific meanings of the remaining sections; each point is to be reflected upon according to principle, so as not to burden the text with excessive detail.

△ The second part, concerning the classification of the various sections, is concluded. This concludes the section on the stages of the afflictions associated with the three roots above. Below follows the section on the stages of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), which is divided into three parts.
First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the presentation of the inquiry.
The characteristics of the six root afflictions have already been explained; what are the characteristics of the various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)?
△ First, the conclusion of the preceding section and the formulation of the question. Below, the second part provides the general answer by means of a verse.

The verse says: "Secondary afflictions (upakleśa) refer to anger (*krodha*) ... up to ... heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), and lack of correct awareness (*asaṃprajanya*).
This summary verse enumerates the names of the twenty secondary afflictions; the first three lines list the ten minor secondary afflictions, while the fourth line [lists the remaining ten].

Regarding the two types [of secondary mental factors] mentioned in the verse, the latter four lines of the verse explain the essential nature and functional activity of the eight major secondary mental factors;
