since these two are uninterrupted, they always function together. The sixth and the five [sensory consciousnesses] may arise simultaneously.
Increasing the number, up to eight functioning together. △ Second, the section on the simultaneous operation of consciousnesses is concluded. Below, three questions and answers clarify the principle:
"If a single sentient being has multiple consciousnesses functioning simultaneously" (up to) "because for them, at all times, there is only one [of each type]."
If "one" (eka) refers to the first [alternative], it is a question; for he asks this because he holds that a single consciousness constitutes a single sentient being.

If "one" (eka) refers to the second [alternative], the author of the treatise restates the position to refute it: if one were to claim that many consciousnesses constitute many sentient beings and few consciousnesses constitute few, [then...]
When there is no mind, one would not be a sentient being. Furthermore, when the minds of others manifest before one, one could still be called a sentient being of one's own;

for you establish that a single sentient being exists because of the presence of a single consciousness. However, this establishes the conventional designation, whereas the correct definition of a sentient being is as follows:
the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the seed of the eighth consciousness, while maturation (*vipāka*) is the present state of the eighth consciousness. Although the names differ...
There are seeds and manifestations whose essence is non-dual; establishing them as a sentient being does not contradict reason in either case.

A single body has only one immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), because [a consciousness] that arises after a long interval of cessation cannot serve as such a condition for a scattered mental consciousness.

The opponent raises an objection based on the principle that a single object-condition gives rise to only a single consciousness. The Master [Vasubandhu] addresses this through a series of concessions and refutations, elucidating the matter through reasoning.

From the words "Since it is admitted... onwards, the Master provides a concessive response: he states that the immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for mental factors are explained in relation to their own respective consciousnesses.

This is just as, for example, the immediately preceding condition of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) induces the arising of a subsequent moment when it takes a virtuous object; its characteristics...
The eleven mental factors, such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, must arise simultaneously; therefore, it is said that they induce many mental factors. How could they not induce many minds?

Furthermore, [the passage] beginning with "Moreover, who... refutes the attachment to singularity. Moreover, [the passage] beginning with "Furthermore, one desires... provides a logical demonstration:

if one does not admit that multiple consciousnesses arise together, then when those many objects appear before one, why would they not be apprehended all at once? If it is argued that although the objects appear simultaneously...

Consciousness arises sequentially; there is no principle of simultaneous arising. Therefore, it is further refuted [by the opponent], saying: "It is illogical that consciousness should arise sequentially when the power of the harmony between the sense faculties and their objects is equal.
Furthermore, below the section on mental factors (*caitta*), the meaning of the simultaneous arising of consciousness is clarified by analogy with mental factors.
Again, the metaphor of waves and reflections illustrates the simultaneous transformation of consciousness. Moreover, below [that], it is further...

Furthermore, this is refuted by the realization of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If the mental consciousness did not share the same objects as the five [sensory] consciousnesses when apprehending those five objects, it would not be clear;
for the first five consciousnesses are devoid of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*). If one were to grant that the mental consciousness can indeed take the five objects as its objects...

Yet they do not arise simultaneously. Therefore, he further objects: "Just as the distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its object a mere reflected image (*pratibimba*) that has long since ceased, how could it be clear?

How can there be only one mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses], such that they are mutually non-associated (*asamprayukta*), just like the five sensory consciousnesses themselves?"
"How is it so? The opponent objects: "How can a single consciousness apprehend five sensory objects (*viṣaya*) as multiple domains?

[The opponent continues: "Just as with the eye and so forth... The Master of the Treatise explains: "For instance, when visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) takes color-form (*rūpa*) as its object, it may take a single color-form or it may take many color-forms.

Therefore, there is no fault in a single consciousness taking multiple types of objects. [The opponent continues: "Both the aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) exist together... The opponent...

An opponent asks: "If it is said that while the aspects (*ākāra*) are manifold and a single consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to apprehend them, yet the visual perceptions (*darśana*) are also manifold, why do they not all arise together to apprehend a single object?
That is to say, if one consciousness can apprehend multiple objects, then a single object should be capable of being apprehended by multiple consciousnesses.

In response to this, the Master of the Treatise answers below, regarding their respective objects of perception (*ālambana*): "Although the visual perceptions are manifold, each has its own specific object; they [arise] within the scope of their own respective consciousnesses."

Regarding the condition (*pratyaya*): only a single consciousness can cognize [the object], as other consciousnesses would be useless. If this is so—[this introduces] the objection from the opponent below.

"The mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses]" and below is the Master’s explanation: mental consciousness is the condition for the arising of the five [sensory consciousnesses]; it assists the five in their arising.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) clearly apprehends its objects, which distinguishes it from the visual and other sensory consciousnesses. The Noble Ones have taught that the mental consciousness possesses discrimination (*vikalpa*), whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not;

how could this be mere empty words? Regarding the question, "If many consciousnesses arise simultaneously, why do they not possess the quality of association (*samprayoga*) like the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*)?", the opponent asks.
To this, the Master [Vasubandhu] replies as follows: [They do not associate] because they are not identical.

Answer: That which is associated must necessarily be simultaneous, share the same object, share the same sense faculty, and share the same substance. Because it possesses these four meanings, it is called "associated.
Now, although the various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, they do not share the same object, nor do they share the same sense faculty.
"Support" (*āśraya*) refers to the faculties (*indriya*). "Entity" (*svabhāva*) refers to the substantial phenomena. "Number" (*saṃkhyā*) refers to the mental factors (*caitta*).
Because these are not identical, they are like the five faculties and their consciousnesses: since their supports are different, there is no sense of association (*samprayoga*).
If one were to ask: "Are these eight consciousnesses one, or are they different? the following answer is given:
The intrinsic nature of the eight consciousnesses cannot be said to be definitively one, because both the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are absent.

Answer: It is clarified that the eight kinds of consciousness are not definitively one, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), bases (*āśraya*), objects (*ālambana*), associated mental factors (*caitta-samprayukta*), arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), and perfuming (*vāsanā*) are each distinct. Nor are they definitively different, like water and its waves. And...

Regarding causality, how could it be definitively distinct? Furthermore, he provides a general analogy, stating that it is "like illusory phenomena and the like," because they possess neither definitive identity nor definitive difference.
As previously stated below, this concludes by revealing the sublime principle of the ultimate and the conventional. As for the aforementioned distinctions among consciousnesses:
That is to say, the aforementioned three types of transformation consist of eight mind-kings and fifty-one mental factors;

each possesses its own distinct essential nature and functional activity. Both their seeds and their active manifestations are all presented according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and do not pertain to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In the true ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), the mind is inconceivable and speech is beyond deliberation;

how could there be distinctions of form, name, or category? As the following verse cites as scriptural evidence: "Because both the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*) are absent," this refers to the true ultimate sense.

Since both the transforming subject and the transformed object are quiescent in their two-fold characteristics, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). △ The third section, the question-and-answer elucidating the principle, is concluded. This concludes the preceding [section].

The first part, the explanation of the three transformations, is concluded. Below, the second part answers five external questions and is divided into five sections. The first section, the provisional designation of self and dharmas, is divided into three parts.
The first is the conclusion of the preceding section and the presentation of the question.
The characteristics of the three types of transformation have already been extensively analyzed (up to the point): "By this, is it the case that all things are merely consciousness?

From "already extensively" onwards, the three types of transformation are summarized as the basis for the two parts—the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*)—which they themselves transform.
"What is meant by 'below'? He asks again: "Regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), you say in your Mahāyāna that they are transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Since they are transformations of consciousness, both the transforming consciousness and the transformed objects each possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why, then, do you say that all phenomena do not exist as separate realities, but that there is only consciousness?
This concludes the first section: the conclusion of the preceding topic and the formulation of the question. Below follows the second section: the presentation of the verse as a general response.
The verse says: "These various consciousnesses undergo transformation... (up to) because that [object] is entirely non-existent, therefore everything is representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

The first two lines clarify the characteristics of the transforming subject and the transformed object, establishing the grasped and the grasper. The latter two lines clarify that both the internal and external are empty, revealing the nature of representation-only.
In the verse, the word "this" refers to the two parts—the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*)—which exist like a magical illusion. That...

"Characters" refers to the real self and real dharmas falsely grasped through delusion; they definitely do not exist. Since both these entities—self and other—are empty, it is said that "all are non-existent.
△ Second, the general response by means of a verse is concluded. Below, the third section explains the meaning of the verse, which is divided into two parts.
First, the correct explanation of the meaning of the verse.
The Treatise says: "These various consciousnesses" refers to what was previously explained [up to] "...not being separate from consciousness, such as mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth.
First, the first line of the verse is explained through two aspects of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The eight consciousnesses are the primary minds (*citta-rāja*); the fifty-one...
The mental factors (*caitta*) are called the "transformer" (*pariṇāma*). The two parts—the seeing and the perceived—are called the "transformed.

Because these two parts, the seeing and the perceived, are transformations of consciousness and arise from causes and conditions, they are termed "dependent origination" (*paratantra*). However, because they merely appear as external objects while manifesting as a real subject and object of grasping, they are said to be "semblances" (*pratibhāsa*).
Below the section on "the transformed," [the text] explains that both subject and object are termed "transformed" according to the second line of the verse. This is because...

The following explains the third line of the verse: by means of the correct principle of dependent origination regarding the transforming subject and the transformed object within the Mahāyāna, one knows that other [schools'] attachments to a real self and real dharmas are definitively non-existent;
for they are devoid of the aspects of seeing and being seen, and thus lack substantial reality. The following explains the fourth line of the verse: as for all dharmas, such as form and mind, if—

That which currently possesses actual activity is called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*). If a phenomenon has already ceased or has not yet arisen, it is called "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) because it lacks such activity.
Furthermore, all phenomena are said to exist substantially (*dravyasat*) because they undergo transformation through causes and conditions.

Because they are transformations of conceptual construction, they are termed "provisionally existent. Therefore, all phenomena do not depart from consciousness. Regarding the term "only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), the *Zhongjing* (Mirror of the Doctrine) states:

"The word 'only' negates the existence of external objects; 'consciousness' distinguishes [it] from the emptiness of the mind. 'Only' negates the attachment of the Sarvāstivādins who hold that objects exist outside the mind;
'consciousness' distinguishes [it] from the 'badly grasped emptiness' held by Bhāviveka and others. Thus, our Mahāyāna establishes Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātratā*)."
The meaning is not to negate those mental factors and so forth that are not separate from consciousness.

Alternatively, "transformation" refers to the fact that the various internal consciousnesses [proceed until] the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established, thereby accords with the Middle Way.
Next, the meaning of the verse is explained by means of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Alternatively, the following section explains the first one and a half lines of the verse:
because the mind that undergoes transformation is itself the faculty of discrimination, and all mental phenomena (*caitta*) of the three realms are illusory.
The subsequent section explains the next one and a half lines of the verse: "this grasped object" refers precisely to that which is transformed. This is the title of the verse.

That which is conceptually constructed is precisely the falsely grasped nature of a real self and dharmas; these are all false attachments to the signs of a self and dharmas that are merely based on the transformations of consciousness.

Therefore, it is said that they are definitively non-existent. Since the first and second fascicles extensively cited scriptural authority and reasoning to refute the definitive non-existence of the self and dharmas, the following section explains the fourth line of the verse: "false and illusory."
Regarding "the existence of conceptual construction," this refers to a verse in the *Sūtra* which states that within the three realms, the mind of false conceptual construction exists;
thus, the mind of *tathatā* (suchness) also exists. This is called "universally established" because it refutes the attachments of the Hīnayāna and others who hold that the mind is non-existent.

As for the phrase "only (*kevala*)... below," it means that "only" excludes the existence of external objects, but does not exclude the mental factors (*caitta*) that are inseparable from consciousness.

Because phenomena such as equality [are established], phenomena such as true emptiness—the ultimate truth—also possess intrinsic nature. According to the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there are no phenomena external to the mind;
this negates the existence of objects and thereby avoids the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*). That there is a delusive mind distinguishes it from the emptiness of the mind itself.

Because it avoids the fault of diminution, the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is established, thereby acceding to the Middle Way. △ The first section, the formal explanation of the meaning of the verse, is concluded.
Below follow two minor points: the nine difficulties raised by the Hīnayāna. First is the difficulty concerning the cause of consciousness-only.

By what scriptural authority and reasoning is the meaning of Vijñapti-mātra (Cognition-Only) established? [This] should be further stated with certainty to establish this scriptural authority. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) states:
"The Hīnayāna raises nine difficulties to challenge the principle that there are no phenomena external to the mind—that it is Mind-Only. The first difficulty says:
'Apart from the mind, we currently perceive material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) as real objects of cognition (*ālambana*). Why does the Master [Vasubandhu]..."

"Encompassing all, they return to the mind; in summary, it is said that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*). First, there is the distinction between form and mind; second, there is the difference between subject and object.

"Is this not already explained?"—below this, the Master of the Treatise answers, stating that although he has previously cited extensive scriptural authority and reasoning to explain the meaning of *vijñaptimātra*, you have not yet understood it despite his having taught it to you. "It is not a refutation"—below this, the Master clarifies his own intention.

This does not mean that one merely refutes the positions of others to establish one’s own; rather, the intention is to extensively clarify *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
Therefore, one should further provide a definitive presentation of the correct principles of the sacred teachings to establish the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra*.
The *Zongjing* replies: "These external objects of form are, first, transformations produced by the perceiving minds of sentient beings, and second, [the manifestations of] the..."
The minds of sentient beings are sustained by this; its root is the mind. Therefore, it is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
As the sūtra says, "The three realms are mind-only," [and so forth], until one can accordingly realize that there is only consciousness and no external objects.

First, four types of scriptural citations are presented, all of which are spoken in the sūtras to prove that there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and no external objects apart from the mind.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* state that the three realms are mind-only (*citta-mātra*). The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* further states that the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are merely manifestations of the mind.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is further stated that all phenomena do not depart from the mind. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*...
Furthermore, it is said that sentient beings follow the defilement or purity of their own minds.

Next, citing the *Abhidharma-sūtra*, it explains that those who have attained the four types of wisdom and entered into consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) are small Bodhisattvas prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*).

Although they have not yet realized the principle of consciousness-only, by relying on the Buddha’s teachings and by observing the Bodhisattvas of the [ten] stages, they achieve these four kinds of wisdom regarding consciousness-only.
He then entered into a contemplation of the outflows (*sāsrava*).

He observed how those Bodhisattvas of the ten stages transform the great earth into gold, churn the long rivers into curd and cream, and manifest mountains of flesh, fish, rice, and so forth. He then said:
"Such transformed things as gold, silver, and jewels do not exist apart from the transformative mind of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; there is no external object (*bāhyārtha*) whatsoever."
Having observed this, one is also able to accord with and penetrate the principle of True Consciousness-Only (*tathatā-vijñaptimātra*).

First, regarding the cognition of contradictory perceptions: if a single object were to exist as a real entity, how could it be established [for those with different perceptions]? (This continues until: "How could it be established? [End of citation].
This refers to four classes of sentient beings whose perceiving consciousnesses are distinct, and whose transformed *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) are likewise contradictory.
Thus, gods see the ground as adorned with jewels; fish and dragons see it as their cave-dwellings; humans see it as clear, cool water; and hungry ghosts see it as a river of pus or a raging fire.
What is called the "image" (*nimitta*) here is not the *parikalpita-lakṣaṇa* (imagined nature), but rather the image of the *nimitta-bhāga*. This is due to the four...
By the power of their prior karma, sentient beings each transform their own objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) differently within a single location;

therefore, this is called "the dissimilar objective aspects of consciousness. As for what is termed "wisdom," it refers to the wisdom capable of taking as its object the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

This wisdom is able to discern that the objective aspects transformed by the individual karmic consciousnesses of these four classes of sentient beings are distinct, and that there is no further mind [other than these].

The four external differentiated objects. Question: As for those four sentient beings, do they each transform their own *nimitta-bhāga* (image-aspect), or is their *vastu* (substantial basis) also distinct?

Answer: Both the image-aspect and the substantial basis are distinct. This is because, due to the differences in the karma of the four sentient beings, the *nimitta-bhāga* transformed by the eighth consciousness is also distinct;
and since the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness serves as the substantial basis (*vastu*), the *nimitta-bhāga* transformed by the first six consciousnesses [is likewise distinct].
The divisions are also distinct. Therefore, one knows that there are no external objects; there is only consciousness. Master Xuanzang said:

"As for the fact that objects are not uniform, they constitute the *nimittabhāga* (perceived aspect) which is transformed by the transforming minds of four classes of sentient beings. Consequently, the objects also become fourfold.
That a single location is perceived differently [by different beings] proves that there is only consciousness."
Second, the knowledge of consciousness that has no object: since those objects do not exist, the rest should likewise be understood as such.

Regarding "consciousness that has no object," this refers to all ordinary beings who, with their own sixth, independently arising, and distracted mental consciousness, take the past, the future, water-moons, mirror-images, and so forth as objects, causing a false *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) to arise through transformation, without there being anything external to the mind.
"Real objects" refers to consciousness that lacks an objective referent (*anālambana-vijñāna*). "The wise" refers to the cognizing mind of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
The Bodhisattva says: "These provisional aspect-objects (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by ordinary beings do not exist apart from the transforming mind (*pariṇāma-citta*);
they are 'consciousness-only' (*vijñaptimātra*). By this same analogy, all real objects likewise do not exist apart from all [minds].
The sentient being’s mind that takes [objects] as its referent has nothing whatsoever apart from the mind itself; therefore, it is said:
"Since those objects do not exist, the rest should likewise be so.
Consequently, one would naturally possess non-erroneous wisdom and should attain liberation without relying on effort.
This refers to a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages who, having given rise to wisdom, observes all sentient beings.
[He sees that] they falsely cling to themselves as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure. The Bodhisattva says: "This is merely the inverted view of the clinging mind of ordinary beings.
Apart from this mind of false clinging, there is truly no realm of permanence, bliss, self, or purity within the bodies of these ordinary beings. If such a thing did exist, it should..."

Ordinary beings do not attain liberation by relying on cultivation; since this is not the case, it is clearly known that there is only deluded consciousness, which is also "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
Regarding the four types of transformation following the three wisdoms: if objects were truly existent, how could they be transformed?
The first three knowledges observe the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), whereas this fourth knowledge observes the realm of noble ones (*ārya*).
These three knowledges are combined into one because all three are the sphere of activity of the noble ones. First, the knowledge that functions in accordance with the mastery of the sovereign:
this is the knowledge arising from a bodhisattva who observes the objects transformed by themselves, none of which are separate from their own capacity to transform.

This mind is its very *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). For Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, they are able to spontaneously transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into butter and curd.
This is the transformation of the objective realm in accordance with true wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*), whereby all transformed phenomena are successfully accomplished.

"Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) has the meaning of changing the original substance; that is, it refers to the transformation of the original substance of the great earth, mountains, and rivers in accordance with [wisdom].
Gold, silver, and so forth are forged and fashioned into various utensils, which sentient beings truly obtain for their use.

If external objects existed apart from the mind, how could it be that the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the fundamental natures (*svabhāva*) of objects such as mountains and rivers all undergo transformation?
Therefore, one knows that all objects do not exist apart from the Bodhisattva’s transforming mind; this applies even to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

One can transform fire into water, change a painting into night, and transmute iron into gold; all such instances are cases where the objective realm shifts in accordance with wisdom, and whatever is transformed is successfully accomplished.

This, too, is *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Generally, those who transform [objects] into gold, silver, palaces, or towers produce what are truly "fruits of concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*).
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, these are transformed through intentional mental application (*manasikāra*). As for Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward, regarding...
The marks and the lands are all transformed through mastery. That superior meditative mind possesses great power;

the gold, silver, palaces, and so forth that it transforms are all successfully accomplished. These serve as various utensils and implements that are truly available for use, yet none of them depart from the Bodhisattva’s internal mind.
This is its "consciousness-only" nature. As for the Śrāvakas and the lesser Bodhisattvas prior to the [first] stage, [it is not so].
When transforming palaces of gold and silver, one takes the palaces of gold and silver transformed by the Bodhisattva as the substantial basis (*bimba*).
The gold, silver, and so forth transformed by the sixth consciousness cannot serve as various utensils; they lack real functional efficacy.

Nevertheless, that which is transformed is a provisionally established derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*), not separate from the internal mind; this is its nature as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Second, regarding the wisdom that functions in accordance with observation: if the object were truly existent, how could it transform according to the mind?

As the Bodhisattva Wuxing (Asvabhāva) said: "When śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas cultivate the contemplation of suffering, emptiness, and so forth, or when they attain the corresponding realization, or when they perform the contemplation of the Four Truths, as they observe each individual phenomenon, there is only..."
Characteristics such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self are manifest; it is not that the meaning of impermanence and so forth exists within the essence of phenomena themselves.
Rather, it is that the meaning of impermanence and so forth exists upon the mind capable of transformation (*pariṇāma-citta*), which then causes all phenomena to become impermanent and so forth.
Thus, one should know that all phenomena do not exist apart from consciousness.
Third, the wisdom that functions in accordance with non-conceptual wisdom: if the object were real, how could it fail to manifest?
When a Bodhisattva’s fundamental wisdom realizes *tathatā* (suchness), the object of suchness and the wisdom are merged; subject and object are of one taste (*eka-rasa*).
Apart from this fundamental wisdom, there is no separate object. Since the object functions in accordance with the wisdom, it is said to be "mind-only" (*cittamātra*). You...

The followers of the Hīnayāna maintain that there are real objects external to the mind; yet if this were so, why would all objective appearances not manifest even when one realizes *tathatā* (suchness)?
That Bodhisattvas accomplish the four wisdoms—and many other such scriptural authorities—provide abundant and authentic proof.

In summary, it is only when a bodhisattva attains these four wisdoms that they are able to awaken to and enter the correct principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Furthermore, the following verses provide scriptural evidence:

the eighth [consciousness] is called *citta* (mind), the seventh is called *manas* (intellect), and the remaining six are called *vijñāna* (consciousnesses). Each has its respective object of perception (*ālambana*), yet all arise as transformations of the mind.
Since the mind is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is said that they do not depart from their intrinsic nature. This applies to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) all manifest from the mind; therefore, it is said that there is nothing remaining. From this point downward, the summary of the sacred teachings concludes the exposition on the meaning of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
In the following text, correct reasoning is further employed to establish four logical arguments (*anumāna*) to clarify the principle of consciousness-only.
"Because it is one of the five well-established consciousnesses such as the visual consciousness, like the others, it does not directly perceive objects separate from its own form.

This establishes the first inference (*anumāna*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is contained within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The *Zhengjìng lù* (Mirror of Correct Proof) states: "The subject (*dharmin*) is the well-established visual consciousness;

'it certainly does not directly perceive objects separate from the forms of its own consciousness' is the thesis (*sādhya*); the reason (*hetu*) is 'because it is one of the five well-established consciousnesses.'"

Because they are subsumed [within the same category]. Just as other well-established (*prasiddha*) four consciousnesses [are accepted], here, regarding what are called "well-established eye-consciousnesses" and so forth, the *Zhengjingshi* (Zhongjing) provisionally takes eye-consciousness as the subject (*pakṣa*);
thus it says, "eye-consciousness is the dharmin. "Because it is one of the five" means that it is subsumed under one of the five consciousnesses;
this is the meaning of the logical reason (*hetu*). It is like the others [the five sense objects] which do not directly perceive anything apart from their own respective forms.

"Et cetera. This means that the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that this visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) certainly does not directly perceive forms (*rūpa*) that are separate from its own consciousness, just as the other four consciousnesses—auditory and so forth—do not directly perceive the four objects (*viṣaya*), such as sounds, that are separate from their own consciousness.
The meaning is that all objects of perception (*ālambana*) are inseparable from their respective consciousnesses;

therefore, in this inference (*anumāna*), the thesis is contained within the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Based on the *Zhengjingshi* (Mirror of the Thesis), all three members [of the syllogism] are employed.

The two characters "universally established" (*prasiddha*) both serve as verbal designations to exclude logical faults. First, regarding the phrase "universally established eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) as it is presented by the proponent:

this excludes an eye-consciousness that is not universally established for both schools. For example, the Mahāyāna school accepts the eye-consciousness of Buddhas in other realms and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) eye-consciousness of a Buddha, whereas the Hīnayāna school does not accept these;
thus, they are not universally established for one of the two schools. The Hīnayāna school, however, does accept that a Buddha possesses [such consciousness].
The defiled eye-consciousness of those with outflows (*āsrava*) and the defiled eye-consciousness of a Bodhisattva in their final existence are not admitted by the Mahāyāna.
These are not established for both schools. Now, setting aside what is not admitted by both schools, we take the eye-consciousness as it is commonly accepted by both as the basis for our thesis.

Therefore, it is said that [the subject] is "universally established" (*prasiddha*). Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) states, "because it is included within one of the universally established five consciousnesses," and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) states, "just like the other universally established four consciousnesses.
These all serve to exclude the visual consciousness and the four consciousnesses beginning with the auditory, which are not universally established for both schools.
If the term "universally established" were not employed, one would commit the fallacy of "specifying the unestablished" (*viśeṣya-asiddha*) regarding the thesis (*pakṣa*).

This does not constitute the fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*). Regarding the reason (*hetu*), it commits the fault of being unestablished for either oneself or the other party (*anyatara-asiddha*).
Regarding the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it commits the fault of the unestablishment of either the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) or the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*).
Because other consciousnesses are also consciousnesses, like visual consciousness and so forth, they likewise do not directly perceive phenomena that are separate from themselves.

This establishes the second inference (*anumāna*), which possesses all four members [of the syllogism]. The *Zhengjingshi* states: "The subject (*dharmin*) is 'the remaining consciousnesses,' which are universally established as existing.

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is 'they also do not directly perceive phenomena separate from their own consciousness. The reason (*hetu*) is 'because they are of the nature of consciousness. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is..."

Just as the five consciousnesses are universally established, the term "the remaining consciousnesses" here refers to excluding those first five and positing the latter three consciousnesses as the subject (*pūrvapakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "because they are consciousness":

since the latter three consciousnesses share the same name as the first five in their aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), the *Zhengjingshi* (Mirror of Correct Principles) takes this nature of being consciousness as the reason (*hetu*).
The analogy provided here states, "just as with visual consciousness and the rest," because their nature as consciousness is identical.

Therefore, the thesis that "those [consciousnesses] also do not directly perceive phenomena other than their own" means that, just as the first five [consciousnesses]—like other consciousnesses—do not directly perceive objects such as form that are separate from their own consciousness, so too the latter three consciousnesses, like the first five, do not directly perceive phenomena other than their own consciousness.
Question: Why does it not state that the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses are the *dharmin* (the subject), but rather says "others"?

"Is it consciousness? He replied: "If one asserts that the six, seven, or eight consciousnesses are the subject (dharmin), since the opponent does not accept the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, one commits the fallacy of 'the subject being unestablished for one party' (anyatarāsiddha).
If, however, one establishes only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) as the subject,"

Within the reason (*hetu*), there is further the fallacy of being "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*). It is countered by using the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as a heterogeneous example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), thereby committing the fallacy of being "uncertain" regarding the common locus (*sādhāraṇānaikāntika*).
Now, we simply speak of "the rest" in general; although the sixth consciousness is explicitly mentioned, the intention includes both the seventh and eighth.
Thus, it is established that seven or eight [consciousnesses] exist within other consciousnesses.
This teaching holds that the object-condition (ālambana) is certainly not separate from either of these two, just like its corresponding subject-condition (grāhaka).

This third inference possesses all four members [of a syllogism]. The *Zhengming Jing* states: "The immediately perceived objects (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the six consciousnesses are the subject (*dharmin*).

It is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that they are certainly not separate from the substance of the six consciousnesses. The reason (*hetu*) is: because they are subsumed under either the 'seeing' or the 'image' portions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) within [the consciousness].
For example, like the 'seeing' portion which acts as the perceiver. Now, when it says "this explains the object," it is establishing the characteristic of the object.

This is divided into the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). "It is certainly not separate from this" means that the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is certainly not separate from the cognizing consciousness (*ālambaka-vijñāna*);
this is the thesis. "Because it is one of the two [aspects]" is the reason; that is, because it is one of the two parts, namely the objective aspect.

"Just like its cognizer" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); for the objective aspect and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are mutually inseparable, just as the objective aspect is to the subjective aspect.

Because they are objects of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*), like associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*), they are certainly not separate from the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*).
This establishes the fourth inference (*anumāna*). The reason (*hetu*) resides within the subject (*dharmin*). The *Zongjing* states:
"All that which is an object of one's own consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*); that it is certainly not separate from my cognizing mind and its mental concomitants is the thesis (*pakṣa*)."
The reason is stated as: "Because it is an object-conditioned phenomenon (*ālambana-dharma*). The concordant example is: "Like associated phenomena (*samprayukta-dharma*).

Now, regarding the phrase "because it is an object-conditioned phenomenon," this takes all that is the object-condition of consciousness as the subject (*dharmin*). Thus, being an object-conditioned phenomenon is stated as the logical reason (*hetu*).
"Like associated phenomena" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); that is to say, the object-conditioned phenomenon is not separate from the subject-conditioning [consciousness], just as...

The associated mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*) do not depart from the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that they are definitively inseparable from the mind and its mental factors;

that is to say, the objects of cognition (*ālambana-dharma*) necessarily take the sovereign mind and its mental factors as their subjects of cognition (*ālambaka*), and therefore are not separate from them.
If one asks: "Why is the latter member of the proposition stated as 'my subject of cognition'? The answer is: if one were not to speak of "my subject of cognition," [the meaning would be lost].
[If one were to say] "it," one would incur the fault of partial mutual support;

for even the Hīnayāna admits that the object of the knowledge of others' minds does not exist apart from the mind that cognizes it. To exclude this fault, [the text] says "my own cognizing [mind]," thereby excluding the cognizing [minds] of others.
These correct principles and authentic proofs are indeed manifold. (Up to: In reality, there also exists a pure portion of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Although there are four types of inference (*anumāna*) herein, all take "non-separation" as their meaning; they collectively reveal the correct principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Therefore, it is said: "These correct principles and authentic proofs are indeed manifold. One should believe and accept this with deep conviction: that the self and phenomena do not exist.

The phrase "refuting what others grasp" negates external attachments. The phrase "emptiness and consciousness are not non-existent" reveals one's own established thesis: emptiness is ultimate emptiness, and consciousness is *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
This meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* is free from both existence and non-existence, accords with the Middle Way.

Below, the Compassionate Honored One (*Maitreya*) cites scriptural evidence for the principle that emptiness and consciousness are not non-existent. The phrase "there is false discrimination" refers to the three realms of existence as false discrimination.
This refers to the discriminating mind. "In these two, there is absolutely nothing" means that within the deluded mind, there is absolutely no grasping at a real self or real dharmas;
"herein there is only emptiness" means that within this deluded mind, there is only true emptiness.
"Therein also exists this" means that within true emptiness, there also exists the deluded mind.

Therefore, when it is said that "all phenomena" refers to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, being neither empty nor non-empty refers to the true mind and the deluded mind—namely, the two natures of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*) and dependent origination (*paratantra*). These are termed "not empty" because they are [respective] real self and real dharmas.
This refers to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). It is called "not non-empty" because of the existence of both the existent and the nonexistent.

"The existent" refers to the deluded mind; "the nonexistent" refers to the self and phenomena. Within the real there is the delusive, and within the delusive there is the real; it is called "existent" because of this presence. This is what accords with the Middle Way.

This concludes the preceding points, which simply mean remaining far removed from the extremes of nihilism and eternalism. Below this verse, the Master of the Treatise explains the intent of the verse.

That is to say, these two verses explain the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) based on the defiled aspect (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*). By inferring through reasoning, one can also see that the pure aspect (*vyavadāna-bhāga*) likewise reveals the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*.
△ The first objection is concluded. Below follows the second objection: the objection that worldly affairs contradict the fundamental tenet.
If it is argued that internal consciousness alone arises appearing as external objects—up to the point where it is said to be "like dream-objects and so forth"—one should resolve this doubt.

Regarding the statement "if there is only internal consciousness" up to "the transformation of the determinate and the indeterminate," the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) records that the Sautrāntika masters raise this objection:
"If you say that there is only internal consciousness and no external objects, how is it that we currently perceive the world of sentient and non-sentient beings?"
Regarding such things as these, there are cases where the location and time are fixed, while the body and its functions are not. Now, the text says:

"If it is only internal consciousness that arises resembling external objects," which restates the Mahāyāna doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The phrase "how could one see... and following constitutes the objection.
This means that one observes that in the world, both sentient and insentient beings have fixed locations and times, yet their bodies and functions are not fixed.
For example, that which is in the east is not in the south; this time is not that time. Thus, place and time are fixed.
Furthermore, among all people, there are those with cataracts and those without cataracts, and what they perceive varies and differs.
This body is not fixed, just as all men and women, swords, staffs, and so forth, which appear to have real functions, are seen in dreams.

[If that were so,] it would lack practical utility; thus, its functional activity would be indeterminate. To resolve this doubt—such as the case of dream-objects and the like—the Master of the Treatise cites Verse 5 of the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*:
"The determination of place and time is like a dream; the indeterminacy of the body is like [the vision of] hungry ghosts;

the common perception of a river of pus and so forth is like a dream that destroys utility. This answers the meaning of the preceding question and reveals the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). [Regarding] place and time...

Regarding "the certainty [of place] is like a dream": this means that within a dream, whether one perceives this location or another, and whether one perceives during a time or not during a time, all are manifestations of the dreaming mind;

thus they may be called "consciousness-only. If that is so, then the objective forms and locations perceived during my waking state—though their places and times are fixed—are likewise consciousness-only.
Regarding "the body is uncertain, as with hungry ghosts": this means that just as hungry ghosts collectively perceive a single [object], such as a river of pus, as being the same for all.
If water can transform into pus-rivers, fierce fires, and other such variations— all of which are manifestations of the karmic consciousness of hungry ghosts—

and these may be called "consciousness-only," then one must recognize that in our own school, those with cataracts and those without cataracts perceive different things depending on their physical conditions.

This is also *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). Regarding the point that "just as in a dream, things that have functional efficacy [are consciousness-only]," this means that although weapons, food, drink, and so forth in a dream lack real functional efficacy, events such as losing [an object] do possess real functional efficacy. Since these are all manifestations of the dreaming mind, they can be termed *vijñapti-mātra*.
Thus, one should know that according to our school, both the waking state and the dreaming state are established as *vijñapti-mātra*. For further details on other meanings, consult our own treatises.

The *Ādarśa* (Mirror) in sixty-three fascicles contains extensive text, which is not cited here. △ The second objection is concluded. Below follows the third objection: Contradiction with the Sacred Teachings.
For what reason did the World-Honored One teach the twelve bases (*āyatana*) [up to] in order to make known that external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*) likewise do not exist?
Regarding the objection from the lower vehicle: The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) records that the Hīnayāna school raises this difficulty:

"If you claim that all things are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*) and that there are no real external objects apart from the mind, for what reason did the World-Honored One state in the *Āgama* sūtras that there are twelve bases (*āyatana*)?"

If all things were merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), the Blessed One would have taught only the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), and would not have spoken of the ten material sense-bases (*rūpāyatana*).

Now, since the Blessed One has indeed taught that there are twelve sense-bases, it is clearly known that apart from the sense-bases of mind and phenomena, there are separately the ten material sense-bases which exist externally to the mind. How, then, can you say that everything is merely consciousness?

Consciousness. There are three types of responses given by the Master of the Treatise (*śāstrakāra*). First, the provisional response (*prajñapti-uttara*); there is no formal scriptural citation for this.

It means provisionally taking the seeds of the five consciousnesses as the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) to answer the position of the Sautrāntika masters. As the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: [The verse follows...]
Consciousness arises from its own seeds and evolves appearing as the semblance of an object; in order to establish the internal and external bases (*āyatana*), the Buddha taught these as ten.
There is an explanation for this verse in the *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source), but the text is too voluminous to be cited here. Second, regarding the direct answer:

it is as stated in the present treatise that [the objects] are transformations of consciousness and do not exist as separate, real entities. This is based on the correct interpretation of our own Mahāyāna school, namely, that the five sense-objects—

Substantial form (*svabhāvarūpa*) is the direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness. This objective aspect is not separate from the eighth consciousness and is likewise *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Regarding the answer by means of the three similes, the present treatise states: "Just as when denying the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), one speaks of the continuity of sentient beings."

This is the Buddha’s intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): to shatter the "unified whole" (*piṇḍa-grāha*) of a self in sentient beings, he provisionally designates the names of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

This causes sentient beings to contemplate that among the phenomena of the twelve bases there is absolutely no self, whereby they enter into the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*). Subsequently, they rely upon consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
One is able to observe that upon all phenomena (*dharma*), there is ultimately no real essence, nor any function such as a superior nature or a sustaining power.

Once the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is eliminated, one then establishes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). △ The third objection concludes. Below follows the fourth: the objection that Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) must itself be empty.
Is this very nature of consciousness (*vijñapti-mātratā*) not also empty? (Up to: For this reason, the Lord Maitreya spoke the two preceding verses.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Doctrine) records that the Hīnayāna critics raise this objection:

"If it is said that all phenomena lack any real function such as maintaining their own tracks, exercising sovereignty, or possessing a supreme nature, thereby establishing the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), then is not the very substance of this consciousness itself [also empty]?"
"Empty. The Master of the Treatise replies: "It is not so; that is to say, the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is also not empty. The Hīnayāna practitioner asks again:
"In what way is it not empty? The Master replies again: "Because it is not that which is grasped as real.

This means that when I previously spoke of emptiness, I was merely emptying away the falsely imagined (*parikalpita*) functions—such as the characteristics of being truly existent, maintaining their own nature, or possessing superior qualities—that are superimposed upon all phenomena.

Phenomena that are false and deceptive are empty; however, they are said to be "empty" because their fundamental wisdom-realized nature of consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātratā) is not empty and is free from names, categories, and so forth.
The passage beginning with "If this consciousness were non-existent... provides a further explanation for why it cannot be empty.
Below the section "Denying the Two Truths," various Buddhas' words of reprimand are cited to warn [the opponent].

Below "One should know," the preceding verse is concluded, establishing the principle that there are things which can be empty and things which cannot be empty. △ The fourth objection ends. Below follows the fifth objection:
that form and appearance are not the mind.

If all form-objects (*rūpāyatana*) also have consciousness as their essence—[extending] up to and including non-material consciousness—if that [consciousness] were absent, then these too would not exist.
The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) records that the Hīnayāna school raises this objection:

"If you claim that all external forms have the mind as their essence, why is it that while the external forms produced by transformation all appear, the transforming mind itself does not appear? For instance, regarding external..."
The physical world—the mountains, rivers, and great earth—remains unchanged for thousands and tens of thousands of years; it continues without interruption and endures for a long time.
The mind that undergoes transformation is not like this. Clearly, one knows that there exist external, real forms apart from the mind.

Why, then, do you say that everything is merely consciousness? Now, when you say, "If all places of form also have consciousness as their essence," this is a restatement of the [opponent's] main point.

"Riding upon the meaning of *Vijñapti-mātra* (Consciousness-only). The phrase "For what reason? (*kasmāt*) introduces the objection. The phrase "The perfuming of names and words" (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*) is the Master’s response. The *Zongjing* commentary explains:
"It is solely because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have transmitted [this habit] from one moment to the next;

through the false perfuming of names and words, they form the understanding that there are external objects, characterized by solidity, stability, and continuity. By the power of this [perfuming], [these appearances] exist."
This aspect appears because it serves as the basis for defiled and pure phenomena; that is to say, all defiled and pure phenomena arise from the appearance of form (*rūpa*). An opponent asks again:
"If you maintain that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), why must sentient beings manifest what resembles external form?
The answer is: "If this were non-existent, there would be no such things as inversion, defilement, purity, and so forth. As a verse says below:

Regarding the scriptural citations that establish the meaning of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), the *Zongjing* commentary states: "The 'confused appearance' (*bhrānti-nimitta*) refers to the objective forms transformed by consciousness;
the 'confused essence' (*bhrānti-svabhāva*) refers to the subjective mind that performs the transformation. One must admit that what is designated as 'form-consciousness' is itself also mind."
Therefore, it is said: "form-consciousness and non-form-consciousness. That which undergoes transformation originates from the mind; hence, it is called "non-form-consciousness.
"If there were no others, there would also be none" means that if there were no transformed objects resembling external forms serving as the signs of confusion, [there would be no consciousness].
Furthermore, there is no essence of consciousness capable of undergoing transformation. Therefore, one must know that it necessarily transforms so as to manifest as external objects.

Thus, all forms and matter do not depart from the mind; they are entirely *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). △ The fifth objection concludes. Below follows the sixth objection: the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
External objects such as form are clearly perceived [up to] they cannot be grasped as being real external forms.
The *Zhengjīng* (Mirror of the True Teaching) states: "For instance, regarding the five sensory objects of form outside the mind, they are clearly realized by the five consciousnesses;

this is what is obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is universally established and accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Why, then, do you deny them and claim in general that 'all is consciousness-only'? Thus it is said.
At the end of the section on "Valid Cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the Master of the Treatise replies. The *Zhengzongjing* commentary explains:

When the five consciousnesses of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) apprehend the objects of the five sense-fields, they grasp the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena without being accompanied by names or words, and without the mind of deliberation. They do not grasp these as external.

It is only the subsequent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that falsely gives rise to conceptual discrimination and then grasps them as external, distinct, and substantially existent objects. Therefore, [this is] direct perception.

Below, the intent of the response is explained and established. The *Zongjing* commentary states: "The five consciousnesses each possess four divisions. The objects of the five sensory realms are the immediate *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the five consciousnesses.
These appear as objective aspects such as form and so forth, manifested through the transformation of the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses.
Furthermore, these objective aspects do not exist apart from the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*); all are but consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). As for the subsequent conceptualizing mind..."

When consciousness arises, one falsely clings to the notion that there are real objects external to the mind; these are in fact non-existent, for they do not correspond to the actual nature of the object.

Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "form and so forth," he exhorts those of other vehicles not to cling to them as being external; that is to say, the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is a transformation of the mind.

Therefore, it is said that they are not form (*rūpa*). Because the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) resembles the underlying essence, it is said to be "resembling form. Since internal form is not external form, it is said to be "not external.
Since internal form appears as if it were external, it is said to be "resembling the external. Just like objects in a dream, all are merely transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*);
how then can one cling to them as real forms existing outside the mind? The sixth objection concludes. Below follows the seventh [objection]: Dreaming and Waking.
The objection of contradiction:
If the forms perceived during the waking state are all like dream-objects, [then] by this one has not yet realized that the objective realm of form is consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The *Zhengjīng* (Zhēnjìng) commentary explains: The Hīnayāna school raises the following objection based on the preceding point: "If the forms of the waking state are all like dream-objects, then..."

Regarding those who deny consciousness (*vijñāna*): for what reason is it that while everyone knows dream-objects are transformations of the mind alone, they do not know that objects during the waking state are also *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)?

To answer this, the text first provides an analogy below the phrase "as when one has not yet awakened from a dream," and then applies the teaching to the analogy below the phrase "during the waking state.

Finally, it cites scriptural authority below the phrase "therefore, the Buddha... The *Zongjing lu* commentary states: "This refers to the seventh consciousness, which is the long night of birth and death."
This is the root that causes the arousal of afflictions and the creation of karma, leading to transmigration through the three realms.
Only upon reaching the stage of true awakening does one realize that all things are but consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

Formerly, King Śarabha, who was handsome in appearance, later left the household life under Kātyāyana and went to the kingdom of Aparāntaka to practice the Way. The King of Aparāntaka [took his] palace...
A man entered the mountains for recreation. When the palace ladies saw that the king’s appearance was upright and handsome, they gathered around him and gazed at him.
King Āpaṇḍi became enraged and whipped him until he was nearly dead; it was not until nightfall that he regained consciousness. He said to Kātyāyana:
"I requested leave from my teacher to return briefly to my own country. Once I have raised an army and destroyed that kingdom of Āpaṇḍi, and slain its king, [I shall return]."
The Master was practicing the Way. Kātyāyana went to him and requested, saying, "If you wish to depart, please stay for one night.
Kātyāyana settled him in a comfortable place and put him to sleep, wishing to cause him to have a dream. In the dream, he saw his entire army set out on a campaign against the kingdom of Aparāntaka;
his own forces were defeated, and he himself was captured by the enemy. His hands and feet were bound tightly, and a red flower was stuck upon the crown of his head. It was most solemn.
The drum sounded as if to kill; the king was seized with great terror and cried out, losing his voice.

Kātyāyana called him by name to awaken him and said to him, "If you march against that [enemy], you will surely be defeated and ruined, just as you saw in your dream. The king said, "I pray that the Master will remove this poisonous intent.
Kātyāyana then expounded for him that all phenomena are like a kingdom—a mere conventional designation without reality.

"In reality, apart from houses, dwellings, and the like, there is no separate realm," and so forth, with various causes and conditions explained at length, down to the point that even a single atom is not a substantial entity.
There is neither "this" nor "that"; there is neither enemy nor friend.

Having heard this Dharma, the King attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), and subsequently gradually attained the fruit of arhatship. Therefore, one knows that all phenomena are but consciousness, as in the awakening from a dream.

It is one and the same. What is seen within waking consciousness is precisely the clearly manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); what is seen within dreaming is precisely the dream-state mental consciousness.
Since the discriminating mind is identical in both cases, how can the differentiated objects be different? If such is the nature of delusion and awakening, why harbor any doubt?
If the states of darkness and clarity are thus comparable, they may be thoroughly understood. △ The seventh objection concludes. Below follows the eighth external [objection].
It is difficult to apprehend another's mind.
External forms are in reality non-existent and cannot be objects of internal consciousness; this is the same as when one takes another's mind, form, and so forth as objects.

The *Zongjing* [Compendium of the Mirror] raises an objection: "Furthermore, if this person’s mind were to directly apprehend and grasp another person’s mind, then it would be separated [from its own object]."
This person’s mind has another mind as its object. If this person’s mind does not adhere when taking another person’s mind as its object, then there is an object that is not being perceived;
if it does adhere, then it contradicts the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). If it adheres without perceiving, how can it constitute the knowledge of others' minds?
Now, to say that external forms truly do not exist, yet might still be objects of internal consciousness, is a concessive argument (*anujñā-vākya*). [The same applies to] the minds of others.
"It truly exists; how could it not be its own object of cognition? This is an objection. To whom does this refer? The Master of the Treatise answers. The *Zongjing* commentary explains:
"Although it is said that another's mind is not the object-domain of this person, if this person directly perceives another's mind, they cannot do so.

However, if they rely upon another's mind as a substrate (*ālambana-pratibimba*) and transform it into their own internal image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) for perception, they likewise possess the knowledge of others' minds."
However, when one transforms the image-aspect (nimittabhāga) to take it as an object, one does not apprehend the actual essence (svabhāva) of another person.

Rather, the image-aspect that is the reflection of another is manifested upon one's own mind; this is called "knowing another's mind. Thus, one knows that the image-aspect of another's mind is not separate from one's own mind.

This is also *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). That is to say, the passage "the consciousness [is] below" explains the meaning of not being a direct object (*asākṣāt-ālambana*). The *Zongjing* commentary states:

When this person’s mind takes another person’s mind as its object, it transforms and gives rise to a *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) that appears before it. This objective aspect lacks any real functional activity;
it does not grasp objects like a hand, nor does it directly illuminate its object by radiating light like the sun. Thus, it takes the other person’s mind as its object.
At that time, it is merely like a reflection in a mirror, appearing as if it were an external substance; yet the image in the mirror likewise lacks any real activity.

It is the same when taking another person’s mind as an object: it is not directly apprehended. What, then, is meant by "directly apprehended"? That which is directly apprehended by the one who is proximate.
This is because [consciousness] transforms itself. Therefore, the sutra below cites evidence for the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only):

that which grasps is mind, and that which is grasped is also mind. This establishes the principle of *vijñapti-mātra*, hence it says: "There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another dharma.
Furthermore, it means that the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises solely from one's own consciousness; appearing as if it were the mind of another person, it is called "grasping that."
Objects are thus for others; the same applies to form and so forth. This is what is meant by "all phenomena are consciousness-only. △ The eighth objection concludes.
Below follows the ninth objection: that objects of different realms are not consciousness.

If there are indeed distinct external objects, how can they be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*)? [This leads to the conclusion that] one must certainly believe that all things are consciousness-only.

The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the School) states that the Hinayana criticizes this by saying: "The meaning of consciousness-only is that apart from the mind, there is not even a single thing that exists."
Only then can it be called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). Since the minds of others take this person’s mind as their object, how can it be established as consciousness-only?
"How extraordinary!"—with these words, the Master of the Treatise rebukes him, saying: "O you of the Hīnayāna, why do you so stubbornly cling to your views and give rise to doubts at every turn?
Does the term 'consciousness-only' merely refer to the consciousness of a single individual? To this, the Hīnayānist replies: "No, how could that be? The Hīnayānist speaks again:
Question: "You should listen attentively," and so forth. The Master of the Treatise answers:

If one says that there is only a single consciousness, then there would be no distinction between ordinary beings and sages, nor between the noble and the base, nor between cause and effect. If there were no Buddhas, what would sentient beings seek? If there were no sentient beings, for whom would the Buddhas teach?

One should know that when I speak of the term "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*), it possesses a profound underlying intent. [The passage] beginning with "the word 'consciousness'" is an explanation.

This establishes the rationale for the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*). Specifically, the term "consciousness" is established to comprehensively indicate that all sentient beings each possess eight consciousnesses,
each possess six classes of mental associates (*caitta*), each possess objective images (*nimittabhāga*) and subjective aspects (*darśanabhāga*),

each possess twenty-four types of dissociated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) distinguished by their various states, and each possess six kinds of suchness (*tathatā*) revealed by the principle of emptiness.

Regarding "the unconditioned": each has eight consciousnesses because they are the self-characteristics of consciousness. Regarding "the six categories of mental factors": they are associated with consciousness. Regarding "the transformed aspects and vision":
these are the transformations of both the mind-king and the mental factors. Regarding "the distinctions of states": [they are so called because]...

This is because the first three dharmas are manifested through their respective stages (*avasthā*). That which is manifested as *tathatā* (suchness) is the actual nature (*dharmatā*) of each of the preceding four dharmas.
Thus, all the dharmas of the five aforementioned positions do not depart from consciousness; they are collectively designated by the name "consciousness.

Therefore, there is a profound intention behind the term "only" (*kevala/vijñaptimātra*). Regarding the statement "the word 'only'": it establishes the term "only" merely to negate the grasping of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), and does not negate the dependent nature (*paratantra*).
Therefore, there is also a profound meaning [in this]. From "If one knows thus" onwards is the conclusion and exhortation that one should have faith.

This means that those who know *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) can realize that there are no phenomena external to the mind, thereby entering into the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Since all phenomena are empty, they realize unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, it is able to rescue sentient beings from birth and death; one who holds the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*) and contradicts the teachings and principles could not accomplish such a great causal matter.
Therefore, those who wish to cultivate the Unsurpassed Vehicle (*anuttara-yāna*) should have faith in the doctrine that all things are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
The second section, the nine difficult questions regarding the Lesser Vehicle, is concluded. This concludes the preceding section on the provisional designation of self and phenomena.
The second section, "The Analysis of Various Kinds of Discrimination," is divided into three parts. First, restating the meaning and posing the question:
If there is only consciousness and no external objects at all, by what means do various kinds of discrimination arise?
"If there is only consciousness and no external objects at all"—this restates the Mahāyāna doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

"By what are various conceptualizations produced?"—this is the interrogative phrase. That is to say: if there is only consciousness and no objective realm, by what means do various mental states arise?
Since there is no object to draw forth the mind, from what does the deluded mind originate? △ 1. Restating the doctrine to pose the question.
[The preceding section] concludes. The following two lines present a summary response in verse:
"By the power of all-seed consciousness (sarvabījakavijñāna), through its successive interaction, various conceptualizations arise."
"By all-seed consciousness" refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), because it is capable of sustaining all seeds.
"Transforming in such and such a manner" points to the successive force described below;

that is to say, from the seeds, manifestations arise in such a way, and from manifestations, seeds are perfumed in such a way—this is the meaning of succession. Therefore, the treatise states: "From the stage of arising, it transforms into the stage of maturation."

Regarding the statement that "the *ālayavijñāna* transforms to give rise to the seeing and object-aspect divisions through the power of mutual interaction," the *Treatise* states that this refers to the eight manifesting consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and their respective object and seeing aspects acting as auxiliary forces.

Regarding the statement that "the various conceptualizations arise through these very conditions being the power of mutual interaction," the *Treatise* states that this refers to the manifesting consciousnesses and so forth taken collectively.
This is called "discrimination. Because the types of discrimination are numerous, it is said to be "various.

The *Zongjing* states that these arise from the false attachment to the existence of external, real selves, dharmas, and so forth, based upon the two aspects of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*).

Part Two: The general response by citing the verse is concluded. Below follows Part Three: the explanation of the meaning of the verse, which is divided into three sections. First: the direct explanation of the meaning of the verse.
The Treatise says: "All-seed consciousness" refers to the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), [up to] "not a consciousness that maintains seeds," which will be explained in detail later.

This explains the first line of the verse. "Fundamental consciousness" is the eighth [consciousness]. "Function" refers to the seeds (*bīja*). "Distinction" indicates the multiplicity of these seeds. Regarding the phrase "producing this":
it explains that the seeds produce only four types of fruits, as others are not seeds. As for the "fruit of outflow" (*niṣyandaphala*), it is the fruit...

Because it resembles its cause. As for the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), it is so called because the fruit is different from the cause. As for the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), it is so called because both cause and fruit exist simultaneously.

"Human effort" refers to the agent; when the task to be accomplished is achieved, it is named the fruit of human effort. As for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), it is so called because it is produced through the joint influence of auxiliary causes.

[The text] below, starting with "excluding the fruit of disjunction," explains the fifth fruit. It does not have the sense of being produced from a seed; rather, it is that which manifests in the present.

The "path" refers specifically to the path of knowledge that is capable of severing [afflictions]. "That which is attained by severing the fetters" refers to what is realized through the abandonment of delusions; it does not arise from seeds.

Regarding the meaning of "successive progression," it means that one must first abandon the phenomena associated with defilement and bondage before one can realize that fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*);
thus, this fruit of dissociation is not what is being discussed here in the context of the seed-state.
Question: Since it is named "all-seeds" (*sarvabīja*), why is it also called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*)? Answer:

Because that which is here described has as its essence the consciousness that produces the seeds of discrimination, it is designated by the name "consciousness" in addition to [being called] "seeds. This is not a separate explanation of consciousness. Regarding the term "seed-consciousness" (*bījavi-jñāna*), there is a distinction:
"there is consciousness that is not a seed" excludes the first seven consciousnesses; "the seed is not consciousness" excludes external seeds. Furthermore, regarding the seed...

"Below" [in the commentary] excludes the eighth consciousness. This means that although the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) is used concurrently in this verse, the intended meaning refers exclusively to seeds;

therefore, it says "to reveal the seeds within consciousness," rather than referring to the consciousness that maintains the seeds. Regarding the phrase "to be explained extensively later," this refers to the extensive explanation of the meaning of seeds within the section on causes and conditions below.
This concludes the explanation of the first line of the verse.
"Because the seeds within this consciousness are assisted by other conditions" [up to] "because they arise as conditions for the manifestation of pure seeds.
The phrase "from this consciousness down to the exhaustion of the seeds of consciousness" explains the second line of the verse.
"Assisted by other conditions" refers to the "mutual force" mentioned in the third line of the verse; because all eight consciousnesses possess mutual auxiliary power, it is so stated.
Other conditions: through the assistance of these conditions, the phenomena of conceptualization arise in this manner.
