Regarding the three types of perfuming—namely, the habitual tendencies of verbal designation (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*), the habitual tendencies of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha-vāsanā*), and the habitual tendencies of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*)—they correspond respectively to what are also called the habitual tendencies of verbal designation, afflictions (*kleśa*), and form-consciousness (*rūpa-vijñāna*).

These are identical to the common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and the uncommon characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*); it is only through these that the seeds within consciousness are established.
"Because they are exhausted. This concludes the preceding section. "Successively descending" explains the third line of the verse; it may be understood according to the text.

"That which is presently manifest" explains the fourth line of the verse. "Manifest consciousnesses and so forth" refers to the eight kinds of consciousness as well as their associated mental factors (*caitta*).
"The many categories of discrimination" refers to discriminations such as saying one, two, and so on, up to eight, nine, ten, and so forth. Below this verse, [the text] restates...
This verse provides a general explanation of the meaning. That is to say, through seeds and manifest consciousnesses mutually bestowing power upon one another, discrimination arises spontaneously.
Why then insist that external conditions must exist for discrimination to arise? Furthermore, pure phenomena (*śukladharma*) likewise do not depend on external conditions;
as with the aforementioned defiled phenomena, they also arise through the mutual generation of pure seeds and pure manifest consciousnesses. 1. The Direct Explanation of the Verse.

The section on the mind is concluded. Below, the detailed explanation of the meaning of conditions (*pratyaya*) is divided into five parts. First, the extensive clarification of the meaning of conditions is divided into two.
First, the question-and-answer presentation of the number:

"How should one understand the distinctions of the arising of conditions through seeds and manifestations as they have been explained? Regarding these characteristics of conditioned arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are four types of conditions."

The question and answer clarify the meaning of the four types of conditions (*pratyaya*). That is to say, both preceding seeds (*bīja*) and present manifestations (*samudācāra*) can serve as conditions capable of producing various forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
How should one understand the characteristics of which phenomena serve as which conditions? In the response, it is stated that there are four kinds of conditions:
the single phenomenon of the seed is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); the remaining three conditions pertain to present manifestations.

The power of successive transformation was explained above; therefore, seeds and manifest activities constitute the four conditions. △ The first section, consisting of questions and answers to indicate the number [of conditions], is concluded.
Below, the second section provides a detailed explanation of the four conditions, divided into four parts. First, the explanation of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The first condition, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). This explains that, in relation to those [phenomena], this [condition] possesses the nature of being a causal condition.
Furthermore, it is divided into two. The *Zongjing lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) explains:

"If all seeds of affliction have been suppressed by the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) such that they never again possess the function of manifesting, they cannot be called causal conditions. It is also like...
When mental seeds produce the manifestation of form, this is not called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

However, when mental seeds produce the manifestation of mind, and form-seeds produce the manifestation of form and so forth, these are all causal conditions. This applies to both the "new" and "original" types of seeds.
Regarding the term "seeds," the following explains them as causal conditions: these seeds, in their meaning, pervade the three natures, the three realms, and the nine stages.
Because each possesses its own distinct functional capacity: that which "induces a subsequent capacity of its own kind" refers to the production of a seed from a seed;
and that which "arises as a simultaneous manifest fruit of its own kind" refers to the production of a manifest consciousness from a seed.
Regarding the statement "this is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to that":

this means that this seed is the causal condition in relation to both the seed that brings about [the result] and the simultaneously arising manifest fruit. Below, under the section on "manifest activity" (*pravṛtti*), the manifest activity is explained as being the causal condition.

This refers to the fact that the term "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*) applies generally to both the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), as well as to the perceived objects (*nimitta-bhāga*), the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the realms (*dhātu*), and the stages (*bhūmi*);

all these are termed "active manifestations. However, with the exception of the wholesome dharmas within the state of Buddhahood and those that are weakly indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), which are not capable of perfuming, the remaining seven [consciousnesses]—both kings and their factors—as well as the realms and stages, perfume the eighth consciousness and produce seeds of their own kind. This...
The preceding seven [consciousnesses] and so forth, in relation to that eighth, constitute the nature of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);
for the eighth mental complex has no [other] perfuming [object], and thus they serve as causal conditions in mutual relation to one another.

This explanation does not concern the meaning of "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*). That is to say, the five [mental factors] associated with the eighth consciousness lack the quality of being "perfumable" (*vāsya*) and thus do not constitute causal conditions.
Suppose it is asked: "If mental factors are not perfumable, is the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) also not perfumable? The answer is: "No;

this is not intended to exclude the eighth consciousness as the support (*āśraya*), but rather to single out the seven preceding [consciousnesses] as the 'perfuming agents' (*vāsaka'), which necessarily require the eighth [consciousness]."

The meaning of "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) is established [only for these]. Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are extremely weak; the wholesome dharmas within the state of Buddhahood are perfectly complete.
Therefore, in these two cases, there is neither increase nor decrease, and they do not perfume to form seeds; thus, they lack the status of being causal conditions.

As for the claim that "manifesting dharmas of the same category, when viewed in relation to one another, are all not causal conditions"—meaning that a preceding manifestation induces a subsequent manifestation—although they are of the same category, they are not [causal conditions].

The preceding manifest phenomenon arises from its own seed; therefore, it is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding all things of different categories that are mutually related, they are not causal conditions:

this refers to the subsequent manifest phenomenon in relation to the preceding seed, and the subsequent seed in relation to the preceding manifest phenomenon, even though these are said to be of different categories.

Yet they do not arise simultaneously, because [the former] is produced by its own parents. Nor is it a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Some say that the subsequent explanations comprehensively resolve other meanings, but none of these fully accord with the principle.

What does fully accord with the principle? Answer: The Noble Ones have taught that, in relation to the *ālaya-vijñāna*, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) constitute the meaning of "causal condition.
This concludes the first explanation of the causal condition. The following two [points] concern the "equal and immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The second [condition], the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), refers to the eight manifest consciousnesses (up to) the dharmas that are equal-and-immediate; therefore, it is not this [present] condition.

This explains the meaning of the second condition in the heading. The eight consciousnesses as mental kings (*citta-rāja*) and all mental factors (*caitta*) are collectively termed "manifest consciousness" (*mukhya-vijñāna*).

This excludes matter (*rūpa*), dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), seeds (*bīja*), and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as these do not possess the nature of this condition. The treatise states: "All... and so forth.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is stated solely with reference to all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

"The preceding aggregate [relative] to the subsequent" excludes simultaneity and the case where a subsequent [aggregate] serves as a condition for a preceding one, because it does not provide an opening and guidance (*avakāśa-āvāhana*). "Of its own kind" indicates that it is not a different consciousness that acts as the condition.

"Immediately preceding" indicates that the preceding [aggregate] serves as the condition for the subsequent, without any intervening gap. "Equally providing an opening and guidance" clarifies the meaning of being a condition.

"Causing that [result] to definitely arise" clarifies that although a subsequent result may be separated by a vast duration—such as the visual consciousness eighty thousand kalpas prior—it still serves as this condition for what follows, because that subsequent result is destined to arise.
This excludes the final moment of mind upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, for since no result is destined to arise from it, it is not such a condition.
The phrase "mostly of the same kind" and below explains the mental factors (*caitta*).
Regarding the meaning of "jointly guiding": "homogeneous seeds" refers to the mental factors (*caitta*) associated with each respective consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because these mental factors are not singular, they are termed "many. They are called "homogeneous" because they are associated with consciousness; since the mental factors arise simultaneously when the mind arises, it is said that they "evolve at the same time.
As for those that are "non-associated" and thus not included within this causal condition, although they are so named...

Regarding mental factors (*caitta*): if they were not associated (*samprayukta*), like other phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, they would not share this common object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
For this reason, the eight consciousnesses do not serve as mutual conditions for one another; this excludes the possibility that the eight consciousnesses are mutually associated.

Regarding the mind and its mental factors, the *Zongjing lu* states: "Since the mind and its mental factors are not of the same category [as the eight consciousnesses], they always arise simultaneously, their substance..."

[Question: Since their functions are each distinct, how can they arise together such that, in relation to subsequent [moments] and among themselves, they possess the status of being mutual conditions?

[Answer: It is said: Mind and mental factors are conjoined as if they were one; they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*), the same support (*āśraya*), arise at the same time, and are subsumed under the same nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they cannot be separated, their differences do not obstruct them, and thus they serve as mutual conditions. [Question: Upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*...
"Is there such a condition based on the mind? He replied: "That [mind] is extremely subtle and inferior; it lacks the sense of being a condition.

It is 'subtle' because it transcends the path of speech and thought, and 'inferior' because it cannot produce a fruit. Since it has already ceased and will not arise again, it is said to lack the meaning of being an equal-and-immediate [condition] for what is yet to arise."
How is this known? The treatise contains an explicit statement [extending to] "the same applies to the relationship between the wholesome and the indeterminate.
This question-and-answer section clarifies the meaning of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Specifically, the treatise states:

"If, at the time when preceding consciousnesses and so forth cease, subsequent consciousnesses and so forth necessarily arise immediately thereafter, then these preceding ones are said to be the [condition] for those subsequent consciousnesses and so forth."

Regarding the "immediately preceding condition" (samanantara-pratyaya): based on the preceding [text], the Master of the Treatise, following the intent of the treatise, establishes that each of the eight consciousnesses possesses the meaning of the immediately preceding condition.
*Ādāna* means "grasping and maintaining"; this clarifies the immediately preceding condition of the eighth consciousness.
The three realms and nine stages are all capable of acting as mutual conditions for one another. Why is this? Because death and birth in the lower and upper [stages] open up to one another equally.

That is to say, when one is born from a lower stage into an upper stage, the mind at the moment of death in the lower stage acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the mind of birth in the upper stage;

the same applies when one descends from an upper stage to a lower one. Therefore, it is said that they act as mutual conditions. "With outflow" (*sāsrava*) refers to the cessation of an outflowing mind.

At that time, it acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the arising of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). The untainted does not act as a condition for the tainted.
Why is this? Because once the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) has arisen, it is never interrupted.

That is to say, at the time of the eighth [consciousness] becoming untainted, the mental complex transforms into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which continues forever until the end of the future, never being interrupted. Since it is without interruption, [it serves as the condition].

"It cannot serve as a condition; the same applies when comparing the wholesome and the indeterminate" means that while a defiled indeterminate state may give rise to an undefiled wholesome dharma, an undefiled wholesome dharma certainly does not give rise to a defiled indeterminate state.
Because they are respectively with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), it is said that "the same applies."

Regarding the question of from which realm this [attainment] subsequently induces the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, the Sūtra does not state that it arises from those [realms], because they do not give rise to the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*).

Through this question and answer, the realms and stages that induce the outflow-free state are clarified. Specifically, "As for the various lower [realms]" explains how the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) induces the outflow-free state;
"The two vehicles... explains how the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) induces the outflow-free state. "There is another interpretation... refutes the preceding view.
The two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) can only generate the outflow-free (anāsrava) state within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

This [text] clarifies that for those who turn toward the Mahāyāna, it is also possible to generate it within the form realm (rūpadhātu). Should one ask: "Does the Sūtra not state that those in the heavens do not turn toward the Mahāyāna?"
How can one cite the manifestation of the eighth [level], the untainted (*anāsrava*), as proof? The answer is:

although the sūtras state that those in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) do not undergo rebirth elsewhere, this refers only to śrāvakas of fixed lineage (*niyata-gotra*); it should be understood that there are also those among them who have generated the great resolve (*mahācitta*).
The seventh *pravṛtti-vijñāna* does not arise in the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi-pratipanna*), because they are not reborn there.

This clarifies that the seventh consciousness acts as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Within the three realms and nine stages, these [consciousnesses] may also mutually serve as such conditions.

Furthermore, regarding death and birth in lower or higher realms, it is the same as the eighth consciousness; for wherever one is born following the eighth consciousness, one is bound by the grasping of that eighth consciousness.
For my sake, [it is said]: "The outflowing [wisdom] below" refers to this seventh [wisdom], the wisdom of transformation within the causal stage.

It differs from the eighth [wisdom], which exists only at the level of fruition; therefore, throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the outflowing and non-outflowing [wisdoms] arise alternately, being able to mutually induce one another.

As stated in the five-fascicle [version]: Since the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is an outflow (*nisyanda*) of the noble path (*āryamārga*) and is utterly quiescent, it too does not exist [as a substantial entity].
This is because its seeds have not yet been permanently severed. Once one has arisen from the noble path of the attainment of cessation, these [seeds] manifest again until they are extinguished;
this is precisely the case where the untainted (*anāsrava*) induces the tainted (*sāsrava*). Furthermore, their nature as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth is identical.

Because the outflows (*āsrava*) and the non-outflows (*anāsrava*) mutually induce one another, it is said that "it is likewise. When the wisdom of the emptiness of arising (*utpatti-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arises, it is called "non-defiled" (*asaṃkliṣṭa*);

when this wisdom does not arise, it is also called "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*). Therefore, in their preceding and succeeding stages, they are able to mutually induce one another. This [refers to] the desire realm below...
The outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) [states] mutually induce one another, but only within the lower two realms (*dhātu*).

This is because Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) are not born in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and because the wholesome roots of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) belong exclusively to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) among the nine levels (*bhūmi*) of the three realms. These pertain to the sixth evolving consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna-pariṇāma*).

This clarifies that the sixth consciousness and its associated mental factors can serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for one another across different realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), and types of outflows (*āsrava*).

This is because those transformed wisdoms (*parāvṛtti-jñāna*) also belong to the stage of a causal practitioner (*hetu-avasthā*); thus, during the stage of nourishing birth (*janma-paripuṣṭi*), they are able to mutually induce one another.

As for the initial arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state occurring only in the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), it is because the wholesome states of the "decisive distinction" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) do not exist in the Desire Realm (*kāma-dhātu*). Furthermore, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses are devoid of the untainted state [in the Desire Realm].
Regarding the possibility that outflows may arise from one another: this refers to these two consciousnesses having three grades of evolving wisdom.

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), it evolves at a low grade; in the eighth stage, it evolves at a middle grade; and at the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*sambodhi*), it evolves at a high grade. When it first evolves at the low grade, it is not yet purely untainted (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, they mutually induce one another with the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*). As for the first five [consciousnesses] and the eighth, they transform only through superior-grade wisdom;
thus, when the untainted (*anāsrava*) is attained, the outflow-tainted no longer arises, because once that wisdom has arisen, there is necessarily no further severance [of the seeds].

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses belong to two realms and two stages (*dhātu* and *bhūmi*). This is because these two [realms/stages] differ in the clarity or dullness of their respective objects.

This clarifies that the five sensory consciousnesses have immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that are each distinguished by realm and stage. Regarding the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body belonging to two realms and two stages:

they pertain to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), specifically the stage of the five destinies living in mixture (*pañcagati-saṃkīrṇa-vāsa-bhūmi*), and the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), specifically the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*viveka-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*). As for the olfactory...

Regarding the statement that "the tongue [faculty] and its two consciousnesses belong to one element and one stage": they exist only in the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu) within the stage of the five destinies living together in confusion (*pañcagati-saṃkīrṇa-vāsa-bhūmi*).
The explanations concerning their mutual arising among their own kind and their mutual relation as wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth are the same as before.

There is one interpretation that it is incorrect for the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) to act as immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*) for one another. There is another interpretation that while the uncontaminated may arise after the contaminated, the contaminated does not arise after the uncontaminated.

Regarding the principle that the arising of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is possible: it is said that the Buddha possesses uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fivefold sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). How could it be that the Buddha also gives rise to the contaminated?
This is because prior to attaining Buddhahood, the five material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are necessarily contaminated.

That is to say, the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), having contaminated objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), manifests as the five material sense faculties; these arise simultaneously with the first five consciousnesses and share the same objects, being contaminated material sense faculties.
To claim that untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) arises [from a tainted state] is logically inconsistent. Tainted objects are obscure, whereas untainted objects are luminous;

how could both luminosity and obscurity arise simultaneously with respect to a single object? The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to being 'immediately preceding' because there is no interval between them;
it is so called because it gives rise to minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the same category or different categories in immediate succession. This is the immediately preceding [condition].
Regarding the meaning of "immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*): "without interval in between" does not necessarily mean being without interval within a single moment.
Even if moments are separated, provided there is no intervening mind of a different nature in between, it is also called "without interval in between.
Otherwise, the mind entering a mindless absorption would not be an immediate condition for the mind emerging from that absorption; however, [it is].

This is its condition. Therefore, within a single continuum, because there is no intervening mind between a preceding mind and a succeeding mind, it is an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Just as it is with mind in relation to mind, one should know that the same applies to mental factors (*caitta*).
Regarding the immediate succession of similar and dissimilar minds and mental factors: this refers to when wholesome minds and mental factors relate to those of their own kind.

It is so. Heterogeneous unwholesome and neutral states of mind and mental factors serve as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for immediately succeeding states of mind and mental factors.

Likewise, unwholesome and neutral states of mind and mental factors are also [equal-and-immediate conditions] in relation to immediately succeeding states of mind and mental factors that are either homogeneous or heterogeneous.

Furthermore, states of mind and mental factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are [equal-and-immediate conditions] in relation to those of the desire, form, and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*). Immediately...
A mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) that have arisen serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

In this same way, it should be understood, as appropriate, that each respective mind and mental factor of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, in relation to those of the form realm and so forth, as well as to the minds and mental factors that arise immediately thereafter in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, function in the same manner.
△ The section on the Equal-and-Immediate Condition is concluded. Below follows the third [type of] condition: the Object Condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The third [condition], the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), refers to those phenomena (up to) which arise even when separated from external objects of cognition.
This explains the meaning of the third condition among the headings. Because there are distinctions between the immediate and the remote, it is divided into two types. Regarding the object-condition:

that which must be a real entity (*dravya*)—a fundamental phenomenon—is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*); relying upon this fundamental reality, one’s own *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) arises through transformation; this is called the [object-condition].

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is defined by combining the aspect (*nimitta*) and the substance (*vastu*). It is called the "object-condition" because it refers to a phenomenon that possesses existence.

As the *Zongjing lu* commentary explains, this refers to phenomena that have substantial reality (*sadravya-dharma*), thereby excluding provisional phenomena as well as the imagined and the image-aspect (*parikalpita-nimitta-bhāga*), which are phenomena lacking substantial reality. Phenomena lacking substantial reality... [text truncated]
However, that which is an object of cognition (*ālambana*) does not necessarily constitute a condition (*pratyaya*).

To function as a condition, it must be a real entity (*dravya*) possessing actual efficacy, capable of drawing forth the arising of consciousness. Thus, the truly perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are entities that possess substantial existence.

Regarding the phrase "bearing its own aspect" (*sākāra*), there are two meanings to "bearing": first, "transformative bearing," which refers to the eight consciousnesses having a remote object-condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
The "essence" (svabhāva) refers to that which arises as an appearance resembling the essence, taking this objective entity as its basis; this is termed "transformation-carrying" (pariṇāma-ādāna).
Second is "clinging-carrying" (upādāna), which refers to all actual *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) that serve as direct objects of cognition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
This is because these *nimitta-bhāgas* are not separate from the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*); thus, the cognizing mind directly clings to these *nimitta-bhāgas*.
Regarding "condition" (*ālambana*), it is termed "carrying along" (*parigraha*). As for what is called "one's own aspect" (*svākāra*), there are also two meanings.

First, when spoken of in relation to the transformed and distant object-condition (*viparīta-parokṣa-ālambana*), it refers to one's own aspect as that which appears similar to the objective substance (*bimba*).

Second, when spoken of in relation to the carried along and immediate object-condition (*parigṛhīta-pratyakṣa-ālambana*), it refers to one's own aspect as the portion of the object-aspect directly carried along upon the cognizing mind itself. This...

This is the characteristic of the aspect of the object (*ālambana-nimitta*). It is not the same as arising with its own aspect while carrying the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of a remote objective condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the statement "mind or associated [mental factors]," Master Ci'en says: "This explains the fruit of the objective condition.
Taking the object as the condition is the cause; that which arises—the mind and mental factors—is the fruit. As for the word "mind," it is...

Regarding the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*), those termed "associated" (*samprayukta*) are the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*). Because these may arise or not arise, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed.

As for "that which is contemplated" (*ālambita*) and "that which is relied upon" (*āśrita*): that which serves as the object of the consciousness is called "contemplated," while that which can induce the arising of the consciousness is called "relied upon.
This substance is divided into two parts below, which are explained separately in the text. If it does not share the same substance as the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), [it is not associated].

"Separated" (*viyukta*) explains the meaning of the direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). If it is separated from the substance of the apprehending subject (*ālambaka*) despite being its object, this explains the meaning of the indirect objective condition.
Regarding "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) and "indirect" (*parokṣa*): "direct" has the sense of being contiguous or proximate;

that is, just as the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*) is directly contiguous with and close to the aspect of the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), with no other parts intervening. "Indirect" has the sense of being distant. It is... [text truncated]

Because they are mutually separated, they are indeed the objective essence (*nimittabhāga*). If [the objective aspect] were not separate from the substance of the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), then the perceiving subject would be the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and its substance would be the self-verifying part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
This means that the objective aspect is the immediate condition (*samanantarālambanapratyaya*) for the seeing-part.

The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is the immediate object-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), and both are inseparable from the essence of the self-witnessing-part.

This specifically excludes the remote object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), namely the fundamental reality (*bimba-dharma*), which, in relation to the seeing-part that acts as the cognizer, possesses the sense of being separate.
It also excludes the image-parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by others, as well as the image-parts transformed by each of one's own eight consciousnesses, which are mutually [separate].
When viewed in relation to one another, none of these are direct [objects]. Now, we take only the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by its own consciousness;

when this is viewed in relation to the *darśana-bhāga* (perceptual aspect), their substance is not separate, and there is no intervening object to obstruct them—only then does the meaning of "direct" apply.

As for the statement that it is "that which is internally relied upon and reflected upon by the *darśana-bhāga*," the term "etc. (*ādi*) includes the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect) and the fourth aspect (*anuvyavasāya*), as well as...

Fundamental wisdom takes suchness and so forth as its objects; all of these constitute direct objective conditions (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding direct objective conditions, the eight consciousnesses are divided into four categories:
First, there are those that have a direct objective condition because they arise through transformation from both the primary substance (*bhūta*) and the mind itself;

this refers to the five consciousnesses taking the five sensory objects as their conditions, wherein the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the direct objective condition. Second, there are those that have a direct objective condition but arise solely through transformation from the mind.

1. There is that which does not arise based on a substantial entity (*dravya*); this refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) taking the three objects as its *nimitta-bhāga* (image-aspect). 2.

There is that which possesses a direct objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and arises neither from a mental transformation nor from a substantial entity; this refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizing suchness (*tathatā*). 3. There is that which possesses a direct objective condition but is not a *nimitta-bhāga*;
this refers to the mutual cognition between the two internal parts [of consciousness]. [The fourth category concerns] the indirect objective condition (*parokṣa-ālambana*).

The objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to those phenomena that are distinct from the cognizing mind. This includes what is transformed by another consciousness as well as what is transformed by a separate consciousness within one's own continuum;

these serve as the objective basis (*ālambanapratibimba*) and so forth. The essence of the direct objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*) consists in being "carried along" (*parigraha*), for it is necessarily inseparable [from the cognition].
Apart from the internal object that is relied upon, the cognizing mind would certainly not arise. As for the indirect...
The essence of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) consists in its transformation and manifestation; if it does not transform, it does not exist.
Therefore, it is said that even apart from the external objects upon which the mind relies for its deliberation, the cognizing mind can still arise. The *Zongjing* states:

"The direct object-condition exists only within the cognizing mind itself. Apart from the internal objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) upon which the mind relies for its deliberation, no mental states whatsoever can function."
Therefore, the Mahāyāna states: "If one takes non-existent phenomena as an object, the mind does not arise.

Regarding the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*), whether the cognizing mind arises or not depends on the fact that the object is a phenomenon external to the mind—such as the grasping at a real self or real dharmas—which, although lacking an essential nature (*svabhāva*), still causes the mind to arise even when separated from those phenomena.

Regarding the eighth mental category (*citta-varga*), there is one interpretation that it exists only [in certain states], while another holds that its presence or absence across all stages is indeterminate.

This explains the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the eighth consciousness. Both of the preceding two interpretations are partial; the first [asserts] that it only transforms itself as the direct [object].
The first [position] relies solely on the physical basis (*rūpa*) and is thus considered remote. The third, the correct meaning, incorporates both:

it holds that the seeds within the eighth consciousness take the bodies and lands as their objects. Regarding these bodies and lands, they are mutually experienced; one may say they rely on the physical basis because each transforms from its own side.
However, since sentient beings each possess their own seeds, they do not take one another as objects. Therefore, it is said: "not for all sentient beings."

Because its own internal seeds are equal to the body and the environment, it should be stated below. Regarding the eighth type, the indirect object-condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*), its existence or non-existence is indeterminate, depending on whether [the seeds] have already been transformed or not yet transformed.

In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) during the seventh mental category, because objects such as the past and future lack external substantial entities (*bimba*), the nature of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for both the seventh and sixth consciousnesses is explained as in the text.
Regarding the nature of the object-condition for the first five evolving consciousnesses, according to the *Zongjing lu*, they possess the direct [condition] but lack the indirect;
for although the first five consciousnesses are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), even though they have substantial entities, [the indirect condition does not apply].
When the notion of a substantial entity arises, it takes only its own transformed aspect (*svavikāra-nimitta*) as the object; therefore, this is called "proximate.
This refers to the five sense objects when they are not transformed by oneself, but exist solely as external substances; therefore, these are called "distant.

If one discusses the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) regarding the eight consciousnesses, the distant objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) definitely exists for the seventh and the first five consciousnesses, because they take that [external substance] as their object.

Because an object must necessarily rely upon a substantial entity (*dravya*), whether other [consciousnesses] are active or inactive, their existence or non-existence is indeterminate. Furthermore, regarding the mutual objects of the various consciousnesses:

only the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the first seven; that is, the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of the eighth consciousness serves as the object-condition for the first five.
The sixth consciousness takes the four parts of the eighth consciousness as its object-condition. As for the seventh, it only...
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness relies upon the seeing-parts of the [first] seven consciousnesses as its objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

These [seeing-parts of the first seven] are all the substantial basis (*svabhāva*) for the four parts of the eighth consciousness. The seeing-parts of the first seven transform and take the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their object; this is the remote objective condition.

Only the eighth consciousness does not take the first seven as its object, because the eighth does not arise in dependence upon the first seven; it takes only its own three objects as its objective condition.

This is because of the principle that within the eight [consciousnesses] as presented in the eighth fascicle, the seventh exists in relation to the eighth, whereas the eighth does not exist in relation to the seventh. △ This concludes the third section, the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Below follows the fourth, the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).

The fourth is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). This refers to any phenomenon that, by virtue of its distinct capacity, brings about the four matters of arising, abiding, accomplishment, and attainment.

This explains the meaning of the fourth condition within the aforementioned heading. The *Zongjing* commentary states: "Regarding 'any phenomenon' (*yǒu fǎ*), this refers to a phenomenon that possesses substantial reality (*sattva*).
This serves to exclude those phenomena that are conceptually grasped but lack substantial reality. 'Possessing superior power and function' means that it indeed exists..."

Because both the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) possess a superior function. This function is not the same as the function of "giving fruit" (*phaladāna*) and so forth; rather, non-obstruction is its predominant function (*ādhipatya*).
By specifying "that which is capable with respect to other dharmas," it excludes that which is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

By specifying "its own substance," it shows that it is distinct from the previously mentioned object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). By stating "whether favorable or unfavorable," it shows that it can function as a condition for both the favorable and the unfavorable.
It serves as a condition for subsequent dharmas that are different from it, but not for those that have already ceased; this excludes the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
That is to say, among the ten causes, the preceding and succeeding ones are concordant, while the ninth is discordant, yet all are this condition. Question:

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), how many types are there in total when categorized by the power or lack of power of the inverse and concordant? Answer: According to ancient exegesis, there are four types: first, the concordant dominant condition (*anuloma-adhipati*).
Superior [conditions], such as water, soil, and green grass, are concordant dominant conditions for the six pāramitās and the fruit of Buddhahood.
The two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), like seeds for the five fruits, are also concordant dominant conditions. Two types of discordant dominant conditions are as follows:
first, those that act as discordant dominant conditions, such as frost and hail acting upon green grass; second, those such as wisdom.
Delusion also contradicts the sovereign [condition]. That is to say, at the single moment when wisdom arises and delusion is severed, there are two types of sovereignty:
wisdom acts as a contradictory sovereign with respect to delusion, while it acts as a concordant sovereign with respect to the principle of the two emptinesses. Third is the sovereign of power.
It is also called "proximate predominance," as when the five faculties give rise to the five consciousnesses and so forth. It is "predominance of incapacity":
that is, when a person's five faculties are considered in relation to another person's five consciousnesses, they constitute predominance of incapacity; it is also called "remote predominance."
Just as when the flame of a lamp is in the process of arising, all dharmas such as the great earth do not obstruct the arising of this flame;
this is called the "distant dominant condition" (*viprakṛṣṭādhipatipratyaya*). Taking only the aspect of non-obstruction, it is termed the "dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*).

Although it is listed below the [other] three conditions, the explanation of the four conditions individually further demonstrates that both favorable and adverse factors alike can function as conditions.

However, although its predominant functions are many according to their respective objects—up to and including wholesome mindfulness (*smṛti*) and so forth—it takes these as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Herein is the general indication; in the text, the names, numbers, and essential natures are explained in detail. Regarding the first five material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*), they consist of both the five superficial organs (*vicitrendriya*) and the ultimate sense organs (*paramārthendriya*).

Their essential nature consists of the pure matter (*viśuddharūpa*) that arises as the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) from the transformation of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). (Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra)
It is said: "The five faculties are established on the basis of the sense of predominance regarding physical support and beauty.
As for the male and female faculties, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, they are the secret parts of males and females, having a portion of the body faculty as their essential nature.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: 'The two faculties are established on the basis of the sense of predominance regarding procreation. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* names them..."

Regarding the predominance of production, there are seven faculties when combined with the preceding five. As for the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), it is a provisional designation based on the seed-state of the eighth consciousness;
as the *Yogācārabhūmi* states, "It is established as a single faculty in the sense of being the predominance for reliance and maintenance.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* calls this the predominance of sustaining. When combined with the preceding seven, there are eight. The mind-faculty (*manendriya*)...
This refers to the sixth sense-faculty, the mind (manas). Because the eight manifest consciousnesses all function in accordance with it, these eight consciousnesses constitute its essential nature.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it possesses the dominant meaning of causing the basis [the body] to function in accordance with its own mastery, one sense-faculty is established.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* also calls it the "dominant factor regarding the object" (*viṣayādhipati*). Question: Is this not simply the mind as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-manas*)?

Answer: Since they belong to the category of dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they are necessarily not equivalent to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Together with the previous eight faculties, there are nine.
As for the five feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*), their essential nature consists of the feelings of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.

The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The five faculties are established based on the sense of dominance regarding benefit and harm. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* calls them "dominant regarding the fruit of experience. Together with the previous...

There are fourteen faculties in total. Regarding the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), these consist of the faculties of faith, diligence (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the nature of wholesome mindfulness and so forth.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "The five faculties are established based on the sense of being predominant over mundane purification.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* refers to them as "predominant over mundane detachment and purification. Together with the aforementioned [five], there are fourteen.
There are nineteen; when the latter three faculties are added, there are twenty-two. The former nineteen faculties are explained according to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*);
the latter three faculties are explained according to the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), and are therefore termed "untainted" (*anāsrava*). This will be explained in detail below.

The essence and stages of the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) are of three kinds. (Up to: It is said that only those prior to the [ten] stages are mentioned because their duration is brief.
Regarding the faculty of "knowing what is not yet known," there are three stages: first, the fundamental stage, which refers to one who is on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

This faculty (*indriya*) takes only the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) as its fundamental basis. Excluding the subsequent moment means that even during the single moment following the path of seeing, it is called the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Therefore, it is said: "Because there is nothing further to be known that has not yet been known.

The intention is that prior to seeing the path, it is named the faculty of "knowing the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*); once the path has been seen, it is named the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātendriya*).

Second, regarding the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*): there are four types of application that are proximate to the ability to induce the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and these also constitute the essential state of this faculty.
Third, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*): from the four lower phrases, the limit of the stage of equipment is clarified;
by the single distant phrase, it is shown to be the essential state of this faculty. Below this, the faith (*śraddhā*) present in all three stages is summarized and revealed.
The nine untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). If it is asked:

"In the wholesome state, since there is no faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), it need not be mentioned; why is there no faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?"—the answer to this question is given below in the section on the preparatory stages (*prayoga-avasthā*).

The first three [lines] provide a general explanation, while the following clarify the characteristics and meaning of this faculty as it is cultivated in conjunction with the auxiliary practices. Regarding the first three formless realms (*ārūpya*):

Except for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the spheres of infinite space and so forth, and the transverse cultivation of the path of seeing—wherein there is also the sense of "the unknown yet to be known"—as well as for the two vehicles who have turned their minds to seek the realization of the emptiness of phenomena, and for bodhisattvas prior to the stages who seek to realize the untainted emptiness of persons on the stages:
all these possess the sense of "the unknown yet to be known. The bodhisattva’s path of seeing properly belongs to this faculty; however...
