this is analogous to the principle of ignorance (*avidyā*) depending on another plane.
These twelve links consist of ten causes and two results (up to this point). Otherwise, it would lead to an infinite regress.

This explains how the aforementioned causes and results belong to the same lifetime or different lifetimes: from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to becoming (*bhava*), these ten constitute the causes of the present life.
Birth and old age-and-death constitute two fruits; as these belong to the future, it is said that they are certainly not of the same world (*adhvan*).

Among the causes, the first seven—craving, grasping, and existence—when already moistened [by ignorance], result in retribution in the present life; since this present retribution is necessarily simultaneous [with its cause], it is said that they "may be the same.
When not yet moistened, they result in retribution in a subsequent life; since this subsequent retribution constitutes a different world, it is said that they "may be different. If...
237. "Each is determined to belong to the same world": the two [links]—namely birth and old age/death—belong together to the future;

the three [links]—namely craving, grasping, and becoming—belong together to the present; and the seven [links]—namely ignorance and so forth—likewise belong to the present. Therefore, each belongs to the same world.
Thus, below, it concludes by clarifying that the meaning of a single cycle of cause and effect is established, thereby avoiding the faults of nihilism and eternalism. That is to say:
The arising of the fruit is not annihilation; the cessation of the cause is not permanence. Regarding the designation of two cycles:
the past consists of two members as cause, and the present consists of five members as fruit; the present consists of three members as cause, and the future consists of two members as fruit.

The intention is to demonstrate that the cycle of rebirth is free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. Since establishing a single causal relationship would suffice, the mention of "two cycles" is, in reality, redundant. Or perhaps it should be...
"If one were to go beyond this, it would lead to infinity" indicates the multiplicity of causes and effects. △ The third section, consisting of questions and answers, concludes here.
The following four sections belong to the various gates and comprise fifteen chapters.
Regarding the distinctions among the categories of these twelve links: (up to) within the seven stages, both the wholesome and the defiled arise.
First, the gate of the provisional and the real: this means that three links—birth, old age, and death—are provisional, while the remaining nine are real.

The six links already moistened by craving—namely, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—are the results already moistened; together they constitute *bhava* (existence).
As for this, karma is moistened by the self and falsely constructed through conjunction; therefore, it is said that "karmic existence" (*karma-bhava*) is a mere designation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) have distinct phases of the three characteristics (*tri-lakṣaṇa*), and are thus designated as "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth: this also demonstrates that the two links of birth and so forth are provisionally established based upon the five links beginning with consciousness.

As for the distinction between the three characteristics: birth and old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*) are distinguished such that the process of growth is called "birth," while the process of decay and transformation is called "old age."
The state of disintegration is called death. The fifth [category] is "inferior. Regarding the second point, "one is not one door," the *Yogācārabhūmi* asks:

"How many have a single entity as their intrinsic nature? It replies: "Five. Therefore, the present treatise states that ignorance, consciousness, and so forth constitute a single perceived object (*dṛśya-bhāga*).

Those that are "not a single entity" refer to the seven members beginning with formative forces (*saṃskāra*). The third point, "only inferior," concerns the third category: the defiled and the non-defiled.
Third, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are of the nature of afflictions; therefore, they are called "exclusively defiled" (*kevala-kliṣṭa*).

Seventh, the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the two members beginning with birth (*jāti*) are the fruits of maturation (*vipāka-phala*); they belong to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature and are thus called "non-defiled" (*akliṣṭa*).

If they can give rise to defilement, they are metaphorically said to be "common to both. As for the others being common to both types: the two members of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are both defiled and non-defiled.

Therefore, below "ignorance" (avidyā), is the fourth section: the Gate of Exclusive and Mixed Characteristics. Ignorance, craving (tṛṣṇā), and grasping (upādāna) are termed "exclusive characteristics" because they are purely defiled.

The nine factors beginning with formative forces (saṃskāra) are termed "mixed characteristics" because they encompass both the wholesome and the defiled. Below "six are exclusively... [the text continues].

The fifth is the section on the non-material and the material. That which is non-material is the mind; therefore, the six factors beginning with ignorance belong exclusively to the mental states (*caitta*).
Consciousness is the mind-king (*cittarāja*). Ignorance, craving, and grasping are defiled mental states. Contact and feeling are the universal mental states (*sarvatraga-caitta*).

As for those that pertain to both types, the six factors beginning with formations (*saṃskāra*) pertain to both the material and the mental, and thus all are classified as "lower. This is the sixth [section].

The gate of the outflows (*āsrava*) and the non-outflows (*anāsrava*). Below [the section on] ignorance (*avidyā*). Seventh, the gate of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*): Ignorance, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are defiled mental factors (*kliṣṭa-caitta*);

they pertain exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the seeds of karma; therefore, they are exclusively wholesome or unwholesome.

Although existence (*bhava*) is also karma, because it is a composite of the member of volitional formations as well as the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is categorized under the member of volitional formations.

Generally speaking, the wholesome and unwholesome [factors] are explained based on the five beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the statement that the "remaining seven" are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*):

these consist of the five beginning with consciousness and the two beginning with arising (*jāti*). These are maturation results (*vipākaphala*) and are exclusively of a non-obscured nature. However, when they arise as wholesome or defiled, they also pertain to all three natures.

Although all [factors] pertain to the three realms, they are either partial or complete (*sarva-bhāga* / *aśeṣa*). (Up to: there is no contradiction in principle regarding the arising in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and so forth.
"Although all" refers to the eighth section on the three realms. That is to say, within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), all factors are complete;
in the Form and Formless Realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), all factors are partial. The subsequent sections explain the meaning that in the upper two realms, all factors are only one part. Six.
Regarding the aspects (*ākāra*): first is suffering (*duḥkha*). This refers to the mental factors (*caitasika*) arising within the body that take desire as their object;

this is the suffering of the cause, as it prevents one from attaining liberation. Furthermore, being associated with the desire realm, the body is oppressed by various conditions such as hunger, thirst, cold, heat, illness, pain, swords, and staves;

this is the suffering of the result. Second is coarseness (*audārika*). This refers to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of the desire realm which can give rise to manifold evils; this is the coarseness of the cause.
This body consists of thirty-six components, accomplished through the foul impurities of excrement and urine; this is the coarse fruit. The three obstructions are as follows:

the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) veils the true nature, preventing its manifestation; this is the causal obstruction. This body is characterized by substantiality and resistance, lacking sovereignty;
this is the resultant obstruction. The four excellences (also called purities) refer to the revulsion toward the inferior desires of the desire realm.
Regarding the suffering of desire: one takes joy in the superior meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the first *dhyāna* and above; this is "superiority of the cause.

Furthermore, one feels aversion toward the sufferings of hunger, thirst, and so forth within the desire realm, and takes joy in the bliss of the flavor of *dhyāna* (*dhyānāsvāda*) of the first *dhyāna*; this is "superiority of the fruit. Regarding the five wonders:

having become weary of the pleasures of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and sensual desires of the desire realm, one perceives that the mind’s distracted and restless movement is coarse; thus, one takes joy in the first [dhyāna].
Regarding the excellence of the cause: it is the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), wherein the mind is fixed and unmoving. Regarding the excellence of the result:

one further grows weary of the foul and impure body of the desire realm as being coarse, and thus joyfully attains the body of the first dhyāna. Like a reflection in a mirror, although it possesses form and color, it lacks substantiality or obstruction.
The six "exits" (also called "leavings") refer to having already grown weary of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśa-nīvaraṇa*) of the desire realm.

Obstruction. This is the cause for emergence, as one rejoices in the mind of the first dhyāna and attains liberation. Furthermore, one feels aversion toward the body of the desire realm, which is characterized by physical obstruction and lacks sovereignty;
thus, one rejoices in obtaining the body of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) in the first dhyāna, which is sovereign and unimpeded.

This is the emergence of the fruit, namely: weariness with the lower [realms] as being characterized by suffering, coarseness, and obstruction; and aspiration for the higher [realms] as being superior, sublime, and an emergence.

These are the six modes of activity initiated by those who seek rebirth in the higher realms. All that is lower belongs to the ninth category of the "Training and Beyond Training" (śaikṣa-aśaikṣa) section, referring to the twelve links [of dependent origination].
These are not possessed by noble ones who are either in training or beyond training (*śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa*). Their contaminated wholesome states take clarity (*vidyā*) as their basis.

The condition (*pratyaya*) is precisely that which is contrary to the link of existence (*bhava-aṅga*). Because one does not create future karma, one likewise does not deludedly seek after the fruit of suffering.
Question: If one does not induce a future existence (*punar-bhava*), how is it that one is born in the higher realms? Answer: Through "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) and so forth.

Cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*) within the tainted heavens is called "mixed cultivation. As for what is called "past karma," this refers to the three heavens: Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala.
Regarding karma:

one interpretation holds that ignorance (*avidyā*) is abandoned solely by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), while the remaining nine [limbs] are all common to both the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

This tenth point concerning the gates of seeing and cultivation is not yet correct; for it is said that the limb of ignorance is abandoned solely by the path of seeing and is not abandoned by cultivation.

The path is severed. [The phrase] "essentially deluded regarding the lower" explains that the various noble ones possess no ignorance; they are not deluded regarding the principle of the truths (*satya*), nor do they initiate karma-formations (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, they also do not create [karma] through delusion regarding future existence (*punarbhava*).

The fact that the two branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) demonstrates that they are innate (*sahaja*) and are not abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*). This is proven by the citation of nine types of minds. The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states:

Regarding the power of continuity, there are nine types of death-consciousness associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvātṛṣṇā*), which cause the continuity of rebirth within the three realms—specifically the desire, form, and formless realms.

First: when one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, the continuity of rebirth is linked by a death-consciousness associated with self-love for a body belonging to the desire realm. Second...

Those who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the form realm, connect the succession of birth by means of a death-consciousness associated with craving for the self-existence of the form realm.

Third, those who pass away from the desire realm and are reborn in the formless realm, connect the succession of birth by means of a death-consciousness associated with craving for the self-existence of the formless realm. Thus it is in the desire realm...
There are not three [types of death]. Death in the form realm and the formless realm each has three types, totaling nine types.

According to one interpretation, all are common to both types of abandonment (the abandonment of afflictions through insight and the abandonment through cultivation); however, those that assist [the path] are abandoned solely through cultivation, though their specific nature is not fixed.

"Righteousness refutes the former" means that the twelve links are common to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). "The treatise says below" refers to citing the *Yogācārabhūmi* as proof.
"If there were no... refutes the view that [ignorance] is severed only by seeing. "If craving... refutes the view that it is severed only by cultivation.

Furthermore, "the treatise says below" again cites the intent of the treatise to prove that the ignorance which directly initiates action is severed only by the path of seeing; it does not say that craving and grasping are [severed only by cultivation].
This refers to abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). "The entire realm" refers to the three realms;

that is to say, all afflictions within the three realms are capable of producing rebirth and leading to conduct that goes toward the evil destinies. It is specifically the ignorance arising from discrimination (*vikalpa*) that can incite them.

It does not state that the afflictions of craving and grasping which moisten rebirth are abandoned only by cultivation. Furthermore, it explains: "That is to say, the treatise states that the formations (*saṃskāra*) which induce future existence..."

The ignorance (*avidyā*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) is able to initiate [the process]; this concludes the preceding section. To clarify the correct meaning, there are two points:

although both [ignorance and craving] are capable of abandoning [their respective objects], the explanation below regarding ignorance shows that while ignorance is the primary factor, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are its auxiliaries.

If one relies on the primary factor to initiate and the primary factor to moisten, then "existence" (*bhava*) would be abandoned solely by insight or solely by cultivation (*bhāvanā*). However, according to the auxiliary factor, it is not fixed; it also extends to both insight and cultivation.

Furthermore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) should be abandoned; [the phrase] "as before" indicates that these various abandonments should be understood as appropriate.
Furthermore, "defiled" below clarifies that defiled phenomena should be abandoned. "All" below clarifies that, according to principle, pure phenomena (*viśuddha-dharma*) should not be abandoned.
Nevertheless, there are two senses in which they are said to be "abandoned": first, "separation from bondage" below refers to the giving (*dāna*) arising within the first six consciousnesses.
All contaminated wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) are grasped as "self" by the seventh consciousness moment by moment; because they cannot eliminate these signs, they are called "bondage.
To sever that [grasping] is called "liberation. Therefore, the commentary states: "It means severing those afflictions that take them as objects and are associated with them.

Both instances of the word "those" (*teṣām*) refer to non-defiled dharmas—that is, the eighth consciousness of the nature of non-obscured neutrality (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-svabhāva*), as well as those present within the first six consciousnesses.

The outflowing wholesome dharmas are grasped as "self" by the seventh consciousness as its object; therefore, since it takes them as its object, these neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are permeated by defiled dharmas, and thus they are said to be "mixed with" them.
Second, "not arising in the lower realms" refers to wholesome and unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas, which take the various destinies (*gati*) as their basis.
When those bases are severed, they will not arise of themselves. Regarding "based on detachment from the lower," this explains [the term] "not."

Defilements (kleśa) also pertain to both types of abandonment: those that are wholesome and those that are non-obscured (anivṛta), which are abandoned only upon perfect enlightenment; therefore, they are abandoned solely through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).

As for the evil destinies and the state of non-perception (asaṃjñi-sattva), these are the bases for those [defilements]; because they are never again produced once the single true path of vision (darśana-mārga) has arisen, they are abandoned through vision (darśana-heya).

The section on the "Twelve Lower [Factors]" concludes by clarifying the previously explained twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). All of them are common to both those abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Ten [of these factors] are associated with the feelings of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), while five are not associated with feeling; furthermore, they are all subsumed under the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), because their nature consists of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

10. The section on pleasure and equanimity (*sukha-upekṣā*). 11. The section on the three feelings (*tri-vedanā-mukha*). This refers to the remaining ten members, excluding the member of feeling (*vedanā*) and the member of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which all pertain to both pleasure and equanimity.
This is because a feeling does not coexist with another feeling. Furthermore, although the stage of aging-and-death can accommodate equanimity, it generally lacks pleasant feeling;
therefore, that [member] is also excluded. Moreover, excluding the member of feeling, the remaining eleven members are suffering (*duḥkha*).
Because they are associated with feeling (*vedanā*). Examining this treatise, among the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), only the link of feeling itself is not associated with all three types of feeling.

Furthermore, although the link of aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is not associated with pleasant feeling, it does extend to painful and neutral feelings. The remaining ten links are all associated with the three types of feeling.
Regarding the "eleven partials" below, the section on the "twelve gates of suffering" refers to the ten links excluding aging-and-death.
Each [of the twelve links] has a small portion subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Question: Why are the links of old age and death excluded? Answer:
The cause of the suffering of change is pleasure; because when pleasure changes, its corresponding suffering necessarily arises, it is called "the suffering of changing pleasure.

The designation "change" is established based on pleasure, and thus old age and death are not mentioned [in this context], because the link of old age and death generally lacks pleasure. Furthermore, each of the twelve links...
A small portion is subsumed under the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because not all of the [twelve] links are entirely suffering.

Furthermore, all twelve links in their entirety are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are the suffering of conditioned formations. Regarding the explanation based on equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*):

these three types of suffering correspond to the three feelings (*vedanā*) mentioned above; the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) corresponds to pleasant feeling, and the suffering of pain corresponds to painful feeling.
The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is identical to the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

Because that feeling of equanimity does not conflict with either suffering or pleasure, this suffering of conditioned existence subsumes the entirety of the previous two types of suffering by taking a small portion from each and combining them into a whole. Furthermore, it is said that the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) is the fruit of suffering.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The feeling of suffering takes the nature of suffering itself as its specific characteristic; therefore, it is called the nature of the suffering of suffering. The suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) is suffering..."

Regarding the cause: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that within this context, pleasant feelings (*sukha-vedanā*) and those phenomena conducive to pleasant feelings give rise to sorrow and affliction at the stage of transformation and decay;

therefore, the transformation and decay of pleasure is the cause of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is the seed of suffering, because "conditioned existence" refers to karma, which is termed the "seed of karma.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "This means that the two sufferings of pain (*duḥkha*) and change (*vipariṇāma*) are accompanied by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*). Because...
The term "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) has the meaning of "seed. It refers to eleven [of the twelve links] in part, excluding the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

As for the statement that it is like the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), this means that since this [suffering of conditioning] follows the suffering of change alone, the link of old age and death is also excluded; thus, there are only eleven parts.

Regarding "The True Meaning" (*sadartha*) below: the conclusion of the preceding instructional intent is as in the text. Regarding "All are under the Truth of Suffering" (*duḥkhasatya*): this refers to the thirteen gates of the Four Noble Truths.

That is to say, the twelve links belong to the gate of cyclic flow (*pravṛtti-mukha*) and are, by nature, the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), thus being subsumed solely under the Truth of Suffering. As for the five that are also subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*):

these are the two branches of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), along with ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*). Combined, these five branches are karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore...
This comprehensively subsumes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

Regarding the mutual relationship of the various factors (*aṅga*), the predominance (*adhipati*) is certainly established. (Up to: It is taught that based on present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), there is only karmic existence (*karmabhava*).

This is the section on the fourteen gates of the four conditions (*catuḥpratyaya*); that is, regarding the mutual relationship of the twelve factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), the predominance is certainly established, because of that predominance.
Because the substance of the superior [condition] is broad, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* speaks of only one;

as for the other three conditions whose presence or absence is indeterminate, they are omitted from the brief explanation because their meanings are restricted. Question: What is meant by "the presence or absence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is indeterminate"?
In the text, there are three parts to the answer and explanation: first, answering that it truly exists; second, clarifying its indeterminacy.
The third example concerns the remaining members. Regarding "craving in relation to what is below," this explains the meaning that the presence or absence of causal conditions is not fixed.

When craving is related to grasping, there are cases where causal conditions exist: when craving intensifies, it becomes grasping. This is because at the initial stage of craving, craving is the seed, whereas grasping occurs subsequently;
thus, grasping is the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of craving. Therefore, craving is the seed for grasping, and grasping is [the manifestation] of craving.
Manifestation has the sense of having causes and conditions. Regarding that which has causes and conditions for its arising, consciousness increases to become existence (*bhava*).

Since that branch of existence (*bhavāṅga*) originally has no separate essence, it is through the moistening of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) that the five factors, beginning with consciousness, constitute the branch of existence.

Thus, existence is the seed of consciousness, and birth (*jāti*) is the manifestation of consciousness. The seed of consciousness as the branch of existence gives rise to the manifestation of consciousness; this is the cause of existence.
Regarding the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*): this first answer establishes that [the link] actually exists. As for the statement "if one says... and so forth:

it means that if the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) were taken as the member of consciousness, then *saṃskāra* would have only a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) in relation to consciousness; however, since the seed of karma (*karma-bīja*) is now taken as the member of consciousness, *saṃskāra* possesses the sense of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) in relation to consciousness.
These two cases clarify that [the relationship] is not fixed. For the remaining members, when compared with one another, there is no causal condition.
This refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
When these members are viewed in relation to one another, none possess the nature of a causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). These three examples apply to the remaining members as well. Question:

Since the others lack the nature of a causal condition, why does the treatise state that there is the meaning of a causal condition when ignorance is viewed in relation to formations (*saṃskāra*)? Answer: It is because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that regarding ignorance in relation to formations and so forth, it is called "ignorance" [in that context].

Regarding the period of clarity (*vidyā-kāla*): the latencies of formative forces (*saṃskāra-vāsanā*) coexist with ignorance (*avidyā*). While they are conventionally designated as "ignorance," they are in reality the seeds of formative forces.
Because they establish the causal condition for formative forces, they are called "ignorance. Question:

Since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the condition for grasping (*upādāna*) and existence (*bhava*) is the condition for birth (*jāti*), why does the treatise state that the various links (*aṅga*) have no mutual causal conditions? Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* relies upon the manifest [state].

Regarding the statement that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are conditions for karmic existence (*karma-bhava*): when referring to past craving and grasping, they serve as the causal conditions for obtaining [existence].

However, in the present case, when comparing presently active craving to presently active grasping, it is not the case that the former is the seed of the latter; therefore, it is not a causal condition. Regarding the statement that only karmic existence is a condition:
when referring to past [karmic existence] in relation to birth (*jāti*), it serves as the causal condition for obtaining [existence]; now, it is only karmic existence [that is the condition].

The seeds of various aspirations give rise to manifest activity; since karma is not consciousness itself, it possesses only the status of a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and lacks the principle of being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Question: The causal conditions have already been explained. How are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) established, given that their presence or absence is not fixed? The following text provides the answer and explanation.

Regarding the relationship between ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), up to [the relationship between birth and] aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the wise should reflect according to reason.
The existence or non-existence of the equal-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) is not fixed.

When it is said that there are two conditions for ignorance and formations, and for craving and grasping, as well as for birth and aging-and-death, this is based on the relationship between active states (*samudācāra*) and active states. This is because...

Ignorance initiates the formations; thus, the formations are identical to ignorance. When the mind of ignorance ceases, it induces the mind of formations. Craving increases to become grasping; thus, grasping is identical to craving.
When the preceding mind of craving ceases, it induces the subsequent grasping. Birth, as well as aging and death, are merely the growth and the decay of consciousness and name-and-form.
When the mind of growth ceases, it induces decay. Therefore, these three— [craving, grasping, and existence]—are one.

In these stages, there is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness arises; it takes ignorance (*avidyā*) as its object. Grasping (*upādāna*) takes craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its object;

old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) take birth (*jāti*) as their object. Thus, the link of ignorance serves as the object-condition for the two links of volitional formations and grasping, as well as for the link of old age and death.
This clarifies that in three positions, two conditions are present: hope (*āśā*) in relation to birth, and feeling (*vedanā*) in relation to craving.

Regarding the absence of an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) while possessing an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): this refers to the relationship between seeds and their manifest activities.

That which arises is what is grasped by the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); thus, even the perfectly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) could potentially be grasped as pervasive conceptualization.
Furthermore, [the opponent] refutes this, saying: "Although it is that object, it is not an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);

therefore, it is not that which is pervasively conceptualized, because the Real necessarily does not induce the production of the false. The second section, "Discriminating the Subject and Object," is concluded. This concludes the preceding explanation of the first four [verses].
The verse ends here. The following two lines explain the fifth phrase.
What are the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)? [From here until] "the grasping of the two is called the thoroughly imagined."
Regarding the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): the previous statement referred to the falsely grasped aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Since these aggregates and so forth are themselves the "dependent" (*paratantra*), the question is asked: what is the distinction? One interpretation holds that the following passage is not correctly identified as the words of Sthiramati’s response. It states:

the false habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) exist conventionally but are non-existent in reality; this image is called the "thoroughly imagined. Here, the image is identical to the seeing-part.
Regarding the characteristics of the two divisions: the "imagined" (*parikalpita*) refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*); the "grasped" refers to the appearance-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Below, regarding the "basis of these two," this explains the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). These two—the seeing and appearance divisions—are the basis, whose substance is the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*).

Because it truly arises based upon conditions, it is called the dependent nature. Question: How is this known to be so? Answer: It is stated in various sacred teachings that [the dependent nature] is false and illusory.

Regarding [the passage] beginning with "discrimination" (*vikalpa*), there is one interpretation which holds that all minds and mental factors (up to the point of... should be understood as being likewise *sāsrava* (with outflows), provided they are not otherwise permitted.
The correct view refutes the former, stating that both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are produced by the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of all minds and mental factors.

Transformation arises from various conditions and is also of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Why then is the grasping at the characteristics of the seeing and seen portions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) considered the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)?
Furthermore, the imagined nature is universally admitted to consist in the false attachment to existence, non-existence, identity, difference, and so forth, based upon these seeing and seen portions.

Only when these two—existence and non-existence—as well as these two—identity and difference—are present can they be termed the "imagined" (*parikalpita*). How could the two portions of seeing and seen themselves be called the imagined nature?
Regarding the phrase "The various noble ones... and below, this cites scriptural evidence that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) does not consist of only a single type of object.

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "How is it established that all consciousnesses are *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)? Briefly stated, there are three aspects: first, 'only measure,' because objects do not exist;
second, 'only two,' namely, because there are consciousnesses consisting of the image (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*); third, 'only various kinds'."
This means that various characteristics arise. Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Only-cognition" (*vijñaptimātra*) means that it is merely the measure of consciousness;
all cognitions are merely the measure of consciousness because the objects of cognition do not exist.

"Only-two" establishes the existence of the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*); that is, one part of this single consciousness constitutes the aspect, while the second part constitutes the vision.
This is because the eye-consciousness and the others each have two parts. Regarding "only various [aspects]":

this refers to the fact that the consciousnesses of the six sense-objects arising from this single consciousness constitute the *nimitta* (aspect), while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) constitutes the *darśana* (seeing). Because the objects of the mental consciousness are not fixed, it is said to be "only various.

Therefore, within a single consciousness, that which is distinguished is the seeing, and that which is distinguished is the aspect; in their totality, they do not depart from consciousness, thereby establishing *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only).

Furthermore, he cites scriptural authority to refute the preceding position. The four factors, beginning with "characteristics" (*nimitta*), are the characteristic-part (*nimittabhāga*), the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*), the self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*), and the self-cognizing-of-self-cognizing-part (*svasaṃvitti-svasaṃvittibhāga*).

Regarding the "eleven consciousnesses," etc.: first, the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), which refers to the five elements such as the eye; second, the consciousness of the body (*kāyasya vijñāna*), which refers to the afflicted consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*);

third, the experiencing-consciousness (*vedakavijñāna*), which refers to the mind-element (*manodhātu*); fourth, the object-of-experience-consciousness (*veditavyavijñāna*), which refers to form (*rūpa*).

The six external objects; the five consciousnesses of direct experience, namely the six consciousness-elements; the six worldly consciousnesses, namely the consciousness that continues the succession of birth and death;
the seventh, the consciousness of number, namely from one up to asaṃkhyeya; the eighth, the consciousness of location, namely the receptacle world;
and the ninth, the consciousness of verbal expression, namely the four kinds of verbal expression consisting of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. These are the nine consciousnesses.
All these are based upon the熏習 (vāsanā, perfuming) of names and words derived from seeing, hearing, and so forth, with their various distinctions serving as the cause.

The tenth is the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, which refers to the distinction of the physical body; it takes the熏習 (vāsanā) of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as its cause.

The eleventh is the consciousness of birth and death within the two paths of good and evil, which refers to the immeasurable varieties of rebirth destinies; it arises from the seeds of the熏習 (vāsanā) of the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).
Regarding the characteristics mentioned above, the treatises all state that they are subsumed under the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature);

they never state that they are the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Otherwise—that is, if seeing and appearance were not considered *paratantra* but necessarily *parikalpita*—it would be difficult to explain how [the treatises] say "the untainted, etc.
This is because even the untainted mind has two parts, and it is accepted that wisdom has two parts.

This is the parikalpita (imagined nature). It follows that noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) should not arise by taking the two parts as its object; and wisdom that takes the two parts as its object should not be the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Since it is not admitted that the two parts within the category of wisdom are parikalpita, one should know that the two parts of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [nature] are likewise not parikalpita.
If they are not parikalpita, how could they not be paratantra (dependent nature)?
Furthermore, if these two parts were merely imagined (*parikalpita*), they could not arise based on the various conditions of the dependent nature (*paratantra*).

This uses an analogy to refute that the imagined is unreal: since the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the subjective part (*darśana-bhāga*) and possesses substantial reality, how could it be the same as a rabbit’s horn, which is unreal?
Furthermore, below this, it refutes [the position] again by means of the meaning of seeds (*bīja*), namely:
If these two parts were of the nature of parikalpita (imagined), they would be false imaginings and would not perfume to form seeds.

Since there would be no prior seeds, the subsequent [moments] would not arise either; thus it is said that when subsequent consciousnesses and so forth arise, they should lack these two parts. Furthermore, the seeds of habitual tendencies are subsumed under the nimitta-bhāga (objective aspect);
how could they act as causes and conditions like the non-existent phenomenon of a rabbit’s horn? If one takes the lower [level] as the object...

Ananta (Sthiramati) maintains that only the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and not the object-portion (*nimittabhāga*) or the seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*).
Therefore, this [text] refutes him as follows: "The object- and seeing-portions must arise with the self-cognizing portion as their cause.

Since the dependent object- and seeing-portions are not the dependent nature, their basis—the self-cognizing portion—is likewise not the dependent nature. Thus it says: "Because there is no distinct cause. The section beginning with "By this" concludes and clarifies [the point].
The correct meaning of the *paratantra-svabhāva*. △ Second, the explanation of the fifth phrase is concluded. Below, three [points] explain the sixth phrase.
The verse says: "That which is produced by conditions through discrimination" (up to) "is all subsumed within this *paratantra*."
Regarding the statement in the verse that "that which arises from conditions is conceptualized," this refers exclusively to the defiled portion of the *paratantra-svabhāva*.
This is because the pure portion of the *paratantra* as well as the *pariniṣpanna* are non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). Alternatively, another interpretation is offered below:

all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), whether defiled or pure, are termed "conceptualization" because they are capable of objective cognition; thus, they are all subsumed within this category.
Within the *paratantra-svabhāva*. △ Third, the explanation of the sixth phrase is concluded. Below, four [points] explain the seventh and eighth phrases.

Because the perfectly accomplished nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness, is true suchness (*tathatā*) whose nature is free from both existence and non-existence.

Below "the two emptinesses," the names are indicated. Below "to reveal this," the meanings are explained. "Specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*) refer to the distinct individual essences of all phenomena.

"Common characteristics" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) refer to the shared nature of impermanence. "Space, self, and so forth" are what are falsely grasped. They are based on the dependent nature and are falsely conceptualized.

Neither of these is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); therefore, both are excluded [from that category]. As for "uncontaminated conditioned phenomena" (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*), they refer to the two fruits:
*nirvāṇa* and *bodhi*. Thus it is said: being free from inversion and ultimate, and possessing pervasive, superior function, they also receive the name "perfected reality.

The reason the former is mentioned and not the latter is that the former is explained in terms of principle—that is, the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*)—while the latter is explained in terms of fruit—that is, the uncontaminated.

...and so forth. Now, regarding the mention of "perfected reality" (*pariniṣpanna*) in this verse, it is stated from the perspective of principle (*tattva*), not because it refers to the fruit (*phala*).

This [refers to] the word "this" (*idam*) below; that is, "this" refers to perfected reality. It provides a general explanation of the meaning of "perfected reality" in the verse: "it is always devoid of the nature of the former.
Regarding the phrase "at that" (*tasmin*) below, it provides a specific explanation of the two characters "at that," thereby completing the meaning of the seventh line of the verse: "always..."

"Far removed from the inferior" explains the eighth phrase through three distinct sections. First, the expression "always far removed" reveals the abandonment of the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Second, the word "from" reveals the abandonment of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Third, the word "nature" (*svabhāva*) reveals the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Therefore, to say "far removed from existence" means to be far removed from the dependent nature;
to say "far removed from non-existence" means to be far removed from the imputed nature. This demonstrates that the character "nature" refers to the perfected nature.
It is established as a substantial entity. △ Fourth, the explanation of the seventh and eighth phrases is concluded. Below, the fifth section explains the final four phrases:
"Because of the preceding principle, this perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) [exists] because the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti) exist in mutual dependence."

From the preceding section, the general meaning of the two lines of the verse has been briefly explained. From "If they were different" (*anya*) onwards, the meaning of being neither different nor non-different is analyzed.
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); that [perfected nature] is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If they were different, then the perfected nature would not be the actual nature of the dependent nature; for the dependent nature must have the perfected nature as its essence. If...

If they were not different, they would necessarily be identical. Thus, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) would be identical to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature would consequently be impermanent, because the dependent nature has the meaning of impermanence.
Regarding the dependent nature, the opposite of the above applies. Below this, the objection concerns the non-distinction between object and cognition:

namely, that the dependent nature is the impure object, which is the focal point of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); whereas the perfected nature is the pure object, which is the focal point of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Regarding the object of cognition (*ālambana*): if they were not different, both would necessarily have no distinction. How is it that these two natures are neither different nor identical?

This is the question. "Neither identical" means precisely "not non-different. That is to say, how are these two natures—the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—neither different nor non-different?
To answer this, an analogy is provided below: as it is said in various holy teachings regarding that form (*rūpa*).
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the mind are dharmas that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self.

Because the dharmas of form and mind each possess their own distinct substance, this constitutes their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That they equally belong to the category of impermanence and so forth constitutes their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

If the nature of impermanence and so forth were different from the dharmas such as the formations (*saṃskāra*), then those formations would not be impermanent and so forth; for [if they were different], the formations...

Regarding the Dharma: because it is characterized by impermanence (*anityatā*). If it were not different [from the conditioned phenomena], then this impermanence would have to be the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those conditioned phenomena, rather than their general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Yet you speak of them as being "common" (*sādhāraṇa*); for the meaning of "common" is only revealed when impermanence is itself impermanent and the conditioned phenomena are themselves conditioned phenomena.
How could they not be different? From here below, the author concludes by applying the analogy to the principle.

This clarifies the meaning of the verses consisting of nine, ten, and eleven lines. "Phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to all dharmas; it is illustrated by the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and is termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
"Nature" (*dharmatā*) refers to impermanence and so forth; it is illustrated by the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and is termed ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Both are neither identical nor separate, because they exist in mutual dependence; this is necessarily the case according to reason.
It is not that one does not realize and see this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) [as being] like illusory phenomena and the like—though they exist, they are not real.
"Not below" briefly indicates the meaning of the verse: this is the perfected nature and the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); that is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Both the perfected and the imputed are manifested by the dependent nature. "Non-conceptual" below explains the preceding phrase "it is not that one does not realize and see."
The latter two lines refer to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Once one has attained the realization of *tathatā* (suchness) and perfected the thoroughly established nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), only then does one give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) to comprehend the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being like illusory phenomena and so forth.

If one does not realize suchness, one falsely clings to the dependent nature as being real. Question: Since beginningless time, the mind and mental factors have taken the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing [part] (*darśana*) as their objects. Already...
[Question: "If one is able to thoroughly comprehend [this], why wait for subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) in order to be able to comprehend it? [Answer:

In the response, the two lines below "not having previously comprehended" (*aprati-pūrva-vikalpa*) are explained. This means that although the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have, since beginningless time, taken the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) as their objects, because the grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) has always accompanied them, they are unable to know that their own minds and mental factors are false manifestations.
Like magical illusions and the like, they do not exist yet appear as if they do. As explained below, eight types of metaphors are used to illustrate their falsity and lack of substantial reality.
The specific meanings of each of these eight metaphors are clearly elucidated in Chengquan’s *Commentary* (*Qingliang shu*); as the text is extensive, I shall not cite it here.

"Based on this [passage] below," etc., cites scriptural authority to establish the preceding meaning. The first line cites authority for the four characters "not failing to see this" from the previous verse.

The intent here is to explain that these three types of self-nature (up to) "therefore, these three are not separate from mind and so forth."

The section beginning with "The foolish" explains that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is likewise not separate from the mind, because it is also falsely grasped upon the phenomena of one's own mind.
