When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, [the afflictions] are severed once and for all. This concludes the eleven explanations of the specific names.
Although these ten categories of meaning are infinite in their distinctions, they are all subsumed within the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

In summary, although the categories of meaning are infinite, the essential framework is briefly indicated by the questions: regarding the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), what is their basis and how are they cultivated?

Answer: Although all ten are indeed cultivated throughout the ten stages, they are assigned according to the predominance of their respective characteristics; thus, one specific practice is cultivated in each stage.
Question: The practices (*caryā*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are infinitely diverse; why are there only ten types? Answer:

Although the ten stages possess infinite doors [of practice], they are all subsumed within the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). This concludes the twelfth summary. △ The twenty superior practices are concluded.
Below, the thirtyfold section on obstructions is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the ten types.

Regarding the ten heavy obstacles: the first is the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*). [This continues] until: "Therefore, there is no fault of the two natures being established simultaneously.
Among the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) mentioned in summary, the ten kinds of heavy obstacles to be abandoned are explained individually in the text.

As for the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being, it is established based on the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization (*parikalpita*). If those seeds are severed, it is transformed and termed the "nature of an ārya" (*āryatva*). It should be...

One should know that these obstacles exist only prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). That which is termed "the nature of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanatva*) refers to the three levels of worthies (*śaikṣa*) and the six paths of existence.

Those who sever only one type [of obstacle] are the followers of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); at the time of their path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they sever only the afflictions of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-kleśa*) and thereby enter the stream of the noble ones, which is termed "the nature of the noble ones" (*āryatva*).
As for Bodhisattvas, who sever both types, the word "both" (*ubhaya*) should be used; at the time of their path of seeing, they sever both simultaneously.

One distinguishes between the seeds of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Upon entering the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), one is said to have attained the nature of a noble one.

Later, in the "Extensive Transformation" section of the tenth fascicle, one is fully able to penetrate [this]; there, the word "simultaneous" (*ju*) should also be employed. Below the two "True" [sections], it clarifies that the natures of ordinary beings and noble ones do not arise simultaneously.

Although there are differences in the narrowness or breadth of severing the delusions of conceptualization (*vikalpa-kleśa*) between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, [this occurs] at the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Because both are real, it is called the "two-fold true path of vision" (*darśanamārga*). The phrase "just as when [the scale] is lowered" is a metaphor for their not arising simultaneously; the phrase "like a balance scale" is a metaphor for the absence of interruption.
Since the afflictions (*kleśa*) are eliminated at the very moment wisdom (*jñāna*) arises, it is said that "the lowering and raising occur at the same time.

As for the statement, "In principle, this must necessarily be so for all mutually contradictory phenomena," it means that wisdom and affliction are contradictory; there has never been a case where wisdom exists while [affliction] is permitted to exist.
Confusion. There has never been a case where confusion exists and wisdom also exists simultaneously; therefore, it is said that there is no fault of the two natures being established together.

The intent of the treatise differs from the Sarvāstivāda school. According to that school’s position, prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned.

When the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) arises, there is no longer any coexistence with the seeds of confusion, and thus it is said that [the nature] is "abandoned. That school then raises an objection: "Since it is based on the path of seeing that [the nature] is abandoned..."

Regarding the establishment of the name "seed": since it is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) that possesses the seeds of afflictions, and these have not yet been severed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), how is it that there is no fault of ordinary and noble ones existing simultaneously?
Therefore, this commentary states: when the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) arises, those seeds are no longer established;
just as when light appears, it does not coexist with darkness, so too there is no fault of the natures of ordinary and noble ones existing simultaneously.

At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the seeds of affliction already no longer exist. (This applies up to) the general statement regarding being "deluded," which is explained hereafter by analogy.

The question and answer clarify the severing of afflictions and the realization of the fruit, based on the distinction in the aspirational mind. Regarding the path of uninterrupted transition—that is, at the time of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)—it is said that once the path of seeing has been attained, the seeds of affliction no longer exist.
What, then, is the further use of the subsequently arising path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? The answer is: it is for the purpose of severing [the remaining] afflictions.

"Realizing cessation" (*nirodha-sākṣātkriyā*). Regarding "because the intended objects differ": at the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is only able to sever the afflictions;

it is only at the time of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that one realizes the fruit. Therefore, it is said that the "intended objects differ. Subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) severs the afflictions, while fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes the fruit; therefore, it is said that the "intentions differ.
"In order to abandon the heavy-obstruction nature (*dauṣṭhulya*) of that category" explains the reason for the arising of the path of liberation.

Furthermore, he himself says: "At the time of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), although the seeds of conceptualized afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) are absent, the seeds of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) have not yet been abandoned.

Because their nature is subtle, they are termed 'incapable' (*akarmanya*). In order to abandon them and to realize the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*) of this category, one gives rise to liberation (*vimukti*).
As for the phrase "of this category," it refers precisely to these aforementioned seeds of conceptualized [afflictions] that have already been severed.

An objection is raised: "Once the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has arisen, one is already designated as a noble one (*ārya*). How, then, can there still be the karmic fruits of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
The response is: "Although the path of seeing has arisen and thereby severed [certain] karmic fruits, it is now said that on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since these are the root of the karmic fruits of the various miserable realms (*durgati*), it is said that on the first stage one abandons two kinds of ignorance (*moha*) along with their seeds."

The term "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) has the meaning of "seed. The first [section], "Grasping at the Lower," explains the two aforementioned delusions; these are collectively the conceptual grasping at the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

However, because there is a distinction between cause and effect, they are divided into two types; thus they are called "categories of delusion" (*moha-pakṣa*), and are generally referred to as "delusion" (*moha*).
Regarding the subsequent explanation based on this: since it is so for the first stage (*bhūmi*), the same applies to the nine subsequent stages.

Alternatively, that [text] speaks only of the sharp and dull categories of hindrances (āvaraṇa-pakṣa), specifically regarding those abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it provides another interpretation to explain the preceding meaning: because afflictions (*kleśa*) are of a defiled nature (*kliṣṭatva*), they are "sharp";

because the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛtatva*), they are "dull. The term "coarseness" (*dausthulya*) therein indicates the seeds of both these sharp and dull hindrances; this is based on...

This refers to those who have already severed [the faculties]. Alternatively, it refers to the state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*) arising from both. Furthermore, this reveals that the two types [of faculties] are co-nascent (*sahaja*).
This is stated according to those currently severing [them]; as when entering the lower [states], an analogy is cited to clarify those who have already severed them:

namely, one who enters the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) simultaneously severs the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), because within these two attainments there is no feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

At the time of entering meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), although there are no active seeds of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), it is nonetheless called "entering absorption" because one has severed its coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

It is the same in this first stage (*bhūmi*): although [the text] initially speaks generally of what is severed on the stages above, while it mentions both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), the intended meaning refers to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The Sūtra speaks of ten kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*), which are the delusions belonging to the ten categories of obstacles; these are not afflictive [ignorance].
Because it is of a nature defiled by affliction (*kleśa*), the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) are also able to sever the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

since these are common to them, they are not what is described in this section on "what is severed exclusively by this bodhisattva. Furthermore, the ten types of non-afflicted ignorance mentioned in the preceding sutra refer solely to the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Therefore, it is known that [this refers to] the stages above the first ground (*bhūmi*).

It is only the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) that are abandoned. If it is asked: "Since what is abandoned in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) pertains to both obstacles (*dvaya-āvaraṇa*), why is it not defiled?
The subsequent passage answers and explains:
"Although the afflictions (*kleśa*) are also suppressed during this stage, they are only suddenly severed when one is about to become a Buddha."

This is an explanation of the terminology. It means that although one simultaneously suppresses the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) in the first stage (*bhūmi*) such that they do not manifest, one may also figuratively say that their "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) is abandoned;
however, this is not the primary intention. Therefore, it is not stated here that the seeds of the afflictions are abandoned.

In reality, the conclusion below clarifies that throughout the ten stages, only the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are abandoned. Question: What about the latent tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*)?

At that time, when he was about to sever [the afflictions], he replied: "I abide within the stage of fulfillment (*paripūrṇa-bhūmi*). Since this period has already been long, it is logical that one should advance to sever the obstacles that ought to be severed.

Regarding the "three times," these refer to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. The provisions (*sambhāra*) are like the practice; traversing one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is called the path of gradual subduing and sudden severance.

This is because it gradually subdues the innate (*sahaja*) [afflictions] and suddenly severs the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) ones. [This constitutes] the path of penetration (*prativedha*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

In the first seven stages, one passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*; this is called the path of sudden suppression and gradual abandonment, because afflictions (*kleśa*) are suddenly suppressed while the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are gradually abandoned.
In the latter three stages of the path of cultivation, up to the stage of ultimate attainment, one passes through one *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*;

this is called the path of permanent suppression and permanent abandonment, because both afflictions and the objects of knowledge are ultimately abandoned. These are the distinctions between the three paths as one dwells in the fulfillment of the stages.
"Since the time has already been long elapsed" refers to the subsequent *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. During this extended period, one should sever the remaining hindrances;

otherwise, there would be no distinction between the paths of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) across the three periods. Furthermore, he cites a sūtra as proof: "one who attains clear observation" (*abhisamaya*) refers to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
That is to say, after the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one directly realizes *tathatā* (suchness), which is an object of direct perception, unlike the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*).

This can only be known through inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, it is said that once a Bodhisattva has attained clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they sever only the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This is because they intentionally retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) to assist their vows in delivering sentient beings, unlike the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) who exhaust all afflictions and swiftly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, below the section on the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the Master of the Treatise provides an explanation by citing scriptural evidence for this meaning.

The second is the obstacle of wrong practice (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which refers to [the portion of] the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) consisting of either the delusion regarding the initiation of karma or the delusion regarding the non-comprehension of karma.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 79, states: "What is the obstacle of wrong practice? It should be known that, in brief, it is the successive production [of subsequent stages]."
There are eight kinds of characteristics: first, the wrong practice of regressive wisdom, because it is regressive; the wrong practice of false mindfulness, because it is false;
the wrong practice of destroying the hundred dharmas, because it is destructive; the wrong practice of manifesting evil intent, because it is evil; and the wrong practice that is difficult to subdue.

Because they are difficult to discipline, they engage in unrighteous and deviant conduct. Because they act improperly, they engage in ignoble and deviant conduct. Because they are not virtuous, they engage in conduct that does not accord with the Dharma.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It refers to the obstacles of deviant conduct regarding the body and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the body and so forth": [it refers to the body, speech, and mind].
This refers to the three types of karma, which together constitute the ten unwholesome actions; these are termed the "obstruction of wrong conduct.

Because one gives rise to great joy upon reaching the first bhūmi as mentioned previously, one is capable of committing transgressions through the three types of karma, which is termed "wrong conduct. Therefore, the treatise itself explains:

"It refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the three types of karma committed through transgression arising therefrom. This serves to distinguish it from the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Regarding "affliction" (*daurmanasya*) and that which arises from discrimination (*vikalpaja*): these exclusively manifest the afflictions known as innate (*sahaja*). Because of transgressions involving error, they obstruct pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Upon reaching the second stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to sever them forever. The following section clarifies the severing of two delusions; the interpretation of their meaning is the same as previously explained.
Subtle transgressions serve as the cause, and the various courses of karma serve as the result; therefore, they are divided into two. Alternatively, there are only two:

the inferior [delusion] and, furthermore, the delusions regarding the arising of karma. Regarding these, the delusion of the arising of karma refers to the initiation of the three types of karmic actions through those subtle transgressions.
The delusion of non-comprehension refers to the inability to understand the illusory nature of those very karmas. And...
Because they cling to [things] as being substantially existent, they are called "deluded.
Third, the obstacle of dullness refers to that which, among the obstacles to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), obstructs the dhāraṇīs and the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.

Because one forgets the three types of wisdom, one is called "dark and dull-witted. This refers to the stage of the Second Ground (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), where although ethical discipline (*śīla*) is extremely pure, because there is no concentration (*samādhi*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), one forgets what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.

Therefore, the Commentary explains: "It refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes the forgetting of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
Following that obstruction, the text clarifies the abandonment of two delusions, the meaning of which is explained as before. First:
The delusion of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-moha*) is itself an affliction (*kleśa*). Therefore, it may be asked:
"Previously, it was stated that a portion of the innate [afflictions] within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is meant; why is the affliction of sensual desire now cited? Answer:

Because that cognitive obstruction frequently arises simultaneously with sensual desire, it is termed the "delusion of sensual desire. Now, when concentration and wisdom are attained, the cognitive obstructions are severed, and sensual desire follows suit.

I prostrate. Because this craving has, since beginningless time, always functioned in dependence upon the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), it is called *dhāraṇī*, which here means "total retention" (*saṃgraha*).
It is named "total" because by retaining a single dharma, one attains all dharmas.

The former [obscuration] takes the cultivation of meditative concentration and wisdom as its cause; the present [obscuration] takes the two types of wisdom—learning and reflection—as its result. Therefore, they are divided into two.
The fourth is the obstruction of the manifestation of subtle afflictions (up to the point where it is said):

"Because one is able to permanently destroy the two types of view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth through greed for meditative concentration and wisdom, these are called 'afflictions' within the third stage. Because there is superior meditative concentration and dhāraṇī, the two inferior types of delusion therein are termed "craving for concentration" and "craving for the Dharma.
The Master of the Treatise himself explains: "The view of self-identity and so forth associated with the sixth consciousness..."
Regarding the inclusion: these afflictions are associated exclusively with the sixth consciousness and not the seventh.
This is because those [seventh-consciousness] afflictions are subdued only at the eighth stage, and even their most inferior grade is subsumed under the indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, they arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) without being conditioned by deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*), and they have followed along with present activity from beginningless time. Because they possess these three characteristics, they are called "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).
Subtle. Because of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one is unable to contemplate the body as impure and so forth, and thus gives rise to the afflictions of craving and attachment.
Now that one has attained *bodhi*, one is able to sever these forever. Since it is stated that this is "a portion of the innate [afflictions] within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*),"...

What is called "subtle affliction"? The answer is: that cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) formerly arose together with the afflictions of self-grasping and was thus designated by the name "affliction.
Now that enlightenment has been attained, that cognitive obscuration is forever extinguished;

consequently, the afflictions of the view of self that arise based upon the cognitive obscuration also never again manifest. Furthermore, it is asked: why is this not the case in the first three stages?
Is that so? The answer is: the first, second, and third stages, and so forth. Regarding the two types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity):
they are called "two" because both the cognitive objects (*jñeya*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) arise based upon the view of a self-identity.
How can one know that [these] coexist with the sixth consciousness (up to the point where) the two types of afflictions and craving also never arise?
Question: Why do these views of self-grasping and so forth coexist only with the sixth consciousness? Answer:

It is because the afflictions associated with the seventh consciousness still manifest during the first seven stages (*bhūmi*), whereas the afflictions associated with the other six consciousnesses [do not].

Because it serves as a basis of reliance, and since the first seven stages (*bhūmi*) do not constitute the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), [the afflictions] only cease to function permanently upon reaching the eighth stage.
This sixth [affliction] is coarse, while that seventh is subtle; because their subduing occurs sequentially, the afflictions subdued within this stage are associated with the sixth [consciousness].

Regarding the statement "below the view of a self" (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) mentioned above, the explanation establishes that the aforementioned terms such as "view of a self" definitively encompass [all relevant categories].

Regarding "attachment to the Dharma" (dharmatṛṣṇā) increasing in the third stage (*bhūmi*): this is because one loves the cultivation of superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and the dhāraṇīs. In the fourth stage, it is because one has permanently severed that which is contrary to enlightenment (*bodhi*).

From here below, [the text] explains the abandonment of two delusions (*moha*). "Attachment to the Dharma" refers to the attachment to meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). Since *samāpatti* is itself concentration (*samādhi*), it is called the "delusion of attachment to concentration.

This "delusion" is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*), which pervasively defiles the mind and its associates; therefore, it coexists with attachment. Thus, it is the "delusion regarding concentration" due to attachment to concentration.
Such is their mutual inclusion. The same applies to the inclusion of the delusions regarding phenomena (*dharmamoha*) and craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

Because the ignorance that constitutes the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—namely, the two types of delusion regarding meditative concentration and phenomena—is severed, the two types of craving associated with those afflictions—craving for meditative concentration and craving for phenomena—also never again arise.

This is because one no longer clings to a self that could "practice" meditative concentration and phenomena; this is the severing of the afflictions. Furthermore, it is because one no longer clings to superior meditative concentrations or great phenomena as being substantially real. This is...
Regarding the abandonment of the objects of knowledge: craving for meditative concentration is the cause, and craving for the Dharma is the fruit; therefore, these are distinguished as two.
The fifth [hindrance] is the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna)—namely, those who seek nirvāṇa within this context.
Seeking to realize bodhi necessarily entails revulsion toward birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because there is this sense of longing and revulsion, it is termed an "obstruction.

This refers to the mind seeking transcendence in the preceding four stages; thus, it shares the same character of longing and revulsion as the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Below that [section], the text explains the abandonment of two delusions, which are precisely this longing and revulsion.
Because of this longing and revulsion, one is obstructed from the non-differentiated contemplation of the ultimate and conventional truths (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*) in the fifth stage.
It is a distinct path; because one attains this path upon entering the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), one is able to sever them forever.
Taking the aspiration for *nirvāṇa* as the fruit and the aversion toward *saṃsāra* as the cause, they are therefore divided into two.
The obstacle of the manifestation of the six coarse characteristics (extending to) the inability to dwell for long periods in signless contemplation.

"Coarse" refers to that which possesses both defilement and purity; this pertains to the five preceding stages. On the path of non-differentiation, when the signs of defilement and purity manifest during the equal contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional, they are termed "coarse manifestations.
Regarding the obstacles to these, the commentary explains the abandonment of two delusions, namely those of defilement and purity.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): because there is defilement and purity, they obstruct the absence of purity and defilement. Therefore, in the sixth stage, when there is neither defilement nor purity, two delusions are permanently severed.
That which observes the process of flow (*pravṛtti*) is the gate of the flow of causes and conditions; thus it is said to be subsumed under the defiled portion (*saṃkleśabhāga*).
Because its characteristics frequently manifest, it is the gate of the cessation of causes and conditions; thus it is said to "grasp the aspect of purity" (*viśuddhalakṣaṇa*). Second.

Because characteristics have not yet been extinguished, it is said that "the contemplation of characteristics is frequently practiced" and one is unable to abide for long in the contemplation of the signless (*animitta*).

Only when one abides in the signless can it be called the path of non-defiled purity in the sixth stage. Observing the process of transmigration is taken as the cause, while the frequent manifestation of characteristics is taken as the result; therefore, these are distinguished as two.
The obstacle of the manifestation of subtle marks (*sūkṣma-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*). [Extending to: being unable to initiate superior practices within emptiness.
When the contemplation with marks (*sanimittabhāvanā*) ceases and the contemplation without marks (*animittabhāvanā*) arises, it is called the obstacle of the manifestation of subtle marks.

This refers to the path of non-defiled purity (*asaṃkliṣṭa-viśuddhi-mārga*) in the preceding six stages; abiding in the contemplation without marks is termed "subtle manifestation. Regarding that obstacle, the commentary explains the abandonment of two delusions (*moha*). That is to say:
Subtle arising and ceasing. Because the characteristic of arising and ceasing obstructs the wondrous signlessness, one permanently abandons the two delusions at the seventh stage.
Regarding "one who diligently seeks the mental application of pure signlessness": this refers to the preceding six stages;

although one diligently seeks the mental application of pure signlessness therein, one has not yet been able to give rise to superior practice within emptiness. "Within emptiness" means within signlessness.
If there were superior practice within the signless (*animitta*), that would indeed be the wondrous signless path of the seventh stage.
Because the cause of arising and the fruit of cessation are opened up as two delusions,

the obstacle to applying effort (*prayoga*) within the eightfold signlessness [is established], since it does not contradict the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Regarding the "obstacle to application" (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*): it obstructs effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), which is the superior practice within emptiness during the preceding seven stages.

Consequently, it obstructs the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the eighth stage, such that [the latter] does not arise spontaneously. Question: What is the distinction between the various stages regarding the presence or absence of the observation of characteristics (*nimitta*)? Answer:

Regarding the first five stages and so forth, the meaning of the presence or absence of the observation of characteristics is explained according to the text. Furthermore, the question is raised: "Since [the sixth stage] is purely..."
The absence of signs (*animitta*) is precisely the meaning of constant continuity and effortlessness (*anābhoga*). What obstructs the eighth [stage] from being effortless?
Therefore, the answer says: "Although it is constant," and so forth. "Sign" refers to the body, while "land" refers to the vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*).

This is because when the seventh stage manifests the body and the vessel-world, they can only appear through the application of mental attention (*manasikāra*) within the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The following passage explains the abandonment [of these obstructions].
The two delusions are precisely the dual aspects of the object and subject of application (*prayoga*). That is to say, there is application which obstructs non-application (*anābhoga*).
Once application has ceased, the body and the land manifest spontaneously and are present before one; therefore, it is said that "two masteries are attained.
The first is the delusion of applying effort toward the signless (*animitta*); this refers to the application and effort involved in manifesting the body and land during the preceding seven stages.
Second is the delusion regarding lack of mastery over signs (*nimitta*). This refers to the aforementioned signs of the body and the signs of the land (*kṣetra-nimitta*);

it is the sense of lacking mastery over them. Therefore, it is further explained as "causing one to lack mastery over signs. Since this also subsumes a portion of the signs of the land, [the question is asked]:
What is the distinction between the presence or absence of the two paths and the two obstacles within the latter three stages (the eighth through the tenth bhūmis)? Below the eighth stage...
Answer: This refers to the two paths, which are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and not tainted (*sāsrava*); therefore, it is said that they "arise spontaneously.

Among the two obstructions, only the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) remains, while the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is absent; therefore, it is said that [afflictions] "never manifest again.

Regarding the statement that "the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons does not contradict that," this means that the afflictions of the seventh consciousness have been suppressed, whereby one attains [the state of a *pudgalanairātmya-jñāna-phala*].
Emptiness [is realized], yet attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) still persists; for the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*) does not contradict that [attachment].
The nine obstacles to the practice of benefiting others are all subsumed under this ninth obstacle.
Spontaneous mastery is termed "non-desire for practice. This refers to the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the preceding eighth stage.

Because one delights in cultivating one's own benefit, one does not desire to exert oneself in benefiting others. Regarding those obstacles, the following explains the abandonment of two delusions (*moha*), which are precisely what obstruct the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Thus, the first type of delusion obstructs three of the analytical knowledges regarding the immeasurable objects...

The following explains the meaning of the three types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*). The Dharma that is taught is the expressed meaning; this is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).
The names and phrases by which it is taught are the means of teaching the Dharma; this is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
Following these, there are further successive words of debate and discussion; this is called the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). As for *dhāraṇī*, this...

"Cloud of Dharanis": because within each one, all things are manifested. Second, "Discernment" (*pratibhāna*): this explains the fourth unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) among the two types of deluded obstacles;
it is called "unimpeded discernment" because one is able to skillfully teach according to what is appropriate. "Delusion regarding the ability... and so forth:
this summarizes the two types of delusion that obstruct the four unimpeded knowledges, naming them the ninth obstacle.
Tenth, regarding the phrase "among all dharmas" up to "obstructing the great cloud of dharma-knowledge and that which it contains":

the obstruction to attaining mastery over all dharmas is also present during the effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the preceding eighth stage, as it simultaneously obstructs the two types of mastery over mind and dharmas.
Therefore, in the ninth stage, the obstruction to mastery over the mind is termed "non-desire for practice. In the tenth [stage]...
Within the stages (*bhūmi*), that which obstructs mastery over phenomena is called "not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena.

One comprehensively observes that all obstructive phenomena of the various stages are the practices of the preceding stage that are able to obstruct the subsequent stage. Now, one contemplates the practice of mastery of mind in the ninth stage.
Regarding those who are not obstructed in their mastery of the dharmas of the ten stages, one should know that this obstruction also arises from within the eighth stage.

This is because it obstructs the mind and dharmas through the absence of effortlessness (*anābhoga*). Below that, the commentary explains the abandonment of two delusions, which are precisely what obstruct supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth;
these refer to the Great Dharma Wisdom and the Great Dharma Cloud, which contain and store all matters such as supernatural powers.

All these are the meanings of mastery over phenomena (*dharmavaśitā*) on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Those who have not yet ascended to the ten stages are obstructed by ignorance, and thus [this mastery] does not manifest before them.

Upon entering the ten stages, one attains mastery over phenomena and is thereby able to sever [these obstructions] forever. "One of great supernormal powers" (*mahābhijñā*) refers to the activities of the supernormal powers that are contained within;
"one who has awakened to the subtle secrets" refers to one who is able to contain the Great Dharma.
The Cloud of Wisdom. Because great wisdom universally contemplates and the great cloud universally covers, one is thus able to awaken to and enter into all phenomena.
Since ignorance can obstruct this, it is said that it should be severed. Question: Once these obstructions are severed, why is one not called a Buddha? The answer below states:
Although on this stage one has attained mastery over phenomena (dharma), because one has realized great nirvāṇa and great bodhi, there remain residual obstructions;
thus, even though one has attained mastery over phenomena on this stage, it is not yet called "ultimate," as there is still that which is inferior.

This explains the remaining obstacles, namely the seeds of the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). Because of what was previously stated, as one dwells for a long duration within the "fulfilled stage" (*paripūrṇabhūmi*), it is logically necessary to advance and sever the obstacles that ought to be severed.

Since that stage is termed "fulfilled" by virtue of being equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), it is said that the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, whereby the remaining obstacles are suddenly severed and one enters the stage of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatabhūmi*). From this point downward, the severance [of obstacles] is explained.

The two delusions are the remaining obstacles. When it is said in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* that they are "abandoned," this refers to their having already been abandoned, not that they are abandoned at the stage of Buddhahood itself;

for these remaining obstacles are abandoned by the Perfectly Enlightened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). "Extremely subtle attachment" refers to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because there is much clinging due to the objects of cognition.
"Extremely subtle hindrance" refers to the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*), because there are many obstructions due to the presence of afflictions.
Because of these obstructions, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (lower volume) cites scriptural evidence regarding the meaning of severing hindrances and realizing the fruit:

that one becomes an *arhat* by severing only the afflictions (*kleśa*), attaining a *nirvāṇa* that is either with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), which is not a state of non-abiding;

and that one becomes a *tathāgata*, realizing great *nirvāṇa* and great *bodhi*, wherein both hindrances are eternally severed and both types of death are eternally extinguished, thereby realizing great *nirvāṇa*.
It is called "the state of non-abiding. To realize great bodhi is called "perfect awakening. △ The first section, the formal explanation of the ten types, is concluded.

In the *Suyuan* (Exegesis on the Ordinary), within the section on the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), the explanation of the meaning of the verses is divided into four parts: first, a detailed exposition of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); second, the meaning of cultivation, abandonment, and realization, which is further divided into three sections;

first, the question-and-answer presentation of the number; second, the specific explanation according to that number, which is divided into four parts; first, the explanation of the ten noble ones (*ārya*).

The Grounds. Second, the cultivation of the ten superior practices. Third, the abandonment of the ten heavy obstacles, which is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation of the ten types [of obstacles].
[Volume Nine ends here. Among these, the second part concerns what is subsumed under the two obstacles.
These eleven hindrances are subsumed within the two hindrances; from the eighth bhūmi upward, they are ultimately non-existent.
This collectively cites the two hindrances of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which encompass all the aforementioned hindrances.

Although ten hindrances were previously indicated, eleven are cited here because, following the severance of the hindrances in the first ten bhūmis, there still remain two delusions regarding attachment and obstruction, which are termed "having a remainder."

Because of these obstructions, there are eleven [types]. The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Good son, within these stages (*bhūmi*), there are twenty-two kinds of ignorance (*moha*) and eleven kinds of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Having eternally severed the most subtle afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one becomes unattached and unimpeded regarding all aspects of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-viṣaya*), manifesting direct realization."
Because it is equal awakening, the eleventh stage is called the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).

Among the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), those arising from conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*) are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they can be severed instantaneously by the true path of insight (*darśanamārga*). When these manifest, from time immemorial...

Up until the stage prior to the first bhūmi, the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are gradually suppressed through preparatory application (*prayoga*). At the first bhūmi, the seeds (*bīja*) are severed;

as for those that are innate (*sahaja*), they are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). This continues up until the stage of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), where they are suddenly severed when the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests.

When that samādhi arises, one has likewise engaged in the four preparatory applications from beginningless time up until the stage prior to the bhūmis, which can only achieve gradual suppression. At the first [bhūmi]...
From the first bhūmi up to the eighth bhūmi, one is able to suppress them all at once until they are exhausted, just like an arhat;

this is a metaphor for the sense that these afflictions will never again manifest. Question: Since they are like an arhat in causing [the afflictions] to never manifest again, why [are they still present] in the preceding seven bhūmis?

[Question: "Yet they still give rise to greed and other afflictions. [Answer: "In the first seven stages (*bhūmi*), although they may temporarily give rise to afflictions such as greed, they do so intentionally for the sake of liberating sentient beings; thus, their arising does not constitute a fault.

From the eighth stage upward, they never again engage in them because, in the eighth stage, there is 'effortlessness' (*anābhoga*), and in the ninth stage, there is 'mastery over the mind. If one ascends..."

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*): because of mastery over phenomena (*dharma-vaśitā*), in the final three stages one brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings through spontaneous activity and the two types of mastery.
Since one does not give rise to greed, hatred, and so forth by means of intentional effort, it is said that afflictions (*kleśa*) ultimately do not occur.
Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that are abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*), these are specifically mentioned because they are manifest in three stages.

To explain the cognitive obstructions: those that arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*) are abandoned through insight, for they can be severed instantaneously by the Path of True Insight (*tattva-darśanamārga*).

When these [obstructions] manifest, from time immemorial up until the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi, their active manifestation is gradually suppressed by means of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The seeds [of these afflictions] have already been severed at the first stage (*bhūmi*). As for those that are innate (*sahaja*), they are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Those ten types of ignorance are termed "non-defiled" (*akliṣṭa*); therefore, they are gradually severed throughout the ten stages until the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-jñāna*). At the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, they are suddenly and completely severed.
When that [concentration] arises, [the process] has also proceeded gradually from beginningless time up to the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi during the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

Prostrate. From the time one ascends to the first bhūmi, [the afflictions] are gradually suppressed and gradually severed; only upon reaching the tenth bhūmi are they forever suppressed and exhausted.
Regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) below the eighth bhūmi, their presence or absence depends on the consciousnesses:

that is to say, the seeds of the cognitive obstructions associated with the sixth consciousness do not manifest as active states during the final three bhūmis. This is due to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wisdom of contemplation and the uncontaminated true [wisdom].
If, because it can be counteracted by the uninterrupted continuity [of the path], the subtle cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) associated with the seventh consciousness can still manifest,

then it is only upon attaining mastery over phenomena (dharmavaśitā) in the tenth stage that the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmanairātmyajñāna) arises, and those obstructions are finally suppressed.

Although the mental states associated with the first five *pravṛtti-vijñānas* have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) to become the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*, they remain in a state of outflow-free purity (*anāsrava*) during the final three stages, wherein the obstacles are suppressed and do not arise.
A question is asked: "Since the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are identical in essence, why are they not abandoned simultaneously?"

The answer states: Although one does not sever the afflictions during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), their seeds are also gradually severed and extinguished. Regarding the three stages in which the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are severed:
first, the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), where the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) are suddenly severed;

second, the stage of the path of cultivation, where the seeds and manifestations of the innate afflictions and cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are gradually suppressed and severed; and third, the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), which is able to...

The seeds of the two obstacles are forever severed and exhausted. Question: Previously it was stated that each of the ten stages (bhūmis) severs one obstacle, two delusions, and their respective coarse residues (dausthulya);

why then is it said here that they are severed only in three positions? Answer: Although they are gradually suppressed and gradually severed throughout the ten stages, [it is in these three positions that they are finally eliminated].
However, because the three paths of abandonment are distinguished by their names and characteristics and are particularly eminent, they are explained specifically here.
Regarding the gradual or sudden nature of abandoning the seeds of the two obstacles: [it is said that] within a single moment, those of the three realms are abandoned all at once.
The question and answer clarify the gradual and sudden abandonment of the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*). First, regarding the two obstacles associated with the seventh consciousness:

both are abandoned suddenly; there is no sense of gradual abandonment. As for the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*): for the two vehicles, it is the transcendence of the triple world (*tridhātu*); for the Bodhisattvas, it is the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

Because the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*) is designated as the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), it is said that when attaining the fruit of no-more-learning in the three vehicles, one simultaneously severs the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of the three realms.
Furthermore, the seeds of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) associated with the seventh consciousness are severed only by Bodhisattvas;

thus, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, all are simultaneously severed. That which arises spontaneously within, without distinction between coarse and subtle, refers to the seventh consciousness, the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*).
The afflictions regarding the knowable (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are both non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), not abandoned by insight (*na darśana-heya*), and are purely innate (*sahaja*).
They arise spontaneously within, which is the meaning of being "innate. Because they do not arise from conceptualization, they are called "without coarseness" (*niṣaudārika*).

"Subtlety" (*sūkṣma*) is spoken of in contrast to "coarseness"; since the name "coarse" does not exist [here], "subtle" is likewise not mentioned. Therefore it is said: "Because there is neither coarse nor subtle. The remaining six... below. Next.
This explains the meaning of the sudden and gradual abandonment of the seeds of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) associated with the first six consciousnesses.

If they are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they are abandoned only suddenly; thus it is said that in the stage of seeing for those of the three vehicles, all are abandoned suddenly within the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*).

If they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it depends on the case: for the two vehicles, there is a distinction between sharp and dull faculties, whereas for Bodhisattvas, it occurs in a single moment. Therefore, it is according to what is appropriate.
Because there are both sudden and gradual [paths], the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the two vehicles occurs entirely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

therein, they realize the first fruit (*phala*). The path of seeing of the Bodhisattva, however, immediately upon the uninterrupted state of the preparatory stage (*prayoga-anantarya*), ascends to the first ground (*bhūmi*);

thus, on the first ground, they realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The first section below explains those of dull faculties who emerge gradually: within the three realms (*tridhātu*), they possess...

There are nine stages (*bhūmi*). In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is only one stage consisting of the five destinies (*gati*) where beings dwell together. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the four dhyānas are called four stages.

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the four emptinesses (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc. are likewise called four stages. Each stage is divided into nine grades, categorized as soft, medium, and superior.

When a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) eliminates the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm up to the fifth grade—that is, the "medium-medium" grade—it is called the first [fruit].

Regarding the stage of the "Approacher to Once-Returner" (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*): upon reaching the sixth category, which is the medium-mild grade, one realizes the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). Because there remain residual afflictions (*kleśa*) such that one will necessarily be born once more, it is called the fruit of once-returning.
When [the afflictions] are abandoned up to the eighth category, which is the mild-medium grade, it is called the "Approacher to Non-Returner" (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).

Upon reaching the ninth category—which is the "mild-mild" category—one realizes the fruit of Non-returner (Anāgāmin). With the afflictions of the desire realm exhausted, one will certainly not return to be born there;
hence, it is called "Non-returning. This third fruit resides in the Pure Abodes of the form realm.

Having severed the nine categories of afflictions for each of the eight higher stages, up to the seventy-first—that is, the mild-medium category of affliction of the ninth stage—it is termed the "candidate for Arhatship" (Arhattva-pratipannaka). [Having severed...]
The final chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Soft-Soft. One who realizes the fruit of Arhatship by exhausting all afflictions is called an Arhat.

Following this, the next section below explains those of sharp faculties who attain liberation instantaneously; that is, regarding the afflictions of the nine stages within the three realms as a single aggregate, they are collectively divided into nine grades.
These are severed individually, starting from the upper-middle and soft grades of the nine, according to the *Daśasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
The third fascicle states: Furthermore, as it has been said regarding the *pudgala* who is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), there are two types:
first, those who attain liberation gradually; second, those who attain liberation instantaneously. Those who attain liberation gradually are as explained extensively above.

Those who attain liberation instantaneously refer to those who, having entered into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), rely upon the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) to give rise to the supramundane path and instantaneously sever [the afflictions] of the three realms. One...
All afflictions are abandoned category by category, yet only two fruits are established: namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*).

"Abandoned category by category" means that one first suddenly abandons the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and so on, down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) category.
"Suddenly abandoning the three realms" refers to the manner of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
It is abandoned [all at once], unlike the worldly path which abandons [defilements] separately according to realm, stage, and category. What is the proof for this meaning?
It is as stated in the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*: "Whatever form there is... up to consciousness—whether past, future, or present;
and so on, in detail, whether far or near—all this taken together is condensed into a single portion. One.
A mass, a single accumulation, a single collection—having thus summarized, one should contemplate that all things are impermanent and all are suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
Based on this meaning, only the first and last fruits can be established, while the second and third are not;
this is called "sudden transcendence. Below this, the Bodhisattva [section] explains the Bodhisattva Vehicle regarding the remaining six.
The afflictions associated with the *vijñāna* (consciousness) are also severed only instantaneously; there is no sense of gradual severance.
This means that those afflictions are suppressed instantaneously upon the first stage (*bhūmi*), and their seeds are severed instantaneously at the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*).

Furthermore, as for the afflictions associated with the other six consciousnesses, they are severed by the Two Vehicles during the stages of seeing and cultivation; however, for Bodhisattvas, they are severed at the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and at the diamond-like concentration.
They are not abandoned through the path of cultivation because they are permanently suppressed.

Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), from the first moment of the first stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, when viewed in comparison with preceding and succeeding moments, it is possible for them to be fully present.

The remaining six consciousnesses are also associated with the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which only Bodhisattvas can sever. Among these, those severed by insight (*darśana-heya*) take coarse external objects as their focus;

being conceptually arisen (*vikalpaja*), they are severed instantaneously upon the Path of Insight (*darśanamārga*). Those severed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) take subtle internal objects as their focus;

because they are innate (*sahaja*), they are severed only during the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). These severances apply universally to the lower realms. This concludes the various types of instantaneous and gradual severance mentioned previously. (2)

Continuing from below: in the separate explanation of when those of dull faculties gradually sever the hindrances, one must invariably give rise to both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) individually.

From the perspective of the cause looking toward the fruit, it is called the path of uninterrupted transition because it is proximate to the fruit; from the perspective of the fruit looking toward the cause, it is called the path of liberation.

Because they are free from causes [of affliction], the wholesome roots conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)— whether arising collectively or individually— which constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) for realizing the liberation obtained through the abandonment of afflictions by means of this path, are called the "path of preparation" (*prayogamārga*).
All preceding stages, in relation to their subsequent advancement, are termed the "path of superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Regarding the bodhisattvas below [the stage of the path of seeing], this explains their sharp faculties, the gradual abandonment of hindrances, the arising of wisdom, and the elimination of afflictions as they partially realize ultimate truth.

It is not necessary for them to separately give rise to the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because within the four types of paths of abandonment—such as the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth—the preceding and succeeding moments are both capable of possessing these qualities. Therefore, it is not...

A separate arising. △ Second, the conclusion on the subsumption under the two obstacles. This concludes the three [sections] above regarding the severance of the ten layers of obstacles. Below follows the fourth [section]:

the realization of the ten true suchnesses (*tathatā*). As for the ten true suchnesses: first, the all-pervading true suchness (up to) because it is not like the eye and other [faculties] which possess distinct categories.

This summarizes the preceding section; the text provides a detailed explanation. "Pervasive" (*vyāpin*) means all-encompassing. "Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to its manifested aspect. This means that this *tathatā* (suchness) pervades all places and manifests its aspect of conduct.
Therefore, at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one suddenly severs the two obstacles of conceptualization, thereby realizing the *tathatā* that is revealed [by such severance];
thus, it is called the "Supreme *Tathatā*" realized in the second stage. As for the second stage...

In the middle [stage], one is endowed with pure *śīla* (ethical discipline), which is called the "precept co-arising with the Path. Since precepts are the root of all virtues, it is said that one is "endowed with boundless virtues.
Because they are the most supreme among all phenomena, they are the "supreme flow" (*viśeṣa-niṣyanda*) of *tathatā* (suchness), realized in the third stage.
This is because within the third stage, through superior meditative concentration and *dhāraṇī*, boundless sublime wisdom flows forth; thus, they are far more supreme than other phenomena.

The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty states: "From *tathatā* flows forth the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); from the fundamental wisdom flows forth the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*);
from the subsequently attained wisdom flows forth great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); and from great compassion flows forth the twelvefold scriptures.

This is called the 'superior outflow' (*viśeṣa-nisyanda*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is without grasping and without the sense of appropriation. This is because, within the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one partially realizes bodhi."

This is called the supramundane path. It is not bound to any realm (*dhātu*). Because it is far removed from the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is no basis for the grasping of self-clinging.
Master Vasubandhu says: Within this suchness (*tathatā*), there is no reckoning of "mine" and no appropriation of "mine.
Like the people of Uttarakuru, it is free from all attachments. One should know that this suchness is neither self-clinging, nor the conceit of "I," nor craving for self.
It is ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is the basis for grasping at the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth. There is no separate *tathatā*, which is realized in the fifth stage;
because in the fifth stage, the two cognitions of the ultimate and the conventional are joined and made to correspond, it is called "without distinction."
The sixth is the *tathatā* (suchness) of non-defilement and non-purity; this refers to the fact that [the bodhisattva] attains mastery over all dhāraṇīs and samādhi-gates.
Regarding "non-defilement and non-purity," this refers to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

Because in the sixth stage one deeply contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which brings forth the manifestation of non-conceptual fundamental wisdom, it is said that its intrinsic nature is undefiled. Furthermore, it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
The Bodhisattva Asvabhāva states: "By means of the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*), non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is brought to manifestation.

One realizes that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure; that there is no differentiation among phenomena is what is realized in the seventh stage. This wondrous path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*) is itself the signless nature of signs (*nimittānimitta*);
thus it is called the 'wondrous signlessness. Therefore, it is said that although various establishments exist, they are without difference. — Cien (Kuiji).
The Great Master said: "Although all the teachings are established based upon suchness (*tathatā*), suchness itself is without differentiation.

Furthermore, although various names—such as 'Dharmadhātu' and 'True Mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)—are established within the teachings, suchness remains undifferentiated. It neither increases nor decreases True Suchness (*tathatā*);

this is precisely what is realized in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Because in the eighth stage one does not follow along with increase through purity, nor decrease through defilement, it is also called 'the mark' (*lakṣaṇa*)."

Regarding that which is supported by the land: within the eight stages (*bhūmi*), during the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), one spontaneously manifests the body and manifests the characteristics of the land, attaining mastery over both.
This is also the meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing herein. As the Bodhisattva Asvabhāva says:
"There is no utility apart from the dharmas; therefore, there is no increase. The essence of the dharmas is not destroyed; therefore, there is no decrease."—Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.
It is said: Among all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one attains mastery because one can manifest them immediately according to one's desire.

For example, if one wishes for earth to become gold, jewels, and so forth, it is accomplished at will. "Marks" refer to the manifestation of the body, while "earth" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
Mastery over wisdom is itself mastery over the mind; therefore, in the ninth stage (*navamī bhūmi*), by realizing this *tathatā*, one attains mastery over the mind.
Because they have accomplished the four kinds of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), they possess mastery over karma and so forth—the various activities of all dharmas.

That is to say, by realizing this *tathatā* within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they attain mastery over the Dharma; thus, regarding the performance of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-karman*), the gateways of dhāraṇī, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
All attain mastery.
Although the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is in reality without differentiation, [the stages] are established in successive order so as to bring it to full perfection.
Should someone ask, "Since *tathatā* is a single entity, how can there be ten? the answer is given: although *tathatā*...
And so forth. Again, it is asked: "Since these are provisionally established such that one [truth] encompasses all, why are the remaining nine kinds subsequently established?

"In this way, the Bodhisattva within the ten stages... (up to) is able to realize the two types of transformation of the basis."
