Through these, one attains realization. △ Third, the conclusion of the cultivation and realization is complete. This concludes the general discussion above on the meanings of cultivation, severance, and realization.
Below follows the threefold transformation of the basis across six stages.
There are briefly six distinct stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). [This concludes the section on] "many" [factors] causing that which is not real not to appear.
Thus, the six types are indicated in general; they are explained individually in the text. "Power" (*bala*) refers to potency; "capacity" (*śakti*) refers to functional efficacy.

This means that during the two stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*), having already realized the characteristics and nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), it is termed "resolute conviction" (*adhimukti*). Having already generated the great bodhicitta...

Focusing the mind is called *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (dread). Training in and cultivating the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) to gradually subdue coarse afflictions is called "diminishing the power of the seeds of defilement.
Diligently practicing the six perfections and generating the three types of heroic vigor is called "augmenting the capacity of the pure seeds. Question:

Since those on the three stages of worthiness prior to the [first] ground have not yet attained the state of a noble one (*ārya*), how can they be said to have undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*)? Answer: Although they have not yet severed the hindrances and so forth, by means of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)...
One attains fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and directly takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; thus it is called "thorough penetration" (*prativedha*).

Having exhausted the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) that arise from discrimination, one realizes the twofold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*); yet since the innate [afflictions] still remain, it is said to be "one part. "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) refers to sustained practice, wherein the initial resolve does not regress.

"Training" (*śikṣā*) refers to repeated study, whereby pure conduct increases accordingly. Therefore, throughout the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one repeatedly cultivates the ten perfections, such as generosity (*dāna*).

Practicing these supreme deeds, one gradually abandons both innate afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and partially realizes the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the ten types of suchness (*tathatā*);

this is called "transformation into reality" (*tattvaparāvṛtti*). It draws forth and encompasses the Mahāyāna. The commentary on the two types of transformation explains that they apply throughout the ten stages.

Among those, the first six stages—where the presence and absence [of signs] interpenetrate—are explained as "transformation through penetration" (*prativedhaparāvṛtti*). Within the latter four stages, the cultivation of signlessness (*animitta-bhāvanā*) is explained as "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding the transformation through cultivation: although it mostly causes that which is not true to not manifest, it is not the case that there is nothing at all [that manifests].
Therefore, it was stated previously that the seventh object of knowledge may still manifest during the eighth stage.

The "transformation through the perfection of the four fruits" refers to the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), because one abandons the two types of heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) and realizes [the fruit].

The transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) mentioned previously was only termed "partial realization"; here, because it is ultimate, it is called "perfection. From the phrase "by means of the three greatnesses" below, the preceding causal practices are restated;

from the phrase "vajra-like" below, the abandonment of afflictions and the realization of the fruit are explained. Within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), there is the Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*).

The ten great samādhis, such as the "Luminous" (Prabhāsvara), are termed the Vajra-samādhi. The seeds of the two innate obstacles, being extremely subtle, are termed the "primordial heaviness" (dauṣṭhulya).

While the cultivation of the causes spans many kalpas, the realization of the fruit occurs in a single kṣaṇa; therefore, it is called "sudden realization. Its future limit can be reached, for once the fruit is attained, there is never again regression.
It constantly transforms sentient beings, providing inexhaustible benefit and bliss. [Those who] fear the Great [Vehicle] and cling to the Small [Vehicle]...

Therefore, it is called "inferior. Because those of the two vehicles delight in solitary tranquility and realize only the emptiness of persons, their minds find no joy in the work of benefiting sentient beings;
they swiftly sever the afflictions and realize true analytical cessation. This is called the "inferior transformation.

That which is capable of succeeding to the Buddha’s position and taking charge of delivering sentient beings is therefore called "vast," namely the Bodhisattva vehicle, which rejoices in the mind of great compassion and benefits others.

Birth is treated as a burden; therefore, one lacks the resolve to escape from birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, one does not take delight in the contemplation of tranquility regarding *nirvāṇa*.

When both types of emptiness are realized together and both obstacles are suddenly eliminated, awakening (*bodhi*) and *nirvāṇa* are attained spontaneously without being sought. This is called the "vast transformation" (*vipula-parāvṛtti*).

Herein, the following section explains the intended meaning of "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) mentioned in the verse; it refers exclusively to the sixth [type], the vast transformation.

The basis is different from that of the two vehicles, which sever afflictions alone; therefore, it is said that one abandons the two types of heavy obstructions (*dausthulya*) and realizes [the result].

△ The three stages of the transformation of the basis are concluded. Below, the four meanings of the transformation of the basis are divided into four parts. First, the path that performs the transformation.

The meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is briefly of four kinds. [This concludes the section on] that which is realized and that which is induced, as these have not yet been accomplished.

Thus, four types are generally indicated; they are explained individually in the text. That which is capable of transforming is "wisdom" (*jñāna*). Wisdom is able to transform delusion back into reality; therefore, it is called "capable of transforming.

Because it first suppresses and subsequently eliminates [the obstacles], it is further divided into two. First, that which is capable of suppressing refers to the seeds of the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa-bīja*).

There is the power of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of birth; this is suppressed by cultivating the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) as well as the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) and so forth.

Therefore, it is said that one prevents the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) from being induced into active manifestation. This applies generally to both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), as well as the meaning of suppressing afflictions (*kleśa*) through either sudden or gradual means.

That is to say, the gradual suppression via the six practices (*ṣaḍākāra*) pertains only to the contaminated; the wisdom of application and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) likewise pertain only to the contaminated.

Gradual suppression applies to both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [paths], whereas fundamental, instantaneous suppression applies exclusively to the uncontaminated; thus it is said, "according to what is appropriate," they suppress those [afflictions] either gradually or instantaneously.

As for the "path of abandonment," this refers to the arising of fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which alone is able to permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles;
therefore, it is stated that this path is certainly not contaminated, nor is it the wisdom of preparatory application (*prayoga-jñāna*). There is...

This explains the "outflows" (*āsrava*). To elaborate: the seventh consciousness clings to a self at every moment, causing the sixth consciousness to be unable to forget the signs (*nimitta*) associated with its acts of giving and so forth;

therefore, it is called the "clinging to the signs of habitual practice. Although this state constantly arises as active manifestation (*samudācāra*) even within the path of outflows (*sāsravamārga*), [it is not yet abandoned].
It neither causes diminution nor provides any benefit; therefore, it is able to constitute the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*). It takes only the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom].
Furthermore, because the wisdom of application (*prayogajñāna*) is induced by the diligent effort and aspiration to seek the fruit to be realized, it can only suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*).

When it comes to the actual moment of abandonment, only the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms (*mūla- and pṛṣṭhajñāna*) are capable of constituting the path of abandonment, as they do not require further application.
There is an interpretation that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (up to the point where it is said) both the fundamental and the subsequently attained wisdoms can correctly sever [the afflictions].
The first interpretation—that subsequently attained wisdom does not sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)—is still logically incomplete. The second interpretation is the correct principle:

namely, that fundamental wisdom can correctly sever both types of latent tendencies—those deluded regarding principles and those deluded regarding phenomena—whereas subsequently attained wisdom severs only [the latter].

Because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding deluded phenomena are clearly perceived through their characteristics and are realized without inversion, the mind that discriminates [these] is called "delusion regarding principles" (*tattva*), while the spontaneous delusion regarding objects is called "delusion regarding phenomena" (*vastu*).
These are the distinct meanings of the two. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (lower section) cites scriptural authority to validate the aforementioned meaning.
The supramundane path of abandonment is the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The mundane-supramundane path of abandonment is the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

The purely mundane path refers to the previously mentioned contaminated preparatory practices (*prayoga*), because such contaminated paths have been practiced before and because they are induced by the grasping at signs.
Furthermore, although the preparatory wisdom suppresses and removes the two types of conceptual grasping prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), it is not yet able to permanently sever them.
It is also mundane; therefore, it is said that there is no purely mundane path capable of permanently destroying the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"From the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these are exclusively mundane, because indistinct perception is constantly present.

From this point downward, the text concludes that both types of knowledge are capable of severing delusions, as their functions differ. Regarding the confusion concerning principle... [text continues].

Regarding "sleep": it pertains to both the paths of seeing and cultivation. The six-fascicle [version] states: "The delusions arising from discrimination, as well as those that are subtle and co-emergent, are all delusions regarding principle.
△ This concludes the first section: the path capable of transformation. Below are the two sections on the basis to be transformed.
Second, regarding the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are two types. [The first] is not mentioned here because it is not the fundamental [basis].
That which is transformed consists of the seeds of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*). Since seeds must have a basis, this is called the "basis of transformation.
This basis is further divided into two: true and false. First, the basis that sustains the seeds refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, which possesses false conceptualization and is capable of...

Because it maintains the seeds of all defiled and pure phenomena, it serves as the basis (*āśraya*). When cultivating the Noble Path, it is transformed so that one abandons defilement and attains purity. Question:
Is not the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) itself the basis for both defilement and purity? Answer:

Other instances of the *paratantra* and so forth serve as the basis for delusion and awakening because they possess the true nature of *tathatā* (suchness); thus, they are capable of giving rise to both delusion and awakening.

It is the fundamental basis; therefore, defiled and pure phenomena arise in dependence upon it. When one cultivates the noble path, it is transformed so that one abandons the defiled and attains the pure phenomena.

Question: Are not the other forms of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) also the basis for delusion and awakening? Answer: Although others also function as such, [the primary basis is this one].
Section Two: The Basis of Transformation is concluded. Below follows Section Three: That Which Is Abandoned through Transformation.

Third, regarding that which is relinquished through transformation, there are two types: (up to) the eighth pure consciousness is not the basis for those [defilements], therefore what is relinquished is as before—both tainted and untainted seeds.
Second, that which is not real, being capable of being severed and abandoned, is termed "relinquished through transformation.
This further divides into two: first, that which is relinquished by severance; the removal of delusions by true wisdom is termed...

"Severance" refers to the permanent non-attainment [of the seeds], which is called "abandonment. "Planting those seeds" means severing the seeds of the two obstacles so that the manifestations of self and phenomena do not arise.
Because these manifestations no longer occur, they do not confront deluded cognition; by this means, one abandons the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

As for that which is abandoned: when the supreme dharmas are perfectly luminous, inferior dharmas naturally recede; when the basis is purely clean, defilements cannot take hold—this is called "abandonment.
Other contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava*) are the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*); inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are the death of transformation (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*).
Once these two types have been abandoned, the manifestation (*samudācāra*) of those two will never again arise, and this is also termed "abandonment. Since...

It abandons the seeds and also abandons the active manifestations (*samudācāra*). From this point downward, it clarifies that *pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death) is inferior and *vibhava-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death) is superior.

The first interpretation is not correct, because it holds that the contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*) and the inferior uncontaminated [seeds] are abandoned when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests.
The second interpretation is the correct principle: at the time of the diamond-like concentration, one merely cuts off the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) to their ultimate degree.

Regarding "subtle seeds": as long as one has not yet abandoned those tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas that are not incompatible with the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), they remain in the state of being causes;
thus, these causal seeds are not contradicted. This implies that it is only at the stage of the fruit (*phala-avasthā*) that they become incompatible with their causes.

As for the statement that "Bodhisattvas should be without the dharmas of birth and death," this refers to the *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformational birth and death), which arises from tainted [seeds] and inferior untainted seeds.
If these seeds were severed, because there would be no further transformation, one might argue that at this stage there should be no consciousness to be perfumed (*vāsya*).

However, this is not so, because even during the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), there still exists the maturation-consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) which maintains the seeds. Furthermore, regarding the claim that one abiding in the path of uninterrupted realization should be called a Buddha:

since the path of uninterrupted realization lacks all [defiled] seeds, why is it not called Buddhahood? Moreover, the subsequent path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) would then be rendered useless; for [the reason is as follows: the preceding...
Once Buddhahood has been attained, what further use would there be for subsequently arising liberation? From this point downward, the correct meaning is concluded.

△ Third, the section on that which is transformed and abandoned is finished. Below, the fourth section on that which is transformed and obtained is divided into two parts. First, the section on that which is manifested is divided into five parts.
First, the general designation of *nirvāṇa*.
There are two types of that which is attained through transformation (*parāvṛtti*). Because its essence is the pure *dharmadhātu*, it is the very nature of the purified realm.

That which is transformed is the aforementioned two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) that were previously abandoned; when these obstacles are exhausted, the fruit is attained, and this is termed "attainment through transformation.

This attainment is manifested through arising and is further divided into two: first, that which is attained by realization (*prāpti-labdha*), namely, Great Nirvāṇa (*mahānirvāṇa*). Question: What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of nirvāṇa?

"Originally pure. What is meant by 'that which is manifested'? Answer: "Although this is originally [pure], etc. Question: "Since there are obscurations and defilements, why is it called the 'originally self-natured purity'?
Answer: "This is based on [the following], etc. △ The general summary of *nirvāṇa* is concluded.
The following two sections provide a detailed explanation of the four types.
Briefly, there are four distinct meanings of *nirvāṇa*. [From "up to" ... because it is eternally quiescent in its functioning, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

That is to say, this *nirvāṇa* is the principle of perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*). Among all phenomena, it is the single, identical true reality (*dharmatā*). By means of the noble ones and ordinary beings...
Because there are distinctions in their states, they are divided into four kinds, which are explained individually in the text. Regarding "the original self-nature":

this does not exclude ordinary beings or [the categories of] form and mind; rather, because all possess the nature of perfectly tranquil *tathatā*, it is called "the principle of *tathatā* regarding the characteristics of all phenomena.
Although there is the phrase "even though," it explains the meaning of being originally pure, equal, and universally shared. It is with [this meaning] that...
Below "All Dharmas," the meaning of the name *nirvāṇa* is explained. The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* is translated here as "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*).
"Quiescence" (*jì*) means it is not identical with all dharmas, because the characteristics of all dharmas manifest individually.
"Perfection" (*yuán*) means it is not different from all dharmas; for that which differs from all dharmas is not perfect. "Free from all marks and all conceptualization" is the explanation.
"Essentially pure; the path of thought is cut off and the way of names and words is severed" explains the departure from conceptual discrimination.

This refers to those who have entered the stage of the noble ones through the Path of True Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). That which is personally realized within is quiescent by its very nature; it is not something made quiescent by effort. Therefore, it is called "primordially nirvāṇic by its own nature.
"With remainder" means that there still exists the basis for the suffering of birth and death within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*).

This is because for all noble ones (*ārya*), the final physical body has never been extinguished; rather, it is only when the seeds and manifestations of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are eternally stilled that it is termed *nirvāṇa*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Abiding in the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*), one still falls within the category of the multitude and still possesses manifold sufferings.
The transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) attained is still associated with the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding the term "the category of the multitude," it refers to...

The body of the five aggregates is a collection of suffering; therefore, it is called "multitudinous suffering. Those who possess even slight suffering, although they have emerged from obstacles, have not yet abandoned the final *pariccheda* (segmented) birth-and-death;
thus, they still possess slight suffering. "Without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*) means there is no basis for the suffering of the final body.

Therefore, it is said that True Suchness (*tathatā*) gives rise to [the transcendence of] the suffering of birth-and-death. When obstacles are exhausted and suffering is extinguished, the Truth is revealed.
Because its essence is perfectly fulfilled and quiescent, it is called *nirvāṇa*. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Abiding in the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*), one does not fall into the categories of sentient beings and is forever free from all suffering; one is forever dissociated from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

As for 'having no place of abiding,' this means not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa. If one were to abide in nirvāṇa, there would be no function of delivering sentient beings; if one were to abide in saṃsāra..."
It possesses no function of severing hindrances; yet it can sever hindrances and can deliver sentient beings, and is therefore called "non-abiding.

Although it possesses the boundless great function of benefiting sentient beings, its essence is fundamentally quiescent, and is thus named "nirvāṇa. This differs from the meaning of the "abiding nirvāṇa" of the two vehicles.
△ The detailed explanation of the four kinds is concluded. Below follows the third [section]: the existence or non-existence [of these states] among ordinary beings and sages.
All sentient beings possess the first [of these four], whereas only my World-Honored One can be said to possess all four.
This distinguishes between ordinary beings and noble ones regarding the presence or absence of nirvāṇa. All sentient beings lack the latter three because they have not yet severed the hindrances.
Those of the two vehicles possess only the [first] three and lack the last one because they abide in [their respective] nirvāṇas. Only my World-Honored One possesses all four.

"Seed" refers to the perfection of realization. △ Third, the section on whether ordinary beings and sages exist or not concludes. Below, the fourth section, "Extensive Discernment through Question and Answer," is divided into three parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa.
How is it that the Sugata possesses a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*) [up to: for this reason, the World-Honored One may be said to possess the four [qualities]?
"Sugata" is one of the ten epithets of the Tathāgata. Because he has skillfully entered into the midst of worldly afflictions (*rajas*), he is called "Sugata. This question asks:
since the World-Honored One is far removed from the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), how can there still be a basis for remaining suffering? The answer says: the World-Honored One...
Although there is no actual basis for suffering, the bhikṣu appears to have severed the afflictions and thus seems to possess a basis for suffering;

therefore, it is said that there is "remainder. Alternatively, when the basis for suffering is exhausted, it can be said that the two vehicles have entered the state of "nirvana without remainder," not because a basis for suffering remains.

It is precisely because one speaks of the Tathāgata as having a "remainder of support" (*sopadhiśeṣa*)—since what is presently manifest appears as suffering—that it may also be described as having a remainder of support.
Therefore, the World-Honored One is perfectly and fully endowed with the four types of nirvāṇa. △ The first section, on the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, is concluded.
Below follow the two [sections] on the Nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas.
Regarding the statement "if Śrāvakas and others [possess] the state of nirvana without remainder" (up to "not as in the case of a certain class entering nirvana without remainder"):
the phrase "Śrāvakas and below" constitutes the question. This refers to two differing explanations found elsewhere.

One explanation states that Śrāvakas possess only the state with remainder and lack the state without remainder, because the state without remainder is the fruit of Buddhahood. The second explanation states that Śrāvakas...

"There is no nirvāṇa at all. How could this be? This answers the second point raised in the preceding question. That is to say, regarding those who have exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*), how could it be that they lack nirvāṇa?
For there is indeed *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), as it certainly exists. Now, the passage beginning with "However, the sound...
explains the existence of *nirvāṇa with remainder*. "Body" refers to the final body; "wisdom" refers to the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions]. Although the afflictions have been severed...
Because the body and wisdom still remain, the meaning of *nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) is obscured; thus, it is said that there is no *nirupadhiśeṇa-parinirvāṇa*.

This does not mean that the state of having no remainder is entirely non-existent. Regarding the passage beginning with "At that time," it answers the first point of the preceding question concerning the teaching that there is no *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are exhausted and one realizes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder).
Furthermore, at this stage, one has not yet realized *nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder); thus, it is said that there is no such thing as "without remainder.
This is because, at a later time, when both body and cognition have ceased and all suffering is forever exhausted, there would otherwise be no meaning to the concept of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Alternatively, the text says "or," providing another interpretation for the second point mentioned in the question: namely, that it is said to be "entirely non-existent" with reference to the fruit of Buddhahood. It does not [refer to the state of an ordinary being].

Based on the preceding three [points], it is said that they do not exist. Furthermore, the subsequent explanation also carries a distinct meaning, clarifying the first point of the aforementioned question:
those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*) are not a lineage necessarily destined to sever suffering and enter parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said that as soon as they have realized *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they resolutely turn their minds to seek the realization of Bodhi.
They enter the path of the bodhisattvas. By the power of their resolute aspiration and joy, they maintain their bodies for a long duration to deliver sentient beings according to their vows.
This is not like certain classes of śrāvakas of fixed nature, who are determined to sever suffering and enter parinirvāṇa.
Based on this distinction, it is said that śrāvakas do not possess a nirvana without remainder. Question: Regarding the two types of nirvāṇa, those with remainder and without remainder—
How is this realized? The following text provides the answer and explanation:
namely, because there are those of the two vehicles who deeply delight in parinirvāṇa [up to] ... therefore it is further stated that they differ from the Buddha.

This is the etymological explanation. "There is that which is inferior" explains the attainment of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. "Those who deeply delight in parinirvāṇa" indicates those of the fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) among the śrāvakas.
"They are able to [attain]" explains the attainment of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. "Manifest suffering" refers to the suffering of birth and death in the present.
"Conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to dharmas with functional activity, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). "Body and wisdom together... [The text continues].
"Abandonment" is termed "nirvana without remainder"; this is the meaning of nirvana. Question: Since there is neither body nor cognition, who realizes nirvana? Answer:

Although at that time there is no final body or cognition, it is manifested by relying on parinirvāṇa; because one enters the state of no-remainder by means of that [prior] body and cognition, one may say that body and cognition exist.
The eighth fascicle states: "Relying on the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), one realizes [nirvana]."

The supreme awakening is not a body resulting from karmic retribution; therefore, it does not contradict reason. Question: Since nirvana without remainder is no different from that of a Buddha, why is there a distinction between the two vehicles and the Buddha?
Answer: It is said that they are without difference based on the essence of *tathatā* (suchness), but they are said to have differences based on the function of *tathatā*.
Thus, one should know that while the *śrāvakas* possess the essence, they lack the function, because they do not possess the capacity to benefit living beings.
Because of this, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses both essence and function in their perfect entirety. △ Second, the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas is concluded.
Below follows the nirvāṇa regarding the two obstacles.

Since the various cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) do not induce rebirth [into saṃsāra], they are subsumed within the two types of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) within True Suchness (*tathatā*), from beginning to end.

Below the section on "all objects of knowledge" (jñeya), there is a question regarding the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa): since it is of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta) and cannot directly induce saṃsāra, how is it that by abandoning it one also attains nirvāṇa?
Below the section beginning with "it can," the answer is given: namely, the cognitive obscuration obstructs the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatājñāna).

Because they do not give rise to compassionate vows for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, when they sever the obstacles, they manifest the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), which is precisely "non-abiding," since they abide in neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
Regarding the section beginning with "If the objects of knowledge... it further asks:

"Since one attains non-abiding by severing the objects of knowledge, and these objects of knowledge are also obstacles to nirvāṇa, why is it that by severing the objects of knowledge one does not [attain] it?"

"Analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Their explanation is that analytical cessation has the meaning of *nirvāṇa*. "Because analytical cessation is free from bondage, and it is not itself bondage"—this is the answer.

That is to say, because one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) analytical cessation, which is free from the bondage of afflictions (*kleśa*). As for that cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), [it is not so].
"Since its nature is not bound, when that [nature] is severed, one does not obtain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If this is so, how can one attain nirvāṇa by severing it? Thus the opponent asks again. "Not all," [the Master replies]. The Master answers:

"That is to say, among the various types of nirvāṇa, some are comprised within analytical cessation, while others are comprised within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); therefore, it is said that 'not all nirvāṇas are comprised within analytical cessation. Otherwise... [and so forth].
This means that if it were not admitted to be included within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), then natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) would not be *nirvāṇa*.

"That which binds" below explains the meaning of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "All objects of knowledge" below explains the meaning of not attaining analytical cessation regarding what is to be known.
"However, by abandoning those" below explains that non-abiding *nirvāṇa* has non-analytical cessation as its nature. Therefore, "the four" below explains the four [types of] *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), there are those that are included and those that are not. The first is *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), and the last is *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa);

these are included only within the unconditioned phenomenon of *tathatā* (suchness). The middle two are *sopadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder);
these are included only within the unconditioned phenomenon of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through analytical discernment).

If it were the case that analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is attained solely by severing the fetters, [it would follow that] in reality, both [types of cessation] are capable of universally obstructing the two fruits.

Question: Among the six unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma), within which of the four types of parinirvāṇa are the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and the unconditioned phenomenon of the cessation of sensation and perception (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha) subsumed?
Answer: Non-analytical cessation is not identical to the ultimate of the two aforementioned nirvāṇas.
"Permanently extinguished. Regarding the two [types of cessation], such as the immovable (*āniñjya*) and so forth, they are said to be "temporary departures. Question:

Within the category of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), is there non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Answer: Analytical cessation is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) that is exclusively ultimate extinction;

non-analytical cessation exists because it is not permanent extinction. Or, alternatively, there is another interpretation: that which lacks a place of abiding is also subsumed under analytical cessation. Question: Since it is subsequently nirvāṇa...
It is also subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). One might ask: "Does this not then confuse it with the two types [of cessation] mentioned in the middle? The answer is:

although both are termed analytical cessation, there is a distinction between them based on two meanings—namely, with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). This is because the attainment of cessation involves the severing of the afflictions that cause birth and death, thereby attaining liberation from their bonds.
Non-abiding nirvāṇa is attained through the cessation of obstacles, because it is realized by completely severing all remaining hindrances.

Therefore, [the text] below explains the four types of nirvāṇa and their relationship—whether they are included or not—included within the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The two unconditioned phenomena, immovability (*āniñjya*) and so forth, are subsumed under non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

this serves as an illustration to show that the latter three types of nirvāṇa are subsumed under analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Regarding the phrase "since it is an object of knowledge" and so forth, the opponent...

[Objection: Difficult. [The text] says "the afflictions below. The Master of the Treatise answers by citing the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) as an example to clarify the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Because the sacred teachings rely on what is predominant, they speak of them as a single obstacle; yet in reality, the two obstacles both obstruct the two fruits. △ The third section, on the two obstacles and nirvāṇa, is concluded.
This concludes the extensive discussion above, comprising four questions and answers. Below, the fifth section provides a general conclusion of that which is revealed.
Among the four types of nirvāṇa thus described, only the latter three are termed "attained through manifestation.
To summarize the four types of nirvāṇa, only the latter three are subsumed under what is attained through manifestation;

the first one is not, because its intrinsic nature is fundamentally pure. △ This concludes the general summary of what is attained through manifestation, which also encompasses the preceding section on the "one thing attained through manifestation."
The attainment is concluded. Regarding the second part, the "attainment produced" (*utpādita-lābha*), it is divided into two: first, a general indication of *bodhi*;
second, the specific attainment produced, namely Great *Bodhi* (extending to this point), which is the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-saṃprayukta-citta-varga*).

"Second, that which is produced and attained, namely Great Bodhi. This is the heading, stating the topic. Question: Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of bodhi is primordially present, why is it called "produced"?

Answer: Although this essence of Great Awakening (*mahābodhi*) is a seed capable of being produced as something primordial, it does not manifest because it is obstructed by the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It is through the power of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that the various noble ones (*ārya*) sever those [hindrances].
Because of these obstructions, [the seeds] are caused to arise from their causal seeds; this is called attaining bodhi. Their continuity is inexhaustible.

Furthermore, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) arises from the conceptualization of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), whereas the seeds of bodhi-wisdom likewise arise from the non-conceptualization of the mind and mental factors.
Now, regarding the turning of what is known to realize *bodhi*: since it has wisdom (*jñāna*) as its essence, it is said that this is precisely the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms.
△ The first section, the general definition of *bodhi*, is concluded. Below, the second section, the detailed explanation of the category of wisdom, is divided into six parts. First:
the essence of the four kinds of wisdom.
What are the mental states associated with the four wisdoms? [The text continues] "...like a great round mirror manifesting various forms and images.
What follows below is the formal question. Regarding the term "mirror-like wisdom" (*ādarśajñāna*), it is named after its metaphorical illustration.

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Furthermore, O Subhūti, as for the great round mirror-like wisdom: just as various reflected images appear in dependence upon a round mirror, so too does [the wisdom] depend [upon the basis]."
Regarding the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, wherein the various images of sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear as reflections:
one should know that the circular mirror and the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom are equal and identical. Therefore, this mirror of wisdom is called the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom).
As for the statement that "this mental state is free from all conceptualization," it reveals that the essence of this wisdom is devoid of all afflictions.

Because it is forever free from the stains of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Regarding the statement that "its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know," this is because they cannot be known by the intellects of the ignorant and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "not deluded or ignorant concerning any objective aspect," the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*): Because it is not deluded regarding any object of knowledge that constitutes an obstruction (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), its nature and characteristics are pure and free from all defilements;
this is because the essence of wisdom is luminous, clear, and stainless.

It is the support for the manifestation and seeds of purely immaculate, perfect virtues, as it is the basis upon which only untainted qualities depend. It is capable of manifesting and generating the [Buddha] bodies and their lands.

Regarding "the shadow of wisdom": all bodies and lands are manifested by this wisdom; the other three kinds of wisdom are the shadows of this wisdom, and thus it is said that [this wisdom] "can produce" them.
"Without interval or interruption, reaching the limits of the future" clarifies the meaning of quiescent permanence.
"Like a great round mirror manifesting myriad forms and images" clarifies the meaning of radiant illumination.
The second is the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), which continues as a single flavor until the end of the future.
It is called "equality" because it derives its name from that which is realized. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, O Subhūti, the wisdom of equality is perfectly accomplished through ten aspects, namely, the realization of the supremacy of all marks."
They delight in equanimity. They realize the equanimity of all dependent origination. They maintain the equanimity that is free from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics.
They possess the equanimity of great compassion that universally rescues others. They possess the equanimity of great compassion that is independent of conditions.

They manifest with equanimity according to the inclinations of all sentient beings. Their speech is received with reverence and affection by all sentient beings with equanimity. All worldly tranquility is...
It is of a single flavor and equal. All worldly phenomena, whether suffering or pleasure, are of a single flavor and equal.
The cultivation and planting of immeasurable merit are ultimately equal. Because one realizes these ten characteristics, it is called "equality. Thus, the treatise says:
"This mental state is the unique basis of the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (the wisdom of wondrous observation). Here, "basis" refers to the faculty (*indriya*), for each wisdom [has its own].
The root upon which [wisdom] relies is called the "exclusive support" (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*).
Sublime contemplative wisdom takes the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) as its exclusive support, and the wisdom of equality likewise relies upon the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

Therefore, it is said that what is established by non-abiding nirvāṇa is the "single-flavor continuity" (*ekarasa-saṃtati*) that extends to the end of the future; this reveals the meaning of permanence (*nityatva*).
The third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
It is termed "wondrous observation" because it is named after its apprehension of the objects of observation. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation sustains all doors of dhāraṇī and doors of samādhi, [and is] unimpeded..."

It explains the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas. Furthermore, it says that it can serve as the cause and condition for the various, immeasurable consciousnesses of signs that give rise instantaneously to unimpeded, sublime wisdom regarding all that is knowable. It also speaks of the various pāramitās worthy of contemplation.

It is adorned with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), and is thus exceedingly delightful.
Regarding the phrase "collecting and observing" (*saṃgraha-vipaśyanā*): "collecting" (*saṃgraha*) means to store or conceal; "observing" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to discernment.

By means of this category of wisdom, one is well able to observe within the gates of dhāraṇī, and is also able to collect and store them so as not to forget or lose them. Thus it is called "the precious jewels of merit."

The "factors" refer to the six perfections, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth. The "differentiation of function" refers to the wondrous applications of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the like.

The fourth, the mental state associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), fulfills the tasks that ought to be performed through the power of one's original vows.
Regarding "that which is accomplished through action" (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*): it is so named because it arises from the performance of the three types of karma. The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"By means of this, the Tathāgata, through the diligent activity of bodily transformation, manifests various fields of arts and crafts, thereby subduing those sentient beings who are arrogant regarding their skills."
By the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he leads all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation.
Through this, the Tathāgata’s transformative activity of auspicious speech proclaims various teachings according to their inclinations; these are both elegant in expression and profound in meaning.
Even sentient beings of limited intelligence will believe upon first hearing them. By the power of such skillful means, he leads [them].

He causes all sentient beings to enter the holy teaching, bringing them to maturity and liberation. This is the Tathāgata’s resolute intention regarding his transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karman*).

Having discerned the eighty-four thousand differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, he leads them to enter the holy teaching, brings them to maturity, and liberates them through the power of such skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). The details of his other bodily, verbal, and mental [activities] would be too voluminous to record.
It does not lead [to that]. △ The first section, on the four bodies of wisdom, is concluded. Hereafter, the mental states (*citta-kalāpa*) associated with these are called "wisdom.
Thus, because these four wisdoms are associated with their respective mental states, it is said that by transforming the eight consciousnesses, one attains these four wisdoms.

In summary, the transformation of the mental states (*citta-prakāra*) through the four wisdoms results in twenty-two factors for each. That is to say, these four wisdoms can transform the mental states such that each possesses twenty-two factors:
namely, the five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors, the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) factors, and the eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors;
to which one factor from the category of vitarka and vicāra is added to make twenty-two. Therefore, what follows below clarifies the association [of these factors] with the eight consciousnesses.
Regarding the "Chapter on Mind": these four wisdoms, together with the five preceding consciousnesses, constitute four types when they function simultaneously.
Therefore, this [text] states that if one does not take the twenty-two factors as their essence, then the conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) of the Buddha-stage could not be fully subsumed.
That which exhaustively subsumes all the Buddha’s merits is the transformation of the eight consciousnesses.

Regarding the "Concomitant Mental States" (cittapakṣa): because one sequentially attains four kinds of wisdom therein. Question: Other sources state that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms;
why then do you speak of "concomitant mental states"? Answer: Although wisdom is not itself consciousness, it exists within both the contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava) states.

Strength and weakness are diametrically opposed. Desiring that sentient beings rely on wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandon consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is taught that consciousness transforms and is attained [as wisdom].
△ Second, the section on the names of the mental factors as wisdom is concluded. Below follows the sequence of the three transformations of wisdom.
Regarding the mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) (up to the point of) "sustaining the untainted seeds so that they are not lost":
this provides a general explanation of the stages of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) for the mental complexes of the four wisdoms.

First, there is an interpretation which is not yet correct, stating that the Perfect Mirror Wisdom first manifests at the time of the Vajra-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), because the seeds of maturation (*vipāka-bīja*) and the seeds of the knowable (*jñeya-bīja*) arise simultaneously.
Because of abandonment, the mental complex (*cittapakṣa*) associated with it also transforms into the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).

If one were to claim that at that time the mirror-like wisdom does not arise, and the seeds of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) have likewise not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), then—since defiled obstructions have already been exhausted and pure seeds are gradually increasing—at that time, which consciousness would be able to sustain these pure seeds?
Next, there is another interpretation [presented] below, which represents the correct principle (*nyāya*): it is said that this mental complex continues until a later time when liberation...
When the path of liberation arises, the seeds and consciousness are both empty; only then does the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arise, whereby one immediately attains the Buddha-way.
Therefore, it is said that at the time of the path of liberation in this stage, one first becomes a Buddha, and thus [the mirror-like wisdom] is able to manifest.

As for the seeds of the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna), they are not suddenly abandoned at the time of the diamond-like path (vajropamasamādhi), because the seeds of the ripening consciousness do not conflict with the uninterrupted path (ānantaryamārga). Furthermore...

The path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) do not [sever] the seeds of the obstructed, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) ripening consciousness, nor the seeds of inferior untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas;
for these out-flowing seeds and inferior untainted seeds are strictly incompatible with the fruit of Buddhahood.

Below the section on the "diamond-like," he refutes the previous position: if the diamond-like concentration were to sever the seeds of consciousness, it would follow that there would be nothing [to support the subsequent state].

Regarding "perfuming" (vāsanā): if there were no basis for perfuming, the pure uncontaminated dharmas would not be able to increase. If dharmas neither increased nor decreased, one would have to attain the fruit of Buddhahood [without effort].
Would one then attain Buddhahood immediately upon the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga)?
Therefore, this section is taught because one first attains Buddhahood from the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), which continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future.
The mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) [continues] in mutual dependence and succession until the end of the future.
This wisdom, while in the causal stage, is associated with the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which is called "unequal" because it constantly clings to a self.

Upon the stage of transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), because there is no longer a constant self, it receives the name "equality. That which manifests at the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and opposes the two types of clinging is this [wisdom].

The six consciousnesses constitute that true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), which severs the seeds of conceptual construction and manifests the wisdom of the two emptinesses; this is termed the "inferior transformation.

Because the seventh consciousness constantly clings internally to a self, its non-conceptual afflictions are exclusively innate (*sahaja*); [this transformation occurs] by means of the sixth consciousness.

At the time of the initial transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the seventh consciousness arises concomitantly, transforming into a portion of wisdom, because it serves as the foundational faculty for the sixth consciousness.

Regarding those in the subsequent ten stages (*bhūmi*) whose grasping has not yet been severed: this refers to the seventh consciousness, wherein the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*) have not yet been eternally extinguished, and wisdom remains intermittent.
Upon reaching the end of the ten stages, one attains ultimate transformation, which persists until the end of the future. Its characteristics are as follows:
It continues without interruption.
The mental states associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) may all arise, even during states of non-conceptualization.

The sixth consciousness associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation [is that which,] while in the causal stage, discriminates the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). Upon entering...
Therefore, at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one abandons the two kinds of obscurations, realizes the two kinds of emptiness, and transforms the two kinds of wisdom.
Regarding the "insight into the emptiness of persons" (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*) that first arises during the stage of seeing for the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*):

this refers to those who, having abandoned only the conceptual grasping at a self (*parikalpita-ātma-grāha*), enter the true Path of Seeing and immediately realize a portion of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); this is termed the "insight into the emptiness of persons. Hereafter...

Proceeding successively until reaching the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): that is, following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while severing the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) within the nine stages, one gradually severs and gradually realizes them.

Because there are no further afflictions to be severed once the seeds of delusion are completely exhausted, it is called the stage of one beyond training. This applies to those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

The uninterrupted [cognition] of the knowable is the wisdom of the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). Or, descending to the lower level, for one who has clarified the Bodhisattva vehicle and is on the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), the "provisions" (*sambhāra*) and "application" (*prayoga*) are collectively termed "practice through understanding.

At the conclusion of the stage of practice through understanding, one immediately enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Or, ascending to the higher level, this refers to the stages beyond the world (*bhūmi*).
If it is not contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is at the time of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); or, at the time of being without mind (*acittaka*), it is simply non-existent.
Discrimination (*vikalpa*). In all the aforementioned stages, the wisdom of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is permitted to arise.

Regarding the category of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), that which first arises at the stage of the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), which are severed exclusively by Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, on the path of seeing, they also sever one portion of the discrimination of attachment to phenomena and transform one portion of wisdom. Below this, the emptiness-wisdom of phenomena is explained.
Regarding the stages of manifestation and names such as "superior stage" (*uttara-bhūmi*) and so forth, their explanations are the same as before.
This is because the mental complex associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) arises through attention (*manasikāra*) that is frequently interrupted.

The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) corresponds during the causal stage to the first five *pravṛtti-vijñānas*, which are capable of performing various karmic functions.
After the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it is able to give rise to transformative activities (*nirmāṇa-karma*), thereby receiving the name "that which is to be accomplished.

The former interpretation is not correct, because it is induced by the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the sixth consciousness; thus, the first five consciousnesses are the initial transformation during the causal stage. The latter interpretation is the correct principle, meaning that upon becoming a Buddha...

At that time, [the pure consciousness] can only just begin to arise. This is because within the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), the matured (*vipāka*) contaminated (*sāsrava*) eyes and other faculties transformed by it are themselves contaminated.
These serve as the uncommon supports (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*) for the eye-consciousness and other cognitions, arising simultaneously with them and sharing the same object.

It is logically inconsistent for contaminated five-fold sense faculties to produce uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness. Why? Because the contaminated is obscure regarding its objects, whereas the uncontaminated is not.
Because the object is clear, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, the maturation (*vipāka*) and the eye-faculty both transform into the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Only then can the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) arise. Unlike the first three [wisdoms], which continue for a long duration, this [wisdom] is intermittent;
it arises only when intentional attention (*manasikāra*) is applied. If one asks: Are these four types of natures innate (*prakṛti-stha*), or are they produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*)? If...

This is the "inherently existing" [nature]. It should possess all four wisdoms at all times. If it were produced through perfuming, the essence of the four wisdoms would likewise undergo increase or decrease.
The answer to this is provided in the subsequent text.
Although these four natures are all inherently present (until: "lest the virtue of a preceding Buddha be superior to that of a subsequent Buddha"), this is the answer.
That is to say, although these four wisdoms possess inherent seeds, due to the two obstacles they become defiled conceptualizations.

If one awakens to *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), through the cultivation of preparatory application (*prayoga*) during the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and upon entering the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they only then arise.
The manifest activity gradually reaches full perfection and continues until the end of the future; it arises solely from seeds and does not perfume to form new seeds.

they are not like the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is substantially real. "Dependent" refers here to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, by which the transformed bodies and lands are designated.

These are not real in the same way that the aggregates and so forth are real. Otherwise—that is, if one were not to [designate them] by means of the aggregates and so forth—[they would not be established].

If [external objects] were substantially existent, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would necessarily fail to be established. Why? Because it would be admitted that both consciousness and its internal objects are substantially existent;

that is to say, since both consciousness and its internal objects are substantially existent, one establishes the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra*. Alternatively, below the section on "consciousness," the meaning of the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is explained again.

Previously, when discussing the internal object, the *paratantra-svabhāva* was explained solely in terms of the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part); now, this is supplemented by including the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part).
Therefore, they are called "mutually perceiving. Both arise from conditions and are equally *paratantra* (dependent origination). Regarding "the false and the real are like consciousness":

the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is false conceptualization, while the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) is a real object; since both are like consciousness, "Consciousness-Only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is established.
The word "only" (*mātra*) excludes the external, meaning it excludes the attachment to objects existing apart from the mind; thus, "Consciousness-Only" is established.
The statement "not obstructing internal objects" means that it does not negate the reality of internal forms as existing objects.
Otherwise—if it were not the case that it does not obstruct internal objects—then even *tathatā* (suchness) would not be real. Why?
Because *tathatā* is the object of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and is thus termed an "internal object. [Section] 7: The Purity and Impurity of Body and Land concluded. Below follows Question 8.
Answer: A summary conclusion.
Since internal objects and consciousness are neither unreal [down to] "because mind and mental factors are necessarily associated," the section beginning with "internal objects" is a question.
It asks: if both mind and object are real, why does one not say "only object and consciousness," but rather...
Is it consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)? Regarding the statement that "consciousness-only" applies to internal objects while also encompassing external ones:

that which is not separate from the mind is called an internal object; that which is grasped as being separate from the mind is called an external object. Since objects encompass both the internal and the external, one establishes "consciousness-only" rather than "object-only.

Or, as for the passage beginning with "Or, various...": this means that by grasping at objects, the mind becomes deluded and sinks into the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); by contemplating the mind, one attains liberation and can realize [enlightenment].
Nirvāṇa. To cause one to contemplate the mind for oneself, the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is established. This does not mean that the internal objects are entirely non-existent;

rather, it clarifies that the objective aspect (nimittabhāga), including True Suchness (tathatā), is never separate from consciousness. That is to say, the internal objective aspect necessarily takes consciousness as its essential nature.
Due to the power of habitual perfuming (vāsanā), it arises predominantly in a manner resembling external objects of attachment. True Suchness is likewise [not separate from consciousness].

The true nature of consciousness refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It arises based upon *tathatā* (suchness) and contains all defiled phenomena; therefore, it is called "consciousness.

Thus, one should know that whether internal or external, conditioned or unconditioned, nothing exists apart from consciousness. Aside from the nature of consciousness, there is no other distinct phenomenon.
Below this, it further clarifies that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), and so forth, are all not separate [from consciousness].
Consciousness establishes the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by encompassing all internal and external forms and minds.
This treatise establishes *vijñapti-mātra* through its three parts; it attains full perfection only in this way, for it is neither redundant nor deficient.

Regarding the title of the commentary, *Cheng weishi* (Establishing Consciousness-Only): it is because the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), the subject-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), and the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) together constitute consciousness-only that it is called "the three aspects combined" (*sanfen hecheng*).
It is named *Cheng weishi* because it is established based on phenomena (*vastu*); since there is no principle apart from phenomena, it is said to be "established.
Furthermore, it is stated below that there is also the name *Jing weishi* (Pure Consciousness-Only), which reveals "only... [the ultimate].
The principle of consciousness is supremely luminous and pure; this is called "Pure Consciousness-Only" (*viśuddha-vijñaptimātra*). This is established based on that principle.

Because there are no phenomena apart from this principle, it is termed "pure. That is to say, this treatise was originally composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu to extract the essential meanings of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

It consists of thirty verses. Now, this treatise, by means of these thirty verses, elucidates the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) regarding its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and its nature (*svabhāva*), whether as cause or fruit, whether true or false, whether provisional or real, and whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because the internal and external dharmas are ultimately accomplished, it is said that "perfection is attained. Although there are thirty verses, this wondrous principle is not diminished by them;
although there are ten fascicles of treatise, this wondrous meaning is not increased by them.

Therefore, it is said: "Because there is neither increase nor decrease. △ The eighth section, the conclusion of the questions and answers, is finished. This concludes the second major division, the Extensive Exposition According to the Teaching.
Below is the third division, the Explanation of the Conclusion, the Bestowal of the Vow.
"Having relied upon the sacred teachings and correct reasoning... may we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.

Regarding "having relied upon the sacred teachings and correct reasoning," this refers to the Bodhisattvas such as Dharmapāla relying upon the sacred teachings previously cited and the correct reasoning of inference (*anumāna*).
Regarding "discriminating the meaning of the nature and characteristics of consciousness-only," this means relying upon the sacred [teachings].

Regarding the exposition of the principles of correct reasoning (*nyāya*), within the detailed explanation of the principles of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), the merit obtained from the meaning of both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) is dedicated to all sentient beings.

This means that by explaining the great significance of Consciousness-Only, one causes all sentient beings to awaken to and enter the subtle principles of the nature and characteristics of Consciousness-Only.
The merit thus obtained is truly not slight; because it is so profound and vast...
I dedicate all my merit to all sentient beings. May we together swiftly ascend to unsurpassed enlightenment.

May all sentient beings either awaken to the wondrous principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) or partake in the merit of *vijñapti-mātra*, so that we may together quickly realize unsurpassed *bodhi*.
